title: Viridi and Good Carbon Deploy One of the Largest Indoor Battery Energy Storage Systems in an Occupied US Residential Building - Batteries News
content:
Viridi and Good Carbon Deploy One of the Largest Indoor Battery Energy Storage Systems in an Occupied US Residential Building
BUFFALO, N.Y., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ —
, the industry leader in fail-safe distributed energy storage systems, and
Good Carbon Co.
, today announced the deployment of a 3.75MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) at
Peace Bridge Place
, a 105-unit affordable housing apartment building in Buffalo, New York. The project is one of the largest indoor lithium-ion battery systems in an occupied residential building in the United States.
At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi’s
RPSLinkIN indoor BESS
is part of a broader clean energy strategy that includes geothermal heating & cooling, domestic hot water, and high efficient building envelope upgrades. The 3.75 MWh system is designed to provide extended backup power for the fully electrified building during outages, while also helping reduce demand on the local grid during peak periods. Good Carbon Co., which focuses on revitalizing multifamily properties in communities throughout Western New York, selected the system to strengthen energy resilience for residents and enable the property to enable flexible, grid-responsive energy management.
Adam Serbert,
CEO of Good Carbon Co, said:
Energy is one of the biggest operating costs in multifamily housing, and how you manage it directly affects the long-term performance of a property
“At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi’s battery and energy management technology will help us reduce peak demand, avoid higher-cost periods and participate in demand response programs. That means lower operating costs, new revenue opportunities and a stronger economic foundation for keeping the property affordable and well maintained. For us, this is not just about one building — it is about creating a model we can apply across future multifamily projects.”
Viridi’s intelligent Energy Management System automatically stores and discharges electricity based on the needs of the fully electrified property and the local grid. It allows Peace Bridge Place to reduce electricity demand during peak periods and respond to utility signals when additional grid flexibility is needed, while providing greater energy resilience for residents. By reducing peak demand and participating in demand response programs, the system can help lower the property’s energy costs while creating new revenue opportunities.
New York State Energy Research and Development Agency
(NYSERDA) is providing support to Good Carbon Co. for the Peace Bridge Place project through its Future Grid Challenge. The Peace Bridge Place project is a
National Grid
pilot focused on integrating flexible, grid-responsive technologies into its distribution network. Viridi’s energy storage and energy management technology will work in coordination with
EnergyHub’s Edge Distributed Energy Resource Management System
(DERMS), enabling the property to respond to National Grid signals during periods of peak electricity demand.
Doreen M. Harris,
President and CEO, NYSERDA, said:
Peace Bridge Place demonstrates how forward-thinking energy storage solutions can ensure New York’s multifamily buildings are meeting the energy needs of its residents while creating a more reliable and resilient electric grid,
“Projects like this embody NYSERDA’s mission to spur innovation that drives New York toward a clean energy future.”
Distributed across seven battery rooms, the 3.75MWh system is integrated with Viridi’s proprietary Energy Management System (EMS), which optimizes the property’s electricity use while enabling it to respond to changing conditions on the local grid in two key ways:
Peak Shaving:
As the building’s grid energy draw approaches a monthly peak, the battery automatically discharges to keep demand below a target threshold, reducing peak demand and associated $/kW demand charges.
Seasonal Demand Response:
During peak events, National Grid dispatch signals are delivered through EnergyHub’s platform to Viridi’s energy management system, which then coordinates the response across the building’s battery and other energy systems
For participating residents, smart thermostat setpoints can be adjusted to “pre-cool” or “pre-heat” apartments before the event, enabling reduced HVAC consumption during the event while the battery discharges. Residents can opt out of individual events at any time. Together, these actions allow the property to reduce its net electricity demand while the local grid is under the greatest strain.
Deploying lithium-ion battery storage indoors at this scale requires rigorous safety standards. The risk of
thermal runaway
— and its potential to propagate from cell to cell — has historically constrained where lithium-ion systems can be installed. The RPSLinkIN system is designed to address that challenge through Viridi’s proprietary Fail-Safe Anti-Propagation architecture, a passive safety layer designed to prevent thermal runaway from spreading between cells.
That safety architecture has undergone industry-standard testing designed to evaluate how battery systems behave during a thermal runaway event. During
UL 9540A testing
, a cell was intentionally driven into thermal failure to determine whether the event would spread to surrounding cells. Viridi’s technology prevented cell-to-cell propagation, with no detectable release of heat, sparks, smoke, gas or flames. RPSLinkIN has also earned UL 9540 Listing from TÜV Rheinland, providing third-party certification of the complete energy storage system.
Jon M. Williams,
CEO of Viridi, said:
This project demonstrates what becomes possible when energy storage is designed to serve the building and the grid at the same time,
“Peace Bridge Place will now be able to reduce peak demand, respond when the grid needs support and strengthen resilience for the people who live there. The bigger opportunity is proving that large-scale lithium-ion storage can be safely integrated into the places where people actually live and work. By unlocking occupied buildings for energy storage, we can dramatically expand where distributed energy resources can play a role in strengthening the grid.”
Peace Bridge Place is also a proof point for Viridi’s ability to scale this technology beyond a single project. At its Buffalo manufacturing facility, the company currently has the capacity to produce approximately 400 MWh of battery systems annually — enough stored energy capacity to equal roughly one day of electricity use for 14,000 average U.S. homes. The facility also has room to expand production as demand grows.
The Peace Bridge Place project brings that broader vision into an occupied multifamily setting, combining fail-safe battery architecture, intelligent energy management and automated grid response to help lower operating costs, strengthen resilience and make the building a more flexible participant in the electric grid.

title: Building AI Kill Switches in Data Centers
content:
As businesses – and societies more broadly – grapple with the risks posed by advanced AI systems, one proposed safeguard is an
AI “kill switch”
: a mechanism designed to shut down an out-of-control model or agent before it can cause serious harm.
More than a few observers (
including me
) have noted that implementing a kill switch of this type is
a lot harder
than many proponents assume. One major reason is that most AI systems run on distributed infrastructure. You cannot simply turn off one server or issue a process-level command to stop a large-scale AI deployment that spans clusters, facilities, or regions.
That said, there may be a realistic approach: building AI kill switches at the data center level. While such a strategy would not solve every problem, it could offer a practical way to isolate certain AI workloads quickly in an emergency.
What a Data Center-Level Kill Switch Would Actually Do
A kill switch implemented at the data center level would allow operators to shut down or isolate AI workloads on a facility-by-facility basis. If an AI model or agent began to behave unpredictably, operate outside its intended scope, or otherwise pose a threat, the facility hosting it could be taken offline or disconnected to contain the risk.
Related:
Can Optical AI Cut Data Center Inference Power Use?
This type of kill switch would not provide fine-grained control over individual AI agents or models inside a data center. It would also not necessarily stop every process immediately. But it could offer a relatively fast and effective way to contain a rogue system by cutting it off from power, connectivity, or both.
Where Data Center Kill Switches Fall Short
Before considering how to build an AI kill switch into a data center, it is important to note the approach’s limitations.
One challenge is scale. Some AI models are distributed across multiple data centers, so shutting down a single facility would not stop the entire system. In those cases, a kill switch would only be effective if every facility supporting the workload could also be disabled or isolated. Even then, partial shutdowns could still matter because they would reduce the compute and storage resources available to the model.
Another concern is propagation. A sufficiently sophisticated rogue AI system might attempt to replicate itself beyond its original environment by deploying copies of models, agents, or data to external infrastructure. A data center-level kill switch would do little to address that problem once replication had already occurred. For that reason,
early detection
would be essential. The sooner operators can identify signs of anomalous or unauthorized AI behavior, the more useful any kill switch mechanism becomes.
Related:
Nvidia Unveils DSX POD Amid Greenpeace Protest
Two Ways to Isolate a Rogue AI Workload
There are two basic ways to shut down or isolate a rogue AI workload at the data center level: cutting power or cutting connectivity. Both approaches are difficult because data centers are engineered to resist exactly these kinds of failures.
Option #1: A Power-Based Kill Switch
The first option is to shut off the power supply to the facility. In theory, this is the most direct way to turn off AI infrastructure. In practice, it is not so simple.
Most data centers are designed with redundant power systems, including
UPS units
backup generators
. If the primary utility power is interrupted, workloads are supposed to stay online. That resilience is a feature, not a bug, but it complicates any attempt to create a deliberate shutdown mechanism. Backup systems are not designed to distinguish between a routine grid outage and an intentional “kill switch” event, so cutting the main power alone is unlikely to stop servers from operating.
There is also the issue of hardware risk. Abrupt power loss can create operational and equipment problems, especially in environments filled with expensive
GPU-based servers
. For that reason, most data center operators would be reluctant to support any mechanism that could damage infrastructure during an emergency shutdown.
Related:
Nvidia Unveils DSX Pod for Faster AI Data Center Builds
Option #2: A Network-Based Kill Switch
The other option is to sever the data center’s network connectivity. This would not necessarily stop AI workloads from continuing to run inside the facility, but it could prevent them from communicating externally, accessing remote resources, or interacting with users and other systems.
Here too, however, resilience makes implementation difficult. Most modern facilities have multiple upstream carriers, redundant network paths, and diverse interconnection points. To isolate a rogue AI workload at the facility level, operators would need a way to turn off all relevant external connectivity paths, not just one.
Could Regulation Make AI Kill Switches Mandatory?
Data center operators are unlikely to make it easy to power off or disconnect their own facilities on demand. Their business model depends on uptime, resilience, and fault tolerance, so voluntary adoption of AI kill switches does not seem especially likely in the near term.
A regulatory path is easier to imagine. Governments could require facilities that host certain classes of AI workloads to maintain a standardized mechanism for isolating those workloads in an emergency, most likely through network disconnection rather than power interruption. Such a requirement would still be difficult to implement, but it is more feasible than expecting operators to redesign facilities around rapid shutdown capabilities on their own.
The effectiveness of that model would depend heavily on consistency across jurisdictions. If only a handful of regions required kill switches, AI companies could simply place high-risk workloads in facilities elsewhere. But if regulators adopted broadly aligned rules, data center-level kill switches could become a practical part of the AI safety conversation.

title: Croatia’s first large-scale standalone 60 MW BESS goes live - Energy Storage
content: Slovenian energy technology company NGEN and Croatian investment platform NextGrid Energy have officially opened a 60 MW / 120 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Šibenik, Croatia. The companies said it is Croatia’s first large standalone battery project of its size connected to the transmission grid. The facility, known as BESS Šibenik, is located at the IMPOL-TLM industrial complex, with official inauguration taking place on November 4. The city is on the coast of Croatia, and north of Dubrovnik and some 50 km south of Zadar. The site was built in phases, with a first 10 MW / 20 MWh phase entering market operation in January 2026. The site uses Tesla Megapack XL BESS, with the project connected to the country’s 110 kV transmission grid. Photos of the site appear to show Sinexcel PCS equipment According to the project partners, the battery has been providing automatic frequency restoration reserve (aFRR) services under a contract with Croatian electricity transmission system operator HOPS since September 2026. The project has supported the balancing market on a fully merchant basis, helping the grid operator manage real-time deviations between electricity generation and consumption. The project was developed and delivered jointly by NGEN and NextGrid Energy, under the joint venture NGEN Smart Energy Systems, and delivered for the owner, IE-Energy, which is referred to as a joint-stock company. NGEN served as the main engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) and technology partner. NGEN developed the software platform and control system, which automatically monitors market and grid conditions while optimizing the system’s operation every 15 minutes and operated as a VPP. “Together with our partner NextGrid Energy, we developed and delivered BESS Šibenik, the first large standalone battery system connected to the Croatian transmission grid,” said Roman Bernard, CEO and co-founder of NGEN Group. NGEN further detailed the merchant basis, saying it has no guaranteed revenues, with income depending on demand for flexibility services, and that its owners and investors fully bear the market risk. The project received backing from the EU Modernisation Fund, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), Raiffeisen Mandatory and Voluntary Pension Funds and IE-Energy. According to previous EBRD disclosures, the roughly €60 million project included a €16.8 million equity investment from the EBRD, a further €16.8 million equity investment from Raiffeisen Mandatory and Voluntary Pension Funds and a €16.5 million capital expenditure grant from the EU Modernisation Fund. NGEN said it is planning additional energy storage projects in Croatia and across Central and South-Eastern Europe. In September, the company commissioned an 85 MW / 170 MWh BESS in Austria . title: Dominican Republic approves rules for 200 MW / 800 MWh BESS at existing solar/wind plants - Energy Storage
content: The Dominican Republic’s Superintendency of Electricity (SIE) has established the framework for a tender to procure up to 200 MW / 800 MWh of new battery energy storage systems (BESS) co-located with existing renewable energy projects. The procurement process, designated EDES-GER-SAEB-01-2026, is open exclusively to solar PV and wind power plants holding active long-term power purchase agreements with distribution utilities Edenorte, Edesur, and Edeeste. Participating plants must not already have energy storage systems installed. The batteries must be new and integrated into the existing facilities. The storage capacity linked to each plant cannot exceed 50% of its net nominal generation capacity. The combined 200 MW / 800 MWh target equates to a four-hour duration requirement. Winning projects will have a maximum of 12 months to install the systems and obtain their commercial operation date (COD) certificate. The tender rules allow power supply to begin ahead of schedule once that certificate is secured, provided all conditions set out in the process are met. The battery systems must be installed on the same site as the generation plants they are paired with. The SIE explained that the tender aims to shift a portion of already-contracted solar and wind generation into peak demand hours on the National Interconnected Electric System (SENI). The regulator considers that adding storage will increase the dispatchability of these power supplies without requiring the construction of new generation plants. The approved schedule sets the contract award date for February 25, 2027. The tender process will include the call for bids, bidder registration, qualification review, bid submission and evaluation, and final award. The SIE also plans to set allowable reference costs prior to opening the financial bids, in line with the price cap and floor rules governing the tender regulations. Winning bidders will sign a new supply contract separate from the existing energy agreement already in force with the respective distribution company. The offered bid price will be structured as a discount against the energy price stipulated in the existing contract, though its application will be strictly limited to the new agreement backed by the battery system and will not alter the terms of the original PPA. Awarded systems must also comply with the technical requirements established under Resolution SIE-178-2025-MEM and applicable ancillary services regulations, with the resolution explicitly citing rules for frequency and voltage regulation. This new call follows a separate tender for up to 600 MW of new solar and wind generation with mandatory energy storage, for which financial bids were opened in April this year. Unlike that earlier process, which targeted greenfield renewable energy plants, the newly approved tender seeks to retrofit batteries onto operational projects that already hold supply contracts with the country’s distribution utilities. title: Dutch residential battery market surges ahead of net metering phaseout - Energy Storage
content: Sales of residential battery storage systems in the Netherlands have more than doubled over the past nine months ahead of the phaseout of the country’s net-metering scheme for residential PV at the end of this year, according to Sunergy Research, a Dutch energy supplier specializing in services for residential solar owners. “Net metering will end on Jan. 1, and the market will change drastically for consumers,” Sunergy Research CEO Rolf Heynen told ESS news . “For many years, solar panels were easy to sell thanks to net metering and a very clear business case, with electricity prices stable at €0.21/kWh. Now, electricity prices have skyrocketed, and dynamic tariffs have made the business case more complex, alongside public discussions about the balancing market, variable grid tariffs starting in 2029, and home batteries.” “With compensation for electricity exports expected to fall sharply, maximizing self-consumption is becoming increasingly important,” Heynen said. “Today, the average Dutch household consumes just 30% of the solar electricity it generates, exporting the remaining 70% to the grid. A home battery can dramatically reverse that balance, potentially increasing self-consumption to around 70%.” Sunergy Research also reported that installations of small home batteries with capacities of up to 5 kWh were more than four times higher in September than in January, while installations of larger systems, ranging from 5 kWh to 15 kWh, nearly tripled over the same period. The company’s data also show that installations of plug-in batteries, a relatively new segment of the Dutch energy storage market, have more than doubled in nine months, making them the largest category in the residential battery market. Heynen said the rapid growth of plug-in batteries indicates that the market is expanding beyond early adopters. “What makes this development particularly significant is the breadth of demand,” he said. “Smaller, accessible batteries are opening the market to ordinary households, while larger, permanently installed systems appeal to consumers who have already invested heavily in electrification. The barriers to battery ownership are falling rapidly.” Sunergy has also launched its Home Batteries Selection Guide, a free, 33-page publication aimed at helping residential solar owners assess battery storage options. The guide identifies two main market segments: plug-and-play batteries for smaller PV installations and permanently installed systems for households with higher electricity demand. Plug-and-play batteries are particularly suitable for homes with around six solar panels and no heat pump or electric vehicle charger, according to the guide. These systems typically offer around 5 kWh of storage capacity, with prices starting at approximately €1,000 ($1,118.9). Larger households may benefit from permanently installed batteries with capacities ranging from 5 kWh to 20 kWh, starting at approximately €4,000. The guide recommends capacities of 5 kWh to 10 kWh for typical single-phase installations and 10 kWh to 20 kWh for three-phase systems, depending on household requirements. Battery sizing should take into account household electricity consumption, solar generation patterns, inverter capacity, backup power requirements and potential electricity trading, the report says. Sunergy also warns that oversized batteries are often recommended to consumers, potentially undermining investment returns. Research estimates cited in the guide suggest payback periods of two to 15 years, with annual savings of approximately €200 to €1,000 for permanently installed systems. The guide also highlights the role of energy management systems (EMS) in coordinating solar generation, battery charging and household consumption. The publication identifies additional revenue opportunities from electricity trading, grid balancing and congestion management. Sunergy also recommends professional installation, adequate ventilation and careful consideration of battery compatibility, expandability and insurance requirements. The guide concludes that appropriately sized batteries combined with intelligent energy management could improve the economics of residential solar as the Netherlands phases out net metering. title: Salt-based thermal storage supports renewable steam in Spain - Energy Storage
content: German pharmaceutical company Bayer has begun testing a system that uses renewable electricity to produce steam at its plant in La Felguera, Langreo, in Spain’s Asturias region. The facility manufactures acetylsalicylic acid, the active ingredient in Aspirin. The project is designed to replace fossil fuels in steam generation. Developed by Iberdrola España, the system combines a 15 MW renewable power purchase agreement, a 2.5 MW self-consumption solar installation and thermal energy storage using salt. The storage system is intended to partially decouple electricity generation from the industrial process’s heat demand, helping maintain a continuous supply of steam. The project aims to meet 100% of the steam requirements for acetylsalicylic acid production with renewable electricity. Testing began with the supply of renewable steam to the plant. The trial phase is expected to conclude by the end of the year, when the system is scheduled to reach continuous operation. The project is structured around a long-term heat purchase agreement (HPA) and uses technology from Spanish engineering company Inerco to integrate the thermal storage system. Iberdrola said the project represents an investment of more than €18 million. More than 60 professionals participated in the initial implementation phase. The project has received public support from Spain’s Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving (IDAE) and Institute for Just Transition, as well as the regional government of Asturias and Langreo City Council. It has also received support from the European Union’s Innovation Fund. title: Sunpin connects 45 MW / 180 MWh battery storage project to grid in Japan - Energy Storage
content: Sunpin Japan, the Tokyo-based subsidiary of California solar and storage developer Sunpin Solar, has completed grid connection for its 45 MW / 180 MWh SP Shiga Otsu Power Storage Station in Otsu City, Shiga Prefecture. Connected on November 5, the four-hour standalone lithium-ion facility is scheduled to begin commercial operations in December 2026. Sunpin Japan led greenfield development in-house, handling land acquisition, permitting, and utility consultations. Group affiliate Blue Point Power Solutions executed the engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) scope and will manage commissioning and long-term operations and maintenance. Once operational, Kansai Electric Power and Enewill joint venture E-Flow will serve as the aggregator, trading the asset across Japan’s wholesale and balancing power markets. The companies involved did not detail revenue sources in terms of merchant operations or tolls, and didn’t disclose the BESS OEM or PCS supplier. Project photography reviewed by ESS News shows 20-foot high-cube liquid-cooled BESS containers. Previously, Sunpin’s US parent Sunpin Solar signed a 10 GWh supply deal with REPT Battero in late 2023, though it’s unclear if this carried over to Japan. Visual details compared closely with REPT Battero’s Powtrix 2.0 DC Container but this is unconfirmed, and a company representative has been contacted for confirmation. title: BYD is going all out on its ultra-luxury EV with coach doors and 1,000+ km of range [Images]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 9 2026 - 7:32 am PT
unveiled the Yangwang Altior, its new ultra-luxury EV with coach doors, over 1,000 km of CTLC range, a 1,000V fast-charging platform, and plenty of premium extras.
Meet the BYD Yangwang Altrio EV
The “super-luxury executive flagship sedan,” as BYD calls it, made its official debut in Abu Dhabi, UAE, over the weekend.
For those who don’t know, Yangwang is BYD’s ultra-luxury sub-brand, sitting at the very top of its brand hierarchy.
The Atrio is Yangwang’s largest and most luxurious sedan, set to compete with high-end brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Benz Maybach.
Measuring 5,600 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,590 mm tall, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase, BYD’s flagship sedan sits squarely between the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom (standard wheelbase) in length.
BYD said the “Golden Body Proportions” are designed to maximize interior space for both front and rear passengers.
Its meticulous front-end design is inspired by “Ding,” a traditional ancient Chinese cauldron, featuring “diamond-cut” headlights, a 137-gemstone dot-matrix grille, and, to top it off, a 24K pure gold car emblem sits up front and center.
BYD Yangwang Altior ultra-luxury sedan (Source: BYD)
The coach doors create a grand entrance, with the front doors opening at an 80-degree angle and the rear doors opening to a 90-degree angle.
Inside, the flagship sedan takes luxury up a notch with a massive, full-length panoramic center infotainment screen that extends from the driver to the passenger side.
BYD Yangwang Altior interior (Source: BYD)
The “Wrap-around cockpit” is designed to create an immersive, premium experience, with four executive seats and a central island for rear passengers that includes vehicle controls, storage, and even a champagne glass holder.
BYD said it offers the most second-row space in its class, but didn’t reveal specifics. The zero-gravity “cloud-like” rear seats feature a four-ball mechanical massage head, you know, for those longer trips.
Meanwhile, the front passenger seat can fold at the push of a button to open up more space for rear passengers.
The interior features premium materials, including full-grain genuine leather seats, diamond-cut detailing, real wood trim, and natural lambswool foot pads.
And that’s not all. It also has a 39-speaker Dynaudio Platinum Evidence high-end sound system that creates an immersive 360-degree “hall-level” sound experience.
The Yangwang Altio is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including a high-speed tire-blowout stability system, emergency float mode, and in-place U-turn or tank-turn control using its quad-motor e4 platform.
It also uses BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Fast Charging Technology, which provides a CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).
The flagship sedan features “extremely fast flash charging,” BYD said, thanks to its 1000V ultra flash charging tech. It takes just five minutes to charge the vehicle’s battery from 10% to 70%. To go from 10% to 97% it takes just nine minutes.
BYD opened orders for the limited-edition “Mountain and River Rhyme” Yangwang Altrio model, which will be extremely exclusive with just 399 units.
Buyers can place a reservation with a 300,000 yuan ($45,000) deposit. BYD didn’t reveal final prices, but the global version is expected to start at around 2 million yuan ($300,000).

title: Electric dirt bikes keep getting called e-bikes. The bicycle industry wants that to stop
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 9 2026 - 4:54 am PT
The line between electric bicycles and electric motorcycles has been getting increasingly blurry – though perhaps not because the vehicles themselves are actually that hard to tell apart.
Instead, much of the confusion comes down to terminology. High-powered electric dirt bikes capable of reaching motorcycle-like speeds are increasingly being referred to as “e-bikes,” despite sharing relatively little with the low-speed electric bicycles millions of Americans use for commuting and recreation.
Now the U.S. bicycle industry is asking federal regulators to make that distinction much clearer.
PeopleForBikes
, the bicycle industry’s leading trade association, recently testified before the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), calling for stronger federal regulations that specifically distinguish electric bicycles from higher-powered e-motos and electric dirt bikes.
“E-bikes and e-motos are fundamentally different products, and federal safety regulations need to reflect that distinction,” explained PeopleForBikes Policy and General Counsel Matt Moore. “When high-powered electric dirt bikes are marketed as e-bikes, it creates confusion for consumers and puts the credibility of legitimate e-bikes at risk.”
The Lectric XP4 is typical of a street-legal electric bicycle, unlike e-motos that greatly exceed electric bicycle limits
There’s a real nomenclature problem hiding underneath all of this. The term “e-bike” is widely used as shorthand for “electric bicycle,” but it isn’t exclusively used that way. Motorcycles have been called “bikes” for generations, and motorcycle media and riders will sometimes casually refer to electric motorcycles as “e-bikes” too, just in the way a biker refers to his Harley as his “bike”. In fact, it all comes from the same root. We don’t call motorcyclists “motorists”, do we? No… we call them “bikers”.
All of that makes phrases like “legal e-bike” and “legitimate e-bike” that were even used by PeopleForBikes in its arguments somewhat problematic when discussing proposed regulation. The term “e-bike” simply doesn’t mean anything specific, at least not legally.
What actually matters from a legal standpoint is whether a vehicle meets the codified definition of an electric bicycle, not whether someone calls it an e-bike – especially when the term e-bike is practically applied so broadly. In other words, perhaps part of separating electric bicycles from e-motos is being more precise with the terminology ourselves: “electric bicycle” has a specific regulatory meaning, while “e-bike” has increasingly become a much fuzzier colloquial term. As much as some would want the term “e-bike” to mean something with pedals, it simply doesn’t – at least not in North America.
I’m certainly guilty of this myself in my writing and videos, falling back on the commonly used phrasing instead of the technical legal terminology, but keeping them separated could help with the growing misunderstanding in the industry.
Legal electric bicycles are a far cry from e-motos, but the terminology can often get mixed up
That distinction has become increasingly important as lightweight electric motorcycles and dirt bikes
have exploded in popularity
. Many feature bicycle-like frames and components, and some
even include pedals
, but their performance can extend far beyond what federal law defines as a low-speed electric bicycle.
The concern goes beyond mere semantics. When a 50-60 mph (80-100 km/h) electric dirt bike gets lumped into the same category as a 20-28 mph (32-45 km/h) commuter e-bike, crashes and reckless riding involving the former can quickly become part of the public conversation surrounding the latter. That can ultimately influence how lawmakers, regulators, police departments, and the general public view e-bikes as a whole.
In fact, many of the supposed electric bicycle crash figures we’ve seen touted in the news aren’t from electric bicycles at all, but rather from e-moto accidents that have been lumped in with electric bicycles, making the latter appear more dangerous than they truly are.
If street-legal electric bicycles were separated from e-motos in crash statistics, the category would be revealed to be much safer than conventional reporting would have us believe.
E-motos like this Annioki A9 can sometimes look similar to electric bicycles, despite hiding much higher performance
All of this and more has led to PeopleForBikes pushing federal regulators to draw a clearer line.
As part of its CPSC testimony, the organization recommended retaining the existing federal definition of a low-speed electric bicycle while creating a separate definition for e-motos, including machines capable of speeds up to 60 mph (96 km/h). It also called for mandatory electrical safety standards for off-road e-motos, which it says currently fall into a regulatory gap, as well as greater scrutiny of conversion kits capable of turning conventional bicycles into vehicles operating beyond their original structural design limits.
The testimony came as the CPSC considers
new mandatory federal battery safety standards for e-bikes and other electric mobility devices
. PeopleForBikes says it supports stronger battery standards, while recommending that regulators rely on existing UL standards without modification.
PeopleForBikes is also asking the CPSC and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to coordinate enforcement against e-motos that evade federal requirements.
None of this means e-motos are inherently bad. They’re incredibly fun machines, and there’s a rapidly growing market for them. But a 60 mph (96 km/h) electric dirt bike isn’t an electric bicycle simply because it looks vaguely like one.
And increasingly, the bicycle industry wants regulators to make sure everyone understands the difference.
E-motos like the Juiced Nomadix can be great fun, but are meant to be used off of public streets. Keep it in the dirt!

title: LiveWire just showed off its biggest electric motorcycle lineup yet
content:
Electric Motorcycles
LiveWire
Micah Toll
| Nov 9 2026 - 7:13 am PT
Customized version of the LiveWire S4 Honcho displayed at EICMA 2026
LiveWire
has spent the last few years expanding beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off. But seeing the company’s latest machines all together at EICMA in Milan really drives home just how much broader LiveWire’s ambitions have become.
I stopped by the LiveWire booth at EICMA 2026, where the company had everything from its new lightweight S4 Honcho models to the freshly acquired DUST electric dirt bikes – plus STACYC’s electric balance bikes for the youngest riders.
It’s quite a spread, and perhaps more importantly, it paints a picture of a company that increasingly wants to have an electric two-wheeler for just about every stage of a rider’s life.
I also had a chance to spend several hours test-riding the S4 Honcho Street in Milan, so be on the lookout for that article and video to experience it with me.
But for now, let’s see what was at the LiveWire booth.
LiveWire S4 Honcho takes center stage
Perhaps the most important bikes at the booth were the S4 Honcho models, LiveWire’s new lightweight and lower-cost electric motorcycles.
The production S4 Honcho Street
made its European debut
at EICMA alongside the dirt-oriented S4 Honcho Trail. The Trail version recently began reaching customers in the US, with the Street now en route to dealerships, and European sales are beginning around the EICMA launch.
These bikes represent a significant departure from LiveWire’s earlier strategy. Instead of trying to compete directly with full-size gasoline motorcycles on outright performance, the Honcho platform is aimed at riders looking for something smaller, simpler, and more approachable.
And now the family is getting even bigger.
Also on display was the new S4 Honcho Skate, making its first public appearance.
The Skate is planned for 2027 and further expands the modular Honcho platform with a stripped-down, playful design.
For those who have followed H-D’s electric ambitions for as long as I have, you might even remember the original
Harley-Davidson electric moped prototype
that seems to have served as inspiration for the Honcho Skate’s design.
Seeing the various Honcho versions together also makes LiveWire’s strategy with the platform much clearer. Rather than creating one small electric motorcycle, the company is building an entire family around the concept.
DUST Moto officially becomes part of the family
The other major attraction at LiveWire’s booth was the DUST lineup.
LiveWire acquired the assets of DUST Moto earlier this year,
bringing the lightweight electric dirt bike company under its umbrella. EICMA marked the first public showing of the production-intent DUST Hightail under LiveWire ownership.
The Hightail had already generated plenty of interest before the acquisition as a lightweight, high-performance electric dirt bike. Now we’re getting our first look at how that machine fits into LiveWire’s broader plans.
The company is targeting a 2027 introduction for the production Hightail.
But it wasn’t alone.
LiveWire also showed the new DUST Spur, another model planned for 2027 and intended to expand the newly formed DUST family.
The DUST acquisition is particularly interesting because it gives LiveWire an immediate foothold in the rapidly growing lightweight electric off-road motorcycle space without having to develop an entirely new platform from scratch.
Fast charging coming to the S2 line?
In what could be a hint at faster charging to come, there was an interesting S2 Alpanista Corsa motorcycle that had been outfitted with a NACS plug and DC fast-charging capabilities.
LiveWire claimed a 20-80% charge in under 10 minutes, which would revolutionize the ability to do long-distance motorcycle touring, or just make it more convenient to get a quick charge and head back to your apartment.
There’s on word on whether the concept will make it to production, but the specs are enticing!
The most interesting part of LiveWire’s EICMA display may not have been any individual motorcycle, but rather what happens when you stand back and look at the entire booth.
On one end you’ve got STACYC electric balance bikes. LiveWire says the brand has already introduced more than 250,000 riders to two wheels.
Then you’ve got the lightweight S4 Honcho family. Above that sit the DUST machines for more serious off-road riding, while LiveWire’s existing S2 motorcycles continue to cover the higher-performance street end of the spectrum.
That’s becoming something of an electric two-wheeler ladder.
A kid can theoretically start on a STACYC, graduate into increasingly capable electric two-wheelers, and eventually wind up on a proper electric motorcycle – all within the same corporate family.
And that feels particularly relevant at a show like EICMA, where much of the motorcycle industry is still trying to figure out exactly where electric motorcycles fit.
LiveWire seems increasingly convinced that the answer isn’t simply to build electric replacements for existing gasoline motorcycles.
Instead, the company is spreading out into categories where electric drivetrains can create different kinds of motorcycles altogether.
Electrek’s Take
I’ve been following LiveWire’s evolution for years, and the company standing in front of me at EICMA looks considerably different from the one that started out selling
a single expensive flagship electric motorcycle.
The big, high-performance bikes are still important, but machines like the S4 Honcho and DUST Hightail are arguably more interesting to me because they can bring entirely different riders into electric motorcycling.
They’re smaller. They’re simpler. And perhaps most importantly, they’re targeting the kind of fun, accessible riding that doesn’t require superbike levels of performance.
There’s still plenty we need to learn about several of these new models, particularly final specifications and pricing for the 2027 machines.
But seeing the Honcho, Honcho Skate, Hightail, Spur, and STACYC machines together at EICMA makes one thing pretty clear: LiveWire isn’t just trying to sell a few electric motorcycles anymore.
It’s trying to build an entire electric two-wheeler ecosystem.

title: Musk says Cybertruck isn't dying from weak sales — the numbers disagree
content:
Tesla Cybertruck
Fred Lambert
| Nov 9 2026 - 5:56 am PT
Tesla Cybertruck production April 2024
Elon Musk now claims Cybertruck orders “far exceed” Tesla’s production rate, and that the truck isn’t being killed because it’s unprofitable. It’s his second explanation in three days for ending the pickup.
The problem is that Tesla’s own numbers say the opposite. The Cybertruck line has been running at roughly a quarter of its installed capacity, and Tesla spent all of 2026 discounting, re-trimming, and repricing the truck to find buyers.
Here’s what Musk posted on X overnight:
“The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people. This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.”
The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.
This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported…
https://t.co/rGmNKV3ILs
He was quote-tweeting a Tesla fan telling people to “get it while you can.” So yes, this is also a sales pitch.
On Friday, Musk
announced Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production
at Giga Texas around mid-2027 “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” That was the first story. Now it’s about “complexity” and “opportunity cost.” Let’s go through it.
“Order rate far exceeds our production rate”
Tesla controls its production rate. That’s the flaw in this claim.
Tesla built the Cybertruck supply chain for 250,000 units a year, and its latest shareholder letter still lists more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. In Q3 2026, it delivered 8,295 “Other Models.” With Model S and Model X out of production,
we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks
. That’s a 30,000-a-year pace, down 48% year-over-year in that category.
If orders had been outrunning production at any point this year, Tesla had about 95,000 units of idle annual capacity sitting right there. It didn’t use it.
And companies with a backlog don’t behave like Tesla did. In February, it offered a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.” It pulled a single-motor RWD version after just 173 sales. It leaned on Musk’s own companies too:
SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025
, about 19% of US registrations that quarter once you add his other firms.
Cox Automotive estimates US Cybertruck sales fell from 14,416 in Q3 2024 to 3,519 in Q1 2026 and 3,744 in Q2. It’s a demand problem everyone could see.
So if orders spiked this weekend, there’s an obvious reason: Musk told the world on Friday that the truck is going away. A last-call rush on a discontinued vehicle is not proof that it was selling.
“Will have to return deposits for a lot of people”
Tesla has been sitting on Cybertruck deposits it was never going to fill for years.
Musk touted more than a million reservations, and crowdsourced tallies
put the list near 2 million by 2023
. Its best US quarter, by Cox Automotive’s estimate, was 14,416 trucks. The reservation book was a vanity number, not an order book.
Two weeks ago, Tesla
cancelled the Cybertruck for Australia and New Zealand
and refunded deposits people had paid in 2019. Returning deposits is something Tesla was already doing because it couldn’t sell the truck in those markets, not because it was swamped.
“Not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable”
This one is a straw man. Our reporting, and most of the coverage Friday, was about sales, not margins. The truck sells at about 12% of the volume Tesla planned for.
Tesla doesn’t disclose Cybertruck margins, so Musk can say whatever he wants here and nobody can check it. But he’s the one who said in 2023 that Tesla had “dug our own grave with Cybertruck” because of how hard it was to build profitably.
And look at what Tesla did the same day it announced the end of production: it
raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10%
and paused orders for the cheapest trim. The cheapest orderable Cybertruck went from $69,990 in early August to $92,490. You do that to squeeze margin out of the last trucks, not because the line was printing money.
The “opportunity cost” argument proves our point
Follow Musk’s logic to the end. If the Cybertruck were profitable and orders really outran production, killing it would mean walking away from guaranteed profit for a robotaxi that had 463 units registered in Texas as of late October and no proven business yet.
The only way that trade makes sense is if the Cybertruck’s profit at 30,000 units a year is small. Which is another way of saying it doesn’t sell enough.
Giga Texas also has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, and the Cybercab runs on its own “unboxed” line. Tesla can’t make use of the Cybertruck line and floor space was never the constraint. To further adapt his logic for shutting down Cybertruck production, Musk shifted his argument from “space” to Cybercab’s line needing some “smart people”, who he implied work on the Cybertruck.
Musk wrote on Saturday that
“there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people”
, but Michael So, who led Cybercab new product introduction and was Giga Texas employee #1, left in April for nuclear startup Aalo Atomics. Last month,
Tesla lost its Cybercab general assembly lead to Rivian’s R2 program
just weeks after the launch. If talent is the bottleneck, it’s the Cybercab team that’s bleeding it.
Electrek’s Take
Musk doesn’t want the Cybertruck to go down in history as a flop, and we get it. It’s his truck. He approved the controversial design, hyped it for four years before it shipped, and boasted that 1 million reservations could translate to 500,000 units a year.
But you can’t run a line at a quarter of capacity, run “10 days only” discounts, pull trims after 173 sales, and sell trucks to your own rocket company, then turn around and tell people demand was never the issue. The data is public. Tesla’s own delivery reports are public.
Our read on what happened is simple. Demand collapsed in 2025 and never came back. Tesla tried every pricing trick it had. When nothing worked, it found a future-facing reason to end it, and now it’s spinning the inevitable end-of-life rush as proof the truck was a hit all along.
Musk loves a big TAM. SpaceX’s IPO filing put its total addressable market at
$28.5 trillion
, and last month he went further, writing that he sees
“a path to SpaceX being worth orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy.”
So apply the same lens to Tesla. Pickups are one of the biggest and most profitable vehicle markets on the planet. Ford sold 801,525 F-Series trucks in the US last year, GM sold 925,656 Silverados and Sierras combined, and Ram moved 374,059. That’s more than 2.1 million trucks from three automakers, easily north of $100 billion a year at today’s transaction prices.
Robotaxis? Waymo, by far the leader, is doing about 500,000 paid rides a week, and analysts estimated its revenue run rate at roughly $355 million earlier this year. Tesla doesn’t even break out robotaxi revenue and we expect it to be a fraction of Waymo’s.
Maybe that flips one day. But that’s the bet here: Tesla is walking away from a giant market it can sell into today for one that only gets big if autonomy is solved in the next couple of years. Musk has made that exact bet before. He promised a million robotaxis on the road by 2020 and has said unsupervised self-driving was a year away almost every year since 2016. He’s lost every time.
And that rush is real, for what it’s worth. Some people want the last of a weird, genuinely impressive truck. That doesn’t make it a business.

title: Tesla launches Robotaxi in San Antonio with a 274 sq mi geofence on paper
content:
Robotaxi
Tesla Robotaxi
Fred Lambert
| Nov 9 2026 - 6:36 am PT
Tesla is launching its Robotaxi service in San Antonio, its eighth city, with a launch geofence covering about 274 square miles. That’s the biggest day-one map Tesla has ever posted, and more than four times the size of Waymo’s San Antonio service area.
But if Tesla’s recent maps are any guide, a big chunk of that area won’t be bookable. In Austin, an independent check found the Robotaxi app only accepted pickups and drop-offs in about 59% of the zone Tesla advertises.
A big map, and no cars spotted yet
Tesla’s official Robotaxi account made the announcement just after midnight local time: “Robotaxi available in San Antonio starting tomorrow, 5am.” It came with a map of the “launch geofence,” a large polygon that runs from Loop 1604 on the north side down to just south of downtown.
Robotaxi Tracker
, which measures operator maps and logs fleet sightings, puts the zone at 274 square miles. That covers about 1.0 million residents (51% of the metro) and 721,000 jobs. San Antonio International Airport sits inside the polygon, but it isn’t served.
Waymo started driverless rides in San Antonio in February with more than 60 square miles and opened to all riders in October, airport trips included. Robotaxi Tracker currently lists Waymo’s San Antonio area at 59 square miles.
What Tesla didn’t say is how many cars will cover its 274 square miles. As of Monday morning, Robotaxi Tracker hadn’t logged a single Tesla Robotaxi in San Antonio.
The launch landed the same day Tesla expanded Austin again. The tracker now measures Tesla’s Austin zone at 443 square miles, up 178 square miles since mid-September.
The map isn’t the service
We’ve seen this movie. Last month, Tesla
expanded its Houston geofence into the shape of a rocket
, and within two days the creator of Robotaxi Tracker
found the app refusing downtown pickups inside it
Since then, Koby Pierce, who tracks Tesla’s service on X, has done the tedious work of checking city after city. He searched thousands of real addresses in the Robotaxi app on an emulator and mapped only the ones where Tesla allows a pickup or drop-off, then compared that with the map Tesla advertises. Here’s the share of Tesla’s advertised land area that actually works:
Austin: about 59% (83% of residents)
Miami: 61% (67% of residents)
Orlando: about 70%
Fort Worth: about 72%
Houston: about 74%
Dallas: 78% (89% of residents)
Austin's dropoff/pickup Geofence is ~41% smaller than advertised.
Seems mostly the East side of town is inaccessible. Unsure the cause. Any ideas?
Dallas is next and should be done by noon tomrrow.
Austin is the one that matters. It’s Tesla’s flagship market, with 453 unsupervised vehicles in service according to Robotaxi Tracker. Yet about 41% of the advertised map Pierce tested, mostly on the east side of town, wouldn’t take a ride request. Pierce points to railroad crossings as a big factor in several cities, which lines up with the strange downtown routing we saw in Houston.
To be fair, Pierce says Waymo is next on his list, and he expects “they’re no better.” Robotaxi Tracker already had to trim Waymo’s Orlando area last month after finding the airport, inside Waymo’s published map, wasn’t selectable. We’ll look at those numbers when they’re out. But it doesn’t change what Tesla is doing with San Antonio today.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due. A 274-square-mile launch in a new city is progress, and Tesla now runs unsupervised rides in eight cities. At the start of this year, it had no unsupervised rides anywhere.
But we need to stop taking Tesla’s geofence numbers at face value, and that includes us. We used Tesla’s 254-square-mile figure for Houston, and it turned out to be overstated. In all six cities Pierce has checked, the real service area is between 59% and 78% of what Tesla posts. In Austin and Miami, it’s about 60%.
So the honest way to read the San Antonio announcement is “up to 274 square miles.” In practice, expect something closer to 160 to 210 square miles, with an unknown number of cars, and the airport already off the table. That’s still bigger than Waymo’s 59 square miles in the city.
The problem is that square miles are the metric Tesla fully controls. Drawing a polygon costs nothing, and the numbers were all over X within hours of the post. Cars per square mile, wait times, and rides completed are much harder to inflate, and nationally Waymo still runs over 4,000 driverless vehicles to Tesla’s 666, per Robotaxi Tracker.
I still consider this a small pilot by any standard, and safety remains the bottleneck. Tesla is still forcing riders through hour-long rides that should take 15 minutes because they have to take routes that avoid areas that Tesla can’t safely navigate without supervision.
Until that’s fixed, robotaxi won’t be able to meaningfully scale beyond these limited demonstrations in geo-fenced areas.

title: Cadillac Is Bringing GM’s Super Cruise Hands-Free Driving System To Europe
content:
Cadillac Is Bringing GM’s Super Cruise Hands-Free Driving System To Europe
The Optiq, Lyriq, and Vistiq EVs will offer semi-automated driving on more than 111,000 miles of roads across 16 European countries.
- General Motors is introducing its Super Cruise hands-free driving system in Europe.
- Three Cadillac electric crossovers will be the first models to deliver the semi-automated feature.
- Based on pre-mapped lidar data, Super Cruise will be available on over 111,000 miles of European roads across 16 countries.
Super Cruise, General Motors’ hands-free driving assistance system, is heading to Europe, where it will be available starting in mid-December on a handful of Cadillac EVs.
The 2025 Optiq, as well as the 2026 Lyriq and Vistiq electric crossovers, will be able to do semi-automated driving on more than 180,000 kilometers (111,000 miles) of compatible roads across 16 European countries beginning at the end of the year. Germany, France, and Switzerland are among the first European countries where the system will go live.
Super Cruise, which is already available in the United States, Canada, China, and South Korea, uses pre-mapped roads, real-time cameras, radar sensors, GPS data, and adaptive cruise control to enable hands-free driving. That said, the system is still considered a Level 2 driver assistant, according to the Society of Automotive Engineers, so it doesn’t make the car run autonomously, and the driver still needs to pay attention at all times when driving.
A driver monitoring system makes sure that the person behind the steering wheel is alert and can take control at any time, if needed.
When active, Super Cruise displays a green light bar at the top of the steering wheel. The system keeps the vehicle centered in the lane and maintains an appropriate distance from the car in front, without the driver having to touch the steering wheel or pedals. It can do lane changes, but the driver has to initiate the maneuver by activating the indicator.
The feature can be used on compatible roads, including highways and dual carriageways, at speeds of up to 130 kilometers per hour (81 miles per hour), including in heavy stop-and-go traffic.
Cadillac has integrated Google Maps into the navigation map display, which shows roads where Super Cruise can be used and how much of a trip can be driven hands-free. The automaker says the driver assistance feature is designed to make driving more comfortable and convenient—so drivers shouldn’t expect to be able to take a nap while on the road.
“Super Cruise brings together Cadillac’s premium driving experience, connected services and advanced driver assistance technology to make everyday journeys more comfortable,” said Maximilian Wittich, Managing Director, Digital Services and Experiences. “We are excited to bring this hands-free experience to customers in Europe and to offer technology that has been tested and adapted for European roads and requirements.”
GM said it did a lot of performance testing and validation, as well as regional route testing and Europe-specific software tweaks to make Super Cruise compatible with European legislation and driving conditions.
Since debuting in 2017, Super Cruise has delivered over a billion hands-free driving miles, GM said. In North America alone, there are roughly 750,000 Super Cruise-enabled vehicles, but the American auto giant estimates that the number of users will exceed 850,000 by the end of the year.
In the U.S., over 20 GM models are compatible with Super Cruise. The system is included for free for the first three years from the date of first registration. When the free trial ends, owners need to pay for a Super Cruise subscription and a Connected Services plan to keep using hands-free driving.

title: Ford Tested 36,000 Mustang Mach-E Batteries. Here’s How They Held Up After 100,000 Miles
content:
Battery degradation is one of the top concerns among potential EV buyers. New data from Ford shows you probably shouldn't worry much.
Photo by:
9:00am ET
Ford collected battery health data from around 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs and shared the results.
Battery degradation is one of the top concerns from car buyers, but Ford's data shows that there isn't much to worry about.
Even Mach-Es with 100,000 or 200,000 miles on the odometer retained most of their original range.
It's one of the top questions I get about EVs: "How long will the battery last?" Understandably, people want to know that their car will go the distance before dropping tens of thousands of dollars on a new car with new-to-them technology.
A growing body of research shows that modern electric cars hold up just fine over years of normal use. And a huge study of
Ford Mustang Mach-E
SUVs further proves the point.
The Detroit automaker collected battery-health data from 36,000 Mach-E SUVs from the 2021 model year that were sold in the U.S. and Canada. The results, released Monday, should help quiet fears that EVs degrade like smartphones, which struggle to hold a charge after a few years of daily use.
On average, the cars had traveled 55,000 miles over 5.2 years and retained 92% of their usable battery capacity. That means a top-trim 2021 Mustang Mach-E with 305 miles of EPA range would in theory be rated for around 280 miles today. All the cars in the study have nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery packs, since Ford didn't introduce a lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery for the Mach-E starting until the 2023 model year.
The 2021 Mustang Mach-Es Ford studied retained 92% of their battery health on average after five years on the road.
Photo by: Ford
physically tests cells in the lab and tries to predict battery degradation using computer models before a model launches, Kevin Vander Laan, the automaker's technical leader of high-voltage battery cells and systems, told me in an interview. But the real test comes after a car spends years on the road.
"Our report card slowly trickles in over time," he said. "So here we are with a five-year report card, and it looks great."
Interestingly enough, putting on twice as many miles as average in the same time period barely impacted overall battery health. Ford says the over 2,000 SUVs with more than 100,000 miles on the odometer retained more than 91% of their battery capacity.
More On Battery Degradation
Those few drivers who put some 40,000 miles on their Mach-Es each year still had strong battery health after five years. Ford says the 30-plus cars in its dataset that had covered more than 200,000 miles showed 88% battery health.
Of course, these are just averages. So your results may vary depending on lots of factors. EVs that spend their lives in the hot American Southwest tend to age more rapidly than those driven in more temperate climates. Likewise, EV batteries that are frequently fast-charged to 100% and drained to near-empty typically wear out faster than those that are kept in the happy zone of 20% to 80%.
Still, Ford says the distribution of results is encouraging for its battery engineers: It says 95% of the 36,000 cars fell between 87% and 97%.
Keep up with the latest EV news straight from your inbox. Sign up for our newsletter!
The results are in line with what other research has uncovered about how EVs age. Some early EVs (notably the first-gen Nissan Leaf) had less sophisticated battery thermal management and saw steep degradation as a result. But modern EVs tend to age far more gracefully.
According to Recurrent, a firm that tracks range retention in used EVs that opt in, the average EV retains 97% of its original observed range after three years and 95% after five years.
In September, battery-health startup Aviloo
released the results
of 500,000 EV battery tests. After 150,000 kilometers (around 93,000 miles), most models studied showed between 90% and 94% health. The
Hyundai Ioniq 5
Mercedes EQA
stood out with readings near the top end of that range. The Mustang Mach-E did just about as well as Ford's own data show: 92.5% battery health. The
came in at 88.9% and 90.3%, respectively.
The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail
Photo by: Ford
Ford makes some familiar recommendations to drivers looking to make sure their EVs last as long as possible. The company says to manage temperature extremes by parking in the shade on scorching days and preconditioning the cabin while the vehicle is plugged in. It also recommends relying on
Level 2 charging
for daily driving, and using Level 3 DC fast chargers sparingly.
Vander Laan says the learnings from this crop of EVs and how they perform contribute to the development process for Ford's next-generation electric cars, like the
sub-$30,000 Fathom pickup
coming next year.
"It's really continuous learning," he said. "We have a design that we deeply understand, the data is flowing in, we're learning learning from that, and feeding that to the engineering teams in the company here."

title: Hyundai Is Recalling Nearly 30,000 Kona EVs Because Their Airbags May Not Deploy
content:
Hyundai Is Recalling Nearly 30,000 Kona EVs Because Their Airbags May Not Deploy
All of the affected vehicles are part of the previous-generation Kona Electric, which went out of production in 2023.
- Nearly 30,000 Hyundai Kona EVs in the U.S. are being recalled for a potential airbag fault.
- The affected vehicles were built in South Korea between 2018 and 2023.
- A software update fixes the problem, but a visit to the dealer is needed.
Hyundai is recalling nearly 30,000 first-generation Kona Electric crossovers in the United States because their airbags and seatbelt pretensioners may not work as intended in the event of an accident.
All affected vehicles, 29,058 in total, were built in South Korea between August 28, 2018, and July 26, 2023, representing model years 2019 through 2023. The problem also affects nearly 9,000 Hyundai Veloster N gas-powered hatchbacks sold here between 2019 and 2022.
2023 Hyundai Kona Electric
The Airbag Control Unit (ACU) is the culprit here. According to the recall report published by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), data that needs to be written to the ACU’s memory may become corrupted during certain driving conditions, causing the airbag malfunction light (MIL) to pop up on the instrument cluster and the airbag system to deactivate.
Without a working system, the airbags will not deploy during a crash, which increases the risk of injury to the driver and passengers.
Hyundai said that the ACU data may become corrupted if a system reboot or a power interruption occurs while the control unit is writing data to its internal memory. The company’s North America office opened a new investigation back in 2024, after the number of airbag warning light warranty claims went up.
The automaker worked with ZF, the supplier that made the airbag control units, to replicate the problem on other vehicles, but couldn’t. However, a fault was induced during bench testing, and a solution was found.
To fix the problem, owners of affected vehicles need to book an appointment with a Hyundai service center, where technicians will update the ACU software for free. In other words, it’s not a hardware fix, but a software fix. According to Hyundai, the new software rolls back to the last known valid data if the transfer is interrupted for one of the reasons described above.
The maker of the Kona EV said that it’s aware of 331 individual incidents related to the ACU issue that affects the electric crossover and gas-powered hot hatch. The car manufacturer is not aware of any crashes, fires, or injuries associated with the ACU data corruption problem in the U.S.

title: This Electric Rolls-Royce Rival Can Spin Like A Tank And Charges In 5 Minutes
content:
China's Rolls-Royce Rival Can Do Tank Turns And Charge In 5 Minutes
BYD's $311,000 electric luxury sedan takes aim at Rolls-Royce with tank turns, outrageous luxury and ultra-fast charging.
- The Yangwang Altior is BYD’s answer to the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Mercedes-Maybach S-Class.
- Unlike its British and German rivals, though, the Altior is electric, with a quad-motor setup that reportedly makes over 1,000 hp.
- Yangwang’s flagship sedan is properly luxurious, with gold and gem-cut elements.
China’s BYD is gunning for supremacy in every possible automotive segment that has traditionally been the stomping ground of European and American brands. After setting the record straight in the hypercar world with the Yangwang U9 Xtreme, the Chinese behemoth is now going after Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Maybach with the new Yangwang Altior.
The Altior, which debuted this weekend in Abu Dhabi, is a massive luxury four-door sedan that goes after the Rolls-Royce Ghost with a long list of features that only the world’s richest people would see as must-haves. It also one-ups its European rivals with something that would probably be labeled as “brash” by some suit-wearing executives.
First up, the Yangwang Altior is completely silent, and not because the Chinese have come up with some revolutionary way of making a massive V-12 engine less chatty than Rolls-Royce, but because it’s powered by an electric powertrain. No fewer than four electric motors and a second-generation Blade battery provide motivation without having to muffle the sound of gasoline exploding under the hood. A fancy suspension, which automatically adjusts settings for the best ride based on information received from a front-facing camera, is also part of the equation.
Thanks to the four individual motors, one at each corner of the car, the Altior can do something that no German or British luxury car has ever been able to: turn on a dime, just like a tank. The Altior also boasts an emergency flotation function that’s meant to help the driver get out of the car if it somehow ends up in water. It’s not exactly something that comes in handy every day, but for the paranoid mogul who thinks about the latest improvements to their doomsday bunker on a daily basis, it may be the one thing missing from every other luxury barge.
Up front, the massive grille that’s reminiscent of Rolls-Royce’s metal nose features individually polished elements and 12 lighting elements that rotate and illuminate one after another as the owner approaches. No fewer than 137 gem-cut elements and a front emblem that’s reportedly 24-karat gold complete the grille.
Open the doors, and you’re greeted with quite a bit of theatre. The front doors open up to 80 degrees, while the rear coach doors can open up to 90 degrees to make ingress and egress as easy as possible. And because imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, custom-made umbrellas are hidden inside the doors, just like on a Rolls-Royce.
While the exterior of the Altior is something that would look at home in Rolls-Royce’s factory parking, the interior reveals its Chinese roots immediately. A huge screen takes up the whole dashboard—a feature that’s all the rage in China, but might seem outdated in a few years. By comparison, more traditional luxury carmakers have usually refrained from plastering screens everywhere, making the interior design a little more timeless.
Apart from the huge screen, though, the Altior can hold its own against the European heavyweights. Plenty of metal switches are used throughout the cabin, and the rear passengers get to enjoy a pair of massaging zero-gravity chairs that can recline and have raising leg rests. Dozens of decorative pieces are dotted around the interior, complemented by traditional embroidery with silk threads, thick pure-wool floor mats, and natural wood trim.
BYD says the Yangwang Altior provides 13.9 inches (354 millimeters) of knee room and 47.6 in (1,209 mm) of legroom. A dedicated relaxation mode makes several pieces fall into place: the sun blinds rise, the seats recline, the ambient lighting softens, and the leg rests rise—all at the press of a button.
When entertainment is needed, a huge 21.4-inch overhead screen swivels down from the headliner, and a 39-speaker audio system handles the sound. A pair of refrigerators keeps drinks cool or warm, with the rear unit holding 1.5 gallons (5.5 liters).
Range-wise, the Altior can deliver more than 621 miles (1,000 kilometers) on a full charge, according to BYD, though that’s based on the rather lenient CLTC rating. Still, recharging from 10% to 70% should take just five minutes on the megawatt-capable Flash Chargers.
The Yangwang Altior carries a pre-sale price of 2.08 million yuan, or about $311,000, with deliveries scheduled to start in the second quarter of 2027. BYD’s Yangwang brand is currently selling cars in the United Arab Emirates and China, but Europe is next, with the first stores expected to go live in the United Kingdom next year.

title: This New EV Motor Spins At 30,000 RPM. Here's Why That Matters
content:
This New EV Motor Spins At 30,000 RPM. Here's Why That Matters
ZF's new drive uses half the magnet material of a comparable system, with nearly 25% less weight and bulk.
- ZF’s new motor spins at 30,000 rpm to deliver the same power in a smaller package.
- The company claims nearly 25% less drive-unit weight and bulk, with half the magnet material.
- Production is targeted for 2030, but ZF hasn’t named any cars that will use it.
An electric motor spinning at 30,000 rpm sounds like something you might find in a high-power EV supercar. ZF has something less extravagant in mind: making the hardware that powers everyday EVs smaller, lighter, and less hungry for expensive materials.
ZF’s new High Revolution Drive combines the motor, power electronics, and transmission all in the same housing. Unlike Mercedes-Benz, though, it doesn't also put the brakes inside the same housing.
Compared with one of ZF’s comparable Select drive units, which spins up to 18,000 rpm, the company claims nearly 25% less weight and volume, half the magnet mass, and a similar efficiency of almost 93%.
ZF High Revolution Drive
This helps because less mass improves EV range, and fewer magnets reduce costs and supply-chain dependence.
According to ZF, spinning the motor faster lets it deliver the same power from a smaller, lighter package. Gears then reduce that speed and increase the turning force sent to the wheels, using a reduction ratio of about 18:1. The version ZF showed produces up to 268 horsepower, with the gearing delivering peak torque of 2,581 pound-feet (3,500 Nm) to the wheels.
The torque measurement comes after the gearing has multiplied the motor’s output. The “two-stage transmission” doesn’t actually mean a two-speed gearbox. It describes successive gear reductions, not two separate driving ratios.
The company says the production High Revolution Drive should deliver 200 to 268 hp and work with both 400- and 800-volt platforms. Reusing its modular Select architecture should simplify installation, shorten development and control costs, and retain manufacturing flexibility. Talks with automakers are underway, with production targeted by 2030.
ZF isn’t alone in trying to squeeze more useful output from a smaller package. One prototype of Yasa’s ultra-compact axial-flux motor produced over 1,000 hp and weighed just 28 pounds. That’s its short-term peak figure, with continuous output estimated at 469–536 bhp.
Yasa’s figure describes only the motor, while ZF’s weight reduction refers to the whole integrated drive unit. Gearing and power electronics still need somewhere to live, and they also add weight.
ZF has also introduced repair kits intended to let workshops fix individual drive unit components, such as gearbox bearings, instead of replacing entire assemblies. That addresses a different problem from shrinking and making hardware lighter, but one buyers may care about considerably more once the warranty expires.
However, ZF hasn’t said whether these two developments are connected, or whether the kits it revealed should be taken as a repairability promise for this new drive. There’s also no mention of which production EV would get this new drive unit. We also don’t know whether those engineering gains will remain unchanged from today’s announcement to something you can actually buy.
Still, this kind of EV development deserves attention even without a four-figure horsepower claim. A family car doesn’t need to break acceleration records, but making its drive unit lighter and less expensive (and possibly easier to repair, too) is exactly what it needs. Whether any savings reach buyers is another question, but giving cars the same power with smaller and less hardware is a good place to start.

首次在国家级森林火灾实战演习中亮相

title: “星云星座计划”发布，覆盖从国产算力芯片到卫星应用的全产业链条
content:
感谢IT之家网友
11 月 9 日消息，据央视新闻报道，在今天（9 日）举办的 2026 太空云产业生态大会上，“星云星座计划”等我国太空云产业化成果发布，标志着我国“太空云”生态建设迈出了从技术验证走向产业化布局的关键一步。
IT之家从报道中获悉，“太空云”是指在轨协同的天基云服务系统，它改变
传统卫星“单星观测、数据回传地面处理”模式
，让天基资源可以
按需调用、即连即用
本次发布的“星云星座计划”是中国科学院空天信息创新研究院与国内科创企业联合研发的全栈国产化太空算力网，是太空云生态产业化落地的重点项目。
从国产算力芯片到卫星应用的全产业链条
。未来，项目将依托
国内计算芯片、服务器整机、卫星制造、卫星应用
等研发单位，构建从“核心器部件研制”到“星座组网与应用”的全栈国产化自主技术体系。分布形成“天地协同”的统一算力网，为自然资源、防灾应急、低空经济等场景提供覆盖全球的太空算力服务。
据专家介绍，该计划未来会
使太空和地面的算力实现无缝融合、统一调度
，太空不再仅仅是数据的转运站，而是与地面地位同等、能力互补的一级算力节点。用户可以像使用地面的云计算一样，随时随地、按需获取太空算力服务。
我国高分辨率遥感卫星的技术水平和在轨数量已达国际领先水平
，高通量通信卫星建设步入高速发展期。未来“太空云”能把遥感、通信、算力等各类卫星通过技术手段整合为智能天基信息服务系统，实现从“功能单星”向“智能星云”的跨越。随着千星规模“太空云”生态加快构建，“太空云”产业化落地将大幅提升我国天基资源综合应用效能，为国民经济高质量发展提供有力支撑。

content:
感谢IT之家网友
11 月 9 日消息，全国高校首个冷门绝学学院于 11 月 6 日在中国社会科学院大学成立。
11 月 6 日，中国社会科学院大学冷门绝学学院成立仪式暨全国冷门绝学联盟启动大会在京举办。
IT之家从官方公告了解到，中国社会科学院大学冷门绝学学院的研究范围覆盖突厥文、西夏文、契丹文、女真文、满文、古藏文、古彝文、八思巴文、纳西东巴文、方块壮文等 10 余种民族古文字，统筹甲骨学、简帛学、古典学等特色研究方向，设立甲骨文与简帛文献、北方民族古文字、西南民族古文字、中西古典文明等教研部，配套建成数智绝学实验室，创办《冷门绝学研究》期刊，
开设本科生“鼎堂班”，构建本硕博贯通式人才培养体系
作为中国社会科学院大学实体机构，冷门绝学学院组建起一支 140 余人的师资队伍，
由 8 位学部委员、30 多名一级教授和国家级人才领衔
，形成老中青梯次接续、专兼职互补协同的学术梯队。
作为开放的协作平台，“全国冷门绝学联盟”由中国社会科学院大学牵头发起，目前共有包括清华大学、中国人民大学、北京师范大学、复旦大学、南京大学、四川大学、南开大学、武汉大学、中山大学、吉林大学、山东大学、厦门大学、兰州大学、中央民族大学、中国藏学研究中心、中国西域研究中心、中国第一历史档案馆、新疆维吾尔自治区社会科学院、云南省社会科学院、内蒙古自治区社会科学院等在内的
全国 82 家高校、科研院所及文博单位参与构成
，基本覆盖了我国冷门绝学研究的主要机构。
