title: A degree in Paris, a gigawatt at the border - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
How French winter temperature reshapes cross-border flows, day-ahead prices and solar revenue in the markets around it.
09 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
High-voltage pylon at the Col de Vernant in commune of Arâches-la-Frasse, Haute-Savoie, France.
When France gets cold, its neighbours feel it at the border. Each degree of French winter cold takes about 1 GW off French net exports and goes with day-ahead prices €5 ($5.6)/MWh to €7/MWh higher in France, Belgium and Germany. Roughly half of the French price response, a third of the Belgian and a quarter of the German is French temperature on its own rather than the neighbours’ weather. Eleven winters of data can also say why the loss sits in the hours solar cannot fill, why the nuclear fleet rather than the thermometer decides whether France keeps exporting, and why a cold spell can leave a solar plant better off.
01. One cold spell, and the pattern of eleven winters
The winter of 2025/26 showed the whole mechanism in four weeks. Between 15 and 21 December 2025, with the French effective temperature, a population-weighted average of the day’s temperature and the two days before it, at 9.8 C, France exported a net 16.3 GW on average to its six neighbours. Between 29 December and 11 January, at 1.9 C, it exported 5.7 GW. On 6 January, at −1.5 C and with French demand averaging 82 GW over the day, France imported a net 3.7 GW. Nuclear output was 52.4 GW in the mild week and 53.3 GW in the cold spell, wind averaged 7.2 and 7.5 GW, and French solar averaged no more than 2.3 GW on its best day of the cold spell. The swing in exports was therefore driven by demand, which rose from 56 GW to 72 GW between the two windows. Lower exports covered about 10.6 GW of that 16 GW rise. The remaining 5 GW or so was met mostly by gas, with smaller gains in nuclear, hydro, solar and wind.
8 GW to 9 GW between a mild day and a cold one
That cold spell is close to the average pattern of eleven winters, counting November to March as winter. On the mildest tenth of winter days, above 11.6 C, France exports 9.0 GW. On the coldest tenth, below 3.2 C, it exports close to zero. Measured within each winter rather than across all eleven, the swing is 8.3 GW, so the loss between a mild day and a cold one is 8 to 9 GW whichever way it is measured. Germany loses 2.1 GW of French supply between the two, on physical flows that include loop flows, Belgium 1.9 GW, Switzerland 1.7 GW, Britain 1.3 GW, Spain 1.1 GW and Italy 1.0 GW, and on the German, Belgian and Spanish borders the flow reverses on average. On cold days the Belgian, German and Swiss borders run near their highest winter import levels in 5 to 6% of hours, against under 1% on mild days. In a cold spell the question shifts from how much France can export to how much it can take in.
02. Where the degree goes
Both the December spell and the eleven-winter average put the swing down to demand, so the share of the extra demand that is met at home decides how much of the loss crosses the border. French demand starts to respond to cold below 15.5 C. Within a winter, once month, weekday and holidays are allowed for, it rises by 1.8 GW for every degree colder. That response has not weakened, at 1.7 GW per degree in 2015/16 and 1.9 GW in 2025/26. Between 15.5 C and freezing, demand climbs by about 30 GW. Below 2 C the average winter day turns France from exporter to importer.
Of the 1.8 GW a degree adds within a winter, nuclear output is 0.43 GW higher, gas 0.36 GW, hydro 0.20 GW, coal and oil 0.11 GW, and net exports 1.04 GW lower. Wind falls by 0.35 GW, as cold French days tend to be still ones, so that loss has to be covered as well, and the five supply terms add up to the 1.8 GW rise in demand plus the 0.35 GW lost from wind. Solar shows no response to temperature within a winter. At 1.04 GW per degree, a winter 1 C colder than the 7.8 C average would remove about 3.8 TWh from net exports.
The neighbours are cold on the same days
The obvious objection is that the neighbours are cold on the same days, so the flows reflect their weather as much as France’s. Holding their temperatures and the French and German wind and solar forecasts fixed gives a larger export response, not a smaller one. The reason is that the neighbours’ own cold pulls French power across the border on the same days, which partly hides the loss in the raw figures. With those controls in place, French demand rises 1.48 GW per degree of French cold rather than 1.8 GW, nuclear output no longer moves with the French thermometer, and 1.29 GW of that 1.48 GW is met by lower exports. The 0.43 GW of nuclear uplift per degree in the raw figures therefore goes with the neighbours’ pull on French supply rather than with French cold itself. The 1.04 GW is the figure for a winter in which the neighbours are cold at the same time, as they usually are; the 1.29 GW is the French temperature effect alone, and it falls almost entirely on the borders. The split between French and neighbouring cold is approximate, because the two move together.
Each border loses between 0.16 and 0.28 GW per degree
On that basis, Belgium loses 0.28 GW per degree of French cold, Germany 0.26 GW, Switzerland 0.21 GW, Italy and Britain 0.19 GW and Spain 0.16 GW, and the six borders sum to the 1.29 GW. Belgian and French effective temperatures move almost in step, so Belgium’s coldest days and the loss of French supply arrive together.
03. The fleet decides how much France can spare
The per-degree figures describe an average winter. Whether France keeps exporting through a particular cold spell depends on what the nuclear fleet is producing when the cold arrives, and the coldest fortnight of each winter shows what France could still spare. In December 2022, at 2.2 C with nuclear output at 40 GW, France imported 8.0 GW. In January 2025, at 3.0 C with nuclear output at 55 GW, it exported 7.2 GW. The coldest fortnight of 2025/26, straddling the turn of the year, was colder than both, at 1.3 C, and France exported 5.9 GW with 54 GW of nuclear output. Cold of much the same depth has produced a 15 GW range in French net exports. Even with nuclear output at 55 GW, the deepest cold of the eleven winters, 0.7 C in January 2017, pulled France into import, though only by 2.0 GW.
The seasonal balance tells the same story. It was −4 TWh in 2021/22 and close to zero in 2022/23, the two winters with nuclear output averaging 42 GW or less. It reached 44 TWh in 2025/26, a winter that was milder than average and had 49 GW of average nuclear output. France was a net importer on 58% of winter days in 2021/22 and on 1% in 2025/26.
04. Solar in a French cold spell
French solar output has more than quadrupled since 2015, so the natural question is whether it can fill any of that winter gap. Its share of French winter generation has risen from under 1% to 3.2%, but December and January output has been 26% to 37% of the summer before it in every year since 2015.
On the coldest tenth of winter days French solar averaged 1.0 GW against 1.3 GW on the mildest, and German solar, on the day-ahead forecast, 2.0 GW against 3.7 GW. The coldest days cluster in December and January, when days are shortest. Within those two months a cold day has more French solar than a mild one, so the lower output on cold days is a matter of the calendar, not of the cold. In the last two winters French solar covered 2.6% of demand on the coldest days. Doubling capacity would take that to about 5%, against a 23 GW gap in demand between the mildest and coldest tenth of winter days.
The loss sits in the hours solar cannot reach
Estimated hour by hour, the export loss peaks at 1.18 GW per degree at 08:00 and at 1.10 GW at 19:00. Both are hours in which winter solar output is close to zero. French demand itself responds least to cold in mid-afternoon, and the export loss follows it, with a trough of 0.93 GW at 15:00.
05. Price formation on a cold French day
On the coldest tenth of winter days the French day-ahead price averaged €113/MWh, against €61/MWh on the mildest. The neighbours moved with it. Belgium averaged €111/MWh against €66/MWh and Germany €101/MWh against €66/MWh, and the French premium over Germany flipped from −€5/MWh on mild days to 12 €/MWh on cold days. Gaps measured across all eleven winters depend on which winters the cold days happen to fall in, and without 2022/23 the French gap is €38/MWh rather than €52/MWh, so the per-degree response, estimated within each month of each winter, is the better guide.
Per degree of French cold, estimated within each month of each winter, the French baseload price rises €6.7/MWh, the Belgian €6.0/MWh, the German €5.3/MWh, the Dutch and Swiss €4.7/MWh, the northern Italian €3.2/MWh and the Spanish €2.8/MWh. In every winter since 2015 the French price rise per degree has been between 4% and 9% of that winter’s average price.
Holding the neighbours’ temperatures and the wind and solar forecasts fixed, as in the export estimate, the French response falls to €3.7/MWh, the Belgian to €2.0/MWh and the German to €1.4/MWh. On these estimates, roughly half of the French price response, a third of the Belgian and a quarter of the German is French cold on its own, and the rest comes with the neighbours’ own cold and the low wind that arrive on the same days.
Within the day, the French price response peaks at €8.0/MWh per degree at 08:00 and €8.4/MWh at 18:00. The Belgian and German curves follow the same shape. The night hours respond least, and midday responds less than either peak.
Capture rates rise on cold days; revenue depends on geography and on what has been sold
That shape has a consequence for solar. The capture rate is the average price solar receives divided by the average price for all hours. It rises in all seven zones on the coldest tenth of winter days compared with the mildest, and reaches parity or above everywhere except Spain. France moves from €0.92 to €1.03, Belgium from €0.93 to €1.03, Germany from €0.96 to €1.05, the Netherlands from €0.91 to €1.04, Switzerland and northern Italy from €0.98 to €1.03, and Spain from €0.82 to €0.97. With little solar on a cold day there is no midday surplus to push the price down, and the first solar hours fall just after the morning peak, when prices are still high, so the price solar receives rises faster than the average and ends up above it. The French solar capture price doubles, from €58 to €118, and the Dutch almost doubles, from €73 to €142.
The price data cover fewer winters than the flow data, and on their cold days solar output is 28% lower than on their mild days in France, 42% lower in Belgium and 52% lower in Germany, a slightly larger drop than in the eleven-winter comparison. Taking average capture price multiplied by average output, French solar earned 47% more per day on the coldest days than on the mildest, because the price gain outran the output loss. Spanish solar earned 13% more and Belgian solar 8% more. German solar earned 15% less, even with baseload prices more than 50% higher, because the output loss was larger than the price gain. Whether a portfolio gains or loses depends as much on how much winter output it has already sold, and in what hourly profile, as on where the plant sits. A producer who has sold a fixed winter volume forward is short that output on exactly the days when buying it back costs most, and the buyer of a pay-as-produced contract holds the opposite position. On these data a cold spell is not a capture-rate problem for winter solar but a volume one.
The storage spread moves from the solar cycle to the overnight cycle
A battery that charges on cheap midday solar and discharges into the evening trades the midday-to-evening spread. That spread narrows on cold days, from €27/MWh to €20/MWh in France and from €34/MWh to €17/MWh in Germany, because the midday price rises with everything else once there is no solar to push it down. The overnight-to-morning spread moves the other way, from €30/MWh to 43 €/MWh in France and from €28/MWh to €41/MWh in Germany between mild and cold days, because the night hours respond least and the morning peak responds far more. A cold spell therefore moves the day-ahead spread a battery can trade in winter from the solar cycle to the overnight cycle rather than removing it, and a battery able to cycle twice a day can trade both.
06. Conclusion
Eleven winters of data make French winter cold a measurable quantity for the markets around it. Each degree takes about a gigawatt off French exports, the six neighbours share that loss, and the French price response has stayed between 4% and 9% of the winter price level in every winter since 2015, including the crisis winters. A model of Belgian or German winter prices that carries local temperature but not French temperature leaves out roughly a quarter to a third of the price response to a French cold day.
For solar, winter output is set by the calendar rather than by the cold, and cold-day prices rise, so the exposure sits in how winter output has been sold rather than in the capture rate. For storage, a cold spell moves the earning window from the midday-to-evening cycle to the overnight-to-morning cycle.
Two forces pull in opposite directions over the coming winters. A fuller French fleet leaves more to export through a cold fortnight, as the last two winters show. Against that, the French demand response per degree is no lower than it was eleven winters ago, at 1.9 GW in 2025/26 against 1.7 GW in 2015/16. Solar growth does little for the peaks in which the loss and the price response are largest. The balance between fleet availability and demand decides whether the next cold spell looks like the turn of 2025/26, with France still exporting 5.9 GW through its coldest fortnight, or like December 2022, with France importing 8.0 GW.
How WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook can help
WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook (EMO) is designed to analyse these market dynamics. The underlying PRIMES model has supported European Commission energy-policy analysis for more than two decades and simulates all major European electricity markets simultaneously through to 2050. Cross-border flows are derived using a replication of the EUPHEMIA algorithm used in Europe’s single day-ahead coupling. Model outputs include hourly wholesale prices, capture rates, negative-price frequency and depth, curtailment exposure, interconnector utilisation and BESS profitability projections at both country and asset level. These outputs provide the quantitative basis for winter risk assessment, PPA and CfD bid analysis and long-term storage revenue modelling.

title: CGN connects first unit of world's highest-altitude CSP plant in Tibet - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Located at an altitude of 4,300 meters, the facility combines PV-powered molten salt heating, thermal energy storage and battery storage.
Vincent Shaw
09 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
The facility is part of a 150 MW demonstration project in Gar County that combines 100 MW of solar PV capacity with 50 MW of thermal power generation.
Chinese state-owned energy company
China General Nuclear Power Corp.
(CGN) connected the first 25 MW generating unit of its 50 MW concentrated solar power (CSP) plant in Tibet’s Ali Prefecture to the regional grid on Nov. 6. The company said the facility, located at an average elevation of 4,300 meters above sea level, is the world’s highest-altitude operational grid-connected CSP plant.
The facility is part of a 150 MW demonstration project in Gar County that combines 100 MW of solar PV capacity with 50 MW of CSP power generation. Total investment stands at approximately CNY 2.4 billion ($330 million). According to CGN, it is the first CSP project in Tibet to achieve grid connection.
The CSP installation consists of two 25 MW steam turbine units. The first was synchronized with the grid on Nov. 6, while the second is scheduled to come online by the end of 2026, bringing the facility to its full rated capacity.
Unlike conventional CSP plants, which use concentrated sunlight to generate heat, the Ali facility uses surplus PV electricity to power a molten salt electric heater with a peak rating of 205 MW. The system converts electricity into thermal energy for storage and subsequent power generation.
CGN said the project is the first CSP facility to integrate PV-powered electric heating, molten salt thermal storage and asynchronous battery storage. The company also claims that the 205 MW electric heater is the largest deployed in a CSP application worldwide. Neither claim, however, has been independently verified.
The plant incorporates a molten salt thermal storage system designed to provide 14 hours of storage, alongside a lithium-ion battery system for rapid frequency response. During the day, PV electricity generated independently of the grid powers the electric heater. Stored thermal energy is then used to drive the steam turbines at night or during periods of peak electricity demand.
The facility also operates as a combined heat and power plant, supplying district heating to Shiquanhe, the administrative center of Ali Prefecture, during the winter months.
CGN said the plant can switch between grid-connected and islanded operation, allowing it to supply electricity independently during grid disturbances. The capability is particularly relevant to Ali, a remote border region that has historically relied on diesel backup generation and electricity transmitted over long distances.
The company has also installed its proprietary distributed control system, which it said has been adapted to operate under the low atmospheric pressure and high ultraviolet radiation levels associated with the site’s elevation.
The project forms part of China’s efforts to expand CSP deployment. In late 2025, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and the National Energy Administration (NEA) jointly issued a policy directive targeting 15 GW of installed CSP capacity by 2030.
CGN also operates a 50 MW parabolic trough CSP plant in Delingha, Qinghai province. The facility recorded 2,824 equivalent full-load operating hours in 2024, the highest figure reported for a CSP plant in China that year.
The grid connection of the first unit marks an initial milestone for the high-altitude facility. However, the performance of its integrated PV-powered heating, thermal storage and cogeneration systems has yet to be demonstrated under sustained operating conditions, particularly during winter.

title: Dutch residential battery market surges ahead of net metering phaseout - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
With the abolition of net metering just weeks away, households are increasingly turning to battery storage to protect the value of their solar energy. New figures from Sunergy Research reveal explosive growth across all battery categories, with plug-in batteries emerging as the market’s biggest breakthrough.
Emiliano Bellini
09 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Residential
Sales of residential battery storage systems in the Netherlands have more than doubled over the past nine months ahead of the phaseout of the country’s net-metering scheme for residential PV at the end of this year, according to Sunergy Research, a Dutch energy supplier specializing in services for residential solar owners.
“Net metering will end on Jan. 1, and the market will change drastically for consumers,” Sunergy Research CEO Rolf Heynen told
ESS news
. “For many years, solar panels were easy to sell thanks to net metering and a very clear business case, with electricity prices stable at €0.21/kWh. Now, electricity prices have skyrocketed, and dynamic tariffs have made the business case more complex, alongside public discussions about the balancing market, variable grid tariffs starting in 2029, and home batteries.”
“With compensation for electricity exports expected to fall sharply, maximizing self-consumption is becoming increasingly important,” Heynen said. “Today, the average Dutch household consumes just 30% of the solar electricity it generates, exporting the remaining 70% to the grid. A home battery can dramatically reverse that balance, potentially increasing self-consumption to around 70%.”
Sunergy Research also reported that installations of small home batteries with capacities of up to 5 kWh were more than four times higher in September than in January, while installations of larger systems, ranging from 5 kWh to 15 kWh, nearly tripled over the same period.
The company’s data also show that installations of plug-in batteries, a relatively new segment of the Dutch energy storage market, have more than doubled in nine months, making them the largest category in the residential battery market.
Heynen said the rapid growth of plug-in batteries indicates that the market is expanding beyond early adopters.
“What makes this development particularly significant is the breadth of demand,” he said. “Smaller, accessible batteries are opening the market to ordinary households, while larger, permanently installed systems appeal to consumers who have already invested heavily in electrification. The barriers to battery ownership are falling rapidly.”
Sunergy has also launched its Home Batteries Selection Guide, a free, 33-page publication aimed at helping residential solar owners assess battery storage options.
The guide identifies two main market segments: plug-and-play batteries for smaller PV installations and permanently installed systems for households with higher electricity demand.
Plug-and-play batteries are particularly suitable for homes with around six solar panels and no heat pump or electric vehicle charger, according to the guide. These systems typically offer around 5 kWh of storage capacity, with prices starting at approximately €1,000 ($1,118.9).
Larger households may benefit from permanently installed batteries with capacities ranging from 5 kWh to 20 kWh, starting at approximately €4,000. The guide recommends capacities of 5 kWh to 10 kWh for typical single-phase installations and 10 kWh to 20 kWh for three-phase systems, depending on household requirements.
Battery sizing should take into account household electricity consumption, solar generation patterns, inverter capacity, backup power requirements and potential electricity trading, the report says. Sunergy also warns that oversized batteries are often recommended to consumers, potentially undermining investment returns.
Research estimates cited in the guide suggest payback periods of two to 15 years, with annual savings of approximately €200 to €1,000 for permanently installed systems. The guide also highlights the role of energy management systems (EMS) in coordinating solar generation, battery charging and household consumption.
The publication identifies additional revenue opportunities from electricity trading, grid balancing and congestion management. Sunergy also recommends professional installation, adequate ventilation and careful consideration of battery compatibility, expandability and insurance requirements.
The guide concludes that appropriately sized batteries combined with intelligent energy management could improve the economics of residential solar as the Netherlands phases out net metering.

title: Ecoprogetti presents automated line for recycling end-of-life PV modules - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The industrial line features a patented technology for the high-efficiency separation of glass from the solar panel, designed to maximise silicon recovery.
Patrick Jowett
09 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Italian PV equipment manufacturer Ecoprogetti has delivered a fully-automated, industrial line for the recycling of end-of-life solar modules to Haiki+ Group, an Italian circular economy and environmental services company.
It has been operational since early 2025 in Sale, northwestern Italy, at a recycling and waste treatment plant. It is capable of processing up to 120 solar panels each hour, equivalent to approximately 4 tonnes an hour. This capacity corresponds to a nominal potential of around 700,000 tonnes annually if in continuous operation. It currently operates with an uptime of 94%, which Ecoprogetti says is one of the highest in the industry.
Ecoprogetti told
pv magazine
its line combines a patented air-based glass removal system with an electromechanical recycling process that separates module components through dedicated stages in order to minimise cross-contamination and preserve the quality of the recovered materials.
“The process includes automatic panel recognition, junction box and frame removal, module flipping, glass removal, material shredding, separation and collection,” the company explained.
Recovery results shared with
pv magazine
show conversion rates of 100% for aluminium and junction boxes, 99% for copper, glass and plastic and 95% for silicon at a purity of 100% for aluminium and junction boxes, 99% for glass, 98% for copper and silicon and 88% for plastic.
The line is capable of recycling mono and polycrystalline, double glass and bifacial solar panels, as well as the glass and backsheet from panels. It can also process modules with broken or cracked glass, missing parts, hail or fire damage, corrosion or delamination, as well as old or worn panels.
Ecoprogetti added that it is the only solution on the market capable of processing both conventional and double-glass PV modules using the same equipment, without requiring additional machinery or extra investment.
The company’s Managing Director Marco Manfron said the line demonstrates that photovoltaic recycling can be approached according to industrial principles of high capacity, automation, operational continuity and quality of the output material.
“The technology installed in Sale represents a tangible leap forward compared to previous solutions, because it makes it possible to process large volumes while reducing machine downtime and improving the quality of the recovered fractions,” Manfron said.
Ecoprogetti’s CEO Laura Sartore
recently spoke to
pv magazine
about the evolution of the global solar supply chain. The company
upgraded an existing PV module manufacturing line
in South Africa in August. It has also been expanding operations in the Middle East, most recently with
Iraq’s first solar module production line
and previously with
production lines in Oman

title: Key takeaways from RE-Source 2026 in Amsterdam - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Europe’s corporate renewable energy buyers and sellers have shifted their focus from price to risk allocation as negative prices erode solar-only contracts and battery-backed hybrid deals move to the center of the market, according to discussions last week at RE-Source 2026 in Amsterdam.
Brian Publicover
09 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
The Beurs van Berlage, a former commodities exchange on the avenue between Amsterdam’s central train station and main square, was built more than a century ago so the city’s merchants had somewhere to agree on prices. But the 1,400 or so people who filled the cavernous red-brick hall on Nov. 4 and 5 came to negotiate deals for renewable electricity, a commodity whose price falls below zero for a growing number of hours each year.
The 10th edition of RE-Source, organized by SolarPower Europe and WindEurope through their joint RE-Source Platform, brought more than 350 corporate energy buyers to some 400 prescheduled meetings with suppliers. But the deal flow they were chasing is thinning: the RE-Source Platform said corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs) have secured 5.9 GW of renewable capacity in Europe so far in 2026, down 9.7% on the same period last year.
Francesco Rossetto, a policy officer at the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER), presented the agency’s annual PPA assessment and described “a market that is cooling down a little bit.” He said activity peaked in 2024 and has held near 2025 levels since. Meanwhile, the share of hours with very low power prices has climbed from 1% to 2% in 2021 to about 10%.
Solar is taking the brunt. Max Plumptre, director of European transactions at Seattle-based PPA marketplace LevelTen Energy, said capture rates – the share of the average market price a solar plant actually earns – have roughly halved in Spain and Germany since 2022.
Swiss market intelligence firm Pexapark said
standalone solar PPA volumes have fallen 43%
this year, and that Italy has overtaken Spain as their largest market, largely because Spanish activity has collapsed. Almost one-quarter of Spanish solar output has been generated during negative-price hours, according to the research firm.
Itamar Orlandi, director of commercial strategy at Pexapark, said solar prices “started to go into free fall about three years ago and that free fall still hasn’t stopped.”
Buyers are responding by asking for more than one technology. Plumptre said nearly every request for proposals on LevelTen’s platform this year has included a hybrid product “in some sort of fashion,” and about 25% of offers in its
latest quarterly report
were hybrid.
Pexapark said PPAs combining several technologies have almost doubled, while Rossetto said capture rates for solar paired with storage are diverging from those for solar alone.
Hybrid hedging
For insulation maker Rockwool, the shift is practical. Kenneth Dupont, energy category director for the Danish company, said it moved away from single-technology PPAs because they do not fit factories that run around the clock. He advised buyers to contract about half of their demand through PPAs and cover the rest with renewable energy certificates.
Spain shows why storage is now central. Silvia Escudero, head of upstream and downstream origination Iberia at
Statkraft
, noted that the country has logged about
920 hours of zero or negative prices
so far this year. With grid connections scarce, she said, putting batteries behind existing solar connections is by far the fastest route to market. However, she warned buyers that a battery’s flexibility carries an opportunity cost, because grid services can be worth more than delivering power to a customer. “A hybrid PPA is not a solar PPA with a battery, it’s much more complex than that,” said Escudero.
That complexity is where traders see their opening. Kristina Herold Høgh, director of RETO origination and contract management at Centrica Energy, said
new contract structures for batteries
are emerging. Profile swaps, which convert a renewable plant’s variable output into a delivery shape that suits the buyer, are becoming more standard.
Herold Høgh cast traders as “problem solvers” that bring the risk capital and credit these deals require. One gap remains in recognizing stored power: one panelist said only one or two European countries issue guarantees of origin, the certificates that prove renewable sourcing, for stored electricity.
Domenico Franceschino, head of origination for West and East Europe at Axpo Solutions, explained how a battery’s location shapes its value, using indicative figures for
tolling agreements
in France, under which an offtaker pays a fixed fee for control of the battery. For seven- to 10-year contracts starting in 2029, he put annual fees at about €80,000 ($89,500)/MW for a standalone battery, €65,000/MW for a co-located unit that can also charge from the grid and €45,000/MW for one that charges only from on-site solar.
The standalone premium comes at a price: cabling and grid fees of about €50,000/MW per year, against about €35,000/MW per year for the battery itself. It “costs more to pay the grid fees than to actually buy the batteries,” said Franceschino.
Pexapark’s Orlandi said “the most valuable asset has now become the grid connection point.” Utilities and traders still take almost all battery offtake, he said, although a handful of sophisticated German corporates have recently signed hybrid contracts.
The obstacle lies in where the money is. Half to two-thirds of a battery’s value comes from ancillary services, the balancing products that grid operators buy, Orlandi said, and most corporates have neither the interest nor the capability to trade them.
Risk allocation
Mathieu Ville, chief revenue officer at battery investor Tavion, questioned why sellers should accept zero-price floors. “Why would you floor me at zero? And if you do, why wouldn’t I cap you at 80?” he said. He was equally skeptical of
state-backed PPA guarantee schemes
. He said they look great “on paper” but have produced only three or four deals in five or six years, which he put down to their pricing and complexity.
Italy is about to test the model again. Francesca Morra, a partner at Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer in Milan, said the country’s energy regulator gave a positive opinion in October on rules for a new organized PPA market. The rules include a guarantee of last resort from GSE, the state-owned energy services company, which she said will be limited and fee-based to comply with EU state aid rules. Her advice was to settle key terms at the term-sheet stage. “The PPA is not an easy animal,” Morra said. “We need lawyers.”
But Ricardo Estévez Solís, senior originator at Centrica Energy, dismissed the idea that the market has stalled. He said that Spanish buyers facing forward prices above €100/MWh for next year are active alongside sellers, and that contracting is shifting from single assets to portfolios.
For large buyers, the question is now certainty. Cédric Saussez, head of green power structuring and origination for Northwestern Europe at
, said customers who once asked how green and how cheap a project was now ask how certain it is.
Rønnaug Sægrov Mysterud, head of energy sourcing at Norsk Hydro, said electricity makes up 30% to 40% of the cost of primary aluminum, leaving the company “extremely price sensitive.” Hydro needs sufficient power at competitive prices and certainty on indirect carbon cost compensation before it signs more PPAs, she said, adding that “the grid cost should not kill the rest.”
Carbon accounting
Carbon accounting rules are adding to the uncertainty. Daniela Fitzpatrick, senior manager energy procurement for Amazon Web Services, said up to 35% of renewable energy contracts globally could be stranded unless revisions to the GHG Protocol, the most widely used corporate carbon accounting standard, protect existing deals. “There’s a real concern that the draft GHG Protocol revisions are
cooling down the PPA market
,” said Fitzpatrick.
The rules may tighten further. Merve Güngör, policy and network manager for the RECS Energy Certificate Association, said the protocol’s standards board is weighing an age limit on eligible assets. “It’s not decided yet. I think 10 or 15 years are on the table,” said Güngör. A final standard is due at the end of 2028.
Javier de la Fuente Iglesias, head of flexibility and physical services at Statkraft, told
pv magazine
that industrial buyers see the value of battery arbitrage but do not yet know how to bring it into their procurement processes.
The premium buyers pay for firmer supply is already visible in pricing. LevelTen data for the second quarter put
hybrid solar-plus-storage PPAs
at a 24% premium to solar-only contracts.

title: Massive solar project at Texas coal plant secures $1.8 billion green loan - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The 1.2 GW Big Rooter Power solar project owned and funded by Panamint Capital will connect with the 342 MW Twin Oaks coal plant, creating a hybrid power station.
Anne Fischer
09 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
United States
Utility-scale
Construction on the first phase of the 1.2 GW Big Rooter Power solar project got underway in July at Panamint Capital’s Twin Oaks power station in Robertson County, Texas. The project will be the largest solar project constructed at an existing coal mining site and the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America, according to Panamint.
The energy infrastructure investor recently closed on the first phase of a $1.8 billion green loan to finance construction. Proceeds from the $769 million first phase will fund ongoing construction of the 491 MW Big Rooter West portion of the project. The over $1 billion second phase of the Green Loan will finance construction of Big Rooter East, the project’s 658 MW second stage.
Located halfway between Dallas and Houston, Big Rooter Power is being built on 1,804 hectares of reclaimed coal mine land and operating interconnection infrastructure at Panamint’s 349 MW coal-fired Twin Oaks Complex. The campus combines power generation, surface mining, energy storage, data center capacity, and high voltage transmission.
“When Big Rooter is complete, the Twin Oaks complex will have 1.5 GW of operating thermal and renewable power, in addition to over 20 miles of new 345 kV transmission, 1.6 GWh of battery energy storage and 790 MW of Batch Zero data center capacity under development across our 10,000-acre site,” said Apolka Totth, Panamint’s chief executive officer.
Panamint reports it signed a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) with an unnamed corporation. “Our long-term power purchase agreement with one of country’s largest companies will ensure the electricity we generate at Big Rooter will power job creation in the American economy into the 2050s,” said Bill Stanton, managing director of development at Panamint.
Construction of both Big Rooter West and Big Rooter East is expected to create over 800 jobs, Panamint reports.
Big Rooter East is the 658 MW second phase of the project and is slated to begin construction in December 2026 and enter commercial operation in August 2029. Financing on that phase is expected to close in Q1 2027.
Panamint reports it is committed to selecting domestic renewable energy companies. Solv Energy will provide EPC services for the project, including solar, substation and transmission infrastructure. First Solar will provide approximately 2 million solar panels manufactured in Ohio, Louisiana and Alabama. California-based Nextpower will deploy its NX Horizon solar tracker systems with Hail Pro-75 and NX Navigator software. In addition, the projects reportedly will use over 34,000 tons of domestically manufactured steel.
Nevada-based Panamint Capital is a woman-led energy investment company founded in 2019 thathad 718 MW of energy generating capacity in operation in 2025.
The company’s sustainability report points to the Twin Oaks station as an example of its redevelopment efforts that focus on preparing existing sites for utility-scale solar, storage and thermal projects. These projects, the report says, “extend the productive use of existing infrastructure through clean energy investments that support local employment and drive long-term economic value in the communities where we operate.”

title: Panasonic releases new residential air-to-air heat pumps - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The reversible air-to-air heat pumps use R32 refrigerant and offer rated heating capacities ranging from 2.5 kW to 10.6 kW. Commercial availability in Japan is scheduled for January 2027.
Emiliano Bellini
09 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The system’s outdoor unit
Japanese electronics manufacturer
Panasonic
has announced its new Eolia X Series of residential split air-to-air heat pumps, designed to provide space heating and cooling in Japanese homes.
Initially conceived for the Japanese market, new range comprises several capacity classes, with rated cooling outputs from 2.2 kW to 9.0 kW and rated heating outputs from 2.5 kW to 10.6 kW. Maximum heating capacity reaches 11.8 kW, depending on the model.
The systems use R32 (difluoromethane) refrigerant, with a global warming potential (GWP) of 675 and refrigerant charges ranging from 0.70 kg to 1.68 kg across the product lineup.
According to Panasonic’s published specifications, the units achieve annual performance factors (APF) of between 5.5 and 7.1 under the Japanese JIS C 9612:2013 standard. These values are not directly comparable with the seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) figures commonly used for European heat pumps. However, they indicate relatively high seasonal efficiency, broadly consistent with modern high-efficiency inverter air-to-air heat pumps, which can achieve SCOP values of around 4 to 5.5 under European average-climate test conditions.
The company said the new generation features improvements to compressor operation during heating. Panasonic claims that the minimum heating output has been reduced by approximately 25% compared with a previous model, enabling more precise heating operation under low-load conditions.
The heat pumps comprise wall-mounted indoor units connected to outdoor units through refrigerant piping. Depending on the capacity class, the outdoor units measure 630 mm to 796 mm in height, 799 mm to 849 mm in width, and 299 mm to 319 mm in depth.
Panasonic also lists heating capacities at an outdoor temperature of 2 C ranging from 4.5 kW to 9.4 kW, depending on the model. The outdoor units incorporate corrosion-resistant components and coated electronic circuit boards.
Sales for the new Eolia X Series in Japan are expected to begin in late January 2027, the company said.

title: Salt-based thermal storage supports renewable steam in Spain - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A renewable steam project at Bayer’s pharmaceutical plant in Spain combines salt-based thermal storage with a 15 MW renewable power purchase agreement (PPA) and 2.5 MW of on-site solar, in an effort to replace fossil fuels used for industrial heat.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
09 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
German pharmaceutical company Bayer has begun testing a system that uses renewable electricity to produce steam at its plant in La Felguera, Langreo, in Spain’s Asturias region. The facility manufactures acetylsalicylic acid, the active ingredient in Aspirin. The project is designed to replace fossil fuels in steam generation.
Developed by Iberdrola España, the system combines a 15 MW renewable power purchase agreement, a 2.5 MW self-consumption solar installation and thermal energy storage using salt.
The storage system is intended to partially decouple electricity generation from the industrial process’s heat demand, helping maintain a continuous supply of steam. The project aims to meet 100% of the steam requirements for acetylsalicylic acid production with renewable electricity.
Testing began with the supply of renewable steam to the plant. The trial phase is expected to conclude by the end of the year, when the system is scheduled to reach continuous operation.
The project is structured around a long-term heat purchase agreement (HPA) and uses technology from Spanish engineering company Inerco to integrate the thermal storage system.
Iberdrola said the project represents an investment of more than €18 million. More than 60 professionals participated in the initial implementation phase.
The project has received public support from Spain’s Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving (IDAE) and Institute for Just Transition, as well as the regional government of Asturias and Langreo City Council. It has also received support from the European Union’s Innovation Fund.

content:
Technology & Products
German solar manufacturer Solarwatt has added a new glass-glass module to its Construct series for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV). The module features bifacial TOPCon cells, delivers up to 227 W/m² and has received general building approval in Germany.
Jochen Siemer
09 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Solarwatt says its modules are particularly suitable for parking canopies.
German solar manufacturer Solarwatt has expanded its Construct series of building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) modules with the launch of the Panel vision M 5.0 construct. The Dresden-based company said the module has received general building authority approval, the so called allgemeine bauaufsichtliche Zulassung, or abZ, from the German Institute for Construction Technology (DIBt), joining several other products in its BIPV portfolio that have held the certification since 2020.
The approval simplifies regulatory procedures for applications that typically face more stringent building requirements, including overhead glazing and facade installations. Solarwatt said the new module is suitable for carports, parking canopies, facades and certain green roof applications.
“With our Construct modules, we significantly reduce the bureaucratic burden on contractors, as the abZ ensures that the primary regulatory hurdles have already been cleared,” said Solarwatt product manager Norbert Betzl. The certification provides architects, planners and installers with greater certainty when designing and implementing BIPV projects.
Solarwatt has not disclosed full technical specifications for the Panel vision M 5.0 construct. However, the company said the module uses bifacial tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) half-cut cells and delivers up to 227 W/m², representing an increase of more than 20% over the previous generation.
The new module features 3.2 mm-thick glass panes, compared with 2 mm glass in the Panel vision GM 3.0 construct. Solarwatt said the thicker glass, combined with a reinforced frame, improves resistance to high snow and wind loads, making the module suitable for applications in alpine regions and on high-rise facades. The company also claims high resistance to hail impacts.
Solarwatt said it has supplied modules with abZ certification for European projects totaling 33 MW since 2020.
The Panel vision M 5.0 construct is available to order through the Solarwatt Pro portal for installation partners. Like the company’s other glass-glass modules, it comes with a 30-year product warranty and a performance guarantee of at least 90% of its original rated output after 30 years.

title: Tongwei unveils 26.03%-efficient TOPCon solar cell with high sheet resistance - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
The solar cell was fabricated using a low-cost photoresist-based etching process to create a selective emitter with a sheet resistance of up to 1,600 Ω/sq in non-contacted regions, reducing recombination losses while maintaining effective electrical contacts. The TOPCon device achieved a certified power conversion efficiency of 26.03% and an open-circuit voltage of 746.5 mV.
Emiliano Bellini
09 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
A research group led by Chinese polysilicon and solar module manufacturer
has developed a tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) solar cell featuring an emitter with higher sheet resistance in a bid to reduce recombination losses, improve surface passivation and increase power conversion efficiency.
“In our work, a non-destructive photoresist-based etching process was used to form a selective emitter structure for TOPCon solar cells,” corresponding author Xiajie Meng told
pv magazine
. “The structure features a sheet resistance as high as 1,600 Ω/sq – to the best of our knowledge, the highest reported for TOPCon to date. This successful implementation confirms that TOPCon remains highly competitive for commercial applications.”
The researchers explained that conventional TOPCon cells face a trade-off between low contact resistance and reduced carrier recombination in the boron-doped emitter. The proposed architecture addresses this limitation by combining heavily boron-doped regions beneath the metal contacts with lightly doped regions between the contacts.
The scientists used a range of characterization techniques to investigate the structural, electrical and passivation properties of the proposed cell architecture, with the aim of identifying optimal design conditions that balance surface passivation, lateral charge transport and metal shading losses.
They used scanning electron microscopy and 3D laser microscopy to examine etching depth and surface morphology, while four-point probe measurements determined the sheet resistance of the lightly and heavily boron-doped emitter regions. They also evaluated contact resistivity using the transmission line method and characterized doping profiles and junction depths through electrochemical capacitance-voltage measurements.
The team assessed minority carrier lifetime and emitter recombination using quasi-steady-state photoconductance measurements. Electron-beam-induced current measurements provided qualitative evidence of junction continuity, while photoluminescence imaging was used to evaluate passivation quality under different illumination levels.
Current-voltage measurements were used to determine key cell parameters, including open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, fill factor, efficiency and series resistance. The researchers also conducted Quokka3 simulations to compare conventional uniform emitters, selective emitters and locally boron-doped finger structures using experimentally derived parameters.
The analysis showed that that high-temperature oxidation reduced surface boron concentrations while increasing junction depth, helping suppress recombination and maintain effective metal contacts.
The scientists also found that increasing the sheet resistance of non-contacted emitter regions from 800 Ω/sq to 2,000 Ω/sq significantly improved minority carrier lifetime and surface passivation, although improvements became marginal beyond 1,600 Ω/sq, while doping uniformity deteriorated, making this value preferable for cell fabrication.
The team then compared three architectures: a conventional uniform emitter, a boron-doped selective emitter and a locally boron-doped finger structure. The selective emitter combined a sheet resistance of 450 Ω/sq beneath the metal contacts with 1,600 Ω/sq in non-contacted regions.
This configuration increased average cell efficiency from 25.82% to 25.98%, representing an absolute improvement of 0.16 percentage points.
Open-circuit voltage increased from 742.6 mV to 745.5 mV, while fill factor improved from 83.54% to 83.76%.
The optimized selective emitter cell also achieved a certified efficiency of 26.03%, with an open-circuit voltage of 746.5 mV, with the results being confirmed by Germany’s
Solar Energy Research Hamelin
(ISFH). The locally boron-doped finger structure also improved passivation but suffered greater fill factor losses, limiting its efficiency advantage. Its fill factor reached 83.34%, compared with 83.76% for the selective emitter, partly reflecting increased series resistance and potentially additional recombination.
The Quokka3 simulations examined the effects of contact width, grid pitch, finger width and wafer resistivity on cell performance and indicated that a contacted-region width of approximately 200 µm offered the highest efficiency among the investigated configurations. Reducing metal finger widths to 7 µm to 9 µm could enable a denser grid with a pitch of around 500 µm to 550 µm, potentially improving efficiency further, the scientists said.
“For the locally boron-doped finger architecture, simulations indicate that using silicon wafers with higher bulk resistivity alongside more closely spaced front contacts could offer opportunities for further performance improvements, although experimental validation is still required,” Meng stated. “More broadly, the study demonstrates the potential of photoresist-based selective etching to produce emitters with exceptionally high sheet resistance in non-contacted areas without compromising electrical contact quality.”
The new cell concept was described in “
High-efficiency TOPCon solar cells featuring super-high sheet resistance emitters via low-cost photoresist etching
,” which was recently published in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells
. The research team included scientists from the School of Optoelectronic Science and Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) and Chinese industrial equipment company Jiangsu Inspiray Equipment Co., Ltd.
“The findings could help manufacturers refine emitter doping profiles and contact designs, paving the way for further efficiency gains and potential industrial adoption of the technology,” Meng concluded.

title: Jakson targets 3 GW integrated manufacturing capacity by 2028, eyes potential 10 GW ingot-wafer expansion - pv magazine Global
content:
Indian PV manufacturer
plans to operationalise an initial 3 GW of integrated ingot, wafer and solar cell manufacturing capacity in India by the end of 2028, Ivan Saha, Managing Director of Jaskson Engineers Limited, told
pv magazine
. Saha said the company may subsequently expand its ingot and wafer manufacturing capacity to up to 10 GW and its solar cell capacity to up to 5 GW, depending on market conditions.
The company intends to develop its ingot-wafer and cell manufacturing projects simultaneously, although the cell facility could become operational ahead of the ingot-wafer plant.
Saha said the company’s strategy centres on vertical integration, with the company seeking to control manufacturing quality across the ingot, wafer and cell stages rather than relying entirely on external wafer suppliers.
“By controlling wafer quality and cell quality, we can have greater confidence in the final product,” Saha said.
He explained that silicon wafer characteristics, including oxygen content, dislocation levels and resistivity, can influence downstream cell performance. Producing wafers in-house would allow Jakson to control these parameters and optimise the manufacturing process.
Jakson currently has approximately 1.2 GW of solar module manufacturing capacity. Saha said the company’s current investment focus is on backward integration rather than substantial additional investments in standalone module manufacturing, which he described as a relatively lower-value segment with higher operating costs.
Instead, JAKSON plans to focus on backward integration through ingot, wafer and cell manufacturing. The company may sell cell production to the market or explore arrangements to convert cells into modules, depending on market requirements.
Saha expects substantial consolidation in India’s solar manufacturing industry over the next four years as manufacturers face increasing pressure to compete on technology, product quality and production costs. “I believe a significant amount of consolidation will happen,” he said.
He expects considerable market restructuring as the industry shifts its focus from announced manufacturing capacity to commercially viable production.
Jakson plans to adopt TOPCon 3.0 technology at its proposed 3 GW solar cell manufacturing facility. The technology incorporates additional process steps compared with conventional TOPCon cell manufacturing to improve conversion efficiency.
Saha said the company intends to adopt the technology directly rather than transition through successive technology generations.
“We expect to be among the early adopters of TOPCon 3.0 in India,” he said, noting that akson is targeting initial cell conversion efficiencies of 25.5% to 25.6%.
Saha highlighted the gap between India’s announced solar manufacturing capacity and actual market supply. He said commissioned and ALMM-listed capacity, together with capacity utilisation, provides a more realistic assessment of available production.
According to Saha’s assessment, India has approximately 17 GW of ALMM-compatible TOPCon cell manufacturing capacity. Based on publicly available financial results of select listed manufacturers, he estimated average capacity utilisation at around 60%. Applying this indicative utilisation rate to the estimated capacity would suggest annual production of approximately 10 GW.
However, not all this output is necessarily available to the open market, as some manufacturers use their cell production for captive module manufacturing.
Saha said the distinction between announced capacity and actual market supply creates opportunities for manufacturers with differentiated technology and integrated operations.
“Our focus is on technology and vertical integration, with an emphasis on high-quality, fully automated and high-efficiency manufacturing,” he said.

title: Latvia switches on 174 MW of solar - pv magazine Global
content:
A 174 MW solar power plant has reached commercial operations in Latvia.
Lithuanian green energy company Ignitis Renewables developed the Tume solar farm in the Tukums municipality.
The project is one of the largest in the Baltic states, according to a statement published by Ignitis Renewables. It spans 302 hectares, features over 282,000 solar panels and is expected to generate enough electricity to meet the demand of 85,000 households annually.
Ignitis Renewables adds it is its first solar project to use solar trackers that will follow the sun’s movement throughout the day, as well as its first to be primarily maintained by in-house specialists.
The company is currently developing a 107 MW/215 MWh Tume battery energy storage system (BESS). With construction underway, the BESS will be integrated with the solar farm upon completion.
Ignitis Renewables CEO Frank Oomen said the project strengthens local renewable electricity generation in Latvia, enhances regional energy security and supports the Baltic energy transition.
The Tume solar farm is Ignitis Renewables’ third in Latvia. It switched on the
94 MW Vārme PV project
in July 2025.
Latvia’s cumulative solar capacity
surpassed 1.5 GW
in August. The country has had a strong year for new solar deployment, installing more solar over the first half of the year than it has across any calendar year prior.
Solar was Latvia’s largest source of electricity generation in May, June
and July
this year, according to figures published by transmission system operator Augstsprieguma tīkls. Research by Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE found the country set an
EU record
for the share of solar within its domestic electricity generation in June.

title: Solar panel waste yields silica nanoparticles for battery anodes - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers funded by a South Korean solar panel recycling program have produced silica nanoparticles averaging 109 nanometers (nm) in diameter from sodium silicate derived from end-of-life solar cell powder. They found that blending the particles into graphite anodes raised battery capacity.
The team reacted silicon-containing cell powder from end-of-life panels with sodium hydroxide and water to make a sodium silicate solution. They then used that solution as the starting material in a modified Stöber process, a method that grows silica particles in an alkaline mix of ammonia and alcohol.
Earlier studies that made silica from solar panel-derived sodium silicate mostly used acid precipitation, which the researchers said tends to produce clumped particles. Their alkaline route yielded spherical particles with limited clumping, without surfactants or polymer additives.
Particles made from the solar waste averaged 109 nm, compared with 97 nm for particles made from commercial sodium silicate under the same conditions.
The researchers tested the material in laboratory coin half-cells, which pair the test anode with a lithium-metal counter electrode. An anode of 95% graphite and 5% silica by weight delivered 370.34 mAh/g after 100 cycles at 0.1 A/g, compared with 308.24 mAh/g for pure graphite. The blended anode’s first-cycle Coulombic efficiency, the share of charge recovered in the first cycle, was 86.17%, against 79.14% for graphite alone. At a higher current of 1.0 A/g, the blended anode kept 24.6% of its capacity, about double the 12.5% retained by graphite.
Elemental analysis found sodium at about 4% and aluminum at less than 1% of the atoms measured in the silica. The researchers attributed these to precursor residue and panel waste. They said the impurity levels in the finished electrode were too low to noticeably affect performance, while noting their measurement method is semi-quantitative.
The silica was tested as-is rather than converted to silicon, which can store far more lithium. The researchers said future work should focus on reducing the nanoparticles to silicon and testing them as silicon anode materials.
The study, “
Synthesis of Silica Nanoparticles from End-of-Life Solar Panels by a Modified Stöber Process for Lithium-Ion Battery Anodes
,” was recently published in the
International Journal of Electrochemical Science
. It was funded by the Korea Environment Industry & Technology Institute through a solar panel recycling research project of South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, and by a National Research Foundation of Korea grant funded by the Ministry of Science and ICT.
Similar routes from solar waste to battery materials have been explored elsewhere, including by
researchers in Australia
in 2023. In South Korea, Gyeongsang National University researchers developed a process in 2024 to
recover high-purity silicon powder from end-of-life panels
for upcycling into compounds such as silicon oxide. The country’s extended producer responsibility rules for PV modules, in force since 2023,
recycled 688 metric tons in their first year
, more than four times the target.

title: SolarEdge exits Australian market - pv magazine Global
content:
Israel-based inverter and battery manufacturer SolarEdge has advised that it is closing its local sales and operations in Australia and New Zealand. The company also announced it will terminate product certification renewals, active marketing promotions and incentive programs in the region.
In a notice to installers,
SolarEdge
says final purchase orders must be submitted by 20 November 2026, with final delivery no later than 18 December 2026.
The company, which now manufacturers inverters, optimisers, solar panels, batteries and EV chargers in the United States, said warranty and technical support will continue via its international call centre and online self-service portal.
The announcement comes after SolarEdge Chief Executive Officer Shuki Nir last week told investors the company was taking actions to “reduce costs, simplify operations, and support profitability.”
“We are making deliberate decisions to exit select underperforming geographic markets and redirect resources towards our core markets and higher growth opportunities,” he said during the company’s third-quarter results call.
“These are difficult but necessary decisions to build a more focused and competitive SolarEdge.”
Nir said the company will redirect resources toward “core regions” and higher-growth opportunities like its
platform and solid state transformers for data centres.
SolarEdge is the second big inverter manufacturer to rethink its position in the Australian market this year after SMA exited the residential and commercial sectors earlier in 2026.
The German-headquartered inverter and battery announced it would withdraw from the Australian residential and commercial markets, focusing instead on large-scale infrastructure, grid-forming technology and hybrid integration.
SMA Chief Executive Officer Jürgen Reinert said at the time that the decision reflected “a
considered view of where the energy transition is heading
and where SMA can make the most meaningful contribution.”

title: What solar installers should ask before handing back office to AI - pv magazine Global
content:
Take one ordinary job. A homeowner fills in a web form on a Sunday night. On Monday someone copies their details into the quoting tool. The quote goes out, gets revised twice because the customer wants a bigger battery, then a third time because the inverter they picked is on back order. When they finally say yes, the job gets typed again into the job management app. The network connection application wants the same details in a different format. The crew takes photos and serial numbers on site, and someone back at the office matches them up for the STC paperwork. Then the invoice goes into the accounting package, again by hand.
None of these steps is hard. But that one customer has now been typed in five or six times by three different people, and every one of those moments is a chance for a wrong serial number, a missed photo or the old quote going out instead of the new one.
That last one comes up more than you’d think. We’ve seen businesses where a salesperson kept amending prices and the office simply couldn’t tell which version was current. Nobody was being careless. The information just lived in too many places. Anyone who’s had to ring a customer and explain that the price they agreed to isn’t the price on the invoice knows how much that costs, and it isn’t only money.
So it’s no surprise installers are being pitched AI to fix it. Some of those pitches are worth a look. Plenty aren’t. Here’s how I’d tell the difference.
Start with the job, not the product
Before talking to any seller, walk one recent install from first enquiry to paid invoice and write down every time someone retyped, checked or chased something. Do it with the person who actually does the admin, not from memory.
That list is worth more than any demo. It shows you where the time really goes, and it gives you something concrete to hold a seller to. If they can’t point at your list and say “we’d take these three steps off you, and here’s how”, they’re selling a product, not solving your problem.
Most owners who do this find the same thing: they don’t have a software shortage. They have plenty of tools that don’t talk to each other. It’s common for a business to be paying for a dozen or more subscriptions and using a small slice of each one.
The questions to ask any seller before you sign
Does it work with what we already run? Your quoting tool, job app and accounting package are where your history lives, and your team knows them. A good partner builds on those. Be wary of anyone whose answer to every problem is “move everything onto our platform”.
Can you show it on one of our jobs? A demo on sample data always looks smooth. Ask them to take a real job, including the messy bits like the revised quote and the missing photo, and show you what happens.
What happens when it gets something wrong? AI makes mistakes. In this industry a wrong serial number or a missing compliance photo isn’t a small error, it’s a delayed claim. A sensible partner can tell you in a sentence how errors get caught before anything is lodged or sent to a customer. If the answer is “it doesn’t make mistakes”, walk away.
Where does our customer data go? You hold names, addresses, power bills, meter details and photos of people’s homes. Ask where that data is stored, who can see it and what the system is not allowed to touch. If keeping it locked down makes things a fraction slower, that’s a trade worth making.
Who do we call when it breaks? Not a portal, a person. Ideally one who understands that a Friday afternoon outage during a busy month is a genuine problem.
Why the best fix usually connects what you’ve got
The most useful improvement in an installer’s back office is usually not a new system. It’s getting the existing ones to pass information along on their own.
When the customer accepts a quote, the job should appear in the job app with the right details. When the crew uploads photos and serials, they should land against the right job and get checked for gaps before anyone goes near the claim. When the job is signed off, the invoice should draft itself from the accepted quote, not from whichever
version someone finds first.
That’s not glamorous. But it’s where the hours are, and the team doesn’t have to learn a whole new way of working to get them back.
It also matters who shapes it. When the office staff and crew help design how the tools join up, they treat the result as theirs. Hand people new software and say “good luck” and it quietly gets ignored. The point isn’t fewer people. It’s letting the people you have handle more jobs without drowning in admin, so growth doesn’t automatically mean hiring another office person.
A small first project for a quiet month
Pick one handover from your list, ideally the one that causes the most rework, and fix just that. For many installers it’s the jump from accepted quote to booked job, or the gathering of photos and serials for the claim.
Run it alongside the old way for a few weeks. Check it against what the team was doing by hand. If it saves time and nobody hates it, move to the next handover. If it doesn’t, you’ve lost very little and learned a lot about what you actually need.
Be wary of anyone who wants to automate the lot in one go. Change too much at once and one fix breaks seven other things.
Treat it like any other supplier
You wouldn’t buy panels or inverters without checking the specs, the warranty and who stands behind them. AI deserves the same scrutiny. Ask what it touches, what it costs, who’s accountable when it goes wrong and what it means for your team.
If a seller can answer those plainly, they might be worth your time. If they can’t, you’ve saved yourself an expensive lesson, and you’ve still got the list of handovers to fix.

title: A Monster Solar Storm Turned a Protected Region Around Earth Into a Particle Accelerator
content:
Ultrarelativistic electrons in an impenetrable barrier following a solar superstorm. Credit: Miyoshi et al., Geophysical Research Letters 2026
A solar superstorm appears to have turned a normally sheltered region near Earth into a natural particle accelerator, boosting electrons to energies capable of penetrating some satellite shielding.
Protecting spacecraft from radiation means understanding where hazardous particles can appear, especially during severe solar storms. Near Earth, an invisible boundary was thought to keep exceptionally energetic electrons out of a relatively protected region. During and after the geomagnetic superstorm of May 2024, Japan’s Arase space probe, operated by JAXA, detected large numbers of them well inside it. Some had energies exceeding three megaelectronvolts, enough to pass through some satellite shielding.
Researchers led by Nagoya University analyzed Arase’s observations to determine how these electrons appeared in a region that normally excludes them. Their evidence suggests the particles gained energy there, rather than entering it already highly energized. The distinction matters because it means a radiation hazard can develop within the supposedly protected region itself.
An electron barrier with uncertain origins
Earth’s magnetic field traps charged particles, including protons and electrons, in two doughnut-shaped regions called the Van Allen radiation belts. These particles can damage the hardware and electronics of spacecraft passing through the belts. At the inner edge of the outer belt, roughly three times Earth’s radius from the planet’s center, the most energetic electrons usually seem to encounter an invisible wall. Under typical conditions, the region inside this boundary is devoid of these extremely fast-moving electrons.
Detailed schematic outlining the process of electron acceleration inside the impenetrable barrier. Credit: Miyoshi et al, Geophysical Research Letters, 2026
Scientists first identified the apparent barrier in 2014, but its origin remains incompletely understood. One possible explanation involves “plasmaspheric hiss,” low-frequency radio waves that sound like static when played through a speaker. These waves occur in Earth’s magnetosphere, the region of space dominated by its magnetic field. Human-made very-low-frequency radio transmissions used to communicate with submarines underwater may also help shape the boundary by scattering radiation-belt electrons into Earth’s atmosphere.
“One of the key questions was how these highly energetic electrons appeared inside the barrier,” said Yoshizumi Miyoshi, a professor at the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University and the study’s lead author. “Were they transported inward from the outer radiation belt, or were they accelerated locally within this region?”
Chirping waves may accelerate electrons for days
The intense solar activity behind the May 2024 superstorm brought northern lights to Hokkaido and as far south as Japan’s Hyogo prefecture. In space, the storm dramatically eroded Earth’s plasmasphere, a region filled with relatively cool charged particles. Its outer boundary retreated unusually close to the planet, leaving the area around the usual electron barrier much less densely populated with plasma. Hotter electrons could then reach farther inward and generate natural, low-frequency electromagnetic waves known as chorus waves.
Arase detected intense chorus waves repeatedly sweeping upward in frequency. “When converted into audio, it sounds like a bird song,” Miyoshi said. These waves ripple through Earth’s magnetic field and can transfer energy to electrons when their oscillations match the electrons’ spiraling motion around magnetic field lines.
“Typically, the plasmasphere recovers on a timescale of about two days,” Miyoshi said. “During the May 2024 superstorm, however, it took approximately 4.3 to 4.7 days for the plasma density to recover to more than half of its pre-storm level in the observed region.”
The resulting low-density conditions persisted for several days, potentially allowing chorus-wave activity and the continued acceleration of electrons inside the previously impenetrable barrier.
Chorus waves rising in frequency recorded by Arase in March 2018 converted into audio. Credit: Erg Science Center
Evidence of acceleration within the barrier
To distinguish local acceleration from the inward movement of already energetic electrons, the researchers analyzed electron phase space density, or PSD. This quantity describes how electrons are distributed according to their energies and motion. Using measurements from multiple Arase orbits, the team examined how PSD varied with distance from Earth while accounting for changes in the electrons’ motion.
A distinct local peak developed near the usual barrier boundary and grew stronger over time. That growing peak provided evidence that electrons were gaining energy within the region, rather than simply being transported inward from the outer radiation belt.
Miyoshi said the findings, published in
Geophysical Research Letters
, show that even parts of near-Earth space considered relatively protected from extremely energetic electrons can experience substantial increases in radiation during severe space weather. The observations also offer insight into how Earth’s magnetosphere responds to extreme solar activity and underscore the value of continuously monitoring the space environment around the planet.
“This discovery highlights the need to understand and predict how energetic electrons behave under extreme space weather conditions,” Miyoshi said. “Such knowledge is important for assessing radiation risks to spacecraft and improving future space weather predictions.”
Reference: “Local Acceleration of Multi-MeV Electrons Inside Earth’s Impenetrable Barrier During the May 2024 Superstorm” by Y. Miyoshi, S. Kurita, A. Shinbori, K. Yamamoto, C.-W. Jun, S. Matsuda, S. Saito, R. Kataoka, D. Wang, I. Shinohara, T. Takashima, T. Mitani, N. Higashio, A. Matsuoka, Y. Kasahara, F. Tsuchiya, A. Kumamoto, T. Hori, N. Kitamura and M. Teramoto, 26 October 2026,
Geophysical Research Letters
DOI: 10.1029/2026GL125879
This work was supported by the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS) KAKENHI Grants 22K21345, 23K25925, 24K07112, 26K00765, and 26H02088.
