Meret Kristen (stehend) und Fabian Engl von der OTH Regensburg werten Blickdaten zu einer E-Mail aus: Die Heatmap links zeigt, wo die Augen am längsten verweilten, die Grafik rechts, in welcher Reihenfolge sie über die Mail wanderten.
| Quelle:
Benjamin Strobel
Download
Eine Eye-Tracking-Studie der OTH Regensburg mit 103 Beschäftigten in der Region zeigt: Auf Betrugsmails fallen Menschen weniger aus Unwissen herein als wegen flüchtiger Blicke im Arbeitsalltag. Zum Europäischen Monat der Cybersicherheit erklärt das Team, warum Schulungen daran wenig ändern und warum Rechtschreibfehler als Warnsignal ausgedient haben.
Das Logo stimmte, die Drohung war unmissverständlich: Wer nicht auf den Link klicke, dessen Kundenkonto werde deaktiviert. Nur in der Absenderadresse fehlte ein einziger Buchstabe, ein „e“. Von den zehn Testpersonen, die in einer Eye-Tracking-Studie der OTH Regensburg am häufigsten danebenlagen, hielten acht die E-Mail für echt. Phishing heißt diese Masche: Kriminelle tarnen Mails als Nachricht eines bekannten Unternehmens, um an Passwörter, Daten oder Geld zu kommen.
Wohin Menschen schauen, bevor sie eine E-Mail für echt oder gefälscht halten, untersuchen Meret Kristen und Fabian Engl, wissenschaftliche Mitarbeiterin und wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter im Software Engineering Laboratory for Safe and Secure Systems (LaS³) an der Fakultät Elektro- und Informationstechnik der OTH Regensburg. „Ein System ist nur so sicher wie der Mensch, der damit umgeht“, sagt Kristen. Laut dem Data Breach Investigations Report 2025 des US-Konzerns Verizon spielte bei rund 60 Prozent der ausgewerteten Datenlecks der Mensch eine Rolle, durch Täuschung, Fehler oder unbeabsichtigte Handlungen.
Falsche Entscheidungen trotz IT-Sicherheitsschulung
60 Prozent der Testpersonen hatten schon einmal eine Schulung gegen Phishing besucht – und erkannten Fälschungen trotzdem nicht zuverlässiger als die übrigen. „Das hat mich ehrlich gesagt überrascht“, sagt Kristen. „Aber man kennt es ja von Datenschutz- oder Arbeitsschutzschulungen: Man lässt sich berieseln, und online klickt man sich möglichst schnell durch.“ Selbst wer sich gut mit IT-Sicherheit auskannte, entschied zwar schneller, aber nicht häufiger richtig. Für Kristen liegt das Problem woanders: „Man klickt nicht auf eine Phishing-Mail, weil man sie nicht durchschauen könnte, sondern weil man abgelenkt ist und schnell seinen Posteingang abarbeiten will.“
„Am Ende einer Phishing-Studie steht normalerweise nur das Ergebnis: richtig oder falsch“, sagt Prof. Dr. Jürgen Mottok, der an der OTH Regensburg Informatik mit den Schwerpunkten IT-Sicherheit und Funktionale Sicherheit lehrt und das LaS³ leitet. „Mit Eye-Tracking sehen wir, wie es zu dieser Entscheidung kommt, worauf jemand achtet und was er übersieht. Daraus lassen sich Schulungen entwickeln, die im Arbeitsalltag tatsächlich helfen.“
Gefährlichster Köder: der Anhang
Für die Studie fuhr das Team im EU-Projekt „Digitale Innovation Ostbayern“ (DInO) mit neun mobilen Eye-Trackern in kleine und mittlere Unternehmen und Behörden der Region. 103 Beschäftigte sahen vor Ort 18 E-Mails in einer gewohnten Outlook-Oberfläche, darunter zwölf echte Phishing-Versuche. Die Eye-Tracker sind schmale Leisten, die am Bildschirm befestigt werden. Zwei Kameras darin erfassen die Pupillen und die Lichtreflexe auf der Hornhaut und berechnen daraus 250-mal pro Sekunde, wohin jemand gerade schaut. DInO ist Ende August ausgelaufen, im Nachfolgeprojekt dina (Digital Innovation and AI) bietet das Team Unternehmen und Behörden weiterhin Eye-Tracking-Studien und Beratung zu IT-Sicherheit an.
Im Schnitt erkannten die Testpersonen gut zehn der zwölf Fälschungen. Am gefährlichsten waren E-Mails mit Anhang: Fast jede fünfte ging durch, bei E-Mails mit Link etwa jede siebte, bei Zahlungsaufforderungen etwa jede neunte. Umgekehrt hielten die Testpersonen jede fünfte echte E-Mail für Betrug. Veröffentlicht sind die Ergebnisse auf der Fachkonferenz SECURWARE 2024 und in der Fachzeitschrift International Journal on Advances in Security.
Kurze, sprunghafte Blicke sorgen für Fehlentscheidungen
In den Blickdaten zeigt sich ein Muster: Wer häufig danebenlag, warf oft nur kurze Blicke auf Absender, Anhang und Text und sprang zwischen ihnen hin und her. Wer alle Fälschungen erkannte, nahm sich für die entscheidenden Stellen mehr Zeit. Hinsehen allein schützt allerdings nicht: Ein Teilnehmer schaute bei der Mail eines unbekannten Schuhgeschäfts vor allem auf den verdächtigen ZIP-Anhang – und hielt sie trotzdem für echt. Dass ZIP-Dateien in kleineren Betrieben bis heute üblich sind, merkten mehrere Teilnehmende selbst an.
Den Erfolg einer gefälschten E-Mail mit einer angeblichen Kontosperrung erklärt Engl mit Gewohnheit: „Schreibt mir eine Firma, die kaum jemand kennt, bin ich erst einmal skeptisch. Habe ich dort aber mein Deutschlandticket oder meinen Internetvertrag, bin ich solche E-Mails gewohnt – und vertraue der Marke.“
Wenn ein Tippfehler Vertrauen weckt
Die Betrugsmails selbst sind über die Jahre besser geworden. „Das ist nicht mehr der ominöse Prinz, der Geld möchte“, sagt Engl. Lange galten Rechtschreibfehler als verlässliches Warnzeichen. Seit KI-Programme fehlerfreie Texte schreiben, taugen sie dafür kaum noch. Engl hält es sogar für denkbar, dass ein Tippfehler künftig eher Vertrauen weckt. Er verweist auf eine US-Studie mit mehr als 3.000 Versuchspersonen: Ein Chat-Kundendienst, der sich vertippte und den Fehler korrigierte, wirkte menschlicher und herzlicher, teils auch hilfsbereiter. „Damit stehen wir eigentlich wieder am Anfang“, sagt Engl.
Inzwischen untersucht das Team, wie weit Menschen einer KI vertrauen. Ein erstes Ergebnis einer noch unveröffentlichten Studie: Ordnet die KI ihren Text zusätzlich mit einer grafischen Bewertung von 1 bis 5 ein, lesen Menschen bei hohen Werten weniger vom Text selbst. „Man sieht nur noch: Okay, das ist gut“, sagt Engl. „Dann muss ich mir das gar nicht mehr im Detail durchlesen.“
Wie schnell KI die IT-Sicherheit verändert, zeigt die PHP-Sicherheitslücke „PHP2Shell“, die weltweit Webseiten bedrohte: Gefunden wurde sie mithilfe von KI, inzwischen wurden Millionen Angriffsversuche registriert.. Um solche Fragen geht es auch beim IT-Security Day „KI: Risikofaktor oder Werkzeug?“, zu dem die OTH Regensburg und die Universität Regensburg ihre Studierenden und Beschäftigten am 11. November 2026 einladen.
Partnerschaft mit schottischer Universität
Seit diesem Sommer wird die Forschung zu Cybersicherheit an der OTH Regensburg durch die Zusammenarbeit mit der Abertay University im schottischen Dundee verstärkt: Vorgesehen sind gemeinsame Forschung und Veröffentlichungen, Gastvorträge und gemeinsame Projekte von Studierenden. In Dundee erforscht Dr. Lynsay Shepherd mit Eye-Tracking, wie Menschen Sicherheitsentscheidungen treffen und wann sie Technik und KI-Systemen vertrauen. Es sind dieselben Fragen, die auch in Regensburg auf dem Tisch liegen: Worauf achten Menschen, bevor sie einer Mail glauben – oder einer Maschine?
Vier Fragen vor dem Klick: Tipps von Meret Kristen
1. Betrifft mich die Mail überhaupt?
2. Wird gedroht oder Zeitdruck gemacht?
3. Muss ich auf den Link klicken? Sicherer: die Adresse selbst im Browser eingeben.
4. Bin ich unsicher? Lieber einmal zu viel nachfragen, am besten bei der IT.

title: Evolving metal extraction processes
content:
Evolving metal extraction processes
Rethinking how metals are extracted could unlock lower-emission production, make better use of mineral resources, and strengthen critical-material supply chains.
Provided byOutokumpu
The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.
Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.
Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?
EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:
“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”
A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem
As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.
That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.
Beyond optimization
For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.
The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.
Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.
Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology
Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.
“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.
Innovation happens at the boundaries
EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.
Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.
“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.
Building a technology platform
A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.
Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.
“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.
The future of materials companies
The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.
Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.
The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.
The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO2, chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.
The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?
The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.
Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore.

title: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
content:
The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
Plus: The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
—Grace Huckins
As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.
I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.
“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it.
The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
—James O’Donnell
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.
Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why.
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair
But Trump says he doesn’t think Huang needs to worry. (AP News)
+ Huang hired a PR firm known for handling sex scandals last year. (Wired $)
+ The allegations will likely spur new chip export restrictions. (Reuters $)
+ They also raise questions about Huang’s lobbying on China. (Verge)
+ And threaten the fate of the economy. (WP $)
2 France has accused Iran of hacking its supermarket fridges
Prosecutors are investigating the leaders of an Iranian cyber unit. (NPR)
+ Hackers are shifting to manipulating physical equipment. (Axios)
+ Is your smart kitchen next? (Wired $)
3 The Iran war has triggered a drop in global emissions
The main driver is energy supply constraints. (New Scientist $)
+ But the decline will likely prove temporary. (Gizmodo)
+ Our climate models have a big blind spot. (MIT Technology Review)
4 The FDA has ordered GLP-1s to carry warnings about blindness
It says the drugs may increase the risk of vision loss. (NBC News)
+ GLP-1s could also exacerbate eating disorders. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Australia is mulling criminal penalties for rogue AI
The proposals follow an AI agent hacking government systems. (BBC)
6 The Pentagon is planning to patrol the Moon
The project’s first five satellites could launch in 2029. (Ars Technica)
7 Two US cities have voted to ditch Flock surveillance cameras
York, Maine, and League City, Texas, have voted to ban them. (Vox)
+ What Flock’s defenders are missing. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Constant surveillance is changing how children grow up
Tracking apps can fuel anxiety and undermine resilience. (Atlantic $)
9 A tiny RNA molecule could explain how life began
Some researchers believe life emerged from self-copying molecules. (Quanta)
10 A sci-fi novel has won the Booker Prize for the first time
The End of Everything was awarded the prestigious honor. (Gizmodo)
Quote of the day
"Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he is Nvidia, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company's strings himself."
—Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, tells Reuters why it will be so difficult to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
One More Thing
China wants to restore the sea with high-tech marine ranches
Just a short ferry ride from the Chinese port city of Yantai sits Genghai No. 1, a strange offshore complex that combines a tourist attraction with an industrial fish farm. It even has a seven-story visitor center shaped like a cartoon starfish. But its main purpose is to breed fish and release them into the ocean.
Genghai is part of China's ambitious marine ranching program. Since 2015, the country has built 169 demonstration ranches and released at least 167 billion juvenile fish and shellfish. But the approach has also proved controversial.
Dive into China's divisive plans to restore the seas with marine ranches.
—Matthew Ponsford
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ “Earth artist” David Popa has created a new land-art portrait in the mountains of Norway.
+ The winners of Wildlife Photographer of the Year capture both the power and fragility of nature.
+ A Minnesota man who stopped a runaway school bus got surprised with a $1,000 cheque from Superman.
+ After more than two decades without regular star shows, Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium has been restored.

title: Mercedes-Benz Lays Out Supply Chain Decarbonisation Plans
content:
Mercedes-Benz Lays Out Supply Chain Decarbonisation Plans
Prioritise Us
on Google
Mercedes-Benz announces steps to decarbonise its supply chain with First Movers Coalition and Hydro offtake agreement. Credit: Mercedes-Benz
CTO Jörg Burzer at Mercedes-Benz Group introduces plans to lower direct and indirect emissions by 2039, targeting greater green steel and aluminium use
Global automotive giant Mercedes-Benz has officially accelerated its challenging "Ambition 2039" supply chain sustainability strategy. By introducing stringent direct and indirect emission decarbonisation targets and signing a landmark offtake agreement to source up to 10% of its aluminium supply from low-carbon aluminium with Hydro, the enterprise aims to execute a sweeping green digital transformation across its procurement networks, reducing overall carbon footprint across all value chain stages by a targeted 70% by 2039 compared to 2019 levels.
“Aluminium is one of the most important levers in our supply chain. By joining the First Movers Coalition, we are sending a clear signal to the market: we want lower-carbon aluminium in our vehicles. This gives our partners planning security and strengthens the resilience of our supply chain,” comments Jörg Burzer, Member of the Board of Management of Mercedes-Benz Group AG, Chief Technology Officer, Development & Procurement.
Jörg Burzer, Chief Technology Officer at Mercedes-Benz
Expanded aluminium offtake agreement with Hydro
Global automotive giant Mercedes-Benz has significantly expanded its strategic supply chain partnership with Hydro. Mercedes-Benz will source primary aluminium from Hydro from 2026 until beyond 2030, with a contractually defined, step-by-step reduction of its carbon footprint. Under the agreement, Hydro will progressively reduce the carbon footprint of primary aluminium supplied to Mercedes-Benz to 3.5 kg CO2e per kg by 2028 and 3.0 kg CO2e per kg from 2030 onwards. The agreement covers at least 10 percent of Mercedes-Benz’s primary aluminium demand.
The primary aluminium Mercedes-Benz currently sources from Hydro, produced using electrolysis powered by renewable energy, has a footprint of around 4.0 kg CO2e per kg. That is around 72 percent below the global average of 14.4 kg CO2e per kg.
The agreement also covers the introduction of aluminium produced from post-consumer recycled aluminium, Hydro CIRCAL, with use planned from 2027. CIRCAL contains at least 75 percent post-consumer recycled content and has a carbon footprint of no more than 2.0 kg CO2e per kg. In summer 2026, Mercedes-Benz was the first car manufacturer company in Europe to announce the integration of Hydro CIRCAL into series production for the next generation of large electric vehicles from 2027.
Hydro notes that achieving further reductions will require continued technology development and investment. Supply Chain Digital recently
reported
that Hydro had produced its first aluminium from aluminium chloride at at its Herøya research and test facility in Porsgrunn, Norway on 19 October. The technology opens up the prospect of eventually eliminating CO2 emissions from both electrolysis and anode production, releasing oxygen instead of CO2.
A Mercedes-Benz CLA inside the electrolysis hall at Hydro's Årdal smelter in Norway, where renewable energy is used to produce Hydro REDUXA, low-carbon primary aluminium. (Photo: Anders Vindegg / Hydro)
Key facts about Mercedes-Benz's Hydro offtake agreement
Hydro will supply at least 10% of Mercedes-Benz’s total primary aluminium demand through this long-term offtake agreement.
Hydro has committed to lowering the carbon footprint of supplied primary aluminium to a maximum of 3.5 kg CO2e per kg by 2028.
Hydro is targeting a further reduction to 3.0 kg CO2e per kg for primary aluminium by 2030.
Hydro will begin to supply Hydro CIRCAL, which utilises a minimum of 75% post-consumer aluminium scrap as feedstock, to Mercedes-Benz in 2027..
Mercedes-Benz announced it was integrating Hydro CIRCAL into series production for the next generation of large electric vehicles from 2027.
Hydrogen-based ironmaking in step towards decarbonising the supply chain
Mercedes-Benz is also seeking to accelerate the introduction of low-emission or green steel produced from a hydrogen-based ironmaking process, after the successful conclusion of a pilot project at HyIron, in which iron ore from Anglo American's Sishen iron ore mine in South Africa was shipped to HyIron's facility before being directly reduced into direct reduced iron (DRI) using hydrogen. By eliminating the energy-intensive pelletisation step, the scope 1 and 2 emissions of the process were lowered to just 10kg per ton of DRI, according to according to HyIron.
During the pilot, the material was then used in steelmaking and formed into a demonstrator component for the Mercedes-Benz EQS. The pilot successfully demonstrated technical feasibility across the value chain. Building on these results, Mercedes-Benz and HyIron have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to advance technical validation towards industrial scale-up and potential next steps.
“In steel, we are building on what we have learned in aluminium: progress happens when partners along the entire value chain work together – from the mine to the finished component. The pilot project with Anglo American and HyIron shows how transparency, responsible sourcing and lower emissions can be considered together. The insights from this pilot will help us decide where such approaches can make a contribution in our steel supply chain,” comments Yanni von Roy-Jiang, Head of Procurement and Supplier Management, Mercedes-Benz AG.
Higher levels of circularity and a lower-carbon footprint can play a role in enhancing the resilience of our automotive supply chains. Together with Hydro, we are making low-carbon aluminium a key pillar in our mass production process.
Yanni von Roy-Jiang, Head of Procurement and Supplier Management at Mercedes-Benz AG
Sharper Sustainability Focus
During the presentation of its detailed CO2 emission reduction strategy at its 'Sustainability Dialogue x Sustainability Update' in Sindelfingen, Mercedes-Benz announced that it was tightening its Sustainability strategy focus around four main pillars.
Decarbonisation: decarbonising the core business along the value chain, with a focus on electrification and on supply chain, logistics and production, in line with Ambition 2039.
Circularity
: expanding the use of recycled materials to 40% within the next decade, in line with Ambition 2039.
Safety: this overarching category now incorporates both traffic safety and digital trust.
People: social responsibility towards employees and respect for human rights across product value chains.
Mercedes-Benz Group is committed to a 90% reduction in production emissions, an 80% cut in use-phase emissions (dependent upon market conditions) , and an overall 70% reduction in CO2 emissions across all relevant value chain stages by 2039 compared to 2019.
Mercedes-Benz plans to target net zero in the course of the following decade. Mercedes-Benz defines net zero as meaning that the CO2 emissions will be reduced by at least 90% compared to 2019.
The Kuppenheim recycling plant is one of the company's strategies of building a circular economy (Kuppenheim recycling plant | Credit: Mercedes-Benz)
Key Partners
Hydro is an aluminium and renewable energy company. Its aluminium operations span the entire value chain, from bauxite mining to finished products. Hydro is an active technology developer researching lower-emission primary aluminium production. Its Herøya Technology Centre in Porsgrunn hosts testing and development of the HalZero process. The programme involves collaboration with Norwegian research institutions including NTNU and SINTEF, while Enova has supported both the test facility and planning for the next development phase.
First Movers Coalition
The First Movers Coalition is a global initiative uniting corporate purchasing power to rapidly commercialise emerging low-carbon technologies. By securing advanced procurement commitments from major multinational enterprises, the coalition accelerates the rapid decarbonisation of hard-to-abate industrial sectors globally.
HyIron has developed a hydrogen-based reduction process for global steelmaking. Its direct reduced iron (DRI) solution offers a solution to reduce emissions from steel supply chains.

Norsk Hydro

title: Vinted Go Expands European Network With Finland Launch
content:
Vinted Go Expands European Network With Finland Launch
Prioritise Us
on Google
Vinted Go is partnering with Unisend as both companies enter the Finnish market. Credit: Vinted Go
Vinted Go is scaling its operations in order to meet consumer demand and grow local businesses, Vytautas Atkočaitis, CEO of Vinted Go, explains
As the recommerce market continues to expand, Vinted Go is launching in Finland.
Vinted’s logistics arm is making it more convenient for Vinted members to buy and sell on the app through a new partnership with Unisend.
Through this, the company is making it more simple for customers to sell their clothes,
preventing fashion from ending up in landfill
Changing consumer patterns
Recommerce – the concept of
selling or renting second-hand
items through online marketplaces – has increased significantly over recent years. Consumers are becoming more economically and environmentally conscious, wanting to save money while still refreshing their wardrobes.
Though charity shops and eBay have been in existence for years, the concentration of these marketplaces have increased. According to OfferUp, 90% of US shoppers bought something second hand in the past 12 months, and 51% of shoppers sold something secondhand in the same period.
As recommerce increases, the need for reliable logistics does too. Recommerce comes with its own challenges – unpredictable volume and condition, case-by-case inspection, value degradation from slow processing.
On C2C sites, such as Vinted, this has extra complexity, as the sellers are non-professionals navigating the market. The logistics challenges of it include fragmented supply chains, vulnerabilities with third-party couriers and high shipping costs relative to item.
Alongside this, many sellers and buyers work, meaning their availability to post or pick up items is limited. As a result, there needs to be some strong last-mile, and first-mile, delivery options. Vinted Go, therefore, is making this process much more streamlined through its partnership with Unisend in Helsinki.
“Second-hand only scales if shipping is effortless and affordable,” explains Vytautas Atkočaitis, CEO of Vinted Go.
Vytautas Atkočaitis, CEO of Vinted Go
“That’s what we’re building: a network that connects members, local businesses and carriers across Europe, offering members accessible, flexible and easy-to-use delivery options. We’re excited to bring that to Finland, starting first in Helsinki, and with plans to go nationwide together with our partner Unisend.”
At a glance
Vinted Go is present in five other European markets
The Helsinki launch includes 300 pick-up and drop-off points
90% of US shoppers bought something second hand in the past 12 months
According to UNEP, the textile industry uses the equivalent of 86 million Olympic-sized swimming pools of water per year
Nearly 40% of consumers surveyed by eBay have sold secondhand items online
Company growth
Unisend, the parcel delivery network operated by Lietuvos paštas, is working with Vinted Go across Finland. The launch has started in the Helsinki area, making use of 300 pick-up and drop-off (PUDO) points.
The PUDO option acts as a more flexible option for many buyers and sellers, particularly when
lockers are used instead of postal stores
. By having accessible reverse logistics infrastructure, businesses meet consumer demand much more effectively.
Lietuvos Paštas is a Lithuanian postal company, operating the LP EXPRESS and Unisend network which consists of 164 post offices and approximately 1,500 parcel machines across Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia. Now, it is entering the Finnish market through Unisend’s partnership with Vinted Go.
"Entering the Finnish market marks an important new stage in Unisend's growth,” says Kastytis Valantinas, CEO of Lietuvos paštas.
Kastytis Valantinas, CEO of Lietuvos paštas
“Over more than two years of operations in the Baltic states, we have built a reliable parcel delivery network trusted by both individual and business customers. Our partnership with Vinted Go allows us to bring this experience to a new market and provide Vinted members with a simple and seamless parcel delivery experience.”
At present, Vinted Go has 18,000 PUDO points, with a presence in five other European markets. The company aims to make shipping more flexible, affordable and simpler for people buying and selling second-hand.
In Helsinki, Vinted members are making use of Vinted Go’s 300 PUDO points, based in shops and local spots. They increase convenience and flexibility, as well as increase footfall in local shops.
The partnership is just part of both companies' expansion plans, with potential to grow into more markets in coming years.
Second-hand only scales if shipping is effortless and affordable.
Vytautas Atkočaitis, CEO of Vinted Go
Vinted Go is expanding its operations to Finland. Credit: Getty
Key partners
Vinted is a Lithuanian online marketplace founded in 2008, specializing in secondhand fashion and accessories. The platform enables users to buy, sell, and exchange pre-owned clothing items across Europe and North America. Operating on a peer-to-peer model, Vinted promotes sustainable fashion by extending garment lifecycles. The company generates revenue through buyer protection fees and additional services. With millions of active users, Vinted has become Europe's largest secondhand fashion marketplace, valued at billions.
Lietuvos paštas
Lietuvos paštas (Lithuanian Post) is Lithuania's national postal operator, providing mail delivery, parcel services, and financial services since 1918. As a state-owned enterprise, it maintains an extensive network of post offices throughout Lithuania, serving both urban and rural communities. The company handles domestic and international mail, logistics solutions, and e-commerce deliveries. Lietuvos paštas has modernized its operations to compete in the digital age while maintaining universal postal service obligations to all Lithuanian residents.
ZigZag is a UK-based returns management platform that simplifies the online shopping returns process for consumers and retailers. The service aggregates multiple courier options, allowing customers to return items through convenient drop-off points or collection services. ZigZag partners with retailers to provide branded returns experiences while optimizing logistics and reducing costs. The platform consolidates returns from various carriers, streamlining reverse logistics. ZigZag's technology helps e-commerce businesses improve customer satisfaction while managing the growing challenge of online returns efficiently.
DHL is a German logistics company and the world's leading international express delivery and logistics provider. Founded in 1969, DHL operates in over 220 countries and territories, offering courier, parcel, freight transport, and supply chain management services. As part of Deutsche Post DHL Group, it serves both business and private customers. DHL specializes in international shipping, e-commerce logistics, and time-critical deliveries. The company employs hundreds of thousands worldwide, utilizing air, road, and rail networks to facilitate global trade.

title: Walmart Agrees to Expand Zipline Retail Drone Deliveries
content:
Walmart Agrees to Expand Zipline Retail Drone Deliveries
Prioritise Us
on Google
Families no longer need to leave the house in order to get essentials and groceries. Credit: Walmart
Walmart SVP Greg Cathey explains how a new multi-year agreement with Zipline will increase efficiency and add 300 drone delivery sites across the US
Walmart and Zipline have signed a multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the US. The retailer expects the expansion of delivery capabilities to increase the efficiency of fulfilment operations for staff and customers.
The new multi-year agreement expands the scope of Walmart's existing collaboration with Zipline. The two companies have been working together on drone deliveries since 2021.
This demonstrates the capabilities that technological advances can add within last-mile delivery options, showing how innovation can support growth.
Network collaboration
Walmart already has the largest network of delivery drones for retailers in the US, but is undergoing further expansion.
Its drone delivery programme has been used to deliver more than two million packages since it began. Drone delivery is seen as an
efficient and fast last-mile delivery option
, as it delivers the order to the destination in a short period of time.
Drone deliveries offer customers a fast way to receive their needed products, within minutes. This acts as an accessible option for customers, as they do not need to leave their house in order to receive their essentials.
“We see customers try drone delivery for the novelty and then continue to come back to it for the convenience when they need something in minutes,” says Greg Cathey, Senior Vice President, eCommerce Fulfillment Transformation at Walmart.
Greg Cathey, Senior Vice President, eCommerce Fulfillment Transformation at Walmart
“Walmart’s stores put us close to the communities we serve. With Zipline, we can build on that proximity and bring this fast delivery option to even more customers across the country.”
At a glance
Walmart has completed more than two million drone deliveries
The retailer is adding 300 new Zipline drone delivery sites
Its aim is to deliver essentials in as little as 30 minutes
Deliveries can weigh up to 8lbs depending on the vendor
Zipline also uses its drones for medical deliveries, saving more than 14,000 lives a year
Last-mile efficiency
Following the success of the drone programme, Walmart is bringing this capability to more communities across the nation. According to Walmart, tens of thousands of items are available for delivery in as little as 30 minutes.
Walmart’s physical presence is vast, with 90% of America living within 10 miles of a Walmart store. Through this, the retailer can build on its existing network to expand delivery.
It is seen as a more efficient and sustainable delivery option – there is no traffic for a driver to sit idly in,
there are fewer emissions
and costs are reduced significantly. Though the packages are of a limited weight, these deliveries are ideal for a forgotten item.
“​​​Five years ago, Walmart and Zipline made our first deliveries together. Back then, the idea of autonomous delivery seemed impossible to most people,” explains Keller Cliffton, CEO and Co-Founder of Zipline.
Keller Cliffton, CEO and Co-Founder of Zipline
“Today, customers order from us multiple times a day. When you can get what you need in 10-30 minutes it takes a huge amount of anxiety out of life. People can plan their lives around their loved ones, not errands. Now, with Walmart, we're going to expand this tech to homes throughout the country."
If their account is within the delivery range, customers will see drone delivery as an option online. They can track the items as they travel to the home, with real-time visibility and updates. It aims to position Walmart as the convenient retailer for customers across the US.
Advancing technology
Zipline is a quickly expanding organisation, currently the world’s largest service by miles flown. In total, it has 150 million commercial autonomous miles in its 10-year service, without a major safety incident, demonstrating its high capabilities.
The drone hovers approximately 330ft above the ground during delivery, with a descending pod containing the order. This ensures safety for the customer and the device, as well as efficiency, as it does not require landing and takeoff.
The company has also announced a US$1.5bn raise at a US$21.5bn post-money valuation. It is growing significantly, having also partnered with Uber to increase delivery capabilities. Zipline is using its increased capital to expand manufacturing capabilities in order to support its
growing drone delivery network
With Zipline, we can build on that proximity and bring this fast delivery option to even more customers across the country.
Greg Cathey, Senior Vice President, eCommerce Fulfillment Transformation at Walmart
The partnership helps consumers save time and provides reliable last-mile solutions. Credit: Walmart
Key partners
Walmart is America's largest retailer, founded by Sam Walton in 1962. Operating over 10,500 stores worldwide, it serves millions of customers daily with affordable groceries, electronics, and household goods. The company dominates through economies of scale, efficient supply chains, and competitive pricing. Recently, Walmart invested heavily in ecommerce, curbside pickup, and automation to compete with Amazon while maintaining brick-and-mortar strength.
Zipline is a drone delivery company founded in 2014, specializing in medical supply transport. Operating in Africa and the US, Zipline's autonomous aircraft deliver blood, vaccines, and medicines to remote healthcare facilities. The company has completed hundreds of thousands of deliveries, reducing delivery times from hours to minutes. Zipline demonstrates how drones can solve critical healthcare supply chain challenges.
Uber revolutionised transportation by launching ride-hailing services in 2009. Through its mobile app, Uber connects passengers with drivers, disrupting traditional taxi industries worldwide. The company operates in over 10,000 cities across 70+ countries, offering various services including UberX, UberEats food delivery, and freight logistics.

title: BYD considers building a battery factory in Portugal - electrive.com
content:
BYD is reportedly considering building a battery factory in Portugal - potentially at the former Galp refinery in Matosinhos near Porto. It remains unclear whether battery cells or complete battery systems would be manufactured there. Such a battery factory would align well with a potential BYD car factory in Spain.
BYD battery production in Chongqing, China (archive image)
Image: BYD
Chinese electric vehicle and battery manufacturer BYD is reportedly considering building a battery factory in Portugal. According to the Portuguese business newspaper
Expresso
, the company is already in discussions with the Portuguese government and the national trade and investment agency AICEP (Agência para o Investimento e Comércio Externo de Portugal) regarding a potential investment. The former oil refinery site of Portuguese energy company Galp in Matosinhos, near Porto, is being considered as a possible location. A source familiar with the matter states that the project is already relatively advanced.
However, there has been no official confirmation from BYD to date. Portugal’s Minister of Economy, Manuel Castro Almeida, merely confirmed a “fruitful dialogue” with a Chinese automaker regarding the establishment of a plant in Portugal, without providing further details. The city administration of Matosinhos also states that it has not yet been formally informed about the project. Nevertheless, Mayor Luísa Salgueiro described such an investment as a “very welcome project”.
Former refinery site as potential location
The former Galp refinery in Matosinhos was closed in 2021. The approximately 240-hectare site near the Atlantic is currently being dismantled. Of this, 100 hectares have already been transferred to the city administration. A 40-hectare site is planned for the University of Porto, while another 20 hectares are set to become a park. The remaining areas do not yet have a designated use. According to Galp, the ongoing demolition work is expected to be completed by the end of 2026, followed by further soil remediation measures.
The location’s advantages include its proximity to the Port of Leixões and excellent transport links. Additionally, the planned lithium extraction at the Barroso mine in northern Portugal is set to begin production in 2028. A battery factory in Matosinhos could therefore benefit from shorter transport routes for some of the required raw materials in the future.
No details yet on the type of battery production
It remains unclear exactly what BYD intends to produce in Portugal. Current reports only refer to a battery factory in general terms. Whether the focus will be on the production of battery cells, the manufacturing of modules, and/or the assembly of complete battery packs is not yet known. BYD has the expertise for all these production steps: the company develops and manufactures its own lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells as well as the associated battery systems.
The second generation Blade battery
A key in-house development is the so-called Blade Battery. Introduced in 2020 and now in
its second generation
, this battery technology is based on particularly long, flat LFP cells that resemble sword blades due to their shape. BYD uses a cell-to-pack concept, where the cells are integrated directly into the battery pack without traditional intermediate modules. This saves space and increases pack efficiency. The Blade Battery is used in numerous electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids from the manufacturer. BYD is thus not only an automaker but also an established cell producer with its own battery technology and manufacturing expertise.
Potential battery hub for the Iberian Peninsula
According to information from
Expresso
, the potential factory could serve as a production hub for the entire Iberian Peninsula. This would also include a
potential future car factory for BYD in Spain
. The Chinese manufacturer is already evaluating additional sites in Europe for expanded production capacity. Besides Spain, France is also being considered as a potential location for further investments. In Hungary, BYD is already constructing its first European passenger car plant in Szeged.
Meanwhile, Portugal is actively seeking investments in the battery industry. Chinese cell manufacturer
CALB is already planning a battery factory in Sines
. This project involves an investment of around two billion euros and a planned production capacity of 15 GWh per year. With a potential second major battery investment, Portugal could further strengthen its position within the European value chain for electric vehicles.
However, it remains uncertain whether BYD will indeed invest in Matosinhos. No details have yet been provided regarding the potential investment amount, production capacity, or number of jobs.

title: CATL explores lithium-air batteries as a long-term research focus - electrive.com
content:
CATL is considering lithium-air batteries as a long-term research option. The technology theoretically promises a significantly higher energy density than today's lithium-ion batteries. However, it is still far from market-ready vehicle batteries or a range of 2,000 km.
SNE Research estimates CATL's market share outside China at 33.7 percent.
Image: CATL
CATL Chief Scientist Wu Kai has positioned lithium-air batteries as a long-term research focus for the company at the
Equipment Powerhouse Forum 2026
. Sodium-ion and solid-state technologies remain closer to commercialisation at CATL. Current attention is primarily drawn to the potential for ranges of up to 2,000 km. The basis for such projections is the very high theoretical specific energy of lithium-air chemistry, at around 3,505 Wh/kg. However, this value describes the electrochemical potential of the reaction, not the energy density of a complete vehicle battery.
The difference from conventional lithium-ion cells lies in the structure. Lithium-air systems use metallic lithium as the negative electrode and oxygen from the surrounding environment as the reaction partner. During discharge, lithium peroxide forms in a porous cathode; during charging, the reaction is reversed, and oxygen is released again.
Because the oxygen does not need to be carried as a traditional cathode material within the battery, this theoretically results in a very high specific energy. However, for a real battery system, electrolyte, electrodes, housing, protective systems, and – above all – components for air processing must be added. Even higher theoretical values of around 12,000 Wh/kg are based on calculations that exclude the mass of the required oxygen.
The gap between theoretical energy density and a production-ready vehicle battery is significant, as demonstrated by current laboratory results. In 2024, researchers from Jilin University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences achieved 757.5 Wh/kg and 241 charge cycles with a lithium-air pouch cell under defined laboratory conditions.
CATL’s lithium-air Batteries still face challenges
Another approach comes from Argonne National Laboratory and the Illinois Institute of Technology. A
solid-state lithium-air cell
introduced in 2023 completed at least 1,000 charge and discharge cycles at room temperature. The architecture used was said to have a theoretical potential of around 1,200 Wh/kg. Both results show progress but are not equivalent to a validated battery for production vehicles.
A central challenge remains the air supply. The battery requires oxygen, while moisture and carbon dioxide must be reliably kept out. Both substances can cause unwanted chemical reactions, damaging electrodes and electrolytes. A vehicle would therefore need a controlled air supply system with filtration and humidity management. This peripheral equipment, in turn, increases weight, space requirements, and energy consumption. Additional unresolved or only partially solved issues include cycle stability, charging efficiency, and the stability of the lithium-metal anode.
The reaction products in the cathode are also problematic. Lithium peroxide can deposit in the pores, hindering oxygen transport. During charging, it must be completely removed without side reactions damaging the electrolyte or electrodes.
A high specific energy alone is not sufficient for use in electric vehicles. Volumetric energy density, power output, fast-charging capability, safety, lifespan, and the weight of the overall system are also decisive. The frequently cited 2,000 km cannot, therefore, currently be applied to a concrete vehicle.
CATL is simultaneously pursuing significantly more market-ready technologies. Sodium-ion batteries and solid-state cells are much further along in the company’s development roadmap. At the same time, CATL is already the clear market leader with established lithium-ion systems. According to SNE Research, the company installed 143.7 GWh of battery capacity outside China in the first nine months of 2026, achieving a market share of 33.7 per cent.
The current trend towards LFP also shows how strongly the battery market is evolving with already available cell chemistries. According to
SNE Research
, the LFP share of the market outside China increased from 15.8 to 27.7 per cent within a year. Chinese manufacturers, in particular, are benefiting from this development.
The technology remains a long-term research option for CATL. Whether it will eventually lead to electric vehicles with four-digit ranges depends less on the theoretical energy density and more on whether the numerous chemical and technical challenges can be resolved in a long-lasting, safe, and affordable battery system.

title: Boston Dynamics' Atlas robot performs a 360-degree jump on wheels
content: Boston Dynamics has given its Atlas humanoid robot an unusual upgrade: a pair of wheels replacing its feet. The experimental setup lets engineers test how the humanoid handles sustained high-speed movement and heavy loads. It also offers a demanding environment for testing the robot’s motors and machine-learning-based control systems.The wheeled Atlas isn’t a planned commercial product. Boston Dynamics developed it as a research platform to investigate how accurately simulation-trained controllers can operate real hardware. The project also explores what happens when engineers push the robot’s actuators close to their physical limits.Simple hardware conversionThe engineering behind the modification was surprisingly straightforward. Boston Dynamics attached standard electric scooter wheels to Atlas using a custom adapter. The adapter connects directly to the robot’s existing ankle actuators.No other major hardware changes were necessary. Engineers also avoided rebuilding the robot’s software model from scratch. They simply replaced the simulated feet with wheels capable of continuous rotation.That simplicity reflects Atlas’ modular hardware design. Boston Dynamics developed the humanoid with manufacturing scalability and easier maintenance in mind. The same design principles also made this experimental conversion relatively uncomplicated.Wheels offered another advantage during testing. They forced the motors to deliver considerable torque while maintaining high rotational speeds. Every acceleration, turn, and stop placed sustained demands on the actuators.Teaching Atlas to rollThe experiment also gave engineers an opportunity to explore reinforcement learning (RL). The technique trains a robot through repeated simulations, allowing its control system to discover effective movements.However, transferring those learned behaviors to physical hardware presents a significant engineering challenge. A simulated motor might behave differently from its real-world counterpart. That mismatch can produce movements that work virtually but fail on the actual robot.Boston Dynamics addressed the problem by refining its simulated motor models. Engineers conducted physical experiments to measure actuator behavior. They then adjusted simulation parameters to reflect the hardware’s actual performance.The team also modified existing reinforcement-learning frameworks. Changes to training commands, reward functions, and posture controls helped Atlas develop smooth rolling movements.The results demonstrated why accurate motor simulations matter. A controller trained against realistic hardware behavior has a better chance of performing reliably outside simulation.Wheels unlock new movementsSome of Atlas’ movements drew inspiration from human motion-capture recordings. Engineers selected examples featuring substantial foot sliding to explore how wheels could reproduce similar movements.Sideways dashes offered an interesting example. Instead of dragging its feet across the ground, Atlas learned to steer its wheels and roll sideways.The robot also performed a 360-degree jump using a trajectory-tracking controller. The system followed recorded human movement data and completed the maneuver on its first attempt.Its approach differed from the foot-based Atlas configuration. Before jumping, the robot rolled its lower body into position to prepare for takeoff. The behavior showed how reinforcement learning could discover new ways to exploit available traction.Boston Dynamics says the findings will influence development of Atlas’ standard configuration. Engineers want to combine accurate actuator models with whole-body learning to improve reliability and expand the humanoid’s capabilities.The wheeled experiment ultimately provided something beyond an entertaining demonstration. It offered engineers a demanding test environment for understanding how motors and learned controllers behave together under extreme conditions.

title: Chilong-1: China starts building 600-MW reactor at hybrid nuclear site
content: Workers have poured the first concrete for the nuclear island at the Xuwei plant in Jiangsu province. The milestone marks the official start of construction on the world’s first commercial “Chilong-1” reactor. The project sets a precedent for using nuclear energy to power large-scale chemical manufacturing.Unlike conventional nuclear sites built almost exclusively for the electrical grid, the Xuwei complex will function primarily as an industrial steam supplier. It provides heat directly to nearby petrochemical refineries while sending surplus electricity to the regional network. Once fully operational, its first phase will provide 32.5 million tonnes of industrial steam each year and generate over 11.5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity. Replacing fossil fuels here will cut standard coal use by 7.26 million tonnes each year. According to official estimates, this will prevent nearly 19.6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.The plant achieves this output through an unusual hybrid design. It will pair two distinct nuclear technologies on a single site. These nuclear technologies are “Hualong One” pressurized water reactors and the “Chilong-1” high-temperature gas-cooled reactor. Using a coordinated control architectureThe system runs in sequence to produce steam with exact thermodynamic properties. Main steam from the third-generation Hualong One first turns demineralized water into saturated steam. The fourth-generation Chilong-1 then takes that steam and superheats it further, yielding three separate grades of high-temperature steam tailored for petrochemical refining.To manage this tandem operation safely, plant operators will use a unified “reactor-machine-heat” coordinated control architecture. It is the first time a commercial facility has run both reactor types under a single integrated heat-delivery framework.Jointly developed by China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) and Tsinghua University, the Chilong-1 relies on fourth-generation nuclear principles that emphasize passive safety. The reactor is designed to remain safe during severe system failures without requiring active operator intervention or external power supplies. Even under complete coolant loss, the physics of the core prevents a meltdown and blocks large releases of radioactive material.A modular layoutThe reactor also uses a modular layout. Individual units produce relatively modest amounts of power on their own, but engineers can link multiple modules together depending on regional energy needs. Beyond supplying industrial process heat, the high temperatures produced by the core make the reactor well suited for large-scale hydrogen production and efficient electrical generation.China Nuclear Power Investment, a subsidiary of CNNC, manages the Xuwei site. The first phase includes two Hualong One reactors alongside the single Chilong-1 unit. Work on the first Hualong One began on 16 January. “It opens a new chapter in providing a replicable and scalable “Chinese solution” for the low-carbon transformation of high-energy-consuming industries worldwide, injecting strong momentum into the realization of global carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals,” the Global Times reported at the time.When completed, the plant will serve as a permanent low-carbon heat and power anchor for the Lianyungang petrochemical industrial base.

title: Claude Fable 5.2 builds a working OS with 1,000 agents in eight days
content: Anthropic’s newest Claude models have taken on engineering challenges that typically demand extensive human expertise and months of work. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have demonstrated significant improvements across software development, robotics, mathematics, and theoretical physics.During internal testing, Fable 5.2 coordinated more than 1,000 agents to build a working operating system. The model also helped researchers tackle two previously unresolved problems involving black holes. In another experiment, it completed a computer-verifiable formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem in just 30 hours.These results suggest the models can handle increasingly complex technical assignments. Anthropic says both versions share the same underlying architecture. However, Mythos targets vetted cybersecurity and biomedical research organizations.Working operating systemOne of the more striking experiments involved building an operating system from scratch. An Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 a basic prompt and an empty project folder.The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days. They wrote code, tested components, and reviewed their work throughout the process.The resulting operating system could boot on a laptop. It included its own kernel, hardware drivers, and permanent file storage. It also featured a graphical interface, login screen, installer, and built-in Claude functionality.Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.They’re capable collaborators on ambitious projects in many fields, and show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. pic.twitter.com/jP0AutLxXb— Claude (@claudeai) November 9, 2026Software engineering wasn’t the only area where Fable 5.2 demonstrated its capabilities. Anthropic also tasked it with designing three electronic devices.These included a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. The model selected components from US distributors and designed circuit boards. It also created 3D-printed enclosures and wrote the required software.All three devices worked without electrical modifications. Their circuit boards reached manufacturing readiness in less than a day.Anthropic also reported a striking result from an internal software migration. A team of agents moved a critical production service from Python to Rust. The resulting service now starts approximately 26 times faster.Stronger robotics and securityFable 5.2 also demonstrated substantial improvements in controlling physical robots. On the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieved a 64.9 percent success rate.That represents a significant jump from Fable 5.1’s 27.6 percent score. It also outperformed GPT-6 Astra, which recorded 29.8 percent on the same evaluation. Opus 5.5 reached 39.4 percent.The benchmark tests how models control a simulated two-arm robot using camera images. Demonstrations included solving puzzle cubes, opening bottle caps, and drawing pictures.Cybersecurity results offered another notable performance gain. Anthropic’s specialized Mythos 5.2 model achieved an 89.6% score on its CVE Rediscovery evaluation.That represents a 10.2 percent improvement over Opus 5.5. It also marks an 11.3 percentage-point increase over Mythos 5.1, which scored 78.3 percent.A separate security company found that other tested frontier models missed one in six confirmed vulnerabilities identified by Mythos 5.2.Faster performance, fewer blocksAnthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than their predecessors. Their standard pricing also starts at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.An optional fast mode increases token generation speeds by up to 2.5 times. However, it doubles the standard pricing.The company also reports improvements to its safety classifiers. Fable 5.2 produces approximately 55 percent fewer unnecessary blocks than Fable 5.1. Cybersecurity-related blocks fell by 60 percent, while biology-related blocks declined by 40 percent.These changes should make the models less restrictive during legitimate work. Mythos 5.2, however, remains available only to vetted organizations pursuing approved cybersecurity and biomedical research.

title: Fast-charging lithium-metal battery holds 94% capacity past 100 cycles
content: South Korean scientists have just unveiled a new liquid-crystal polymer separator, which, when tested in a lithium-metal battery, retained 94 percent of its capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at a 4C charging rate.The separator was built by the a research team at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST). It could reportedly improve battery stability and charging speed, meaning drivers could charge their EVs in just 15 minutes.The study was led by Dong Ki Yoon, PhD, and Hye Ryung Byon, PhD, professors at KAIST’s Department of Chemistry. “Lithium metal batteries can store more energy than conventional batteries,” they stated. “However, during charging, lithium can accumulate in sharp, branch-like structures known as ‘dendrites.'”For the separator, the researchers used liquid-crystalline polymers to control how the lithium ions move inside lithium-metal batteries. Both Yoon and Byon believe that their find could address slow ion transport and dendrite formation.A highway for lithium ionsLithium-metal batteries can store more energy than conventional ones. However, during charging, lithium can accumulate on the electrode surface and, as a result, form dendrites. These tiny needle-like metallic crystals grow on the anodes, and they can damage the separator between the electrodes, which could cause short circuits and increase the risk of fires. To address this problem, the team created a porous separator made from liquid-crystalline polymers, which have an ordered structure like solids. They also share some properties with liquids. For the project, the team incorporated polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains into the material to facilitate lithium-ion transport.The scientists then monitored the alignment of the liquid-crystal molecules and arranged them either vertically or horizontally to examine how their orientation affected ion movement. The vertically aligned separator created direct pathways for lithium ions to travel toward the electrodes.In contrast to the horizontally aligned separator, it reduced the tortuosity (winding nature), of the ion transport pathways by about 2.5 times. This allowed the lithium ions to move faster and more uniformly. What’s more, it suppressed the dendrite formation and improved the battery stability.Longer battery lifeUltimately, the researchers tested the separator in a working lithium-metal battery to evaluate its performance. To their massive surprise, the cell retained 94 percent of its initial capacity after 100 charge-discharge cycles at 4C. In simple terms, a 4C charging rate means a battery can fully recharge in 15 minutes. According to the team, controlling how molecules are arranged could potentially make batteries charge faster and last longer without compromising safety. Yoon emphasized the significance of this finding for future battery development.He said that molecular alignment plays a key role in battery performance. “We expect this approach to contribute to the development of high-energy-density next-generation battery technologies, for which long driving ranges and rapid charging are essential,” he concluded in a press release.The scientists believe the approach could contribute to the development of high-energy-density batteries for future EVs, where rapid charging and longer driving ranges are essential. Further tests will, however, show whether it works in larger batteries as well.The study has been published in the journal ACS Nano.

title: Google expands chipset lineup with 80% better inference performance
content: Google has added two specialized systems to its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) lineup, targeting secure AI computing and workloads requiring massive memory capacity. The expansion gives Google four distinct TPU configurations in one generation, reflecting the growing demands of enterprise AI infrastructure.The new systems, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, address challenges emerging as businesses deploy autonomous AI agents. One prioritizes confidential computing for sensitive workloads, while the other targets models handling enormous amounts of contextual information.Google says its TPU business now serves nearly 100 customers. These include AI research labs, financial trading firms, retailers and universities. Customers can also deploy TPUs directly inside their own data centers.Two systems, two prioritiesTPU 8tx targets organizations that process sensitive information or operate under strict regulatory requirements. Google has integrated hardware-level confidential computing into the system, protecting data and model weights during active processing.Typically, processors must decrypt information before working with it. That creates potential exposure even when storage systems and network connections use encryption.Today, we're expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two new systems built specifically for the agentic era — bringing our total to four distinct eighth-generation TPU systems launched in a single year.TPU 8i Max was built for massive context windows and the highest… pic.twitter.com/Ljj622Z5zL— Google (@Google) November 9, 2026Google addresses this vulnerability through hardware-based isolation. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t, paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also incorporates Google’s low-latency Boardfly networking technology.The configuration delivers up to twice the latency reduction compared with TPU 8t, according to Google. Performance penalties from its additional security protections remain minimal.Organizations can also fine-tune proprietary models using private datasets. They can distill larger models into smaller versions without transferring sensitive information between separate computing clusters.TPU 8i Max tackles a different limitation: memory bandwidth. Large AI workloads increasingly require processors to access enormous amounts of information without waiting for data transfers.Google combines two TPU 8i chips within a single package to address that bottleneck. The resulting system doubles compute capacity, on-chip SRAM, and high-bandwidth memory bandwidth.It also fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint. That allows data centers to accommodate more computing capacity within the same physical space.Four accelerators for AIThe expanded lineup now covers different stages of AI development and deployment. TPU 8t handles large-scale model training, while TPU 8i focuses on low-latency inference and reasoning.TPU 8tx adds confidential computing capabilities. TPU 8i Max targets applications requiring extensive context windows and greater compute density.Google originally introduced TPU 8t and TPU 8i at Cloud Next in April. The company reported up to 2.7 times better training performance for TPU 8t. TPU 8i offered up to 80 percent better inference price performance against the previous generation.Making TPUs easier to useHardware improvements represent only part of Google’s broader strategy. The company is also trying to reduce the software expertise required to deploy workloads on its accelerators.Its open-source TorchTPU project brings native PyTorch support to the platform. Developers can run existing PyTorch code and Hugging Face models without rewriting their applications.Google has also introduced TPU development agents compatible with Claude Code, Cursor and Google Antigravity. These tools can automate onboarding, identify performance bottlenecks, and optimize custom kernels.Another addition, TPU Sync, creates a unified memory architecture across TPU memory, host memory, and shared storage. Google says it can reduce key-value cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90 percent.The company is also expanding its infrastructure management tools. Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing help developers coordinate large TPU clusters and reconfigure computing resources more efficiently.Google’s broader bet is that AI infrastructure must evolve beyond faster individual processors. As autonomous agents handle increasingly complex tasks, memory, networking, and security will play equally important roles.

title: Ionic liquids help scientists precisely shape metal-organic frameworks
content: Researchers at the Tokyo University of Science have developed a method to shape porous materials called metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) into microscopic patterns without destroying delicate structures.Previously, carving these materials into tiny components for advanced electronics or chemical sensors required expensive liquid-nitrogen cooling to prevent them from collapsing under energy beams. Liquid ionic filler soaks into the MOF’s microscopic pores, strengthening the structure so it can absorb heat and clear electrical charges during standard room-temperature etching.This low-cost, scalable technique makes it much easier to incorporate over 100,000 known MOF variations into practical technologies like high-sensitivity sensors and micro-catalysts.Ionic liquid treatmentScientists building microscopic electronics have faced a major challenge: their best raw materials crumbled under the tools meant to shape them.Now, a team of Japanese researchers has unlocked a way to sculpt these delicate crystals using a technique as simple as filling a sponge with liquid.MOFs are widely considered important for modern materials science. Discovered in 1974 by Professor Richard Robson at the University of Melbourne, these custom-engineered materials link metal ions with organic molecules to create hyper-porous structures. Imagine a microscopic cage where a single gram offers thousands of square meters of internal surface area. The material’s tiny pores can store gases, trap environmental pollutants, and catalyze complex chemical reactions.Engineers have long eyed MOFs for next-generation chemical sensors and micro-electronics. Translating that potential into practical hardware required carving the material into precise micro-scale patterns.Standard semiconductor manufacturing relies on dry etching, blasting materials with high-energy ion beams to strip away microscopic layers. MOFs, however, are far too fragile for such high force.Striking a standard MOF crystal with an ion beam causes the delicate lattice to collapse into giant, ruined cavities. Until now, the only way to shield these fragile architectures during etching was to freeze them with liquid nitrogen. This has been a costly process that requires specialized cryogenic equipment.Led by Assistant Professor Yumeng Zheng and Professor Kentaro Kinoshita, the team devised a room-temperature solution. And soaked a copper-based MOF in an ionic liquid, filling 50 percent to 60 percent of its internal pore volume. The liquid acts like a microscopic structural reinforcement.High-tech future applications Blasting the treated samples with a focused beam of gallium ions revealed a dramatic difference. The ionic liquid absorbed the thermal heat of the beam while redistributing electrical charges across the material. Hardness tests confirmed that all liquid-treated samples became tougher, while thermal analysis showed the material resisted breakdown at much higher temperatures.Interestingly, the MOF retained its structural integrity. It etched precise shapes into the material at room temperature, including micro-pillars, a 5 × 5 µm² square, and even a Chinese character with line widths as narrow as 130 to 300 nanometers.The findings could finally clear the path toward mass-producing MOF-powered technology. Manufacturers can now shape these materials with existing microfabrication machinery because they no longer need cryogenic cooling.“We can foresee applications in high-sensitivity sensors, separation and analysis devices, and catalytic devices. This technology has the potential to become a foundational technology for bridging the exceptional material functionalities of MOFs with their use in practical devices,” concluded Prof. Kinoshita. The findings were published in the journal Communications Materials.
