title: James Webb Discovers a Nearly Pristine Galaxy From the Dawn of the Universe
content:
JWST image of the massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416 (background) and a three-color composite of the extremely faint galaxy LAP1-B (inset). Invisible in the NIRCam image, LAP1-B was detected through sensitive NIRSpec observations of hydrogen and oxygen emissions. The inset shows gas velocity and spatial distribution (blue: hydrogen Lyα; green: oxygen [OIII]; red: hydrogen Hα), with Lyα shifted by 200 km/s for clarity. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA & K. Nakajima et al., Nature.
Some of the faintest galaxies near the Milky Way may be survivors from the earliest chapters of cosmic history. Their ancient stars preserve clues about how galaxies formed, but astronomers have struggled to connect these nearby relics to the small, primitive galaxies that existed billions of years ago.
An international research team led by Associate Professor Kimihiko Nakajima of Kanazawa University has now identified a possible link. A tiny galaxy called LAP1-B, seen as it existed 13 billion years ago, contains remarkably little oxygen and has several characteristics that resemble some of the oldest galaxies still found near the Milky Way.
The chemical evidence reaches back to a time when the universe was only beginning to acquire the elements familiar to us today. Shortly after the Big Bang, the universe consisted primarily of hydrogen and helium. Heavier elements, including the carbon and oxygen essential for life, were produced later inside the first generations of stars and eventually released into space.
A galaxy with almost no oxygen
Astronomers have long wanted to study galaxies from this early period to understand how those elements first accumulated. The challenge is that such galaxies are extraordinarily small and faint, making their chemical composition difficult to measure even with powerful telescopes.
LAP1-B became accessible thanks to gravitational lensing, a phenomenon in which the gravity of a massive object bends and magnifies light from something farther away. In this case, a massive galaxy cluster amplified the distant galaxy’s light approximately 100 times, allowing researchers to examine an object that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study.
Building on earlier detections, the team observed LAP1-B for more than 30 hours using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They used spectroscopy, a technique that analyzes light to identify the chemical elements present in a distant object.
The observations revealed an oxygen abundance just 1/240th that of the Sun, a record low that places LAP1-B among the most chemically primitive galaxies ever characterized.
“I was instantly thrilled by the extreme lack of oxygen revealed in the data,” says Associate Professor Nakajima, the research team leader. “Finding a galaxy in such a primitive state is astonishing. It’s a chemical signature that clearly indicates a primordial galaxy caught in the moments shortly after its formation.”
This diagram compares galaxy stellar mass and oxygen abundance. LAP1-B (red circle) has an exceptionally low stellar mass and just 1/240th the Sun’s oxygen abundance, a record low for a star-forming galaxy, revealing its chemically primitive state. Brown symbols represent distant galaxies, while the dashed line shows the trend in nearby galaxies. Credit: Nakajima K. et al., Nature (2026), Springer Nature.
The researchers also found an unusually high ratio of carbon to oxygen. That distinction matters because the relative amounts of different elements can reveal how a galaxy acquired its chemical ingredients. In LAP1-B, the elevated carbon-to-oxygen ratio closely matches theoretical predictions for material scattered into space by the explosions of the universe’s first-generation stars.
Together, these measurements suggest that LAP1-B was observed during an exceptionally early stage of chemical enrichment, when the products of the first stars were beginning to accumulate in its gas.
“Usually, we act like ‘cosmic archaeologists,’ trying to guess the past by looking at old stars in our own neighborhood. But now, we can analyze the gas directly from the original scene 13 billion years ago,” emphasizes Nakajima. “We are witnessing the moment when a galaxy first inherited the chemical building blocks created by the universe’s earliest stars.”
A possible ancestor of cosmic fossils
The galaxy’s extremely small size provides another clue about its origins. The team estimates that LAP1-B contains less than 3,300 times the Sun’s mass in stars and is associated with a halo dominated by dark matter, the invisible material thought to account for much of the mass in galaxies.
Those characteristics resemble a class of nearby objects called ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs). These exceptionally dim galaxies contain ancient stars and relatively few heavy elements, leading astronomers to suspect that they preserve conditions from the universe’s earliest periods of galaxy formation.
This diagram compares oxygen abundance and carbon-to-oxygen ratios. LAP1-B (red circle) closely matches predictions for material produced by the universe’s first stars (purple region) and the chemical composition of present-day ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (blue outline). Its unusual chemistry suggests enrichment by the earliest stars 13 billion years ago. Grey symbols represent ancient Milky Way stars and distant gas clouds, while orange indicates later stellar enrichment. Credit: Nakajima K. et al., Nature (2026), Springer Nature.
“UFDs are not only the faintest galaxies; they are composed of ancient stars over 12 billion years old and are often described as ‘fossils of the universe,'” explains Professor Masami Ouchi (NAOJ/University of Tokyo), a member of the research team. “Astronomers suspected they might be the remains of the universe’s earliest galaxies because they lack heavy elements, but astronomers never had a direct link—until we found LAP1-B.”
LAP1-B offers a rare opportunity to examine what a possible predecessor of these nearby galaxies actually looked like billions of years ago. Its low oxygen abundance, unusual carbon-to-oxygen ratio, and dark matter-dominated structure are consistent with the idea that today’s ultra-faint dwarf galaxies descended from small systems that formed very early in cosmic history.
“It is a profound surprise to find that LAP1-B looks exactly like the ‘ancestor’ we had only imagined in theories. This helps us solve the mystery of why these cosmic fossils have survived in their current form to the present day.”
The search for even earlier galaxies
Although the findings provide a compelling connection between early galaxies and nearby cosmic fossils, LAP1-B represents one example. Examining more objects with similarly primitive chemical compositions could help researchers determine how common these early systems were and how they developed into the galaxies observed today.
The team plans to continue using JWST to search for even more chemically primitive galaxies, with the ultimate goal of identifying some of the first galaxies ever formed. Such observations could help establish when the earliest stars began producing heavier elements and how those materials spread through the young universe.
Associate Professor Nakajima concludes, “We hope this discovery marks a historic step in understanding how the elements that make up our own bodies were first born and accumulated across the Universe.”
Reference: “An ultra-faint, chemically primitive galaxy forming in the reionization era” by Kimihiko Nakajima, Masami Ouchi, Yuichi Harikane, Eros Vanzella, Yoshiaki Ono, Yuki Isobe, Moka Nishigaki, Takuji Tsujimoto, Fumitaka Nakamura, Yi Xu, Hiroya Umeda and Yechi Zhang, 13 May 2026,

title: James Webb’s Mysteriously Bright Galaxies May Finally Have an Explanation
content:
Artist’s illustration of gas being cleared from the surroundings of a star-forming region in the early universe. Credit: Matt Twombly for Simons Foundation
Calculations suggest powerful ultraviolet light from young stars could sweep gas out of early galaxies while leaving dense star-forming regions intact, offering a clue to their mysterious brightness.
The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed something unexpected about the early universe:
bright galaxies were far more common
just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang than astronomers thought possible. A new analysis suggests these galaxies may not necessarily be producing more light than expected. Instead, powerful ultraviolet radiation from young stars could be clearing away gas and dust, allowing more of their light to reach us.
Researchers at the Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute in New York City and the University of Texas at Dallas investigated this possibility by examining how ultraviolet light called Lyman-alpha radiation interacts with material surrounding young stars. Their findings, published November 4 in
The Astrophysical Journal
, suggest that this radiation can drive gas and dust out of less dense regions of galaxies, potentially explaining why some of the earliest galaxies appear unusually bright.
“Our results show Lyman-alpha radiation can push low-density gas and dust away really, really fast,” says Shyam Menon, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Astrophysics and the study’s lead author. “It can sort of clear the ‘fog,’ allowing us to see stars in the early universe much more clearly than we would otherwise.”
Hydrogen makes ultraviolet light unusually powerful
Lyman-alpha radiation forms when an electron collides with a hydrogen atom or joins a hydrogen ion, and it can be especially abundant in regions where young stars are forming. When this light encounters gas or dust, it transfers momentum to the material, creating pressure that can push it outward.
What makes Lyman-alpha radiation particularly powerful is how hydrogen responds to it. While most absorbed light is released at a different wavelength, hydrogen atoms almost immediately re-emit Lyman-alpha radiation at the same wavelength, allowing nearby atoms to absorb and release it repeatedly. These repeated interactions increase the force exerted by the light, potentially pushing surrounding material away from regions where stars are forming.
An infographic explaining how radiation propelled light-blocking gas and gust. Credit: Lucy Reading-Ikkanda/Simons Foundation
Astronomers have long suspected that this pressure could reshape stellar nurseries by removing gas needed for star formation, possibly even stopping the process under extreme conditions. However, the repeated interactions between radiation and hydrogen are difficult to reproduce in computer simulations, making it challenging to determine how much influence the radiation actually has.
“We’ve known for a very long time that Lyman-alpha radiation could be important because it carries a lot of force,” Menon says. “But we’ve never actually been able to estimate how important it is in a realistic environment because of how challenging it is to model.”
Where ultraviolet light overcomes gravity
To address this problem, Menon and collaborator Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas analyzed snapshots from an existing simulation of a star-forming region in the early universe. Rather than tracking every interaction between light and matter, they calculated how much pressure Lyman-alpha radiation would exert on the surrounding gas and dust.
Their calculations revealed that the radiation behaves differently depending on the density of the surrounding material. In dense star-forming regions, gravity remained strong enough to hold gas and dust in place despite the outward pressure, suggesting that Lyman-alpha radiation had little effect on star formation there. In less crowded regions between stars, however, the radiation could overcome gravity and drive material outward at high speeds.
Multiple views of a 2.5-million-year simulation visualizing a gas cloud as it is cleared away and the formation of stars. From left to right, the views show the gas density, ionization, and temperature. Credit: Shyam Menon (Flatiron Institute) and Aaron Smith (UT Dallas)
“When the density is low enough, the Lyman-alpha radiation can push the gas to really high speeds, launching explosive winds that can shoot material clear out of the galaxy,” Menon says.
These winds could help explain the unexpectedly bright galaxies detected by the James Webb Space Telescope. By removing loosely distributed gas and dust from between stars, the radiation may create clearer paths for starlight to escape, making distant galaxies appear brighter without requiring them to produce unusually large amounts of light.
Three-dimensional simulations remain a challenge
Important questions remain, particularly about the properties of dust in the early universe and how radiation interacts with moving gas as stars form. Researchers will need more comprehensive simulations that account for these processes together to better understand their influence on early galaxies.
Recent work by Olof Nebrin of Stockholm University and study co-author Smith has demonstrated that these interactions can be modeled in two dimensions, although more realistic three-dimensional simulations remain a challenge.
“But the hope is that in the coming years, with improvements to computing power and the development of more effective algorithms, we can eventually do these simulations in three dimensions.”
Reference: “Lyα Radiation Pressure in Dense Star Clusters: Implications for Star Formation and Winds at Cosmic Dawn” by Shyam H. Menon and Aaron Smith, 4 November 2026,
The Astrophysical Journal
DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeaed6

title: Massive Study of 2.8 Million People Reveals New Secrets of Alzheimer’s Disease
content:
The largest genetic study of Alzheimer’s disease to date has uncovered dozens of previously unknown genetic associations, offering new insights into the disease’s complex biology. Credit: Stock
A genetic analysis of 2.8 million people points to specific brain cells that may influence Alzheimer’s, offering researchers new leads to investigate in the search for treatments.
Alzheimer’s disease is the leading cause of dementia, which is projected to affect more than 150 million people worldwide by 2050. Genes play a substantial role in Alzheimer’s risk, but scientists still do not fully understand which genes matter or how they influence the disease. Connecting those genetic clues to what happens inside the brain could help researchers identify possible targets for treatment.
An international team has now identified 127 regions of human DNA associated with Alzheimer’s risk, including 48 that had not previously been mapped in this context. The findings offer a more detailed view of the biological processes involved, pointing to roles for both the brain’s immune cells and several specific types of nerve cells.
Led by Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and published in
, the research is the largest genetic association study of Alzheimer’s to date. Researchers analyzed genetic data from approximately 2.8 million people with diverse genetic backgrounds, including 183,620 people with Alzheimer’s.
Alzheimer’s clues point beyond immune cells
“We already knew that immune processes play an important role in Alzheimer’s disease. What makes this study particularly valuable is that we can now connect new genetic risk factors to more specific biological processes, while also uncovering evidence pointing to the involvement of other brain cell types. This gives us a more detailed picture of the biology underlying Alzheimer’s and provides new directions for investigating potential treatments,” said research lead Danielle Posthuma of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
The analysis strengthened the evidence for the involvement of microglia, immune cells in the brain that help clear away harmful substances and damaged cellular material. Linking genetic risk factors to the processes these cells carry out gives researchers more specific biological connections to investigate.
For the first time, the researchers also identified several specific types of neurons, the cells that receive and transmit information, that were enriched for genetic signals associated with Alzheimer’s. In other words, the genetic evidence pointed toward these particular cell types more often than expected. The findings suggest that they may play a key role in the disease’s development, opening research directions beyond the immune system.
Shared data expands Alzheimer’s genetic map
Pooling data from 30 research groups allowed the team to detect genetic associations that might have gone unnoticed in smaller studies. The collaboration brought together academic researchers, biobanks, and industry under the International Psychiatric Genomics Consortium. Its Alzheimer’s disease working group is co-led by Posthuma and Ole Andreassen of the University of Oslo.
Among the contributors was the University of Exeter-led
study. Professor Anne Corbett of the University of Exeter, who leads PROTECT, said, “This exciting new genetic analysis has uncovered new information on how our genes influence our risk of Alzheimer’s disease. We’re delighted that the PROTECT-UK study contributed to these important new findings. PROTECT collects genetic samples from all participants through a simple at-home saliva sample. This data can then be combined with cohorts from around the world to help us to better understand dementia risk and how it can be treated.”
The genetic associations provide starting points for further investigation, rather than proof that targeting a particular gene will produce an effective treatment. Follow-up research must establish which associations reflect a causal role in Alzheimer’s and whether intervening in the processes involved would be safe and meaningfully beneficial.
Reference: “Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation” by Emil Uffelmann, Douglas P. Wightman, Shahram Bahrami, Alexey A. Shadrin, Vera Fominykh, et al., 28 October 2026,

title: NASA Warns a Monster El Niño Could Surpass the Historic 1997 Event
content:
The 2015-16 El Niño was also very strong, as elevated sea levels in October 2015 (middle) show. But its pattern differed from those in October 1997 (top) and October 2026 (bottom): less of the elevated water reached the coast of South America, which contributed to different weather patterns that year. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory maps by Lauren Dauphin, using NASA-SSH altimetry data provided by Josh Willis, Severine Fournier, and Kevin Marlis, NASA/JPL-Caltech
An El Niño that could beat 1997’s record is taking shape in the Pacific, leaving scientists watching for its next move.
El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that returns roughly every two to seven years. Its most recent
very strong
events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, disrupted weather worldwide. Consequences included
fires in Indonesia
and the Amazon, crop failures caused by
drought in southern Africa
heavy rain
and coastal flooding in Southern California.
Satellite measurements show that the
current El Niño
resembles the 1997–98 event, with warm water stretching across the equatorial Pacific to South America. But that oceanic resemblance does not guarantee the same weather during winter 2026–27, as the outcome also depends on how the atmosphere responds.
How El Niño Builds Momentum
Every El Niño starts with a change in the tropical Pacific’s winds. Trade winds normally push warm surface water westward, leaving sea levels higher in the western Pacific than in the east. When those winds weaken, warm water begins moving back toward the central and eastern Pacific.
As warmth spreads eastward, the trade winds weaken further and sometimes reverse, allowing still more warm water to follow. This feedback loop helps El Niño intensify.
But strength alone does not determine its effects. The location of the warmest water and the atmosphere’s response also shape the outcome. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.”
Satellites Reveal the Ocean’s Heat
Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface. Across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, unusually high water therefore provides a signal of El Niño’s heat buildup.
The maps compare
sea surface height
anomalies on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). JPL scientists processed measurements from
TOPEX/Poseidon
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich
, respectively. Red shows higher-than-average sea levels, white indicates normal conditions, and blue marks lower levels. Seasonal effects and long-term trends have been removed to highlight El Niño and other short-term natural changes.
“What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.”
Why The 1997 Comparison Matters
Although the 2026 El Niño developed much more abruptly, by October it shared two defining features with 1997: lower sea levels in the west and higher levels in the east, with warm, elevated water reaching South America. Willis thinks that resemblance could translate into similar impacts, including the abundant rainfall seen across California and the southern United States in 1997–98.
The powerful 2015–16 event shows why the arrangement of that heat matters. A map based on
measurements from October 12, 2015, appears alongside the 1997 and 2026 comparisons. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator did not reach as far against South America. That winter, rainfall effects were concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States, with significant flooding in Mexico.
NOAA’s October 8, 2026,
El Niño outlook
assigned an 83 percent chance of a strong to very strong event through the first three months of 2027. Still, its effects during winter 2026–27 and beyond remain uncertain. El Niño’s influence passes through a chaotic atmosphere, and its signal becomes harder to distinguish beyond the tropics.
“There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”

title: Researchers Discover New Lace Bug Species on Japan’s Remote Ogasawara Islands
content:
Omoplax desecta (adult). Credit: Jun Souma
DNA uncovered a hidden species among Japan’s lace bugs and hints that a tree introduced by humans could help give rise to another.
Lace bugs living on two groups of Japan’s remote Ogasawara Islands had been classified as a single species, despite differences in their diets and coloring. Comparisons of their DNA have now revealed that they belong to two species, a distinction supported by subtle physical differences.
The archipelago lies roughly 900 to 1,000 kilometers (560 to 620 miles) south of Tokyo and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site. Its land snails and plants are celebrated for including species found nowhere else. About 440 insect species are also known to be unique to the islands, but their evolution has received far less attention.
Omoplax desecta (nymph). Credit: Jun Souma
DNA distinguishes two lace bug species
Among those insects is
, a genus of lace bugs thought to have diversified rapidly across the islands. Jun Souma, of Hirosaki University’s Shirakami Research Center for Environmental Sciences, investigated these insects with Naoyuki Nakahama, of the Graduate School of Agriculture at Osaka Metropolitan University.
“The reason I took a particular interest in
Omoplax desecta
is that it feeds on both the native plant
Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi
and the introduced plant
Calophyllum inophyllum
in the Chichijima island group,” Souma said. “This is quite unusual for lace bugs, which typically exhibit high host specificity. I was also intrigued by the fact that it is distributed across multiple island groups, which is different from other
species.”
To investigate relationships among the insects, the researchers analyzed 52 specimens using MIG-seq, a method that provides DNA data from across the genome. Populations classified as
Omoplax desecta
on the Chichijima and Hahajima island groups were genetically distinct. The study is published in the open-access journal
Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi. Credit: Jun Souma
The genetic evidence helped explain differences Souma had noticed in the Hahajima insects.
“I had wondered why it fed exclusively on
Rhaphiolepis indica var. tashiroi
and why there were no individuals with dark brown to black pronotum, which are sometimes seen in the Chichijima island group,” Souma explained. The pronotum is the plate just behind an insect’s head. “After conducting population genetic and phylogenetic analyses, I began to suspect that this population might be a distinct species. Upon closely observing their morphological characteristics, I was certain of this.”
Subtle differences in male genitalia confirmed the distinction. The Hahajima population is now described as
Omoplax sandoru
, named after the local name of its host plant.
A new diet could divide a species
Omoplax desecta
in the Chichijima group, the introduced tree offered another clue to how these insects might diversify. The DNA data indicate that its shift to feeding on
Calophyllum inophyllum
happened once, and recently. Whether that change will eventually produce another species remains a possibility rather than an established outcome.
“I also find it interesting that the introduction of
Calophyllum inophyllum
Omoplax desecta
,” Souma added.
Calophyllum inophyllum. Credit: Jun Souma
Lookalikes aren’t always the closest relatives
The researchers also reconstructed an evolutionary tree to trace relationships among the insects. That allowed them to test whether species with similar appearances and food preferences were one another’s closest relatives.
“The most surprising finding of my research was that species feeding on the same plant and appearing very similar are not necessarily sister groups,” said Souma, referring to groups that are each other’s closest evolutionary relatives. “Adaptive radiation among insects on oceanic islands may be more complex than comparisons of morphological characteristics and life histories would suggest at first glance.”
Jun Souma, conducting observation on Calophyllum inophyllum where Omoplax desecta feeds. Credit: Jun Souma
Adaptive radiation is the diversification of related organisms into species adapted to different ecological roles. Here, the findings point to both geographic isolation and shifts between host plants as drivers of species formation.
The researchers could not obtain DNA from two rare species, leaving gaps in the evolutionary picture. Further sampling will be needed to trace how these insects reached the islands and diversified.
Reference: “Genome-wide SNP data reveal phylogenetic relationships and further new species of lace bugs (Hemiptera, Heteroptera, Tingidae) endemic to the Japanese oceanic islands (the Ogasawara Islands), providing insight into their speciation” by Jun Souma and Naoyuki Nakahama, 8 October 2026,
DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1294.205145

title: “This Should Not Happen”: Scientists Discover a Strange New Way To Control Atoms
content:
Impression of the experiment where the spins of the electron (blue) and the nucleus (orange) within a single atom are independently controlled by wave signals from the probe tip of a tunneling microscope. Credit: Studio Scixel
A new technique allows researchers to manipulate magnetism deep within a single atom.
Scientists have used radio waves to control the magnetic spin of a single atomic nucleus, achieving a result that challenges their understanding of how atomic magnetism works. The experiment, conducted at
Delft University of Technology
and published in
Nature Communications
, demonstrates that nuclear spin can be manipulated under conditions where researchers did not expect it to respond.
Unlike the relatively strong magnetism associated with electrons, nuclear magnetism is extremely weak and more isolated from its surroundings. “By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons,” says lead researcher Sander Otte. “But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.”
An Unexpected Response From the Atomic Nucleus
To investigate magnetism at the atomic scale, Otte’s team uses a modified scanning tunneling microscope capable of directing electrical signals at individual atoms. Previous experiments primarily examined electron spin, which is easier to detect and manipulate. Nuclear spin could be observed indirectly through the hyperfine interaction, a quantum coupling between the magnetic properties of an electron and the nucleus.
In the latest experiment, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues applied two signals simultaneously, one targeting the electron and another targeting the nucleus. By examining their effects separately, the researchers discovered that they could flip the nuclear spin even when it was largely disentangled from the electron spin. This contradicted their expectation that the nucleus would not respond independently to the microscope’s electrical signals.
“According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen,” says Otte. “The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.”
Controlling Atomic Magnetism With Precise Frequencies
The researchers achieved this control by adapting double magnetic resonance, an established technique, to work with a single atom. The method allowed them to address the nucleus and electron independently using signals tuned to their respective magnetic resonances. In quantum mechanics, spin can change between specific allowed states, and each transition requires a signal with the appropriate frequency.
“You can compare it to the strings of a guitar,” Vennema explains. “Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The ‘notes’ of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.”
Implications for Quantum Information Storage
Nuclear spins are promising candidates for storing quantum information because they are relatively well protected from external disturbances that can disrupt delicate quantum states. The ability to control an individual nuclear spin could eventually support new methods for storing and reading quantum information, although practical applications remain a future possibility.
For now, the experiment leaves a fundamental question unanswered: What physical mechanism allows the nuclear spin to respond when its coupling to the electron spin is insufficient to explain the observed behavior? Understanding that process will require further investigation.
“Back to the drawing board, then,” says Otte. “That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out.”
Reference: “Nuclear magnetic resonance on a single atom with a local probe” by Hester G. Vennema, Cristina Mier, Evert W. Stolte, Leonard Edens, Jinwon Lee and Sander Otte, 24 October 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78801-5

title: Amazon and Google Win Big From Anthropic IPO
content: If you’re looking for a cheaper way of getting exposure to Anthropic than buying the stock directly, consider Amazon or Google. Anthropic’s updated IPO filing on Tuesday shows just how many shares each of those two tech giants will own in Anthropic, along with how much money they’re making on their early investments in the AI firm. Neither tech giant will own voting shares in Anthropic, so antitrust cops won’t have to worry about their influence over its management. But their stakes are significant. In theory, Amazon could own around 20% of Anthropic’s outstanding shares. But because of a self-imposed ownership cap, Amazon won’t hold more than 12% of Anthropic. The rest of its holdings are convertible notes that can convert to equity over time. Regardless, Amazon’s economic return is pretty damn good. Forgetting about the ownership cap for a minute, Amazon’s entire 20%-or-so stake would be worth about $258 billion at the midpoint of Anthropic’s proposed IPO pricing range. That’s from an investment totaling around $18.6 billion. (Anthropic’s final IPO price may well end up higher than the preliminary range, a Financial Times report tonight suggests). Google hasn’t done quite as well. It will end up with a roughly 10% stake worth $132 billion, on an investment of about $33 billion. Still, that’s not bad! Both Amazon and Google have committed to put more money into Anthropic through 2030, under certain conditions, so their investments could grow. (Google’s ownership is also capped, at 14.99%, which will limit how quickly it can convert any convertible notes it gets for future investments). And these numbers represent just the equity investments. Both Amazon and Google are also destined to get a lot of cloud business from Anthropic. Anthropic’s latest filing says it has committed to spend at least $121 billion with Google Cloud through July 2033, “regardless of actual usage.” Additionally, it is committed to spend up to another $150 billion on computing capacity using Google’s TPU AI chips. Anthropic has also committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s cloud unit through 2036—again “regardless of actual usage.” Anthropic has made similar commitments with Microsoft (totaling $49 billion through 2033) and SpaceX (up to $120.5 billion through 2029). Anthropic is a competitor to big tech firms in AI and, increasingly, in software. On Tuesday, for instance, shares of Microsoft and Google fell after Anthropic launched new workplace software apps that compete with productivity applications sold by Microsoft and Google. But it’s swings and roundabouts in this industry. Anthropic owes its existence to advances from big tech firms that were looking to generate some cloud business. Those bets have worked out spectacularly for Big Tech. CoreWeave’s New Financing Tactic For neoclouds looking for ways to finance their data center expansion, getting customers to “prepay” has become a popular tactic, particularly now that interest costs have skyrocketed. CoreWeave is the latest neocloud to call out the benefits of prepayment. “This year we have collected prepayments on 70% of our deals, with customers funding up to 100% of the contract value upfront,” said CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator on Tuesday’s call. But anyone prepaying for computing capacity is likely to ask for some concessions. If interest rates are low, it can be cheaper to borrow money than to take the hit on rates that come from getting customers to prepay. Indeed, CoreWeave hasn’t always been a fan of prepayments. In February, Intrator bragged that it was “very exciting for us” that CoreWeave could reduce its dependency on prepayments thanks to the falling cost of capital. At current interest rates, Intrator said on Tuesday, prepayments are more attractive. “Looking ahead, we will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields,” he said. Davidson will be joining OpenAI to focus on “the future of travel,” he said in an X post. • SoftBank wrote off $3.7 billion spent on non-refundable advance payments to secure data center equipment, reflecting a review of its data center plans, the company said in reporting its September quarter results. title: Anthropic, Others Warn of AI Acceleration
content: In recent weeks, my colleagues and I have been trying our hand at being venture capitalists: today, the end result of that process is our annual list of the 50 most promising startups of this year , published today. We’ve had a pretty good track record in past years: AI startups we’ve previously highlighted include OpenRouter , when the model-routing startup was valued at $500 million; Cursor , when the coding agent was valued at $400 million; and Perplexity , when the AI-powered search engine was valued at $150 million. OpenRouter was recently acquired by Stripe for more than $7 billion, Cursor in August was acquired by SpaceX for $60 billion, and Perplexity was most recently raising at a more than $30 billion valuation. Each year, however, it gets more difficult to pick promising AI startups that fall within our requirements of having raised less than $100 million and being valued less than $1 billion. These days, it feels like the moment any young AI company has a hint of revenue traction, investors are all over them. Still, we’ve managed to uncover a number of under-the-radar gems in this year’s list. In fact, we had trouble whittling down the entrants for our AI infrastructure and security categories, which included everything from companies that help developers train their models using multiple cloud providers to those that use AI to protect employees’ devices. Such companies have become even more important as the rate of AI-powered cyberattacks have increased .— Stephanie Palazzolo Now, onto today’s column… AI researchers that focus on ensuring AI doesn’t harm humans have reason to be a little rattled. Two recent reports suggest AI is advancing even more quickly than previously thought, and that’s increased these safety researchers’ worries that AI will escape human control to wreak havoc. The first report , from AI research nonprofit METR , found Anthropic’s internal AI use is helping it improve the capabilities of its models at around twice its previous speed. Anthropic gave METR access to internal information for the report, published last Thursday. The second report was from the AI Futures Project , a nonprofit whose “AI 2027” forecast, published a year and a half ago, gained attention among safety researchers for predicting superhuman AI would likely arrive by the end of next year. In its new report, out Tuesday, AI Futures Project predicted the advent of superhuman AI researchers—models so good at doing AI research that Anthropic might prefer to fire all their human researchers—by late 2027, compared to 2029 or later in their original forecast. Driving these forecasts, researchers increasingly believe that recursive self-improvement, a continuous loop where one generation of AI models helps build the next generation, may be becoming a reality at AI companies far faster than previously expected. “We're at the beginning of the takeoff period,” Daniel Kokotajlo , the ex- OpenAI researcher who heads the AI Futures Project, told The Information. “All those things that people have been warning about for years and for decades: superintelligence, recursive self-improvement, catastrophic loss of control, it seems like those things are a real possibility in 2027.” Along with these forecasts, Anthropic also updated its IPO filing on Tuesday morning to say it now expected its models to be able to double its non-AI-assisted rate of capabilities progress. Because it had met that threshold, Anthropic’s safety commitments say it should now undertake stronger safety and monitoring measures such as systematically testing that Claude’s behavior and propensities are aligned with human values. Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic employee whose public resignation in September over Anthropic’s efforts towards superintelligent AI made him a minor celebrity, told me he was “glad Anthropic put out some information about this.” “But I don’t think they shared nearly enough,” he said in a statement. “Given the stakes, I think they have a responsibility to provide experts with enough information to assess how fast things are going.” The new reports don’t beat around the bush. In its report, METR wrote that AI R&D acceleration could lead to “extreme and risky capabilities.” “If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict,” METR researcher Ajeya Cotra wrote of last week’s research acceleration finding. These warnings may sound alarmist to a lot of readers. But what spooks some researchers is that AI 2027 has an uncannily good track record with its predictions. The original forecast was initially dismissed as “a work of fiction” by critics including New York University neuroscience professor Gary Marcus . But the report correctly predicted the rise of AI agents and assistants and models speeding up AI research. Some of AI 2027’s predictions were misses. It predicted mass protests against AI, a single leading AI lab in the U.S., and a centralized, government-controlled lab in China, which haven’t come to pass yet. Critics such as Princeton professor Arvind Narayan have argued that even fast progress in AI capabilities takes time to impact society. Google DeepMind research scientist Sebastian Krier over the weekend criticized METR’s report as relying on flawed measures, and argued that one factor that might slow down Anthropic’s progress is the fact that developing and running these uber-advanced models has gotten so expensive. But for some AI researchers I spoke to this week, such criticisms haven’t diminished their sense that AI is moving incredibly fast—faster than most people thought—and so are the risks. Their expected probabilities of doom, or P(doom) , have just shot up. Here’s what else is going on… Earnings Report CoreWeave reported third quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, more than double the year earlier number of $1.365 billion, but its losses also ballooned. SoftBank wrote off $3.7 billion spent on non-refundable advance payments to secure data center equipment, reflecting a review of its data center plans, the company said in reporting its September quarter results. title: Booz Allen Switches to Nvidia’s Nemotron
content: Nvidia is managing the worst hit to its reputation in its three-decade history from the revelations that its CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly working for China’s spy agencies (read our latest on that here ). But in one bright spot for the AI chip giant, there are early signs of headway in its efforts to build the world’s best open-source models . Booz Allen Hamilton—the $10 billion-market capitalization government contractor—several months ago switched from primarily using Anthropic’s models to run its software for cybersecurity and defense to using Nvidia’s Nemotron models, CTO Bill Vass told me. That move has resulted in significant cost savings, he said, though the company declined to share specifics. (Booz Allen spends tens of millions of dollars annually on AI, according to a person familiar with the company.) “What we've been doing is the opposite of tokenmaxxing,” the term for using as much AI as possible, Vass said in an August interview. When it comes to actually building, rather than running, its software, Booz Allen developers still mostly use Anthropic’s Claude Code unless its customers ask them to use other coding tools, Vass said. That’s likely because Claude Code is still lauded as the best tool for software engineering. However, Vass said he is interested in having the firm’s developers use Nemotron models for coding as their capabilities improve. Nemotron has been making inroads with contractors and government agencies in part thanks to its relationship with Palantir. The software firm and Nvidia have partnered more closely lately, as both companies have positioned themselves as suppliers of AI that can help enterprises avoid relying on frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. Nvidia recently signed a big deal to use Palantir’s software internally to manage its supply chain. And Palantir in late June launched a product aimed at helping U.S. government agencies and enterprises use Nvidia open source models through its software. Some government customers have already switched from closed-source frontier AI models to Nemotron, Palantir CEO Alex Karp told me this summer. It’s not just big customers trying Nemotron. Open-source coding software platform Kilo Code says Nvidia’s Nemotron models accounted for nearly 17% of the roughly 50 trillion tokens processed through its software in October, up from 8% the previous month. Individual developers as well as those from small and large enterprises primarily use Kilo Code to access open source models for coding work. Despite that progress, Nvidia’s models are still eclipsed by frontier models. Nemotron models accounted for just about 4% of tokens processed through OpenRouter over the past month, down slightly from a peak of 7% one week in August. OpenRouter, the Stripe-owned software that lets businesses autonomously switch between different models from one place, processes a lot more tokens than KiloCode (about 700 trillion monthly) and for a broader set of tasks than coding. So far in November, Anthropic accounted for a higher share (31%) of OpenRouter customers’ spending than any other AI provider, while Nvidia accounted for less than 1% of spending. Tokens as Benefits Those OpenRouter statistics show that most companies are still spending the lion’s share of their AI budgets on Anthropic’s models. As those firms look to moderate spending, they’re diverging on whether to dictate firm token caps to their software engineers, as I laid out in this story today with Phoebe and Catherine. That’s becoming a sticking point for engineers. Maria Colacurcio, the CEO of human resources software startup Syndio, said talent acquisition leaders at Syndio’s large enterprise clients have begun receiving requests from new job candidates to get higher token budgets as part of their employment packages. The requests come after the candidates are offered the job for higher or unlimited token budgets and access to the latest OpenAI and Anthropic models. “So there's all of these sort of side addendums being created where candidates are getting basically agreements to these carve outs,” she explained. Right now, these aren’t formal benefits. “Nobody‘s writing it down. It’s not really part of policy,” she said. If AI prices stay high and enterprises further restrict spending—as companies such as Apple, Microsoft, and Disney have—tokens could potentially become a formalized, coveted employee benefit. title: Introducing The Information’s 50 Most Promising Startups of 2026
content: As artificial intelligence changes how companies get hacked, investors are paying up for startups that promise to keep defenders ahead. That dynamic shaped this year’s The Information 50 , our annual list of the most promising startups. For the first time, our list includes a category devoted solely to security, and it holds some of the list’s biggest bets. Two of the four most highly valued companies in this seventh edition of the list are security startups valued at more than $1 billion apiece, and six of the security firms are run by Israelis, which have a long history of breakout hits in this field. At a time when many people use AI to research new companies, our reporters didn’t use AI to find candidates. They just had good ol’ fashioned conversations with dozens of founders and investors—including many that pointed us to startups they missed out on—and collected hard data on revenue and growth rates at the companies. You can view the list here , and join our conference call for The Information subscribers at 12pm PT / 3pm ET to discuss the list with several of the founders whose companies are on it. To qualify for the list, startups must have raised $100 million or less in equity funding while being valued at less than $1 billion, or be less than two years old and valued at $1.5 billion or less. The cap in prior lists was $1 billion, but valuation inflation prompted us to relax it. Security is one of seven categories this year, alongside enterprise apps, AI infrastructure (mainly software), deep tech (bio, energy, defense), robotics, crypto and fintech, and Asia. The seven startups in our security category are products of the AI era. All were founded in 2024 or later, and most use AI agents to do work that has long fallen to human security staff, such as triaging alerts, hunting threats and probing for weaknesses. The pressure on defenders is coming from several directions. AI-driven attacks are generating more security alerts, and companies are producing more code thanks in part to AI, which has increased potential weak spots. Hackers also keep getting in through the devices employees use at work, as in the recent $6 billion crypto heist of Binance, which began with hackers tricking an employee into downloading malware. Startups are positioning themselves as cheaper alternatives to cybersecurity-focused models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, which can scan customers’ code for vulnerabilities. Those models are expensive and often turn up dozens or hundreds of potential holes, leaving companies unsure what to patch first. Tenzai’s AI, for instance, tries to hack customers the way sophisticated attackers would, aiming to find the vulnerabilities that pose the biggest immediate risk, and it is cheaper to run than Mythos or Astra. Another security startup focuses on protecting more than business’ code: securing networks, cloud infrastructure and employee devices, too. Others on the list want to replace tools security teams already use, including so-called endpoint software that protects employee devices; or do the grunt work of a corporate security operations center, deciding whether alerts are malicious, responding to threats and hunting for new ones. Two of the security startups on the list that got started this year don’t want their data in the public cloud. One of them, Cylake , founded this year by Palo Alto Networks co-founder Nir Zuk, sells hardware and software to companies and governments that run computing in their own data centers or private clouds. Zuk says the majority of cyberattacks will continue to be related to tricking employees (including phishing), hiring people who become insider threats or inserting malicious code in other software and hardware (so-called supply chain attacks), rather than to AI that exploits application vulnerabilities. As Rene Bonvanie, Cylake’s chief marketing officer, put it, “Attackers will successfully get in; the focus in cyber has to shift on deploying techniques to catch them as fast as possible based on their behavior.” The Rest AI agents run through much of the rest of the list . In the enterprise apps category, one startup’s product fields calls and books appointments for HVAC and plumbing businesses, and another startup’s AI agents scour invoices and supplier contracts, then try to negotiate better terms. These startups are battling for customers against a slew of other startups as well as SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, which are pushing their own workplace agents. Some of the list’s most capital-efficient companies are involved with software “infrastructure” for AI. One of them makes models run faster and more cheaply on Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices chips, generating more than $40 million in annualized revenue with 16 employees. Another startup in that category provides performance and cost benchmarks for AI models, is on pace to generate more than $100 million annually yet has a valuation of less than $100 million. It also hasn’t raised much capital. Startups in the deep tech category are working on compact gas turbines, truck-borne batteries and aluminum-fueled backup generators, among other things. The category also includes AI drug discovery startups. Four of the seven robotics startups collect, sell, manage or evaluate the physical-world data robot developers need. Another firm that generates data for humanoid developers, Noitom Robotics (“motion” spelled backwards), which is listed in the Asia category, says it counts all the major American frontier AI developers as customers. Other highlights from the list: We broke our unwritten rule of not naming the same company in multiple The Information 50 lists. In this year’s list, AI agent startup Town was included despite being named to last year’s list because it has pivoted its business model since then and is widely viewed as an attractive acquisition target. Most companies on the list generate revenue, but some are just getting started. Eight generate no revenue, up from six last year. Two others didn’t disclose revenue, and two describe theirs as nominal. The startups on our list, mirroring other AI firms, are hitting sales milestones earlier than ever. Twenty-three companies generate more than $10 million in annualized revenue, up from 20 last year and 13 in 2024. Four generate more than $70 million, the same as last year. Twenty-four companies were founded in 2025 or 2026, including seven founded this year. The oldest, a longevity drug developer, was founded nearly a decade ago but has gained renewed traction this year. The vast majority of companies are small. Just nine have more than 100 employees, the same as in each of the past two years. At least five have fewer than 20. Many founders, including Zuk, previously started or worked at successful technology firms. Greylock showed up most often among investors that led funding rounds in companies on our list. The 60-year-old firm backed five companies on the list, including three of the seven security startups. Sequoia Capital and Battery Ventures each led rounds in five; Andreessen Horowitz , Benchmark , and Y Combinator each led or co-led rounds in four startups on our list, and CRV and Lux Capital led or co-led three. Outside Asia, corporate investors were scarce again. Nvidia , Qualcomm and Samsung all backed robot-data startups on our list, and the OpenAI Startup Fund backed one of the AI agents on our list. That’s a far cry from our 2024 list, when OpenAI invested in eight of the companies. In Asia, tech giants showed up as key investors once again; they included Ant Group , Meituan and Tencent . Other Chinese entries count regional and university-affiliated funds such as Henan Investment Group, Kunshan High-tech Venture Capital and Tsinghua Holdings Capital among their leading backers.

title: OpenAI Revenue Jumps to $10 Billion in Third Quarter Amid Growing Losses
content: OpenAI has told investors that revenue jumped nearly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, rebounding from a period of slower growth as demand for its more recent models and enterprise products picked up, according to a person familiar with the matter. However, the company’s operating losses also grew during the third quarter from $10.1 billion to $10.9 billion, the person said, demonstrating how it is still struggling to make its sprawling business model profitable. There are signs of progress: Its adjusted operating margin improved from -150% to -109%. The company shared some financial metrics with investors during a call on Tuesday as it seeks to close a new fundraising round at a $1.25 trillion valuation. OpenAI’s revenue growth is higher than the 17% gain in the second quarter from the first. The third-quarter revenue figure was 2.6 times the year-ago quarter. Demand for the company’s recent model releases, including GPT 5.6 and Astra, as well as image models drove sales of its models through its application programming interface. The company’s topline also benefited from growing ad sales, which reached a $1 billion annualized pace in August. OpenAI’s loss was far larger than that of rival Anthropic, who reported an operating deficit of $567 million in the third quarter. At the same time, OpenAI’s revenue is still trailing Anthropic’s, which hit nearly $17 billion in the third quarter, up 47% from the second quarter. Anthropic’s revenue overtook OpenAI’s in the second quarter of this year as the company’s focus on building tools for enterprises, including its popular Claude Code coding tool and Claude Cowork agent, paid off. OpenAI, which started as a consumer app, scrambled to get a bigger piece of these developers’ dollars. It started to throw more resources toward its own coding tool, Codex, abandoned some projects like a video app , and pursued more contracts with large companies. OpenAI President Greg Brockman said last week that OpenAI’s enterprise business doubled during the third quarter and now makes up a majority of OpenAI’s revenue. Unlike Anthropic, OpenAI still has a large consumer business. The company said last month it has 1.2 billion weekly active users, the vast majority of which are using the platform for free. In the third quarter, the company reached nearly 100 million paying users, the person with knowledge said. It added about 200 million non-paying users and 22 million paying users, the person said. OpenAI has been trying to make money from its consumer business through advertising, which has emerged as a bright spot for the business after reaching a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate in August.

title: The Anthropic-OpenAI Valuation Gap
content: If you want proof of the widening gap in sentiment between public and private investors, take a look at the valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI. On Tuesday, Anthropic disclosed it was targeting a valuation of between $1.26 trillion and $1.4 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. The prospectus update comes on the heels of OpenAI’s most recent fundraising, which valued the company at $1.25 trillion . That means Anthropic expects public investors to value it at only 12% more than OpenAI, assuming it achieves the valuation at the high end of its range. That is in spite of the fact that Anthropic generated 70% revenue than OpenAI in the third quarter and has been growing far faster for much of this year. Still, Anthropic’s advisers may be guiding the valuation downward now to make sure there’s plenty of demand for the stock on the first day of trading. There’s a good chance Anthropic can increase the IPO price or sell even more shares if investors’ demand is strong, as some Anthropic investors are expecting. As I reported today , OpenAI told investors it had generated $10 billion in third quarter revenue, up nearly 50% from the second. Increased use of Codex and demand for image models helped growth rebound from a sluggish second quarter. Still, OpenAI trails Anthropic, whose third quarter revenue neared $17 billion in the third quarter, up 47% from the second. Of course there are important differences in how each company reports revenue generated from sales of their AI through cloud partners—but not enough to make up for the sales gap. And Anthropic looks like it’s held onto its lead in the current quarter. Anthropic’s annualized revenue pace—roughly its last 28 days time 13—hit $81 billion in October, up nearly six times the comparable figure in February . OpenAI’s annualized revenue was nearing $50 billion in September, double its February pace . (Its October pace couldn’t be learned.) Anthropic is also a more efficient business compared to OpenAI. As revenue picked up steam in the third quarter, OpenAI operating losses rose to $10.9 billion, slightly up from $10.1 billion in the second quarter, said a person familiar with the matter. Anthropic also reported an operating loss, but a far smaller one. It swung to a $567 million loss in the third quarter, mostly due to costs to secure short-term computing capacity and $2 billion to match donations made by employees. Public investors have been notably skittish about tech stocks, sending the Nasdaq Composite last month to its worst month since March 2025 on concerns about the returns on AI investments. Those jitters grew after the Democratic sweep in Congress made it likely that more AI data centers will face delays. That cautiousness doesn’t seem to have spilled over in a big way to private markets yet, as Morgan Stanley tech banker Diana Doyle reminded me last month. The real referendum on whether public and private markets are converging will happen in the next few months, after Anthropic lists its shares and while OpenAI fills out the second, $9 billion installment of its fundraise. Just on fundamentals, the fastest growing company should sport the highest revenue multiple. But private investors have been known to inject a bit more hope into their valuations than public shareholders—suggesting this gap could hold. title: Why HubSpot, Snowflake and Others Are Avoiding AI Spending Caps
content: While some companies are curbing employees’ AI use to contain soaring costs, many others in the tech industry are pushing ahead with full-throttle spending. As the chart below shows, large cloud providers including Amazon Web Services and software firms such as Palantir, Snowflake and HubSpot haven’t put firm caps on engineers’ spending as employees use AI coding tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex to build apps and features. Neither have the frontier labs themselves. And venture capitalists say many of their portfolio companies are still urging employees to use as much AI as possible. Meanwhile, Salesforce in recent months has moved to implement team-level spending caps for its forward deployed engineers, who are focused on building AI agents for customers, according to a person familiar with the company. Not all those employees are aware of the caps, though: one Salesforce forward deployed engineer told The Information they believed their budget was unlimited. The different practices show how industry leaders are taking sharply divergent views on how to manage AI use more than half a year after concerns erupted about soaring spending. In April, The Information reported Uber had already blown through its full-year AI budget and that Meta Platforms employees had been competing to consume as many AI tokens—the units of information processed by AI models—as possible in a phenomenon known as tokenmaxxing. Around that time, many companies began voicing concerns about the high cost of AI tools. Meta has told staff that it plans to implement caps on engineers’ AI spending, and Uber developed its own software for coding called a harness that can swap between different AI models to cut costs. At enterprise software company Workday, the per-engineer budget starts very low, typically ranging between $100 and $300 monthly, according to an engineer at the company. (A Workday spokesperson said that budget is a “starting point,” not a firm “ceiling,” and Chief Technology Officer Gabe Monroy said in an interview that additional budgets are granted for special projects.) For startups invested by Salt Lake City-based Oquirrh Ventures, the budgets are bigger, even though the companies are all far smaller than Workday, with $15 million to $80 in annual sales. Eight tech companies backed by the venture firm have around $500 per engineer spend budgets, said Oquirrh founder Ron Heinz. Some companies are still trying to encourage engineers to use coding tools. Duncan Lennox, chief product and technology officer at HubSpot, said the software company has been pushing engineers to use its in-house coding tool that can swap between Anthropic, OpenAI and open-source models. Of the company’s more than 2,000 engineers, about 15% regularly used the coding tool for their jobs at the start of the year. By late September, that figure had surged to more than 90%. Cost is “not a significant issue,” Lennox said, because the coding tool has improved engineers’ productivity so much. That’s also true for most of the roughly 50 portfolio companies of venture capital firm S3 Ventures and the more than two dozen early stage portfolio firms of Bain Capital Ventures, none of which have firm token caps. “As an early stage, venture-backed company, your imperative is to be at the frontier of technology, both in the product you deliver but also the tools you give your employees,” said Bain Capital Ventures partner Alysaa Co. “So I think we’re seeing very little control on spending,  and I think that’s the right approach.” S3 Ventures partner Eric Engineer said part of what’s making its portfolio companies less nervous about cost is that they’re reducing their workforces or slowing hiring. Compared to the cost of hiring another engineer, he said, spending large sums on AI coding tools is “not a big deal, and they’re not feeling like they need to put a cap on it if they’re getting the value.” Tech companies such as Rippling and Uber have token budgets, but they are relatively high and engineers can request higher spending levels, which are typically granted. Similarly, software firm Autodesk gives teams a budget equal to $2,500 per engineer for each month, but team leaders decide how that budget is allocated to their teams. Of course, some companies are pulling back. Walmart recently lowered the token budgets for engineers, according to an employee. Apple also cut its engineers’ daily budgets to $200 from $300, according to Bloomberg. Microsoft recently slashed monthly budgets for engineers by a tenth, The Information reported last month. And one Disney software engineer said the company has paused employee requests to tap its tiered AI coding tool budgets, which range from $50 per month to $25,000. Other companies that don’t have caps are moving toward them. Blackstone is set to introduce caps on engineers’ spending with new settings from its main cloud platform, AWS, that can limit AI spending per employee, according to a person familiar with the company. In the coming quarters, the private equity firm will likely set its budget around $5,000 per month for power users of coding tools and AI models, while employees who use less AI users may have a lower limit of $250 per month, though they’ll be able to request higher amounts. Matt Garman, chief executive of AWS, said during Blackstone’s technology conference in San Jose last week that the hyperscaler has let employees “go crazy” experimenting with AI tools for productive purposes but advises them not to waste company money. He pointed to the example of one employee he said used company AI tools to create a TV sitcom. “ And I was like, ‘Great. Is that the best use of company money?’ Like, probably not,” he said. While Amazon doesn’t have spend limits now, it’s moderating costs by using tools that autonomously route engineers’ requests between different frontier and open-source models, which has in some cases reduced costs by 40% for engineering work, Garman said. Amazon and other AI providers also are planning or providing features to make it easier for customers to track spending. Customers of Anthropic’s Claude Enterprise can set spending limits for their company or individual employees and can view a dashboard launched this summer showing AI usage. OpenAI has similar capabilities. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the companies most central to the AI boom are letting their own employees use as many tokens as they need. An OpenAI spokesperson said its lack of a cap is because the company thinks arbitrary limits would constrain experimentation—though OpenAI does have internal dashboards that show per-employee usage and doesn’t encourage tokenmaxxing, according to the spokesperson. At Nvidia, one employee said AI budgets are as high as $50,000 monthly per engineer and up to $10,000 for non-engineers. Another employee said they know of only one person in the company to ever hit the cap, and that person was using open source AI to generate data for model training.

11月8日，“数智江淮·科创兴皖”2026人工智能创新生态大会在安徽合肥举行。紧扣“算力为基、电力为擎”的下一代数智基础设施命题，“算电协同产业研讨会”同期召开。依托安徽作为国家算力网络重要布局区域的天然禀赋，本次研讨会通过主题演讲、前沿发布、成果展示与高端对话等多元形式，联动政府、企业、科研机构与生态伙伴，深度探讨算电协同与人工智能融合发展的产业路径，旨在助力安徽“十五五”开好局、起好步，加速构建中部数字经济新高地，为千行百业提供绿色、高效、可靠的算力供给新范式。
安徽省新型储能产业创新联盟秘书长张炜表示，当前，算电协同已成为能源转型与数字经济提质增效的关键。安徽新型储能产业基础扎实，2025年全省新型储能产业营收达1131.3亿元，同比增长26.6%，已形成从硅片、电池、组件到储能电芯、系统集成的完整产业链，拥有阳光电源、国轩高科等龙头企业。下一步，联盟将推动算力设施与光储企业专项对接，联合科研机构、检测认证机构和龙头企业组建算电协同专业委员会，探索制定团体标准和技术指引，把光储产业优势转化为算力产业的能源优势。
华为综合能源服务军团副总裁陈斌提出，人工智能正成为培育新质生产力、赋能实体经济的核心驱动力。安徽紧扣国家战略布局未来产业，合肥综合性科学中心人工智能研究院与华为公司将发挥院企协同优势，共同打造省级高水平产学研用合作平台，加速前沿成果转化落地，助力建设全国人工智能创新与数智产业发展新高地。安徽在算力端依托芜湖作为国家“东数西算”八大算力节点之一的优势，正加快筑牢以华为昇腾为代表的自主创新软硬件底座；在电力端，安徽作为长三角重要能源供给基地，以强韧电网支撑算力中心绿色低碳演进，推动“比特流”与“瓦特流”深度融合。
在主题分享环节，华为综合能源服务军团副总裁陈斌表示，算电协同是数字经济与能源革命深度融合的必然趋势。2026年，国家首次将算电协同纳入新基建工程，四部委发布《关于促进人工智能与能源双向赋能的行动方案》，提出到2030年人工智能算力设施的清洁能源供给保障能力达到世界领先水平，届时算力需求将激增。面对算力与绿电时空错配，华为提出规划、建设、调度、市场四个协同统筹破解发展痛点：通过“算电同址、发训网推”让绿电就近消纳、降低用能成本，推动从“供电保障”向“算电一体化”生态运营演进。算电协同从绿电到Token实现价值重构，可帮助发电企业实现第二增长曲线。
安徽省电力设计院综合能源公司副总经理袁辉认为，随着智算中心加速发展，算力与电力深度耦合，算力中心设计需统筹选址、能效、绿电与冷却等关键环节。她结合国家数据中心项目申报要求介绍，芜湖作为国家级数据中心节点城市，到重要城市时延不超过
毫秒，且兼具水资源与电力优势；项目需满足PUE、综合能耗、绿电比例不低于80%、节点上架率不低于65%等窗口指导要求。在算效提升方面，可通过高效电源模块、800伏直流供电、AI优化配电与制冷等方式降低损耗；在冷却方案上，需综合服务器功率密度、建设地气候与水资源条件、全生命周期投资成本确定风冷或液冷路径。
会议提出，算力与电力双向赋能已成为数字经济发展的关键支撑，安徽依托完整的先进光伏与新型储能产业链、日益密集的算力基础设施布局，正加快把产业优势转化为算力产业的能源优势。面向未来，随着算电协同标准体系逐步完善、示范项目加快落地，“比特流”与“瓦特流”的深度融合将持续释放绿色动能，为千行百业提供更绿色、更高效、更可靠的算力供给，助力安徽加速构建中部数字经济新高地，为全国算电协同产业发展贡献可复制、可推广的实践经验。

title: 中国石油乙丙橡胶单月销量首破万吨大关
content:
（通讯员 王臻 王涛涛）11月9日，笔者从化工销售运营中心合成橡胶产品线获悉，中国石油乙丙橡胶市场攻坚取得突破，产品不仅成功在电线电缆、车用材料等多个高端领域实现进口替代，而且9月份的销量首次突破万吨，产业链效益同步攀升，创下历史最好水平。
近期，乙丙橡胶下游市场需求持续低迷，整体以刚需为主，库存承压明显。为破解产品经营难题，化工销售事业部、运营中心坚持以市场为导向，充分发挥专业化管理效能，联动生产、研发、销售等企业组建产销研用攻坚小组，连续开展市场走访40余天、服务客户20余人次。今年以来，公司新增客户58家，市场开拓成效持续显现。
乙丙橡胶作为中国石油打造的“产品巨人”，化工销售聚焦开拓高端市场，主攻新能源汽车密封、光伏线缆和家电密封制品等高增长高附加值领域。其中，二元胶产品进口替代率明显提高，目前市场占有率超55%；三元车用密封条专用料打破了高端车用乙丙橡胶长期依赖进口的格局，成功进入航空航天、核电线缆等高门槛应用场景，成为该领域的核心供应商。
进入9月份，合成橡胶产品线抓住下游刚需订单集中释放窗口期，精准对接客户需求，当月销量环比提升32%。截至目前，今年产品总销量同比增长43.7%，在市场下行周期中跑出逆势增长曲线。

title: 云南石化：标定“实打实” 开工“妥妥的”
content:
图为云南石化工作人员检查即将送检的石脑油半成品样品。 黄晓洪 摄
“标定工作是对装置大检修后能耗水平、催化剂使用情况的全面检验，为装置后续安稳长满优运行提供数据支撑。”11月6日，生产运行部工作人员徐焱说。
为保障标定工作科学有序，云南石化充分研判高负荷工况下的各类运行风险，提前制定针对性管控措施。先后组织4次标定对接会，逐一明确各装置加工负荷、标定时间、采样频次及分析项目，同步敲定物料平衡核算、设备效率测算、技改技措项目验证等工作要求。通过提前对接、逐项梳理，打通了从生产操作到化验分析的全流程节点，推动标定工作从“按计划实施”向“高标准管控”升级，确保标定过程规范严谨、数据真实可靠。
截至目前，云南石化已完成20套装置高负荷标定，摸清了高负荷下装置的运行性能、设备效率与瓶颈短板。标定结果显示，各装置具备高负荷运行条件，主要技术经济指标达到预期水平。（王慧 唐龙 文）

title: 兰州石化设备内磨损检测有了“智慧助手”
content:
技术人员使用新系统进行润滑油铁谱分析。王淼 摄
（记者 武庭宇 通讯员 孟凡薇）11月5日，兰州石化研究院（科技创新中心）数智化专业研发团队技术人员使用新研发的润滑油铁谱图像智能分析系统，对一批新采集的机组油样进行磨损状态检测。屏幕上，铁谱图像上传、识别、分类、诊断等流程一气呵成，原本依赖人工经验的分析工作，如今有了智能化助手全程辅助。
润滑油铁谱分析结果被称为设备内部磨损的“晴雨表”。铁谱分析通过分析油液中的金属磨粒来判断设备的磨损程度，是保障机组长周期运行的关键技术。然而，传统的分析模式长期依赖人工显微镜观察，既耗时耗力，又因缺乏相应标准，难以精准记录测量数据。
“过去，我们全靠肉眼在显微镜下计数、分类，一天最多处理20个油样。”从事铁谱分析多年的工程师李磊感慨道。人工计数存在误差，磨损趋势模型难以建立，制约了设备预知性维修水平的提升。
为解决这一难题，兰州石化立足关键机组长周期运行保障需求，将人工智能技术引入铁谱分析。
“数据标注是最大的瓶颈。”研发负责人胡建斌介绍，通用模型难以精准识别磨粒形态。研发团队将325份铁谱图像按类型逐张标注、交叉验证，将疲劳、切削、黏着、腐蚀等磨损形态与故障原因一一对应，反复训练模型。
在技术攻关中，团队坚持“软硬兼施”。通过显微镜物镜测微尺进行比例尺标定，并优化光源系统以提升成像色彩还原度，为智能识别奠定了高质量的图像基础。同时，系统通过嵌入式开发，无缝集成于现有分析软件，确保了业务流程的平稳过渡。
目前，该系统已在多台关键机组试点应用。单份油样分析全流程耗时由30分钟压缩至5分钟以内，磨粒识别准确率稳定在90%以上。“系统不仅提升了检测效率，而且为决策提供了依据。”一线技术人员李宝生表示，过去靠肉眼反复确认的结论，如今有了数据支撑，大幅降低了误判与漏判风险。
从人工识别到智能诊断，润滑油铁谱图像智能分析系统的上线，为设备维护从经验判断向数据驱动转型提供支撑。“智能系统不会取代分析师，而是将我们从重复性劳动中解放出来，去从事更有价值的综合研判和维修决策。”胡建斌说。

title: 冀东油田：风雪井场“攻坚令”
content:
图为员工顶风冒雪进行修井作业。 杨军 摄
11月8日清晨，河北唐山迎来今年冬天的首场降雪。冀东油田高53-27井作业现场，井下作业公司特种作业分公司带压一队二班正在召开班前风险辨识会。
“今天的作业工序是起打捞管柱，安全风险是机械伤害、卡钻、液压钳伤人，大家施工过程中要注意安全。尤其是一岗和二岗，要注意雪天钻台湿滑，防止摔伤。”技术员姜璐瑶说。
室外大雪纷飞。一岗孙国明望着窗外，有些犹豫：“是不是等雪小点再干？”带班干部、队长李立东说：“工序不等人，班前巡回检查完后就干。”他环视了一圈现场，又说道，“在座的也有党员，党的二十届五中全会公报学习了吧？今年还剩不到2个月，作为基层班组，我们要牢记全会强调的，要做好岁末年初各项工作。干活的时候，各岗位要紧盯结冰打滑、设备冻堵等风险。同时，做好防寒保温，坚决守住年终安全底线。”
9时，修井机的轰鸣声震落了滚筒上的积雪，全班队员在风雪中忙碌起来，争分夺秒地冲刺年终生产任务目标。

title: 华北石化加氢裂化催化剂完成国产化替代
content:
（通讯员 张守志）11月6日，从华北石化传来消息，该公司在290万吨/年蜡油加氢裂化装置上，成功应用华北石化与石化院联合研发的加氢裂化催化剂，实现一次开车成功并连续稳定运行，完成国产化替代，为进一步增产航煤提供了新的技术支撑。
近年来，华北石化深挖装置潜能增产航煤，不断提升保供北京大兴国际机场的能力。技术团队开展联合攻关，结合装置特点，量身定制了增产航煤的催化剂方案，成功开发并应用了PHT-01/PHC-03/PHC-06加氢精制/裂化催化剂组合技术。其中，PHC-06催化剂创新采用了兼具选择性裂化和异构功能的先进介孔分子筛材料，大幅增强了蜡油分子定向转化能力，满足了最大量生产优质低冰点航煤的技术需求。
装置完成催化剂装填并开工后，顺利产出符合3号喷气燃料标准的合格航煤产品，航煤收率提升至40%。
目前，装置各项运行参数平稳。华北石化与石化院正组织进一步优化操作，以提高航煤收率、增加航煤产量。此次自主研发催化剂在大型蜡油加氢裂化装置上的成功应用，标志着该类型催化剂国产化替代迈出实质性一步，也为华北石化减油增化、转型升级提供了有力的技术支撑。

title: 四川石化：从算“产量账”到算“效益账”的观念突围
content:
11月6日，四川石化智能运营中心的大屏幕上有节奏地刷新着生产数据，趋势曲线平稳变化。与此同时，生产装置区里的设备轰鸣声昼夜不息。就在这日复一日的坚守中，今年，公司累计原油加工量突破亿吨、乙烯产量突破千万吨，乙烯单月收率不断创出新高。
时针拨回到“十四五”开局，炼化行业发展态势已变：一头是成品油需求见顶，另一头是高端化工材料长期依赖进口。这意味着，依靠规模扩张的路走到了尽头，转型发展势在必行。四川石化以乙烯为龙头，向内抓平稳、向外盯市场、向深挖需求、向新求突破，一步步蹚出转型之路。
坚持大平稳出大效益
10月30日8时，化工一部工艺工程师董万军早早来到岗位，调出DCS监控界面，目光顺着乙烯裂解气压缩机的参数趋势缓缓移动；装置现场，外操孙乐巡检到机组前，与内操马建山逐项核对仪表参数，不放过任何细微偏差。
“大平稳出大效益”是四川石化员工长期秉持的信条，在乙烯装置运行中得到生动印证。
但实现平稳运行并非易事。随着装置持续高负荷运行，部分裂解炉对流段积灰问题逐渐显现，直接制约乙烯装置高效运行。对此，公司开展“一装置一策”攻关行动，制定台历化清洗等6项管控措施，运行瓶颈逐一突破。
以裂解气压缩机为代表的乙烯三机组，被称作乙烯装置的“心脏”。公司组建“机电仪管操”五位一体常态化特护小组，每月召开例会，逐项分析运行工况，陆续解决存在的问题，关键机组保持连续多年零故障运行。
装置稳得住，还要“吃得好”。公司及时动态优化乙烯原料构成，让裂解炉COT等工艺参数随“料”而变、动态寻优。
在日复一日的精细守护中，乙烯装置收率显著提高，不断创出历史新高。
把资源、生产、市场统筹起来
装置稳了，产品怎么排？
“我们要把资源、生产、市场统筹起来，集中研判最优方案。”在公司月度经营例会后，计划经营部管理人员蔡桥玉说出了自己的体会。
面对竞争日趋激烈的化工产品市场，“产什么就卖什么”的老路越走越窄。四川石化摒弃旧观念，立起“市场需要什么，就生产什么”的新标尺。
于是，四川石化锚定“稳产、增优、提效、去库”方向，打出了紧跟市场变化提升经营质效的“组合拳”。
四川石化开发的抗冲共聚产品可用于蓄电池外壳等下游制品生产，市场需求逐渐旺盛。公司抢抓机遇，组成联合服务团队，会同销售企业对接产销两端，走访市场、开发客户，根据用户需求滚动排产。短短3个月，主力牌号单月销量攀升近28%。
近年来，公司不断优化生产组织，保障高效产品高负荷生产，同时坚持以销定产，精准把握产品出厂节奏，将产品库存维持在合理水平。线性低密度聚乙烯、高密度聚乙烯、乙二醇等乙烯下游高效产品的产销量均实现显著增长。
从算“产量账”到算“效益账”，市场导向理念渗透进四川石化生产经营的每个环节。
客户难题就是攻关的课题
“PP-H M0200的弯曲模量较竞品高出不少，但改性客户希望热变形温度再高点，这个调整难度不小，还请你们继续攻关。”“客户需要一款抗穿刺性能较好的新型膜料，你们能否开发一下？”
在四川石化规划和科技信息部，科技新材料管理人员黄健打开通信软件，置顶的几个下游企业对接群中，讨论一轮接着一轮。
市场需要什么，怎样解决客户的难题？这些直接来自一线客户的声音，成为公司新材料研发的主攻方向。
客户的难题就是攻关的课题。公司攻关小组深入调研新能源汽车零部件、高端家电外壳等下游市场需求，反复开展配方筛选、小试评价和转产推演。经过数月的连续攻关，PP-H M0200产品在保持高刚性优势的同时，热变形温度显著提升，满足了用户对轻量化与耐热性的双重严苛要求。
与此同时，聚丙烯纤维专用料纺丝性能、气味控制等技术难题也被相继攻克，填补了公司在纤维料市场的空白。在新型膜料领域，公司正围绕高抗穿刺性能等关键指标加快攻关步伐，推动产品结构向中高端持续升级。
向高端突围，绕不开“卡脖子”的坎。
长期以来，高端牌号聚烯烃生产所需的催化剂、助剂等高度依赖进口。公司把国产化替代列为攻关重点，从通用聚烯烃“三剂”国产化起步，与科研院所协同攻关，历经多轮实验验证和迭代优化，逐步向高端聚烯烃催化剂和添加剂领域延伸突破。近期，公司完成了抗冲催化剂及给电子体国产化工业试验，实现了国产成核剂替代。
“目前公司已形成车用料、改性塑料两大拳头产品，高端聚烯烃产品矩阵正逐步成形。”公司研发中心一级工程师鲁成祥说。
相同的产量，变化的是逐渐增大的产品附加值。四川石化让研发方向从实验室走向市场，让客户需求真正牵引技术攻关。
记者观察：观念一转 赛道自宽
“要把资源、生产、市场统筹起来，集中研判最优方案”，这本身就是一次从“产什么就卖什么”到“市场需要什么就生产什么”，从算“产量账”到算“效益账”的观念改变。
四川石化破除旧观念，把市场导向、效益导向、需求导向树立起来，让生产组织、产品排产、库存管理、客户服务都围绕效益转，围绕市场转，围绕高质量发展转。
转，不是简单地换赛道，而是换思路。从以产量为中心转向以效益为中心，从生产型转向经营型，从产品型转向材料型。观念一变，路径更宽；思路一转，空间更大。
转型的密码，写在几组关键词里：以稳筑基、以需定产、以新破局。稳是底盘，需求是方向，创新是突破口。效益的持续提升，反映出的不只是装置实力，更是观念之变、经营之变、创新之变。密码不写在纸上，它写在装置的长周期运行里，写在客户的订单里。

title: 广西石化高端双端官能化溶聚丁苯橡胶稳定规模化量产
content:
（记者 李芳 通讯员 周晓红）11月6日记者获悉，广西石化建设的12万吨/年溶聚丁苯橡胶装置顺利实现双端官能化产品SSBR2055DF2稳定量产，公司高端合成橡胶量产能力日趋成熟、国产替代步伐持续提速。
广西石化12万吨/年溶聚丁苯橡胶装置依托中国石油完全自主知识产权技术建设，是集团公司首建、国内同工艺规模领先的标杆项目。装置精准聚焦新能源轮胎高端材料供应短板，专注于官能化高端橡胶产品的研发生产。自2025年10月投产以来，装置已成功稳定产出SSBR3540DF、SSBR2055DF2、SSBR1530DF三款高端产品，丰富了公司高端橡胶产品矩阵，有效填补了国内高端轮胎橡胶市场缺口，为国内橡胶轮胎产业提质升级提供了坚实的原料支撑。
今年，为实现产品稳产优产，公司组建专项技术攻坚团队，持续开展工艺迭代优化。技术人员深度对接下游市场需求，结合客户生产反馈精准优化产品分子结构，精准适配轮胎行业生产工艺标准。同时有针对性地破解首次量产中，装置后处理干燥系统波动、生产负荷受限等难题，完成关键设备系统性升级改造，彻底打通满负荷连续生产瓶颈，实现产能、质量、稳定性全方位提升。
此次高端双端官能化溶聚丁苯橡胶稳定规模化量产，有效补齐了国内产业链短板，保障了轮胎关键原材料供应链安全。
目前，该装置已全面具备双端官能化系列产品满负荷稳定生产能力。SSBR2055DF2产品凭借优异性能和高性价比，可等量替代进口产品，顺利进入国内头部轮胎企业供应链评价体系。广西石化正持续深耕高端精细化工领域，不断优化产品品质、拓展市场场景，以自主可控的高端新材料，赋能交通行业绿色低碳发展，助力企业打造世界一流炼化一体化品牌。
SSBR2055DF2：国产高性能轮胎材料“韧星”
SSBR2055DF2是中国石油自主研发、广西石化独家量产的高端双端官能化溶聚丁苯橡胶，被誉为国产高性能轮胎材料“韧星”，是绿色节能轮胎升级换代的核心战略性材料。
若将汽车轮胎比作车辆前行的“足底跑鞋”，SSBR2055DF2便是支撑跑鞋性能的核心弹性骨架，兼具柔韧度、抓地力与耐久性，在原材料端提升了轮胎的综合品质。产品采用先进的间歇法聚合与双端官能化改性核心技术，通过优化分子链结构，大幅增强橡胶与白炭黑填料的结合强度，彻底改善传统橡胶生热高、滚阻大、耐磨性能弱、湿滑抓地力不足等缺点。
该产品综合性能严苛对标国际标准，成功平衡“低滚动阻力、高抗湿滑、强耐磨损”三大核心性能。既能有效降低车辆行驶能耗、助力交通领域节能降碳，又能大幅提升雨雪、湿滑路面制动稳定性，全方位提升行车安全系数，同时具备优良的耐老化、耐候特性，可实现四季全天候稳定适配。
在市场应用层面，SSBR2055DF2精准匹配当前行业发展趋势，主攻中高端乘用车、新能源汽车四季胎胎面胶核心市场，适配城市通勤、高速行驶、复杂路况等多元使用环境，高度契合新能源汽车低能耗、长续航、高安全的核心需求。
产品工艺兼容性强、混炼性能稳定，可直接等量替代进口高端牌号，适配下游企业规模化量产节奏。作为国产高端橡胶标杆产品，SSBR2055DF2凭借稳定品质、成本优势、自主供应链优势，持续助力轮胎行业降本增效、转型升级，为国内新材料产业自主可控、绿色高质量发展注入持久动力。（李芳）

title: 渤海钻探第一钻井公司：“数智大脑”助钻机提速
content:
页岩油区块施工现场。 张秋亮 摄
员工正在进行起钻作业。 张秋亮 摄
11月9日，渤海钻探第一钻井公司顺利完成吉林油田英台地区深层天然气钻井项目，实现13开13完，钻井周期与钻完井周期均缩短20%以上。

title: 热饮暖心
content:
11月9日清晨6时，烟台气温骤降至4摄氏度。环卫司机王师傅完成清扫作业，驶入山东销售烟台分公司金沙江路加油站爱心驿站。
加油员丁宁递上一杯刚磨好的热咖啡：“王哥，天凉了，喝杯咖啡暖暖身子。”在氤氲的香气里接过咖啡，王师傅笑着说道：“这杯咖啡下肚，浑身就热乎了。”
秋季气温骤降，山东销售烟台分公司因时、因地制宜，在26座爱心驿站同步升级服务内容，将凉茶、冷饮服务改为供应咖啡、奶茶、热饭、休憩等暖心服务。
分公司统一梳理各驿站服务清单，明确季节切换节点和饮品供应标准，让户外劳动者随时有个“歇脚地”、喝上一口“应季水”。
驿站各设一名“驿站管家”，由站经理兼任，负责设施巡检、物品补给和诉求登记，咖啡豆、姜茶包等消耗品按周盘点、及时补充。
与此同时，各驿站主动与周边环卫公司、快递公司以及物流车队等建立联系，互留联系方式、互通作业时段，用一杯咖啡、一次洗衣、一处歇脚，架起了一座座连心桥。（史凤凯 摄）

title: 锦西石化尿素脱蜡装置VOCs项目一次开车成功
content:
（记者 李吟竹 通讯员 曹肃 宫柳杨）11月5日，记者从锦西石化获悉，该公司尿素脱蜡装置VOCs（挥发性有机物）环保隐患治理项目顺利打通全流程，实现一次开车成功。此项目是锦西石化今年重点环保治理项目之一，投运后可有效解决装置储罐呼吸线无组织排放问题，进一步提升废气治理水平。
项目建设期间，锦西石化严格落实安全文明施工管理要求，压实各环节质量管控责任，紧盯节点推进现场施工。各专业人员紧密衔接、协同联动，高效完成设备安装、管线配管、仪表接线等工作。
中交完成后，项目团队立即启动标准化试运行工作。现场技术与操作人员严格按照VOCs治理专项开工方案，分步推进各项调试任务。先后完成3台无动力设备投用、系统贯通试压与气密试验、5台机泵单机运转及联锁逻辑调试，并将装置内各储罐及单元并入治理系统。
作业全过程严格执行标准化操作流程，落实双人复核、逐项签字确认制度，严守试运操作规范。各班组人员紧盯现场、精细管控，逐罐逐线核查管线密封点位，细致排查VOCs泄漏风险，反复校验仪表监测数据与联锁动作的可靠性。对试运期间发现的微小隐患，项目团队坚持问题导向，做到立查立改，确保每一道工序合格后方可进入下一阶段，保障开工过程平稳有序。
该项目开车成功后，实现了VOCs废气集中收集与无害化处理，补齐装置环保短板；稳定满足现行环保管控要求，降低装置环保合规风险。通过稳定尾气治理工况，减少现场异味，为装置日常平稳生产操作创造有利条件。

title: 【答疑室】光伏储能电站项目当前进度如何？鸿富瀚回应
content:
【中国能源产业发展网】获悉，据中证金牛座报道，近日，有投资者在互动平台向鸿富瀚提问：公司的光伏储能电站项目当前进度如何？2026年11月10日，鸿富瀚回复称，公司光伏储能电站项目已实现并网发电，具体经营数据以年度经审计数据为准。
公开回复显示，围绕光伏储能电站项目进度这一提问，鸿富瀚给出了并网发电的阶段性进展，同时将经营数据的披露口径指向年度经审计数据。除项目进展外，公司在回复中还提及了业务布局方面的安排：重点布局液冷、机器人两大新兴业务，培育新的业绩增长点，积极拓展海内外市场。
消息面上，近日，国家能源局发展规划司副司长邢翼腾在新闻发布会上表示，截至2026年9月底，全国已建成投运新型储能装机规模达1.67亿千瓦/4.35亿千瓦时，同比增长63%。从发布会披露的其他数据看，平均储能时长为2.61小时，同比提升约0.27小时；全国新型储能等效利用小时数约915小时，同比增加约10小时。
对于储能市场的后续空间，机构认为，随着算力用电需求增长，绿电直连及源网荷储协同有望进一步打开储能市场空间。万联证券研报显示，2026年10月，中国储能招标规模为17.0GW，同比增长70.0%。
万联证券研报同时指出，储能招投标规模是装机规模的前置指标。在强制配储取消后，招投标规模保持高增长，显示装机需求韧性，有望支撑未来储能装机规模增长。
按公开披露口径，鸿富瀚光伏储能电站项目已实现并网发电，经营数据以年度经审计数据为准；国家能源局公布的全国新型储能装机规模、平均储能时长与等效利用小时数均对应截至2026年9月底的情况；万联证券研报将储能招投标规模视为装机规模前置指标，并指出强制配储取消后招投标规模保持高增长。
