title: Predicting power output from artistic BIPV pixel by pixel - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers have developed a model linking artwork colors to power output and potential hot-spot risks in colored BIPV arrays. Simulations of 50 masterpieces show how selectively darkening bright pixels can improve electrical performance.
Lior Kahana
12 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Illustration of BIPV façades displaying Girl with a Pearl Earring
A South Korean research team has developed a novel model to predict power output and hot-spot risk in colored building-integrated PV (c-BIPV) systems featuring artistic images. The researchers modeled PV arrays displaying 50 masterpieces, including Johannes Vermeer’s
Girl with a Pearl Earring
and Vincent van Gogh’s
Café Terrace at Night.
“Unlike a uniformly colored module, an image-based array contains many differently colored cells. Because each color requires a different optical reflection profile, the photocurrent generated by each cell can vary across the array,” corresponding author Hyung-Jun Song told
pv magazine
. “This spatial mismatch can reduce power output and, under certain bypass-diode configurations, expose cells to reverse bias and hot-spot risk.”
The novelty of the research, Song added, lies in directly linking the visual characteristics of a candidate image to the electrical performance and reliability of the entire PV array. “For every pixel, we estimated the minimum-loss selective-reflection spectrum needed to reproduce its color and calculated the resulting photocurrent. We then used equivalent-circuit simulations to evaluate the series-connected array under different bypass-diode configurations,” he explained.
Schematic of an artwork-based colored PV array | Image: Seoul National University of Science and Technology
In its work, the group has converted each of the 50 artworks into a 36 × 36-pixel mosaic, with each of the 1,296 pixels representing an individual series-connected PV cell. They assigned each pixel the average color of its corresponding image region. For each color, they calculated an ideal dual-band selective-reflection spectrum, selecting the reflection-band parameters that most closely reproduced the target color. They then calculated the photocurrent generated from the sunlight transmitted through the colored layer, accounting for the underlying cell’s wavelength-dependent internal quantum efficiency.
Using a single-diode equivalent circuit calibrated to commercial TOPCon cells, they modeled each cell’s current-voltage characteristics at 300 K. They simulated the fully series-connected array in LTspice. The simulations compared configurations without bypass diodes and with one diode protecting between one and 36 cells, assessing maximum power output and the number of cells operating under reverse bias at the maximum power point as an indicator of potential hot-spot risk.
“One of the most surprising findings was that the overall brightness or colorfulness of an image does not necessarily determine its photovoltaic performance. Instead, the spatial distribution of brightness plays a much more important role,” Song said about the results. For example, the simulated array displaying
Café Terrace at Night
achieved 91.7% of the power output of an equivalent black reference array without bypass diodes, compared with 74.3% for
Girl with a Pearl Earring
“We found that even a small number of extremely bright pixels can limit the power output of an entire series-connected PV array,” the researcher added. “We also identified an interesting trade-off associated with bypass diodes: installing more diodes can improve power output, but it may simultaneously increase reverse-bias conditions and the associated hot-spot risk.”
Illustration of BIPV façades displaying
Café Terrace at Night
Girl with a Pearl Earring
, installing one bypass diode per cell increased normalized power from 74.3% to 84.4% of the black reference array’s output, a 13.6% relative improvement. However, 24 of the 1,296 cells entered reverse bias at the maximum power point. Selectively darkening those 24 pixels instead raised normalized power to 84.8% without bypass diodes, while avoiding reverse-biased cells under the simulated conditions.
“Based on these findings, we developed a screening framework that classifies artistic images according to their expected power performance and hot-spot risk, using only two image-derived parameters: the brightest pixel and the overall brightness variation,” the academic added. “The framework was further examined using additional images, demonstrating its potential to assess the electrical suitability of candidate artwork without requiring a full circuit-level simulation for every image.”
Concluding, Song said that his team is planning a few follow-up studies. These include incorporating measured reflectance spectra into a more realistic optical model, expanding the image database, and developing an AI-assisted tool to assess uploaded images and suggest modifications that improve power output and reduce hot-spot risks while preserving their appearance.
The article “
Prediction Model for Power Output and Hot-spot Risk in Colored Photovoltaic Arrays with Artistic Image
” has appeared in
. Researchers from South Korea’s
Seoul National University of Science and Technology
Gachon University
have participated in the study.

title: Spanish IPP deploys automated solar installation platform at 457 MW Texas project - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Matrix Renewables is using Terabase Energy’s Terafab V2 automated construction platform at its 457 MW Tormes Solar project in Navarro County, Texas. The system combines robotic module assembly, automated quality inspection, autonomous transport vehicles and digital construction management tools.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
12 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
United States
Utility-scale
The Terafab platform
Spain-based independent power producer (IPP)
Matrix Renewables
is deploying Terafab V2, an automated solar construction platform developed by US-based Terabase Energy, at part of its 457 MW Tormes Solar project in Navarro County, Texas. California-based Solv Energy is serving as an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor on the project.
Terafab V2 combines robotic assembly, AI-assisted quality inspection and autonomous vehicles to streamline module assembly and transportation, shifting labor-intensive construction activities from the solar field to an automated production line installed on-site.
According to Matrix Renewables, PV modules and structural components are delivered to the on-site assembly line, where robotic equipment mounts the modules onto tracker torque tubes. The completed assemblies then pass through an integrated quality inspection system before being transported to their installation locations.
The modular “factory” is designed for rapid deployment and relocation within a construction site. Terabase says the latest version can be moved and set up in approximately four hours, allowing the assembly line to be repositioned as construction progresses.
Following inspection, robotic equipment loads the completed assemblies onto autonomous vehicles, known as rovers, which transport them to designated locations in the solar field. Workers then unload the assemblies and install them onto prepositioned tracker supports.
Terafab V2 incorporates a manufacturing execution system (MES) to coordinate assembly operations, material flows, quality inspections and transportation.
The platform also integrates construction planning, inventory management and logistics software with a digital twin of the project site. AI-assisted tools support workflow optimization and the coordination of automated equipment.
The system’s modular architecture allows multiple assembly lines to operate at a single project, increasing production capacity according to construction requirements.
Terabase says Terafab V2 is designed for continuous operation, with a production cycle of approximately two minutes per assembly. According to the company, each line could achieve an output of around 20 MW per week under continuous operating conditions.
The company claims its automated construction approach can double labor productivity compared with conventional utility-scale PV installation methods. Actual output depends on project configuration, equipment utilization and site conditions.
Terabase has been developing its automated solar construction technology for several years.
pv magazine
reported in August 2022
, the company raised $44 million in a Series B financing round to support its digital and robotic construction platforms. Earlier that year, it had deployed its technology to install 10 MW of capacity at a 400 MW solar project in central Texas.
May 2023
, Terabase announced the launch of its Terafab automated installation system and opened a manufacturing facility in Woodland, California. The company described the plant as a “factory to make factories.”
Later that year, Terabase completed its
first commercial Terafab installation
, using the system to build 17 MW of a 225 MW solar project in Arizona developed by Leeward Renewable Energy, with RES serving as the construction contractor.
The V2 platform represents a further step in the company’s automation strategy. In
April 2026, Terabase told
pv magazine
that the upgraded system had completed field testing and was ready for commercial deployment.
The new version features a more compact factory design, increased automation and faster assembly operations. It is currently optimized for First Solar Series 7 modules and Nextpower trackers, although Terabase plans to expand compatibility with other module and tracker technologies.
Terabase said the first-generation Terafab platform had been used to install approximately 40 MW of tracker-mounted solar capacity across several US projects.
While the current system automates module assembly, inspection, loading and transportation, the final installation of the assembled PV tables onto tracker supports still requires workers. Terabase has said it is developing additional robotics to automate this step in a future version of the platform.

title: Sweden plans new inverter and battery database - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Sweden plans to launch a voluntary database for solar inverters, battery storage systems and bidirectional EV charging equipment in 2027, replacing its existing pre-assessment system for new listings. The database will provide standardized technical documentation to support grid connection assessments by network operators.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Inverters
Sweden is preparing to replace its existing list of pre-assessed solar and battery inverters with a new digital database in 2027, according to Swedish energy industry association Energiföretagen Sverige.
The new system, called Rikta Rätt 2.0, will provide standardized technical information on inverters used in solar photovoltaic and battery energy storage installations, helping electricity distribution system operators (DSOs) assess grid connection applications.
“The basic requirements for inclusion in the new database will be limited to contact information, manufacturer name and type designation. However, inclusion will not constitute an approval or demonstrate compliance with technical requirements,” a spokesperson for Energiföretagen Sverige told
pv magazine
. “The database will provide relevant technical information and supporting documentation for each model. Manufacturers must provide supporting documentation where required, for example certificates when claiming conformity with a particular standard.”
Rikta Rätt 2.0 will not require additional product testing solely for inclusion in the database. Technical information will generally be supported by certificates, test reports and other documentation from existing testing and conformity assessment procedures.
“The approach is similar to the current Rikta Rätt process, but more transparent: the database will show technical information and supporting documentation on which the network operator can base its assessment.,” the spokesperson added. “The categories and associated requirements are still being finalized, but the documentation requirements are expected to remain close to those applied in the current Rikta Rätt.”
Inverter models already included in the current Rikta Rätt list will remain on
the PDF version of the list
CSV version
will be removed from the Energiföretagen Sverige’s website at the end of 2027.
“There will be no automatic migration to Rikta Rätt 2.0. Manufacturers and importers will need to apply for inclusion in the new database and provide the information and documentation required for the relevant categories,” the spokesperson specified.
According to Energiföretagen Sverige, the transition will not change the existing grid connection approval process for solar PV installations, as individual network operators will retain responsibility for assessing compliance.
“The final compliance assessment is already carried out by individual network operators, but we understand the concern about potentially inconsistent requirements. Grid conditions vary, and the aim is to provide a common structure while allowing requirements to be adapted to actual conditions. Compared to the current Rikta Rätt, the new approach should result in less restrictive and more appropriately targeted requirements. It will be sufficient for an inverter to meet the requirements relevant to actual grid conditions, at a level of detail manageable for manufacturers and network operators,” the spokesperson stated. “We do not expect approval times to increase significantly once the new procedure is established. Instead of checking whether a product is listed in Rikta Rätt, network operators will check a small number of relevant data points in the Rikta Rätt 2.0 database.”
Cybersecurity is not currently planned as a separate category within Rikta Rätt 2.0, although Energiföretagen Sverige may consider adding further categories as regulations evolve.
“Manufacturers and network operators are subject to an increasingly extensive cybersecurity regulatory framework. Cybersecurity is already part of the requirements relevant to CE marking, with requirements will become more extensive in the coming years. Verifying actual compliance as part of a product assessment remains challenging, particularly where conformity can be demonstrated through manufacturer self-assessment,” the spokesperson added. “We will continue to follow regulatory developments and consider whether additional categories should be incorporated into the Rikta Rätt 2.0 database in the future.”
The voluntary Rikta Rätt 2.0 database is scheduled to open in early 2027, while new listings under the existing system will cease in September 2027.

title: Viessmann launches propane ground-source heat pump compatible with PVT systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy uses R290 refrigerant and delivers heating capacities ranging from 6 kW to 16 kW, with a maximum flow temperature of 70 C and a seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) of up to 5.5.
Emiliano Bellini
12 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy (ie) heat pump
German heating specialist
Viessmann
has launched the Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy (ie), a new inverter-driven brine-to-water heat pump designed for indoor installation in new and existing residential buildings.
The system uses propane (R290) as its refrigerant and features an integrated active safety system for refrigerant management.
The heat pump is available in three versions, designated 06, 12 and 16, with modulating heating capacity ranges of 1.8 kW to 9.3 kW, 3.2 kW to 12.2 kW, and 3.2 kW to 15.6 kW, respectively. Their nominal heating outputs at a brine inlet temperature of 0 C and a heating water temperature of 35 C (B0/W35) are 3.25 kW, 5.26 kW and 6.16 kW, with corresponding coefficients of performance (COPs) of 4.7, 5.0 and 5.0.
All three models measure 1,018 mm × 600 mm × 680 mm. The smallest version weighs 167 kg, while the two larger models weigh 185 kg each. The floor-standing units require an installation footprint of approximately 0.5 m2.
Viessmann said the system achieves an SCOP of up to 5.5 in low-temperature applications, with seasonal space-heating efficiency of up to 212% and an A+++ energy efficiency rating.
The heat pump delivers flow temperatures of up to 70 C, making it suitable for heating system retrofits as well as new installations, according to the manufacturer. The smallest model has a sound power level of 34 dB(A) under European Union Energy-related Products (ErP) testing conditions.
The system can also be connected to photovoltaic-thermal (PVT) collectors, which can serve as an alternative heat source to conventional geothermal boreholes while simultaneously generating electricity. Existing boreholes can be reused when replacing older ground-source heat pumps.
Viessmann said up to four units can be connected in a cascade configuration, providing a combined heating capacity of up to 64 kW. A single universal controller manages the entire cascade.
The heat pump incorporates the company’s One Base Intelligence control platform, which enables integration with photovoltaic systems, battery storage, electric vehicle charging equipment and compatible third-party devices. Its integrated energy management system supports weather-based optimization and dynamic electricity tariffs, while the ViCare app enables remote monitoring and control.
An optional natural cooling function uses the relatively low ground temperature to provide indoor cooling during summer. According to Viessmann, the feature can reduce indoor temperatures by up to 3 C.
The Vitocal 300-G intelligent energy is available for order, with deliveries scheduled to begin on Nov. 30, 2026. A compact version with an integrated domestic hot water storage tank is expected to become available in April 2027.

title: Financial institutions back 2 GW of solar in Türkiye - pv magazine Global
content:
A total of eight international financial institutions have signed letters of support for the financing of two solar power plants in Türkiye with a total planned capacity of 2 GW.
The two solar plants, to be located in the Sivas, central Türkiye, and Taşeli, southern Türkiye, will each have a capacity of 1 GW.
They will be undertaken by Riyadh-headquartered developer Acwa Power. They form part of an agreement
signed by Türkiye and Saudi Arabia in February
that stipulated Saudi Arabian companies would develop 5 GW of solar and wind projects in Türkiye.
Acwa Power is aiming for both power plants, representing a total investment of approximately €1.6 billion ($1.77 billion), to be operational by 2029. They are expected to provide electricity to a combined 1.3 million households.
The financial agreements were signed by the Asian Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, Deutsche Investitions-und Entwicklungsgesellschaft, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, International Finance Corporation, Islamic Development Bank, Société Générale and Standard Chartered.
The agreements were entered into on the sidelines of COP31, which is ongoing until November 20.
Speaking about the remaining 3 GW in the 5 GW deal with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye’s Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said the remaining capacity could be wind or solar projects.
“We also aim to include storage in this,” Bayraktar added. “For example, when you add the high-voltage power lines that will carry electricity from Karaman to Istanbul or to the west, this means a package worth 5-6 billion dollars.”
Türkiye kicked off COP31 by unveiling its new national energy policy, including a target of
installing 175 GW of solar and wind by 2040
. The aim builds on its goal of reaching 120 GW of combined solar and wind capacity by 2035.
The country’s cumulative solar capacity stood at around 26.9 GW by the end of the first half of 2026, after adding
2.1 GW across the first six months of the year
4.7 GW across 2025
Türkiye’s most recent renewable energy tender concluded recently, awarding
785 MW of solar capacity
across 11 projects.

title: Longi launches new products for the Australian market - pv magazine Global
content:
What new module technology is L
ONGi introducing in Australia?
Brett Robinson: We’ve released two major products at this show. The first, the X12, is for the domestic market. The X12 is a back contact, 54 half-cell module, 1,800 x 1,134 x 30 mm. It has an efficiency exceeding 25% and a top power class around 510 watts. It’s a perfect size for the compact roofs in Australia.
For our C&I side, we’ve released a product called the X10 Ultimate. It’s got a slightly lower efficiency rating compared to the X12, but the unit cost is a bit lower as well. The key to the product is that it is 2,382 x 1,134 mm in size, but the power class approaches 680 watts.
What is L
ONGi doing for utility scale scenarios?
Robinson: In the past year, LONGi delivered more than 1.4 GW across all Australian solar PV segments and, in particular, our back contact Hi-MO 9 modules have been selected for many projects across Australasia. For the utility market, we launched the Hi-MO 9 Prime, which is 2,382 x 1,134 mm in size. While the module’s output will approach 680 watts, at the moment it’s around 665 watts, which still leads the market in products currently available for purchase. With the Hi-MO 9 Prime, we’ve increased the average power class by between 7 and 10 watts, which is a 1.5% to 2% increase in the panel output. And LONGi offers customers a 30-year warranty.
How does L
ONGi support Australian installers?
Robinson: We have an exclusive distribution agreement with Raystech, which is an Australian-owned family business with offices all over Australia and in New Zealand. They have undertaken and commit to undertaking training work with installers so they can become LONGi approved installers with accreditation from Australia’s Clean Energy Council.
What is your take on the Australian solar and storage market and how it’s evolving?
Dennis She: With its high penetration of renewable energy, I think Australia is very unique. One-third of homeowners already have solar on their roof. But the challenge will be not only to produce more renewable energy, but to make it more reliable, dispatchable, and flexible, to support a more resilient grid.
How is L
ONGi addressing the growing demand for integrated solar and storage technologies across both residential and C&I sectors?
She: Our strategy is to develop a fully integrated product in-house, so we created the “LONGi ONE” to combine solar and energy storage as a single solution with higher efficiency and more reliability. “LONGi ONE” customers get our turnkey one-stop service for the whole lifetime of the system.
What are the key innovations in L
ONGi’s latest energy storage solutions and what is their value for the Australian market?
She: LONGi has what we call 5S native full-stack innovation, which includes the BMS, iCCS, EMS, PCS, and TMS. The first value is that the system is much safer, because all the components talk to each other. Secondly, it’s about the segmentations. There are a lot of applications for energy storage in Australia, and LONGi has a different kind of product for each segmentation, developed based on the demand or requirement from customers’ real applications.

title: Major solar-storage project provides round-the-clock power in DRC Congo - pv magazine Global
content:
Africa’s largest copper mine is now running on solar baseload power thanks to a large-scale solar-plus-storage power plant.
The Kamoa-Kakula Copper Complex, located in the Central African Copperbelt near Kolwezi in the Democratic Republic of Congo, has been powered by a 233 MW solar plant coupled with a 123 MVA/526 MWh battery energy storage system since the facility entered commercial operation on August 12. The system provides the copper complex with a continuous 30 MW power supply, with output currently peaking at 55 MW.
The facility is owned and operated by project developers CrossBoundary Energy, with Germany’s Dhybrid Power Systems GmbH responsible for engineering the battery system and providing the facility’s control platform.
Figures provided by Dhybrid state that during its first month of operation, the facility displaced around 4 million liters of diesel, worth roughly $11 million.
The project combines over 357,000 solar modules from Aiko, Sungrow solar inverters and medium-voltage stations, battery containers from Risen SYL and EPC Power power conversion systems.
Dhybrid says its universal power platform (UPP) acts as the central control layer for the entire plant, coordinating the solar and battery inverters, power quality meters, protection relays, meteorological sensors, UPS and HVAC units and managed network switches, equating to over 1,300 devices in total.
A statement from the company explains the UPP’s forecasting algorithm tells the operator twenty-four hours ahead what the plant can deliver. “The operator sets the value, and the platform decides every second how to split up to 180 MW of solar between the mine and the batteries, how far to charge for the night, and how to hold the setpoint through cloud cover and load swings,” the statement explains. “The customer only sees constant power output.”
Dhybrid has been awarded a contract to expand the battery system by a further 35 MWh, to an installed capacity of 561 MWh, with targeted commercial operations in January 2027.
The complex has also set a target of raising its on-site solar baseload capacity to 120 MW within 18 months.
The project is DRC Congo’s largest operational solar asset, according to figures available in the Africa Solar Industry Association’s (AFISA) project database. The database lists a total 1,381 MW of operational solar in the country, alongside a further 132 MW under construction.

title: Mexico's distributed solar capacity tops 5.65 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Mexico’s cumulative distributed generation capacity reached 5,675.47 MW at the end of June 2026, according to figures published by the National Energy Commission (CNE) on Nov. 4. The country added 485.76 MW in the first half of the year, up 9.4% from the 5,189.71 MW recorded at the end of 2025. Solar accounted for nearly all the new capacity, with 484.36 MW added during the period.
The number of processed interconnection applications increased from 600,651 at the end of 2025 to 655,417 in June 2026, an increase of 54,766, or 9.1%. Solar accounted for 655,124 cumulative applications and 5,649.34 MW of installed capacity, compared with 600,368 applications and 5,164.98 MW at the end of 2025.
Jalisco led Mexico’s states in cumulative distributed generation capacity, with 808.58 MW, followed by Nuevo León with 596.22 MW and Chihuahua with 424.85 MW. Together, the three states accounted for 32.24% of the national total. Guanajuato, Coahuila, the State of Mexico, Sonora and Yucatán followed.
Cumulative investment in distributed generation reached an estimated $14.58 billion, according to the CNE, up approximately $1.25 billion from $13.34 billion at the end of 2025. Investment in solar installations accounted for an estimated $14.46 billion of the total.
Net metering accounted for 648,260 processed interconnection applications and 5,596.65 MW of installed capacity. Systems up to 50 kW represented 98.23% of applications under this scheme, with 636,775 registrations and 3,557.98 MW of capacity. Installations ranging from 250 kW to 500 kW accounted for 2,600 applications and 1,081.98 MW.
The latest figures update the
year-end 2025 statistics
previously reported by
pv magazine México
in June. They confirm that solar remains the dominant distributed generation technology in Mexico, ahead of biogas, biomass, cogeneration and small-scale wind power.
The comparison covers installations registered under the distributed generation framework introduced in 2017, excluding legacy contracts under the former small- and medium-scale generation scheme. This provides a consistent basis for comparing figures from December 2025 and June 2026.

title: New glass-to-glass PV module design enables rapid delamination - pv magazine Global
content:
An international research team has developed an induction heating-assisted delamination method for end-of-life photovoltaic modules to improve recyclability and facilitate the recovery of individual components.
“We designed a glass-glass photovoltaic module that is easier to take apart at the end of its life,” corresponding author Yonghwan Lee told
pv magazine
. “Using induction heating, we rapidly separated the layers of our test module and recovered 99.8% of its original mass, including the glass, the silicon cell and the polymer encapsulant.”
Lee said the team was surprised by how quickly and cleanly the silicon cell separated using the new technique and modified module design.
“In our fastest test, the module layers separated in just 5 seconds. We recovered the cell intact, with no visible polymer residue on its surface, without having to remove the entire encapsulant layer first,” he said.
The researchers first used Comsol Multiphysics simulations to investigate induction heating in passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC) cells and heat transfer through the surrounding module layers. They examined the effects of operating frequency, coil current, coil-to-cell distance and electrode thickness on heating.
They then produced simplified samples comprising a 2 cm × 2 cm PERC cell laminated onto tempered glass with ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulant, leaving the rear of the cell exposed. They tested the method using a water-cooled copper induction coil operating at 270 kHz to 300 kHz to rapidly heat the cell’s metal contacts, triggering localized EVA decomposition at the cell-encapsulant interface. The samples were suspended with the cells facing downward to enable gravity-assisted separation.
The tests showed that induction heating created a temperature difference of more than 200 C between the cell and glass at a coil current of 100 A, enabling localized EVA decomposition at the cell interface. With gravity-assisted separation, the cells detached in approximately 14 seconds.
Microscopy revealed no significant polymer residue or structural damage on the recovered cell surfaces, while spectroscopy indicated that the remaining EVA largely retained its chemical structure.
The researchers then fabricated modified glass-glass mini-modules incorporating a single PERC cell, EVA encapsulant and two tempered glass sheets measuring 5 cm × 8 cm and 1 mm thick. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) release films, each with a central opening measuring 1.8 cm × 1.8 cm, were inserted between the cell and EVA on both sides to allow gases generated during heating to escape. The researchers suspended the mini-modules in a custom support jig and applied induction heating at coil currents of 100 A, 150 A and 200 A.
The modified mini-modules separated in 18.6 seconds at a coil current of 100 A, compared with 8.3 seconds at 150 A and 5.4 seconds at 200 A. The process recovered 99.8% of the total module mass, with negligible losses of glass, cells and release films.
After delamination, the researchers mechanically scraped the EVA from the glass, resulting in less than 10% encapsulant mass loss. Analysis of the recovered cells showed no significant surface residue.
“For us, this points to a way to recycle modules quickly and brings the goal of 100% material recovery closer,” Lee said. “Our next step is to apply the process to full-size commercial PV panels and scale it up for use in commercial recycling operations.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Inductive heating for photovoltaic module recycling and near-complete component recovery
,” which was published in
Communications Materials
. The research team included scientists from South Korea’s
Korea Electronics Technology Institute (KETI)
and Australia’s
University of New South Wales (UNSW)

title: New open-access atlas maps 2,697 agrivoltaic projects across 109 countries - pv magazine Global
content:
German consultancy AgRadiance has launched the
AgRadiance Atlas
, an open-access interactive platform that maps agrivoltaic projects worldwide and provides information on relevant regulations, support policies, and court rulings.
The atlas currently includes 2,697 projects across 109 countries, up from 37 projects identified worldwide in 2018. It provides geographical data for each project and allows users to examine regulatory conditions in individual countries and regions.
Each project is linked to its original publicly available source. The database also includes 151 projects classified as postponed or canceled.
The atlas tracks 523 regulations, policies, and court rulings relevant to the projects it covers. Users can select a country or region to view identified projects, the applicable regulatory framework, and a summary of local market conditions.
Users can filter projects by development status, agricultural activity – including fruit and berry cultivation, viticulture, horticulture, biodiversity conservation, and beekeeping – power capacity, and dates associated with different development stages. Records date back to 2009, allowing users to track project development over time.
In Spain, the atlas lists 10 operational projects, two under construction, two permitted projects, and five announced projects. It also includes two decrees governing agrivoltaic projects, along with four official orders and local strategic plans.
In Germany, the atlas identifies 229 projects and 74 regulations, policies, and procedures. It also provides a summary of the national market. Information for each territory is accompanied by references to publicly available sources.
The database is updated using publicly available planning and permitting documents from countries including Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, and the United Kingdom.
The atlas is intended to serve as a reference tool during the early stages of project development. Users can identify existing and proposed projects in a particular area, including canceled or stalled developments, and review applicable regulatory requirements before conducting site visits.
The platform is freely accessible without registration. Users can also view historical versions of the map dating back to 2009 to examine how projects have progressed through different development stages.
AgRadiance plans to expand the platform by linking the atlas directly to its web-based design tool. The integration will allow users to move from reviewing existing projects and regulatory conditions to mapping individual plots of land and assessing potential PV system configurations.

title: Researchers show LBIC phase mapping accurately detects solar module interconnection defect - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers at Karlstad University in Sweden have used light beam-induced current (LBIC) phase mapping to investigate the local electrical behavior of half-cell solar modules and have found that the technique shows potential for assessing electrical contact quality and detecting localized defects with high spatial resolution.
LBIC mapping is a non-destructive, spatially resolved optoelectronic characterization technique used to investigate the electrical properties and performance of photovoltaic cells and modules. It involves scanning a focused light beam across a solar cell or module while measuring the resulting photocurrent to identify spatial variations in electrical performance.
Unlike conventional LBIC mapping, which primarily measures photocurrent amplitude, LBIC phase mapping uses modulated illumination to measure the phase shift of the photocurrent response, providing additional insights into local electrical resistance and contact quality.
“Our experiments demonstrated that LBIC phase mapping can detect variations in contact quality, including regions with good contacts and regions with intentionally reduced contact area and discontinuous wire contact,” corresponding author Markus Rinio told
pv magazine
. “The results demonstrate the potential of LBIC phase mapping as a sensitive local diagnostic technique for identifying variations in interconnection quality.”
“A central contribution of our work is the development of an analytical equivalent-circuit model and the derivation of an equation describing the relationship between the measured LBIC phase shift and the electrical parameters of the solar cell,” said co-author Majid Salari. “In particular, the equation establishes how changes in local series resistance (Rs) influence the phase response. This provides a physical and analytical basis for interpreting LBIC phase maps in terms of local electrical properties, rather than relying solely on empirical correlations between phase shifts and defects.”
For their experiments, the scientists used an 828 nm laser with a power of 22 μW, a spatial resolution of 6 μm, and a typical penetration depth of 15 μm in silicon. The laser was modulated at 640 Hz to generate an alternating photocurrent, which was measured using lock-in amplifiers to minimize noise and improve precision.
They explained that although the photocurrent oscillates at the same frequency as the laser illumination, a phase shift occurs between the two signals. This shift reflects the electrical impedances encountered as photogenerated charge carriers travel through the cell and are collected at its contacts. Analyzing these phase shifts provides additional information about local electrical properties, including series resistance and contact quality.
The team used 156.75 mm × 156.75 mm monocrystalline bifacial silicon solar cells with five busbars, supplied by Chinese manufacturer Lightway Solar. The cells were cut in half using laser scribing followed by mechanical cleaving, and their internal quantum efficiency (IQE) and phase shifts were mapped using LBIC measurements.
The half-cells were then laminated using The Tape Solution (TTS), an interconnection method developed by Sweden-based Sticky Solar Power. The process involves attaching low-temperature solder-coated wires to both sides of the cells using transparent tapes, followed by simultaneous lamination and soldering.
To assess interconnection quality, the researchers deliberately reduced the contact area between wires and busbars in selected regions by applying less pressure. They then compared LBIC phase maps recorded before and after lamination to identify changes in electrical contact quality. They noted that although the five-busbar M2 cells are no longer representative of current industrial standards, they provided a simplified platform for validating a methodology that could also be applied to larger solar cells.
The experiments showed that phase shifts became more negative after lamination, consistent with increased local Rs associated with the interconnection wires. Regions with high-quality contacts showed average phase differences of around 150 millidegrees, compared with approximately 250 millidegrees in areas with deliberately weakened contacts. Optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) supported these findings, revealing nearly continuous connections between solder and silver pads in well-connected regions and visible gaps in areas with poorer contacts.
The researchers also compared LBIC phase mapping with electroluminescence (EL) imaging, finding that the latter could not easily distinguish the localized resistance variations detected by LBIC. They said the results highlight the technique’s sensitivity to interconnection defects and its potential for diagnosing electrical performance losses in laminated solar modules.
Moreover, the researchers attributed the increased LBIC phase shifts after lamination primarily to higher local Rs, based on the proposed equivalent-circuit model. By measuring the same cells under identical conditions before and after lamination, they minimized variations arising from the measurement setup. Regions with deliberately weakened contacts showed significantly larger phase shifts than those with better connections, a finding also supported by cross-sectional microscopy.
“We acknowledge that possible changes in parallel capacitance or other effects cannot be completely excluded,” said Rinio. “However, our analysis indicates that the changes in local Rs are the primary explanation for the observed behavior.”
The researchers also found that LBIC phase mapping could distinguish between well-connected contacts and those with reduced contact areas or discontinuous wire connections, with the latter showing larger phase shifts associated with higher local series resistance. Completely disconnected contacts would be expected to produce even stronger electrical disturbances, provided other contacts remain functional. However, the technique has not yet been systematically tested across the full range of contact conditions.
“Therefore, we would not claim that the current study establishes a definitive distinction between partially soldered and completely disconnected contacts,” Salari explained.
The research findings are presented in the study “
Probing interconnection defects in solar modules via LBIC phase mapping
,” published in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells

net metering scheme
to use the monetary value of surplus electricity generated at one property to offset electricity bills at other eligible locations. The move could improve the economics of rooftop solar for households and businesses with multiple properties.
The new methodology, implementing Law No. 160/2026, expands Romania’s existing quantitative compensation system. Surplus electricity credits can be allocated across multiple properties belonging to the same prosumer, provided they are served by the same electricity supplier.
The regulation maintains quantitative compensation for eligible PV installations of up to 200 kW, allowing electricity exported to the grid to be offset against electricity imported from the grid. Installations above 200 kW and up to 400 kW remain subject to financial settlement based on wholesale electricity market prices.

title: Sungrow launches C&I storage solution with modular scenario dock and full SiC PCS - pv magazine Global
content:
Sungrow launched the PowerStack 3.0 series, its latest commercial and industrial energy storage platform, positioning the product as a shift from standardized physical integration toward what the company calls “scene-in-one” architecture designed to serve pure storage, solar-plus-storage, solar-storage-charging, and microgrid applications from a single hardware base.
The core of the launch is a “1+N=S” design — a standardized main cabinet paired with interchangeable expansion docks — which Sungrow describes as an industry-first approach to C&I storage. In the solar-plus-storage configuration, the company says a single power conversion system can absorb PV power conversion, eliminating the need for a separate PV inverter and supporting twice the rated PV capacity on the DC side. For the microgrid dock, Sungrow claims seamless grid-to-island transition without an external static transfer switch. These specific performance claims come from the manufacturer and have not been independently verified.
On the hardware side, PowerStack 3.0 uses 684 Ah laminated LFP cells, a full silicon carbide power conversion system rated at up to 99.2% peak efficiency, and a stated system round-trip efficiency of at least 92%. Energy density is listed at 256 kWh per square meter, which Sungrow says reduces footprint by 43% compared with conventional solutions. The system carries IP55 enclosure protection and C5 corrosion resistance, operates from −30 C to 50 C, and tolerates up to 30% grid harmonic content — specifications aimed at harsh industrial environments and weak-grid sites. Liquid cooling with AI-driven thermal management is said to cut auxiliary power consumption by 33% versus the previous generation.
The control architecture consolidates what Sungrow previously handled across four layers — energy management, cluster management, and local control — into a two-layer fusion controller. Each cabinet retains independent dispatch capability, with automatic host failover designed to keep the station running if a single unit drops offline. Units can be paralleled from one to 20 to scale from small commercial sites to campus-level installations.
Sungrow has also embedded an AI assistant, branded Bubbly, across the product lifecycle. The company claims the system can generate a site-specific design and revenue forecast in 30 seconds, complete complex scenario commissioning in three minutes, and lift operating revenue by 12% versus a self-consumption baseline through forecast-driven dispatch optimization. These figures are manufacturer projections based on internal modeling rather than field-validated results.
PowerStack 3.0 succeeds the company’s 255CS and 510CS C&I lines, and Sungrow says it is targeting Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East — regions where C&I storage demand is growing as electricity price volatility, demand-charge management, and behind-the-meter renewable integration drive more complex use cases. The underlying technology — large-format laminated cells, SiC conversion, and liquid cooling — has migrated from Sungrow’s utility-scale PowerTitan platform, reflecting a broader industry pattern of utility-grade hardware moving downstream into distributed applications.

title: A Natural “Varnish” May Explain How 37,000-Year-Old Cave Art Survived
content:
New analysis reveals that these cave drawings are partially covered by calcite mineral, which has kept them safe for tens of thousands of years. Credit: Adapted from ACS Omega 2026, DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061
A new technique uses UV light to reveal a natural mineral varnish that may have helped preserve Chauvet Cave’s 37,000-year-old charcoal drawings.
About 37,000 years ago, Paleolithic people entered a limestone cave in southeastern France and drew the animals around them, including cave bears, cave lions, bison, and horses. An ancient rockfall later sealed away the artwork, leaving it undiscovered until the 1990s. Today, Chauvet Cave holds some of the oldest artwork in existence, along with clues to how the cave itself helped preserve it.
Getting close to those clues requires care. The site is so historically important and fragile that its location is kept secret and access is secured behind a huge steel door. Inside, prehistoric footprints lie in front of the artwork. Researchers examining the walls must also protect these traces of the people who once walked through the cave.
Researcher Philippe Walter describes the purpose of that painstaking work. “We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time.”
Due to the presence of prehistoric soil and footprints immediately in front of the cave walls, researchers had to set up their analysis instruments nearly 8 feet away. Credit: Adapted from ACS Omega 2026, DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061
Studying cave art without touching it
In a study reported in
ACS Omega
, Walter and his colleagues investigated the charcoal drawings without touching the cave walls. They focused on mineral deposits that had formed over the artwork, looking for evidence of how the drawings were created and how the cave’s geology may have contributed to their preservation.
To work around the fragile footprints, the team placed a portable spectrometer on a protective walkway about 8 feet (2.5 meters) from the wall. This instrument measures light, allowing the researchers to examine materials from a distance.
Their approach used ultraviolet, or UV, fluorescence spectroscopy, a technique researchers have used to
reveal fluorescent mineral deposits invisible to the naked eye
. Certain materials emit light when exposed to UV illumination. By shining a UV beam onto the wall and analyzing the resulting glow, the team could investigate both the mineral deposits and the pigments in the artwork.
Natural varnish and possible torch marks
Two different colors offered clues to what had happened on the cave walls:
Thin layers of calcite glowed blue under a blacklight. These mineral layers had been left behind by water flowing over the limestone surface, forming a natural varnish that covered parts of the artwork.
Some areas fluoresced orange. That glow could come from hot charcoal or other burning materials, such as a lit torch, rubbed against the wall to create the drawings.
“Our methodology is much like forensic investigation: We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time,” says Walter.
The team anticipates applications beyond cave art, from forensic science to monitoring biofilms aboard the International Space Station. Biofilms are communities of microorganisms that grow on surfaces. A project applying the technique to monitoring them aboard the station is already underway.
Reference: “In Situ Ultraviolet Fluorescence Spectroscopy for the Characterization of Translucent Calcite Coatings over Prehistoric Cave Art” by Yohan Boulard, Thiéry Guillou, Carole Fritz, Gilles Tosello, Maguy Jaber and Philippe Walter, 29 September 2026,
ACS Omega
DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061
The authors acknowledge funding from the French Ministry of Culture, the French National Centre for Scientific Research (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), and Sorbonne University.
Disclosure: One of the authors is a founder of Lumentis, a company developing imaging instruments for historical artwork analysis.

title: Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It
content:
Immunotherapy is a type of cancer treatment that harnesses the body’s immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. Unlike traditional treatments that directly target tumors, immunotherapy strengthens or redirects the immune response, offering promising results for many cancers. However, it can sometimes cause the immune system to attack healthy tissues, leading to potentially serious side effects. Credit: Shutterstock
Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.
Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.
Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.
“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.
Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in
that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.
Diet helps recreate immunotherapy side effects
Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.
“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”
Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe. Credit: University of Pittsburgh
Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence
cancer patient outcomes
responses to immunotherapy
. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.
The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.
Gut microbes can worsen or ease inflammation
Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.
The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.
Stabilizing immune cells reverses inflammation in mice
Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.
Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.
“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”
The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.
“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.
Reference: “Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade” by Dipyaman Patra, Katelyn Wolfgang, Chenxian Ye, Lora Rigatti, Kelsey Ertwine, Kristin M. Morder, Jessica Jana, Ishita Baral, Drew Hurd, Kaitlin Bossong, Steven Mullett, Yingtong Dou, Stacy Gelhaus, Dario A.A. Vignali, Diwakar Davar, Anthony R. Cillo, Greg M. Delgoffe and Abigail E. Overacre-Delgoffe, 22 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055

title: Could Vitamin B12 Hold the Key to Treating a Rare Genetic Disorder?
content:
Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient that helps the body produce healthy red blood cells, maintain nerve function, and synthesize DNA. Credit: Stock
A search for genes linked to lifespan uncovered an unexpected connection between RNA splicing, metabolism, and developmental disorders.
A mutation linked to a rare developmental disorder appears to interfere with more than the way cells process genetic instructions. Researchers discovered that it also disrupts vitamin B12-dependent metabolism in tiny roundworms. Supplying the vitamin restored key metabolic processes and corrected developmental abnormalities in the animals, raising questions about whether a similar approach could eventually help people.
The findings concern Verheij syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that causes developmental delays, growth problems, and short stature in children. The condition is associated with changes in a gene involved in RNA splicing, an essential process that prepares messenger RNA for protein production. During splicing, cells remove unnecessary sections of RNA and join the remaining pieces to form instructions that can be used to build proteins.
A Genetic Mutation Reveals a Metabolic Problem
The discovery emerged from experiments with the roundworm
C. elegans
, a widely used model organism in biological research. Scientists were initially searching for genes that influence lifespan when they identified a mutation in a splicing-related gene associated with Verheij syndrome in humans. Worms carrying the mutation grew more slowly and remained unusually small, resembling some of the developmental problems seen in affected children.
Further genetic screening and metabolic analysis showed that the mutation altered biochemical pathways that depend on vitamin B12. These pathways support normal growth and cellular function. When researchers administered vitamin B12 to the affected worms, the disrupted metabolic processes returned to normal, and the animals’ developmental defects were corrected.
In the disease model shown on the left, C. elegans worms exhibit a stress response, which is visible in green. Administration of vitamin B12 counteracts this effect, as can be seen on the right. Credit: W. Huang / Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing
“We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism,” says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. “Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.”
Could the Findings Apply to Human Patients?
To investigate whether similar metabolic disruptions occur in humans, the researchers examined publicly available data from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at University Hospital Cologne, to obtain blood samples from patients with Verheij syndrome. The analyses provided evidence that metabolic pathways affected in the worms may also be altered in people with the condition.
However, the results do not establish that vitamin B12 supplementation can treat Verheij syndrome in humans. Additional research is needed to determine whether the metabolic changes contribute directly to patients’ symptoms and whether correcting them could provide clinical benefits. The findings also suggest that metabolic dysfunction may deserve greater attention in other genetic disorders involving defective RNA splicing.
“Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases,” says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. “A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.”
Reference: “Vitamin B12 alleviates spliceosomopathy via phospholipid remodeling” by Jonathan Kölschbach, Hormos S. Dafsari, Emily Baum, Anna Löhrke, Chun Kew, Ivan Dikic, Wenming Huang and Adam Antebi, 7 August 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76295-9

title: More Than a Billion Years of Earth’s History Is Missing – Scientists May Finally Know Why
content:
More than a billion years of Earth’s geological history have mysteriously vanished from rock formations across several continents. New research suggests that slow, deep-seated movements within the planet may explain how these enormous gaps formed and why they remain visible today. Credit: Stock
Earth’s rocks are missing more than a billion years of history in some places, and the slow rise and fall of continents may explain how those chapters disappeared.
A study led by University of Wollongong (UOW) PhD candidate Santosh Dhungana suggests that the slow rise and fall of continents helped create the Great Unconformity, a vast gap in Earth’s geological record. Published in
, the research links this missing history to currents of hot rock in the mantle that moved continents vertically over hundreds of millions of years.
Normally, rock layers preserve a sequence of events, with younger deposits accumulating above older ones. At the Great Unconformity, that sequence jumps: sedimentary rocks from around the beginning of the Cambrian period, roughly 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite more than a billion years old.
“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance,” Dhungana said.
Regions for which a mantle flow model predicts a dynamic topography history conducive (orange) or non-conducive (grey) to Great Unconformity formation and preservation. Laurentia (‘LAU’), Baltica (‘BAL’), and North China (‘NCH’) are three regions where the Great Unconformity is well documented. Credit: Associate Professor Nicolas Flament and Santosh Dhungana
The Grand Canyon exposes one of the most striking examples of this geological gap. It lies within what was once the ancient continent Laurentia (modern North America). Similar boundaries appear in Europe, Australia, Africa, and Asia, although the missing intervals vary from about 200 million years to well over a billion.
Tracing Earth’s Missing History
Explaining the Great Unconformity requires accounting for both the removal of rock and the survival of the eroded surface beneath younger deposits. Dhungana said that although scientists had offered several explanations, those ideas had not been thoroughly tested against Earth’s behavior over time.
To investigate, he and his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, modeled mantle convection across hundreds of millions of years. The mantle consists of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly. Its currents can
gently lift enormous stretches of land
or allow them to sink.
Santosh Dhungana and Associate Professor Nicolas Flament. Credit: Michael Gray/University of Wollongong
The models indicated that mantle currents raised the ancient continental cores of Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe), and North China during the Neoproterozoic Era, from about one billion to 540 million years ago. This prolonged uplift would have exposed rock to erosion. The era was followed by the Cambrian period, when animal life diversified dramatically.
How Sinking Continents Preserved The Gap
The next stage helped preserve what erosion had left behind. During the Phanerozoic eon, which spans the past 540 million years, the continental cores gradually sank. Seas spread across their worn surfaces, and accumulating sediment buried the boundary between the ancient rocks and the younger geological record.
Top: The Great Unconformity was formed by continental-scale erosion of ancient crystalline basement during Neoproterozoic times, followed by continental-scale sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times. Bottom: Mantle flow models predict Neoproterozoic dynamic uplift followed by Phanerozoic dynamic subsidence for Laurentia (‘LAU’), Baltica (‘BAL’), and North China (‘NCH’). Credit: Associate Professor Nicolas Flament and Santosh Dhungana
The modeled pattern matched the geography of the evidence. North America, northern Europe, and North China, where the Great Unconformity is especially well preserved and documented, all showed the prolonged rise followed by sinking that the researchers proposed.
“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface,” Associate Professor Flament said.
“Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed, but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.”

title: Popular Weight-Loss Drugs May Have a Surprising Effect on Your Brain
content:
GLP-1 medications, such as semaglutide, mimic a naturally occurring hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite, and digestion. Commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, these drugs can promote weight loss by reducing hunger and slowing stomach emptying. Credit: Shutterstock
Popular weight-loss drugs may offer benefits that extend beyond metabolism, potentially helping preserve memory and other cognitive abilities.
Medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes may also influence memory and other cognitive abilities. But whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide can actually protect the brain remains uncertain, particularly after major clinical trials failed to demonstrate a benefit in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease.
In Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE+ trials, semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer’s progression, even though it produced changes in several biological markers associated with the disease. Researchers from the
University of Gothenburg
University of Copenhagen
have now examined the broader evidence in a review published in
, exploring whether these medications could still help preserve cognitive function in other groups of patients.
Why Weight-Loss Drugs Could Affect Memory
GLP-1 medications influence biological processes involved in both metabolism and brain function. Animal experiments suggest they can affect learning and memory, but studies involving humans have produced inconsistent results. Analyses of patient health records have linked GLP-1 treatment to a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes, although these observational findings cannot establish that the drugs directly provide protection.
The potential benefits may differ depending on the cause of cognitive difficulties. People with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience problems with attention, planning, and mental processing speed. These difficulties are frequently associated with metabolic disturbances and poor vascular health, raising the possibility that treatments targeting these underlying problems could help maintain cognitive abilities.
Stina Börchers, the review’s first author and a researcher affiliated with both universities, believes that identifying the right patients and treatment timing will be essential.
Stina Börchers, Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg, and University of Copenhagen. Credit: Josefin Bergenholtz
“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” says Stina Börchers.
Understanding How Metabolic Treatments Influence the Brain
A central unanswered question is whether any cognitive benefits arise from direct effects on the brain, improvements in metabolic health, or both. Better regulation of blood sugar and other metabolic processes could indirectly support brain function, while GLP-1 signaling may also influence neural processes more directly. Separating these mechanisms could help researchers determine which effects are most relevant to preserving cognition.
Christoffer Clemmensen, Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen. Credit: University of Copenhagen
Christoffer Clemmensen, the review’s senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity medications to investigate these connections.
“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function,” says Christoffer Clemmensen.
The Next Step Toward Protecting Cognitive Health
The researchers are calling for clinical trials that measure memory and other cognitive abilities from the beginning of treatment. Such studies could help establish whether these medications preserve cognitive function, which patients are most likely to benefit, and whether starting treatment before cognitive difficulties appear makes a difference.
They also caution that potential benefits must be weighed against risks in older or frail patients. Rapid weight loss and declining muscle mass can reduce physical functioning, potentially limiting the overall advantages of treatment. Future studies will need to account for these effects when assessing whether obesity medications can support long-term brain health.
Reference: “Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition” by Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg and Christoffer Clemmensen, 5 November 2026,

title: Scientists Discover That Male and Female Hearts Age in Surprisingly Different Ways
content:
Scientists have discovered that the heart does not age uniformly, with inflammation and tissue scarring concentrated in unexpected locations. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals surprising differences in how male and female hearts age at the cellular level.
The heart may age very differently from one region to another. A detailed study of mouse hearts found that molecular signs associated with chronic inflammation and tissue scarring were concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root, rather than being distributed evenly throughout the organ.
Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) identified these hotspots by mapping thousands of cells from young and aged mice. Published in
Aging Cell
, the findings suggest that structures often overlooked in cardiac aging research may play a central role in how the heart changes over time.
Why the Heart’s Valves May Be Aging Hotspots
Previous studies of cardiac aging have largely concentrated on heart muscle, particularly the left ventricle, which pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and throughout the body. Because mammalian heart muscle cells have very limited capacity for regeneration, understanding how they deteriorate with age has been a major research priority. The JAX team instead examined the entire heart, using single-cell and spatial genomics technologies to identify both the molecular activity of individual cells and their locations within the organ.
“The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine,” said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. “It turns out they’re home to many of the cells we’re interested in, and that’s where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated.”
“Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue,” Rosenthal said. “We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don’t age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don’t age at the same rate either, even within one individual.”
Maps of young (top) and aged (bottom) mouse hearts showing where immune cells called macrophages (left) and fibroblasts (right) are most abundant. Blue indicates fewer cells and red indicates more cells. The highest concentrations of both cell types appear around the aorta and heart valves, regions identified as hotspots of age-related change. Credit: The Rosenthal Lab, The Jackson Laboratory
How Immune Cells and Fibroblasts Influence Cardiac Aging
Aging is associated with persistent, low-grade inflammation, sometimes called “inflammaging.” The researchers focused on two cell populations involved in this process: immune cells that help regulate inflammation (macrophages) and structural cells responsible for maintaining connective tissue and producing scar tissue (fibroblasts). In older mouse hearts, macrophages showed increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and tissue remodeling, while fibroblasts exhibited molecular patterns linked to fibrosis (or scarring).
“To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life,” Rosenthal said. “What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging.”
The team also detected increased activity in two genes within the identified hotspots.
produces an inflammatory signaling molecule, while
(also known as p21) helps regulate the cell cycle and is commonly associated with cellular senescence. Their activity points to changes in signaling between neighboring cells, not simply isolated changes within individual cell types. “We’re not talking about single genes. We’re talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts,” Rosenthal said.
A Surprising Discovery in Young Hearts
Some molecular markers traditionally associated with senescent cells were already present in young mouse hearts. Cellular senescence occurs when cells permanently stop dividing, often following stress or damage. Senescent cells can contribute to inflammation and tissue deterioration, but the researchers found that the presence of commonly used senescence markers does not necessarily establish that a cell has entered this state.
“What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren’t where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us,” Rosenthal said. “That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don’t mean a cell is senescent. There’s nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart.”
Male and Female Hearts Show Different Molecular Changes
The study also identified differences in how fibroblasts responded to aging in male and female mice. In males, older fibroblasts showed greater involvement in molecular pathways associated with fibrosis. In females, aging was linked more closely to pathways involved in heart development and protein production. These findings describe differences in gene activity, not demonstrated differences in cardiac function or disease risk.
Rosenthal noted that cardiovascular disease patterns also differ between men and women, with disease risk generally increasing after menopause in women. However, the mouse findings do not establish a mechanism for those human differences. Comparisons with previously published human heart data did identify several shared molecular programs associated with aging, including pathways involved in cellular stress responses.
“Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process,” said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.
What the Findings Could Mean for Cardiovascular Health
Age is the leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease, but separating changes caused by aging itself from those associated with lifestyle, environmental exposures, and disease remains difficult. Although the study did not establish whether the identified cellular changes directly impair heart function, the controlled conditions in which the mice lived helped researchers examine the biological effects of aging.
“Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself,” said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. “Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta.”
The researchers are now investigating how exercise, diet, and disease influence the interactions between immune cells and fibroblasts. Their goal is to distinguish changes that occur during normal aging from those that may increase the heart’s susceptibility to disease. Although the current findings do not immediately suggest new treatments, the cellular map provides a foundation for studying how inflammation and fibrosis develop in specific regions of the aging heart.
