title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in One of the Deadliest Cancers
content:
Fox Chase researchers identified ANO6 as a potential pancreatic cancer target that may slow tumor growth and reduce immune suppression. Credit: Fox Chase Cancer Center
Researchers have identified another potential approach to treating pancreatic cancer, with early experiments suggesting that blocking a protein could slow tumor growth and strengthen immune defenses.
Pancreatic tumors can be surrounded by tissue so dense that it compresses blood vessels, making it difficult for nutrients to reach cancer cells. Even under these conditions, the cells continue growing. How they obtain the materials needed to survive has remained an important question.
Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have identified one way pancreatic cancer cells obtain cholesterol and other fats, known as lipids. Their study, published in
Nature Cancer
, also identified a protein that helps control this process and could offer a potential target for cancer treatment.
The research focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common type of pancreatic cancer. These tumors contain large numbers of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), cells that produce and organize connective tissue. As CAFs and their collagen fibers expand, they can compress nearby blood vessels, restricting the tumor’s blood supply.
Cells that restrict blood flow also feed tumors
Despite contributing to this nutrient shortage, CAFs also help cancer cells overcome it.
“We found that CAFs can act as a source of these nutrients,” said Edna Cukierman, PhD, a professor and co-leader of the Cancer Signaling and Microenvironment Program at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Using laboratory and animal models, we discovered that CAF units acquire cholesterol from the bloodstream and transfer it to nearby pancreatic cancer cells through a process called trogocytosis”
Trogocytosis occurs when one cell takes small pieces of another cell’s membrane during direct contact. In this case, pancreatic cancer cells acquire pieces of CAF membranes containing cholesterol and other lipids that support their survival and growth.
The researchers discovered that this transfer depends on a protein called anoctamin 6 (ANO6), which helps prepare the CAF membrane for the exchange.
“These findings help explain how pancreatic cancer cells obtain essential nutrients despite the unusual structure of the pancreatic tumor microenvironment,” said Igor Astsaturov, MD, PhD, a professor at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Cancer-associated fibroblasts are not passive bystanders. They actively support tumor growth by transferring lipids to cancer cells.”
When researchers reduced or eliminated ANO6 in CAFs, the cells became less effective at supporting pancreatic cancer cell survival. In mouse models, tumors supported by CAFs with functional ANO6 grew substantially faster than those without functional ANO6.
Cholesterol may exhaust cancer-fighting T cells
The same nutrient transfer process also appeared to interfere with the immune system.
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are immune cells that recognize and kill cancer cells. When these T cells come into contact with CAFs, they can acquire membrane material containing cholesterol. Excess cholesterol in the tumor environment can contribute to T-cell exhaustion, making these immune cells less effective at fighting cancer.
“With Serge Fuchs, professor at the University of Pennsylvania and co-author on the paper, we were surprised to find that the same cellular mechanism can benefit the tumor in two ways – by supplying cancer cells with lipids while also weakening cancer-fighting T cells,” said Astsaturov. “Targeting ANO6 could potentially disrupt both of these tumor-supporting functions at the same time.”
In mouse models, blocking ANO6 reduced cholesterol accumulation in T cells within tumors and improved markers of their activity. Laboratory experiments also showed that T cells exposed to CAFs with reduced ANO6 were better able to kill cancer cells.
Two drugs reduce tumor weight in mice
The researchers then tested whether drugs that interfere with ANO6-dependent activity could slow tumor growth. In mouse models, treatment with niclosamide or clofazimine significantly reduced tumor weight. Niclosamide also reduced cholesterol delivery to pancreatic cancer cells.
These findings suggest that targeting ANO6 could both restrict a nutrient source for pancreatic tumors and improve the immune response against them. However, the results remain preclinical, and further research is needed to determine whether selectively blocking ANO6 would work as a treatment in patients.
Trogocytosis is also only one of several ways pancreatic cancer cells may obtain lipids. The researchers suggest that the drugs tested could potentially help treat other difficult cancers, although that possibility requires further investigation.
“We believe our findings identify ANO6 as a potential therapeutic target that could simultaneously disrupt the nutrient supply supporting pancreatic cancer cells and reduce the immune-suppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment,” said Astsaturov.
The findings also build on nearly a decade of research into how the tissue surrounding pancreatic tumors supports cancer growth.
“Excitingly, reducing ANO6 expression also disrupted the stromal synapse-mimicry circuit we previously identified, which coordinates tumor nutritional support, CAF-unit metabolism, and immune suppression. These findings position ANO6 as the missing mechanistic link that unifies nearly a decade of discoveries by our team,” said Cukierman.

title: Scientists Just Found a Key Ingredient for Superconductivity at Room Temperature
content:
Superconductors are materials that allow electricity to flow without electrical resistance, eliminating energy losses caused by heat. They could transform technologies ranging from power grids and magnetic levitation trains to quantum computers. Credit: Shutterstock
Researchers have discovered that a key requirement for superconductivity can persist even at room temperature.
Scientists searching for a superconductor that works at room temperature have identified a potential way forward. New research from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich shows that electrons can form the pairs needed for superconductivity even at room temperature. The findings, published in
, suggest that a different requirement may be preventing these materials from conducting electricity without resistance.
The key appears to be how paired electrons behave collectively. Although the pairs can survive at much higher temperatures than previously understood, they must also act in a coordinated way for superconductivity to emerge.
Why Superconductivity Remains So Difficult to Achieve
Electrical resistance causes energy to be lost as heat whenever current passes through an ordinary conductor. This is useful in a toaster, where resistance heats a metal wire until it glows, but undesirable in power transmission and electronic devices. Superconductors eliminate electrical resistance, potentially enabling more efficient energy storage, levitating trains, and advanced quantum computers.
First authors Maialen Ortego Larrazabal and Jiasen Niu with the measuring equipment Credit: LMU, Faculty of Physics
The obstacle is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C (-436°F), often using expensive liquid helium. Superconductivity was first discovered in 1911, and researchers made major progress in the mid-1980s when they identified materials that could become superconducting at temperatures around -173°C (-279°F). Yet these higher-temperature superconductors presented a mystery: the established theory explaining conventional superconductivity could not account for their behavior.
“We don’t understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all,” says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. “And if you don’t understand it, you can’t systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.”
Electron Pairs Can Survive at Room Temperature
Superconductivity requires two essential conditions. First, electrons must form partnerships known as Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated quantum state called phase coherence. Without both conditions, a material cannot sustain superconductivity.
In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and phase coherence emerge together as the material cools below a critical temperature. The new research shows that these processes can occur separately in high-temperature superconductors. Electron pairs can form and remain stable at temperatures far above the point where electrical resistance disappears, including at room temperature.
“This is really good news,” says Swart. “We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren’t possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.”
The Remaining Barrier to Room-Temperature Superconductivity
The findings indicate that the interaction binding electrons into pairs can remain sufficiently strong at room temperature. This shifts attention toward phase coherence, which may be the limiting factor preventing superconductivity at higher temperatures.
“The ‘glue’ that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature,” says Swart. “This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.”
The researchers have not demonstrated room-temperature superconductivity, but their results help narrow the search for what is missing. Swart plans to investigate how phase coherence develops and what prevents electron pairs from achieving it at higher temperatures.
“If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.”
Reference: “Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor” by Jiasen Niu, Maialen Ortego Larrazabal, Thomas Gozlinski, Yudai Sato, Koen M. Bastiaans, Tjerk Benschop, Jian-Feng Ge, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Genda Gu, Ingmar Swart and Milan P. Allan, 5 November 2026,

title: Scientists Ranked 20 Protein-Rich Foods on Health, Affordability, and Sustainability. One Surprising Food Came Out on Top
content:
Tofu is a versatile, plant-based protein made from soybeans that provides all nine essential amino acids. Credit: Shutterstock
Tofu took the crown in a showdown of 20 protein-rich foods judged on health, affordability, availability, and their toll on the planet.
Protein-rich foods can look very different when cost, access, health, and environmental impact all enter the picture. In a study published in
Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
, Dr. Chris Macdonald developed a framework that combines these four considerations to compare commonly consumed protein sources.
Among the 20 foods assessed, tofu took the top spot, while cheddar cheese finished last. The results followed a clear pattern: plant-based foods occupied the entire highest-scoring fifth, and animal-based products made up the lowest-scoring fifth.
Tofu’s lead came from strong results across both parts of the assessment. It earned a perfect 16 points for environmental performance, placing in the best-performing fifth for greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, land use, and freshwater use. It also scored 20 out of 24 points for health and accessibility, including full marks for providing all nine essential amino acids.
Together, these measures explain why the rankings go beyond protein content alone. They weigh the environmental costs of producing protein alongside nutritional factors and practical considerations such as price and availability.
Two bar charts comparing greenhouse gas emissions and water pollution produced by plant-based and animal-based protein sources per 100 g of protein. Credit: Chris Macdonald
Looking Beyond A Single Food Label
The paper argues that ratings focused on one feature can leave consumers with an incomplete picture. A product’s performance in one area does not explain its trade-offs elsewhere. Macdonald presents the framework as a way to help people understand those competing considerations and the food systems their purchases support.
As the paper states, “Against deliberate corporate obfuscation and marketing myths, the goal of a holistic score is not to create a new label, but to foster a new literacy, one that empowers us to see the reality of the systems we are funding.
Ultimately, beyond the spreadsheets and scores, lies a fundamental reckoning: our protein choice is a referendum on the compassion we are willing to show to animals, to the planet, and to future generations.”
The research builds on Macdonald’s work at the Better Protein Institute, which examines how much protein people need for optimal health, how to shift consumer behavior effectively, and where investment could support future protein sources. By questioning common assumptions and starting from first principles, that work addresses some of the most frequently Googled questions about dietary protein.
Reference: “What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI Score” by Chris Macdonald, 1 July 2026,
Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems

title: This $10,000-a-Pound Spice Could Help Save Colorado Farmers

Saffron is the world’s most expensive spice, prized for its vibrant crimson color, distinctive flavor, and delicate aroma. Harvested by hand from the tiny stigmas of purple Crocus sativus flowers, saffron requires extraordinary labor to produce. Credit: Shutterstock
Beneath Denver’s solar panels, a spice nicknamed “red gold” is yielding a promising harvest that could help Colorado farmers earn more with less water.
Colorado State University Spur
, horticulture graduate student Reece Bailey is investigating whether saffron could become a profitable addition to the state’s farms. His experiments in the campus’s urban gardens and
green roof research areas
are testing how the crop handles Colorado’s climate, how much water it needs, and whether growing it beneath solar panels improves production.
The appeal starts with its extraordinary value. A pound of saffron typically costs between $600 and $5,000, with some varieties reaching $10,000. Vanilla, the second most expensive spice, sells for roughly $90 to $225 a pound. Those prices caught Bailey’s attention, but the research must establish whether the potential earnings justify the work.
These tiny purple saffron flowers have been a prized crop for thousands of years. Credit: Colorado State University
Why Saffron Could Suit Colorado
Colorado may seem an unlikely home for a spice closely associated with the Middle East. Yet Iran, which produces roughly 85% of the world’s saffron, has mountainous, semiarid conditions that resemble parts of the state. Bailey sees that overlap as a reason to investigate whether “red gold” could find a foothold on Colorado’s high plains.
The crop also offers an unusual combination of low water demand and late production. Saffron typically blooms in November, potentially bringing farmers income after other harvests have ended. Under suitable conditions, Bailey said, it could provide that additional crop without requiring extra irrigation.
“One thing that’s always been interesting to me is new ideas and novel ways of integrating crops into our environments,” said Bailey, who grew up in Aurora and has worked on Spur’s green roof for three years.
The Work Behind “Red Gold”
The world’s most expensive spice comes from a remarkably small harvest: the three slender red stigmas inside each purple saffron flower. Collecting enough to produce a pound of dried spice requires roughly 75,000 flowers.
That harvest is painstaking. Flowers open for only a few hours each morning, and workers carefully extract the stigmas, often with tweezers. The amount of hand labor helps explain both saffron’s price and the challenge of turning it into a profitable crop.
The rooftop of the Terra building at CSU Spur is home to a rooftop garden filled with a variety of native plants. It overlooks the Rocky Mountains and downtown Denver. Credit: Colorado State University
“It’s certainly not the easiest crop to grow or the easiest crop to work with, but the investment can be well worth it,” Bailey said.
The Colorado Department of Agriculture has committed $80,000 through its
Specialty Crop Block Grant Program
to investigate that possibility, particularly as a source of supplemental income late in the season and during dry years.
A Potential Boost for Farm Income
“For a lot of farmers, the price for their goods isn’t keeping up with the price of inputs, so what we’re really trying to do is find new crops that will work with Colorado’s climate and for our producers’ bottom line,” said Sam Hahn, the department’s next generation and specialty crops program manager. “Saffron has a high labor input, but it could really be a boon for our farmers.”
Successfully growing the flowers would answer only part of the business question. Farmers would still need to assess startup costs, bulb suppliers, equipment, labor availability, and buyers. A valuable spice does not automatically translate into a profitable harvest.
Its labor demands could nevertheless create another benefit. Hahn said the November bloom might provide agricultural jobs during a period when many farmworkers are typically unemployed, while helping farms adapt to a changing climate.
“It’s so important that we experiment with these high-value crops to see if it can supplement the market in our state and keep us competitive,” Hahn said.
Saffron Thrives Beneath Solar Panels
Some of the most promising results are emerging 75 feet (23 meters) above the ground. Bailey’s plots occupy the roofs of two CSU Spur buildings, with Denver’s skyline and the Rocky Mountains in view. One grows among native Colorado plants, including sunflowers. Another sits beneath solar panels in an agrivoltaic system, where the same space supports crops and electricity production.
Reece Bailey is studying how saffron fares in Colorado’s arid, high-elevation environment. Credit: Colorado State University
“I’m always curious about how different plants evolve and how they adapt to green roofs, and lately, I’ve come to realize that saffron is almost the ideal plant for these environments,” said Jennifer Bousselot, Bailey’s faculty adviser and an associate professor of horticulture and landscape architecture at CSU.
Spur’s rooftop gardens have carefully selected soil characteristics and are designed to use water efficiently. Saffron also tolerates some shade, and Bailey’s research so far has found that
yields nearly double beneath the partial shade of solar arrays
“This could provide cash flow value for farmers who want to use solar as an energy source, or who happen to be in an urban agriculture setting,” Bailey said.
Testing a Crop for Dry Years
Water use offers another reason to keep testing. Bailey said saffron requires roughly half as much water as corn and could potentially survive on rainfall alone, making it an appealing candidate for a region where irrigation water is under pressure.
“This crop is incredibly drought resistant,” Bailey said.
The experiments extend beyond Spur’s rooftops to CSU’s Foothills Campus and Denver Botanic Gardens Chatfield Farms, at the base of the mountains south of Denver. At Chatfield Farms, Lauren Hazlett, one of the head growers working at the solar array, has welcomed the sight of flowers appearing as other plants fade.
“I never thought I’d ever be able to see saffron growing, especially in Colorado—it’s something I always associated with the other side of the world,” she said.
Bousselot and Bailey have also sent bulbs to farmers in Paonia, Pueblo, and Montrose. Their reports will help show how saffron performs in working farm operations and whether its potential benefits carry beyond the research plots.
There is already a long history of finding uses for the spice. Alexander the Great, king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon, reportedly bathed in saffron to help heal battle wounds. Doctors once prescribed it for bubonic plague, and Cleopatra used its fragrance to attract potential suitors. Today, it flavors dishes such as paella and risotto and is increasingly sought after in perfumes.
Modern research is also exploring its medicinal properties. Some studies suggest saffron may support mental health and help alleviate depression, while others have investigated its possible
anti-inflammatory effects
. Those research areas could add to its commercial appeal, although Colorado’s trials are focused on whether farmers can grow and sell it successfully.
“Up until now, we haven’t really been able to study saffron in Colorado at a deeper level, but the demand is there, and I only think we’ll be talking about it more and more,” Bailey said.

title: Why Did Polynesians Suddenly Sail Across the Pacific After 1,700 Years? Scientists May Have Found the Answer
content:
A traditional Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe on display. Population pressures and advances in sailing technology may have helped transform Polynesian migration. Credit: Shutterstock
The real history behind Moana may be tied to a devastating drought that pushed Polynesian voyagers toward wetter islands and helped reshape human settlement across the Pacific.
In Disney’s Moana, a young Polynesian girl sails beyond her island’s barrier reef to save her threatened home. Scientists have now uncovered evidence that a real environmental crisis may have helped drive one of history’s greatest ocean migrations, pushing Polynesian voyagers across the Pacific after centuries without expanding farther east.
The findings offer a fascinating connection to the story behind Moana, which recently returned to theaters in a live-action adaptation.
A 1,700-year pause in Pacific expansion
Around 3,000 years ago, the ancestors of modern Polynesians arrived in Samoa and Tonga. For approximately 1,700 years, their eastward expansion appeared to stop. This mysterious period became known as the “Long Pause.”
Then, between AD 900 and 1050, everything changed. Within roughly 250 years, Polynesian voyagers had reached and settled islands across the Pacific, including Tahiti and Hawai’i, with their expansion extending to the continental Americas.
Swamp and lake sediments are found across the Pacific islands often in remote volcanic crater lakes or mountain rain forests like here on Tahiti. Credit: University of Southampton
Researchers from the University of Southampton and the University of East Anglia believe a prolonged drought helped trigger this extraordinary movement.
David Sear, Professor of Physical Geography at the University of Southampton and lead author of the study, said, “We have confirmed the theory that the end of the Long Pause coincided with a period of mega drought in the homeland islands of Samoa and Tonga – and also a period of increasing rainfall in the receiving islands. As they headed east, they found wetter islands with nobody on them.”
Ancient mud reveals a devastating drought
To uncover what happened, the team examined ancient mud buried beneath swamps and lakes in Samoa, Tonga, French Polynesia, and the Cook Islands.
Dr. Mark Peaple, a paleoclimate research fellow at the University of Southampton, conducted the geochemical analysis. He studied chemical traces left by freshwater algae and leaves, focusing on different forms of hydrogen called isotopes. Their proportions change depending on rainfall, allowing scientists to reconstruct how wet or dry the islands were thousands of years ago.
Prof David Sear (l) and Dr Mark Peaple (r) coring a swamp in Polynesia to collect mud samples that contain records of rainfall over thousands of years. Credit: University of Southampton
The evidence revealed a severe drought beginning shortly before the migration and continuing during it. When the Long Pause ended, Samoa and Tonga were experiencing their driest conditions in the last 2,000 years. Meanwhile, islands farther east were becoming wetter.
Climate modeling led by Manoj Joshi, Professor of Climate Dynamics at the University of East Anglia, helped explain why. Changes in Pacific Ocean surface temperatures over several decades had shifted a vast tropical rain belt eastward, leaving Samoa and Tonga with less rainfall.
“The climate changes we identified would have transformed daily life on these islands. Reduced rainfall would have affected freshwater availability, food production and the resilience of communities, creating powerful incentives for people to seek opportunities elsewhere,” Joshi said.
Dan Skinner, a research fellow at the University of East Anglia who conducted climate modeling experiments, identified prolonged drought lasting years or even decades as a definite factor behind the migration.
Professor David Sear with mud extracted from swampland in French Polynesia. Credit: University of Southampton
More people and better sailing technology
But worsening conditions were probably not the only influence. Sear explained that growing populations would have placed additional pressure on limited resources. At the same time, Polynesian sailors may have improved their voyaging canoes, moving from U-shaped to V-shaped hulls and developing better rigging. These advances could have helped them sail against the prevailing winds, which generally blow from east to west across the South Pacific.
Together, environmental pressure and improved sailing technology may help explain how Polynesian communities undertook such remarkable journeys.
“There was a huge explosion of migration, and within 250 years they had landed and settled every little dot in the South Pacific, from tiny coral atoll islands to larger lands. It was a very rapid process,” Sear said.
Reference: “How Did changing climate in the tropical South Pacific contribute to the eastward migration and settlement of Polynesia?” by David Sear, Mark Peaple, Peter Langdon, Daniel Skinner, Manoj Joshi, Adrian Matthews, Charlotte Hipkiss, Tim Osborn, Gordon Inglis and Justin Sheffield, 5 May 2026,
Journal of Pacific Archaeology

title: AI Inference Startups Are Quietly Buying Their Own Chips
content: The fast-growing crop of startups that lease computing capacity from cloud firms and then resell it, without spending a nickel on their own AI chips, are at a crossroads. Finding it harder to line up enough computing capacity to serve their customers, some are starting to buy their own chips, which is likely to drastically change the economics of their business. The difficulty in getting enough compute also has pushed some of these startups to look for computational resources from dozens of smaller neoclouds, which tend to have more available capacity than larger hyperscalers such as Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. News this week of a hack of Fireworks, one of the best known of these startups, highlights the risk of that approach. The hack was caused by weak security measures at a small cloud used by Fireworks, according to a person with knowledge of the situation. The hack has prompted some of Fireworks’ customers to consider switching to alternative providers. Startups like Fireworks are known as inference providers—because they cater to customers who need chips to run AI models, a process known as inference. They don’t own chips or data centers, instead devoting their efforts to building software that can help customers better optimize running AI models. These firms have grown quickly. Fireworks, for instance, passed $1 billion in annualized revenue in July, the company said, up five times from what it was generating a year earlier, while others like Fal have doubled their revenue pace in a matter of months, The Information reported in September. Fireworks was most recently valued at $17.5 billion, the highest of the group. But the growing difficulty of securing compute could jeopardize the sector’s rapid growth. In some cases, cloud firms are becoming less willing to lease capacity to rivals. CoreWeave earlier this year decided to stop selling compute to Baseten, according to someone with knowledge of the strategy. CoreWeave launched its own inference service in March this year and didn’t want to devote computing resources to a rival, the person said. Someone close to Baseten disputed the idea that Coreweave had reduced the compute it provides to Baseten. A spokesperson for CoreWeave said: “We have good relationships with inference providers and many of them are our partners, consuming CoreWeave services where it makes sense for their business model, which we are happy to support.” Paddy Srinivasan, CEO of cloud firm DigitalOcean, said he prioritizes “customers that have real-end user demand…versus those reselling our capacity…honestly, because we have so much demand from companies that are actually building software on our stack.” DigitalOcean operates its own data center space. Some inference providers have responded by striking deals with a wide range of smaller cloud firms. Modal, for example, went from working with all the major hyperscalers as cloud partners and a few neoclouds in its first four years as a company to signing up to 30 additional neocloud partners in the past year, when it couldn’t get Nvidia Blackwell chips at the prices and quantity it wanted from larger cloud firms, said CEO Erik Bernhardsson in an interview. Modal still works with hyperscalers, though it tends to rent other chips from them, Bernhardsson said. Some cloud industry executives said inference providers that don’t own their own hardware could be left high and dry if demand for computing capacity disappears or bigger firms decide to cut them off. Inference companies are “like the WeWork of the [graphics processing unit] world, where WeWork went out and signed these long-term leases over office space and then turned around and tried to sell it on a short-term basis. It works well while it works, until either demand or financing dries up,” said Kent Draper, chief commercial officer for Iren, which has built its own data centers. “People are seeing the benefits of vertical integration.” No Choice Some inference providers have decided they have no choice but to invest in their own hardware. Fal, which focuses on hosting video and image AI models, has recently started buying its own Nvidia chips to place in leased data centers, said Raghu Rao, who joined Fal in July to help build out its data center strategy. Fal will use the $1.65 billion in venture capital funding it raised earlier this month to help pay for extra compute capacity, including GPU purchases and renting cloud space from AWS. Fal is also hiring staff to help with the data center effort, Rao said. Fal’s plans to buy hardware haven’t previously been reported. “As we’ve grown tremendously, there’s been a need to both lease as well as own our own hardware,” Rao said. Fal has also expressed interest to investors in borrowing money to help it finance hardware purchases, according to a person with knowledge of the plans. Rao declined to comment on the possibility of debt financing. In recent months, inference providers have been talking to lenders and intermediaries about borrowing money to pay for compute contracts with neoclouds, according to someone involved in the deals. The providers are seeking ways to use borrowed money rather than the equity they have raised from venture capitalists to secure the compute they need, the person said. Together, meanwhile, started buying its own hardware last year and was planning to have 250 megawatts of its own data center capacity by the end of 2026, The Information reported in March. Baseten is also looking to buy Nvidia GPUs to place in data centers that Baseten intends to manage, according to people with knowledge of the plans. CoreWeave itself has made a similar transition. Until now, it has mostly operated data centers owned by other companies. But it revealed last year that it is building its own campus, believing that is the best way to control its hardware. Not all inference companies think they need to own hardware, though. Fireworks leaders have told investors the company believes acquiring the physical chips and building and operating data centers is a commodity, and Fireworks has a more defensible moat in building software that can run models quickly, according to ae person familiar with its strategy. It does not currently have plans to buy hardware, another person with knowledge of Fireworks said. Modal has also told investors it’s interested in purchasing more of its own hardware for data centers, a person with knowledge of those plans said. In an interview, Modal CEO Bernhardsson said the company will do whatever it needs to do to get capacity it needs, but he doesn’t think differentiation comes from owning hardware, echoing a critique hardware owners like Iren have lobbed at inference providers such as Modal. “The hardware layer…is not…where I feel like a lot of value is created. At the end of the day, you’re just buying chips and reselling them,” Bernhardsson said. “So we focus on the software layer. That’s where we’re always going to add the most value.”

title: Alice Huang’s Companies Invested in DeepSeek, Promising Nvidia Chips
content: The network of companies tied to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy in a romantic relationship with Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang, recently invested in Chinese AI star DeepSeek, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter. The investments were meant to forge closer ties with DeepSeek so Alice Huang’s companies could supply a steady stream of Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips, which are banned from sale to China, according to one of the three people. The investments, which haven’t previously been reported, illustrate the hidden yet important role Alice Huang and her companies have played in China’s AI industry. DeepSeek shot to global stardom in early 2025, after its R1 model showed capabilities comparable to those of OpenAI’s latest model at the time but was trained at a fraction of the cost. Nvidia’s Huang, whose resignation as CEO was announced on Thursday morning, had been one of DeepSeek’s most prominent admirers. In his keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in January, he said DeepSeek’s R1 was “really, really exciting work.” “We’re so happy with it,” he added. But DeepSeek, like other Chinese AI firms, has been held back by a persistent AI chip shortage, resulting from U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips in place since late 2022. While DeepSeek has been at the forefront of adapting to Huawei chips, it is still trying to gain access to more Blackwell chips, which can be used for research, and as a fallback in case Huawei chips don’t work. During DeepSeek’s second funding round between July and October, DeepSeek employees introduced companies connected to Alice Huang and her family, Century Litong and its parent company, Shanghai-listed Jiangsu Lettall Electronics, to several investors, the people said. The DeepSeek employees made clear that Century Litong and Lettall, collectively referred to as “Litong Inc” in the industry, were a substantial supplier of blackmarket Nvidia AI chips, and therefore deserved allocation in the hotly contested funding round, the people added. Litong Inc. ended up participating in the funding round, which raised 105.5 billion yuan ($15.8 billion) in October, the people said. The companies invested through special purpose vehicles set up by DeepSeek’s investors for the funding round. As a result, no entity from Litong Inc appears directly on DeepSeek’s shareholder list . One of the investments went through a special purpose vehicle set up by Beijing-based venture capital firm Monolith Management, according to stock exchange filings and Chinese corporate records. Lettall invested 95 million yuan ($14 million) in the entity, the records show. Monolith, founded by former Sequoia Capital China partner Cao Xi, is the third-largest investor in DeepSeek after two rounds of funding. It couldn’t be learned how much money in total Litong Inc put in DeepSeek, but a person with direct knowledge of DeepSeek’s second funding round said the group of companies invested through multiple vehicles. Century Litong has priority access to Nvidia’s chips thanks to its status as one of the chip designer’s preferred cloud partners, which it attained just four months after it was founded in 2023. The company operates data centers and rents out AI chips including Nvidia’s graphics processing units. Litong imported 240,000 Nvidia chips worth at least $7.5 billion into China since 2023, despite tightening U.S. export controls, The Information reported earlier this week. The close ties between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang made the imports possible, The Information reported. Century Litong has managed to import Blackwell chips despite a U.S. crackdown on chip smuggling since late last year, according to two other people with direct knowledge of the situation. Alice Huang never held a stake or an executive position at Century Litong or Lettall (whose name in Mandarin is also Litong). The Information mapped out her relationship with these companies through a myriad of former ownerships and corporate transactions that involved her sister Huang Yu and her husband Kang Wei. DeepSeek’s second funding round drew nearly 30 investors, many of them Chinese tech giants and state-affiliated firms. It was the biggest Chinese AI company fundraising so far. The round valued DeepSeek at about 615.5 billion yuan ($92 billion). Tencent and battery giant CATL were the biggest backers.

title: Anthropic’s PE-Backed Venture, Ode, Pushes to Get Paid for AI Results
content: Private equity firms and AI labs are sorting out how to charge clients and hire enough engineers for joint ventures they’ve launched to build custom AI tools for businesses. That comes as private equity firms are looking to the technology to boost profits, including at companies they’ve struggled to sell. One such team-up is Ode with Anthropic , which launched in July with $1.5 billion in capital commitments from investors including Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman. Ode currently charges most of the several dozen businesses it works with a fixed fee to develop and launch custom AI products, people familiar with the partnership say. The company lets clients retain ownership of the AI software it builds, the people said, allowing them to keep using or even sell the tools once completed without paying Ode ongoing fees. Those terms help Ode attract customers that balked at the terms offered by the team of engineers at Anthropic that embeds with enterprises, which seeks to retain ownership of the custom software it builds and license it back to customers, one of the people said. But Ode has been looking at other ways to earn more on AI projects. Some Ode executives initially proposed coinvesting in companies that were also its customers, but Blackstone’s team pushed back on the idea, one of the people said. Instead, Ode decided to charge performance-based bonus fees on top of the fixed project fees, allowing it to earn more if clients hit specific financial targets. Less than 10% of Ode’s clients are paying those performance-based fees, one of the people said, though Ode is aiming to grow that share. Setting the fees can be difficult because the company and its customers both need to agree on how to measure any AI-driven gains, including setting a baseline and financial or product-related goals. The fees may be negotiated once a contract is signed and Ode then does some early exploratory work and collects data, giving both sides enough information to set terms before moving on to the building phase, the people said. Ode inherited some of its business from Fractional AI, a startup founded in 2024 that the venture acquired in May for an undisclosed sum. Fractional already worked mostly with private equity–backed companies to automate tasks and build custom AI software, and Fractional co-founders Chris Taylor and Eddie Siegel became Ode’s CEO and chief technology officer, respectively. One of those clients, risk and compliance software company LogicGate, paid a fixed fee in the low seven figures for a project that began under Fractional last summer and finished this fall, said LogicGate CEO Diego Panama. (LogicGate’s backers include growth equity firm PSG, which led the company’s $113 million funding round in 2021.) Ode engineers built a custom agent that shortened LogicGate’s client onboarding from 120 days to 90 days or less. LogicGate received full intellectual property ownership and training to run the tool independently, Panama said, and it subsequently began selling the agent to other businesses and has signed several deals. The agent is set to launch publicly at the end of the month. Around half of Ode’s clients are software or business services companies, while the rest come from industrial and other sectors. Its client base is split roughly equally between portfolio companies of Ode’s backers, including at least six Blackstone companies, and other businesses. All of the Blackstone portfolio companies working with Ode currently pay fixed fees, including accounting firm Citrin Cooperman, where Ode engineers built a new onboarding system, similar to the work they did at LogicGate. Blackstone typically sets targets to improve earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in a specific division when evaluating how an AI project is working. Other AI services firms are experimenting with similar fee structures. Hyde , backed by Bain Capital Ventures and General Catalyst, launched last year and helps businesses build custom AI models using their own data. Clients then own the customer models and can run them themselves or pay Hyde to host them. Hyde typically assigns two engineers to work with clients for around four weeks per project, charging for that work plus a recurring fee for using its software platform. (Clients also pay for compute based on usage.) Around half its contracted revenue includes a portion of fees tied to results—its fee for an automotive client, for example, is tied to whether agents meet certain car sales goals. Hyde CEO Anirudh Sanga said demand for Hyde’s services has roughly doubled monthly for the past three months. At the same time, a shortage of engineers is limiting how much business AI services firms can take on. Anthropic itself has sought to address the shortage, announcing a $100 million effort last month to train 10,000 deployment engineers at customer and partner companies by the end of next year. Upstart AI services firms are also competing with major tech firms for talent. Microsoft in July committed $2.5 billion to its Microsoft Frontier Co. with the aim of placing 6,000 engineers inside enterprise customers, partnering with consultancies like Accenture and EY . As of November 2025, Fractional had an annual revenue run rate of over $12 million. At the time of the May acquisition, it was generating around $30 million in ARR, which has since nearly tripled, according to people familiar with the matter. But Ode is being selective about the clients it takes on because it doesn’t have enough engineers to handle all potential business, one of the people said, though it has enough demand for at least two to three times its current workload. OpenAI Deployment Co. has faced similar constraints. The venture, backed by TPG and other investment firms including Brookfield Asset Management and Bain Capital, has sought to hire more engineers to expand available capacity. Ode has made several acquihires and acquisitions since launching, including one of Casper Studios , which designed specialized AI products using Claude. Ode remains open to exploring more deals, a person familiar with the venture said, but is looking to expand its services or geographic reach instead of simply adding more people. Hyde, for its part, isn’t currently seeking acquisitions, but it has declined several takeover offers, Sanga said, mostly from large companies looking to quickly establish their own AI deployment team. This time around, our fintech and crypto category featured new twists on trading and betting and startups positioned to benefit from growth in emerging areas like agentic payments . There’s Fomo, a viral trading app that plans to branch out from memecoins to tokenized stocks, and Catalyst, a startup offering agents that help people trade across venues like prediction markets and crypto exchanges. On the payments side, Natural is offering bank accounts for AI agents, while stablecoin-backed card provider Kast is expanding beyond retail customers by courting merchants. title: Commerce Department Finalizing Long-Awaited AI Remote Access Rule
content: The Commerce Department is finalizing a long-awaited rule that will prevent Chinese AI firms from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through data centers in other countries, according to two people familiar with the process. The move could help the department push back on criticism that it has acted too slowly to create policies to limit China’s access to advanced AI technologies—rules that have been opposed by influential companies such as Nvidia. The rule, which could be announced as soon as this month, will expand existing semiconductor-related controls from the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and extend them to seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to prevent remote access and chip smuggling into China, the people said. Commerce is currently consulting with other government agencies on the rule before it can be finalized, they added. The change will implement a policy that Nvidia has pushed against in previous lobbying efforts, as it would put more stringent requirements on data centers abroad that are major buyers of its chips. Commerce’s decision to finalize the rule could, in part, reflect Nvidia’s waning influence in Washington. Nvidia’s board has been investigating CEO Jensen Huang for an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset and is reportedly considering whether to remove Huang from his position. The Bureau of Industry and Security has faced growing criticism that it has moved too slowly in implementing new export control policies at a time of heightened AI competition with China. The remote access loophole, in particular, meant restrictions on chip exports to China could be easily circumvented, allowing Chinese AI companies to train their models using the most advanced U.S. chips. That criticism of the Bureau of Industry and Security and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler has heightened in recent days after news reports that the Commerce Department halted an investigation into Megaspeed, a Singaporean company embroiled in a scandal involving its former top executive and Huang, after Nvidia intervened . Several prominent Republican lawmakers have called for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to explain why the agency has not moved to block Megaspeed from buying advanced chips. The so-called remote access loophole has long been a focus area for export control policy experts, who argue that it allows Chinese AI companies to gain access, through data centers largely in Southeast Asia, to advanced chips that would otherwise be restricted. There have been previous efforts under the Trump administration to address the loophole through Commerce rules, The Information has reported . And the White House recently provided feedback to Congressional staff requesting a provision be added to export control measures currently being debated in a must-pass defense bill that would have required the Commerce Department to create a rule preventing remote access to certain chips, The Information reported Monday. If finalized, the new Commerce rule could allay some of these concerns by taking action on an issue at the top of the wish list for many China hawks. Remote Access Under the current Commerce Department regime, certain countries such as Saudi Arabia and Vietnam need licenses to receive exports of advanced AI chips. The licenses include controls and conditions such as restricting remote access to companies, as well as different security measures that prevent chip smuggling. Along with Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, the new countries that will now be subject to those licensing requirements include Brazil, Indonesia, Norway and South Africa, said the two people familiar with the rule, which extends to Nvidia Blackwell chips and above. One of the people said that in addition to preventing remote access to advanced AI chips, bringing those new countries under the licensing regime could also combat smuggling. That’s because the rule will now require customers seeking chip exports to tell the Commerce Department who is receiving the chips and what they’re going to be used for, and will subject them to ongoing monitoring. The rule will likely face pushback from governments in those countries, as well as U.S. companies who operate there. Under the new rule, however, U.S. company-run data centers in those countries will not require licenses to receive exports of chips, as long as they restrict remote access of AI chips of a certain capability to countries where the U.S. has arms embargos, such as China, Russia and Venezuela. Those U.S. companies will instead be subject to new reporting requirements, including informing the Commerce Department if they have any customers from arms-controlled countries. The companies will also have to report who the customers in those countries are and how much compute they have, one of the people said. While the new rule is restricted to seven additional countries for now, it could expand, according to one of the people, who said the rule is designed to put other countries on notice that chip smuggling and remote access in a way that is contrary to U.S. interests will not be tolerated. The Commerce Department is also planning to formally rescind the Biden-era AI licensing framework known as the diffusion rule, one of the people said. In May 2025, the Trump administration announced its intention to rescind the rule and issue a replacement, though it never formally scrapped it.

title: Exclusive: SES AI CEO Says Drone Sales Could Lead to Profit
content: In 2021, SES AI CEO Qichao Hu proudly appeared in a company video brandishing a technological breakthrough: a full-size next-generation lithium-metal battery ready to power an electric vehicle, produced in the company’s new factory in South Korea. But in the five years since then, Hu has found no EV maker prepared to deploy that battery in a commercial car, putting millions of dollars of SES’ investment at risk. So this year, Hu threw in the towel and completely rebuilt the South Korean manufacturing line. Now it’s configured to make batteries one-tenth the size of the EV battery—the perfect scale to power drones. And though SES lost $73 million last year, Hu thinks drone battery sales could eventually allow the company to turn a profit. The pivot reflects the impact of the drone boom on the next-generation battery industry after a roughly four-year-long industry slump. In recent months, startups that had earned either very little or no revenue ever have started to see some real money flow in. Virtually all of the next-gen startups, like SES, continue to lose money. But Hu said the early drone revenue received so far means SES is finally earning some money back on the more than $55 million in accumulated equipment and other capital costs incurred since he founded the company in 2012. “All the technology that we’ve developed the last 14, 15 years, now we are monetizing all that technology,” he told me. It’s the latest abrupt strategic turn for SES, which Hu founded out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he was a postdoctoral researcher. The original idea was to develop a battery that used lithium metal as the anode. The industry as a whole had been seeking to develop such a battery since the 1970s because pure lithium metal delivers exceptional energy density, which would translate into extraordinary EV driving range. But no one could manage that feat because lithium metal can explode or catch fire when it comes into contact with air or moisture. Over the subsequent years, Hu developed various working versions of the battery. In 2016, his lab produced a design known as anodeless, because it created its own lithium-metal anode internally on the first charging cycle, thus not requiring some costly equipment. It delivered energy density exceeding 500 watt-hours per kilogram, well over twice that of conventional lithium-ion batteries. But it would sustain only 10 or so charge-discharge cycles. “We were like, ‘OK, who’s going to want these things?’ No car company would want that. So we just basically filed a patent and then shelved it,” Hu said. Hu went on with development until his big 2021 unveiling of the full-size battery. Honda, Hyundai and General Motors all invested in the company, with loose plans to use the battery in future EVs. Then came the downturn in U.S. EV sales. Suddenly, expensive next-gen batteries no longer interested major car companies, which instead began looking to power their EVs with cheaper “good enough” conventional batteries. All three carmakers ended their battery development projects with SES. To survive, Hu repeatedly changed his plans: He moved SES into stationary storage batteries; he developed a materials discovery system using AI; he added silicon and lithium-iron-phosphate batteries to SES’ repertoire. Those gave SES some cash—last year, the company generated $21 million in revenue, and it projects $30 million to $35 million in revenue this year, most of it from stationary storage batteries. But Hu is now focusing on the drone boom, triggered by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which has taken that anodeless battery off the shelf and into use for interceptor drones. “Drones have thrown a lifeline to a lot of the battery startups in the U.S.,” he said. Last month, SES finished the first stage of reconfiguring the drone battery production line in its Chungju, South Korea, factory. It has the capacity to produce 1 million battery cells per year, enough to power approximately 150,000 small quadcopters. Hu said the company will triple the capacity in the second quarter of next year to 3 million battery cells. He said he is responding to a “flood of orders,” but these are still only from countries and companies validating the performance of SES’ batteries. He said he is on the verge of getting commercial production orders that will take up most or all of the planned production. Compared with the EV market, selling drone batteries is easy, Hu suggested. Car companies spend five or more years putting new batteries through tests before making any commercial production commitment—and so far, virtually no next-gen battery startup has gotten past this gauntlet. “Drones are way faster. It’s maybe nine months of validation,” he said. “For some of the smaller drone companies, it could be like three months or just a week.” Most battery startups I speak with have also pivoted to supplying the drone industry, and I asked Hu whether the market for drone batteries is getting saturated. He said it isn’t. “The drone market is still quite early and still evolving, whether it’s defense or civilian commercial applications,” he said. “I do think battery companies need to move quickly and establish some level of scale to actually matter in the space.”

title: Jensen Huang Is Out; Are Inference Providers Screwed?
content: What a week. Jensen Huang , the CEO and cofounder of the world’s second-most-valuable company, resigned, Nvidia said Thursday morning , after reports of extramarital affairs both with a woman alleged to have spied for Beijing as well as a woman who reported to him at Nvidia . Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress will become interim CEO, the company said, while it searches for a permanent successor. Much remains uncertain, including implications for Nvidia’s business of selling advanced AI chips and for Nvidia’s aggressive investments in AI model developers and infrastructure startups that are holding up the AI economy. I’m sure we’ll be getting into all of it in the upcoming days. Meanwhile… It’s not only a tough week to be Huang, but it’s also a tough week to be an inference provider , a well-funded category of startups that help developers use open-source models at high speeds across Nvidia servers. Most recently, Fireworks , one of the most heavily-funded startups in this category, suffered a security breach that exposed customer data to hackers and has also prompted some large customers to consider ditching the service. (In a note to customers, Notion , one of Fireworks’ customers, suggested that, although the inference provider promised it was using zero data retention , meaning that it wouldn’t store any data from Notion after processing a request, Notion later learned that data was actually being retained.) While that incident was bad enough on its own, it exposes a potential systemic vulnerability for the rest of the inference market: the cloud firms that inference providers lease capacity from And that makes me wonder whether it will have a chilling effect beyond Fireworks. The breach was caused by weak security measures at a small cloud provider that Fireworks uses, we reported Wednesday . And increasingly, inference providers are turning to these smaller cloud providers because they can’t rent enough servers from the major cloud providers, such as Microsoft , Amazon and Google , Cathy and I reported in the same article. Capacity shortages have gotten so dire that inference providers like Modal have started using more than 30 different small clouds to access servers they can turn around and rent to their own customers. Many of these cloud providers are young startups themselves and don’t have the security expertise of a major cloud provider. So you can imagine that the sort of breach Fireworks suffered might not be out of the realm of possibility for its competitors, including Baseten , Modal and Fal . Already, I’ve heard of at least one customer of these inference providers that is considering moving its business off these startups. If it did that, it would run open-source models either in its own data centers or with the hyperscalers because its leaders are so spooked about what happened with Fireworks. I’d imagine that other developers, especially those that were affected by the Fireworks breach, would be wary of using alternative inference providers that are sourcing their compute from the same small neoclouds as well. These security concerns could further accelerate the trend Cathy and I wrote about on Wednesday where inference providers buy their own Nvidia servers and stand them up in data centers themselves, rather than renting such servers from other clouds. In building their own data centers, the inference firms could get more control of the security of the cloud services they provide and also improve their gross profit margins, since they’re not paying to rent servers from cloud providers that themselves need to hit certain profit margins. (Margins have been a hurdle for inference providers since they first emerged on the scene three years ago.) This buy-versus-rent approach has its own downsides, though. Finding the power, land and chips to build a data center or even just leasing an existing data center requires a lot of specialized expertise that most companies don’t have. That could explain why inference providers like Fal have job postings for staff to help with data center efforts. And it’s not clear whether the inference providers can do a better job at sourcing chips and managing data centers than the dozens of other cloud providers that are already doing so. Plus doing so requires billions of dollars at a time when the capital markets are seizing up for smaller borrowers (see: the recent neocloud crisis). That’s why Fireworks, for example, has explicitly told investors that it believes acquiring chips and building data centers is a commodity and that its true defensible moat lies in developing software that can run models quickly. Of course, dozens of other firms are trying to do the same thing. Here’s what else is going on… People On The Move Meta Platforms is changing the leadership of its massive data-center operation, with longtime executive Santosh Janardhan telling employees that he is stepping down as head of global infrastructure and will leave the company early next year. Dave Brown , a veteran of Amazon Web Services whom Meta hired in July, will take over as infrastructure head. Big Number Anthropic 's IPO roadshow drew orders for multiple times the 825 million shares on offer within its first day or two on the road, demand that has been credited with helping fuel a broader rally in AI-related stocks, according to Bloomberg. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Torus , which builds modular shipping container–sized AI datacenters, raised $500 million in growth capital led by Magnetar. Edelbyte , which built a data platform for AI agents, emerged from stealth with $70 million in total funding, combining a $25 million seed round led by Sequoia Capital , and a $45 million Series A funding round led by Quiet Capital. Bay , a Tel Aviv-based startup that offers AI agent security software, raised $50 million across seed and Series A rounds. Battery Ventures led the $37 million Series A and YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners led the $13 million seed round. Operand , a New York-based startup that offers AI-powered due diligence software for private equity firms, raised $31 million across seed and Series A funding led by Khosla Ventures . Nebuly , which measures the ROI of enterprise AI agents, raised $21 million in Series A funding led by Planven. XpertDox , which uses AI to code medical bills, raised $20 million in Series A funding led by Savant Growth. Biomatter , which uses AI to design custom enzymes, raised $18 million in an oversubscribed Series A funding round led by Astanor. Plurai , which tests AI agents before they reach customers, raised $13 million in seed funding led by Team8. United Airlines said Wednesday it will ban AI agents and assistants from booking its flights, following similar bans by banks and retailers that cited privacy concerns. SpaceXSI ’s vibe-coding agent, Grok Build , leaked data from thousands of users who used the platform, a new report from security firm Claroc showed. Some of the data included sensitive business information and medical exam results. title: New Startup Voya Energy Proposes Replacement for Loud Diesel Generators in Data Centers
content: In 2023, Shayle Kann, a venture capitalist with Energy Impact Partners, was mulling a longstanding fixation—how to get rid of the loud and polluting diesel generators used to provide backup power for most AI data centers. He put the question to the head of his technology team: Isn’t there some material rivaling the enormous energy density of hydrocarbons that could do the same job cleanly and quietly? The result was Voya Energy, a Hayward, Calif., startup that promises to replace diesel generators with a novel electrochemical process that converts scrap aluminum into electricity without emissions, toxic waste or noise. In August, Kann’s firm led a $35 million Series A round for Voya at a $113 million valuation. Voya leads a lineup of three energy technology companies that made the 2026 edition of The Information 50 , our list of the most promising tech startups, published Wednesday. The other two are Critical Loop, a Long Beach, Calif., startup that offers fast backup power generation, which we profiled last month after it landed a big deal to power an aerospace facility for Anduril Industries; and Parallax, a San Francisco startup that makes natural gas turbines using 3D-printed technology. All three startups fit neatly into the biggest technology boom in decades, offering ways to power AI data centers. Richard Wang, a battery expert whom Kann recruited to be Voya’s CEO, said he expects to deploy pilot versions of the aluminum generator in 2028 and to deliver commercial models to AI data centers and other customers in 2029. But for now, the idea is little more than a concept: No one appears to have ever used metals as fuel to power a commercial industrial facility, and Voya has made only a rudimentary version of the equipment necessary to do so. The idea is that a machine turns scrap aluminum like soda cans into small pellets. A mechanical system loads those pellets into a generator and combines them with an electrolyte, which releases electricity held electrochemically inside the aluminum. The generator delivers that electricity to the data center, and the spent aluminum converts to aluminum trihydrate, which can be used to remake pellets, according to Wang. Voya’s origins start with Kann and his Energy Impact colleague. By early 2024, they had stumbled across a concept that had been around awhile—that the electricity stored in some metals could efficiently deliver a lot of power, just as fossil fuels do. They decided to try to fund a startup to see if they could make that idea work as a business. In 2024, a friend introduced Kann to Wang, a next-generation battery expert. Wang attracted attention in 2021 when he sold Cuberg, a lithium-metal battery startup he co-founded a few years earlier while a graduate student at Stanford University, to Northvolt for an undisclosed amount. Early in 2024, Northvolt shut down Cuberg (and a few months later Northvolt declared bankruptcy). Wang was now out of work. A friend introduced him to Kann, who told him about his idea of how to replace diesel generators. Wang wasn’t impressed. “This looks half-baked,” Wang recalled responding. “I don’t think this is ready to be a company yet, honestly, and I don’t know if I’m the right person to do this right now.” But Wang agreed to join Energy Impact as a technology fellow and explore the concept. After four or so months, he had warmed to the idea. “You look at the ease of producing the metal, the ease of consuming the metal to make electricity, how easy it is to convert it back and forth between metal and metal oxide,” he told me. Wang had started with the periodic table and narrowed down the metals that would be best as electricity generators to magnesium, zinc, iron and aluminum. Aluminum quickly won the bake-off. “Aluminum stands out naturally as having the highest energy density, being an incredibly abundant, very available commodity resource,” he said. Wang told Kann he had changed his mind. “He came to us and he was like, ‘I think this should be a company and I would like to run it,’” Kann said. In April 2025, Energy Impact led a $13 million seed round for Voya. The standard system Wang has in mind would involve two storage containers, one a standard 20-foot-long container with a 2-megawatt aluminum generator, and the other a 10-foot one containing enough aluminum pellets to produce 100 megawatt-hours of energy. Wang said the advantages of such a system include that aluminum rivals hydrocarbons in terms of energy density and can be stored at an industrial site in a much more compact space than diesel because it’s not flammable and releases no emissions. Voya claims the system converts 57% of the pellets into electricity, higher than diesel’s average 35% conversion efficiency. The one ultrapolluting aspect of using aluminum is the smelting stage. By relying on scrap aluminum, Voya is initially avoiding dealing with the smelting question. But Wang said there are ways to sharply reduce the amount of energy used to smelt the metal and the emissions released in the process. “Our ultimate ambition is to really think about designing our own smelting cells and systems and ultimately plants that are of our own creation, because we think that’s the pathway to get to the lowest-cost-possible aluminum,” Wang said.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns, Creating Uncertainty for the AI Sector
content: Nvidia CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resigned in a stunning turn of events that upends the world’s second-most-valuable company and rattles one of the foundations of the AI economy. Finance chief Colette Kress will become interim CEO, Nvidia said in a statement on Thursday morning. The move came three days after the board announced an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.” U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly concluded earlier this year that Huang had developed a close relationship with a woman they believed was spying for Beijing. Huang on Sunday also apologized to Nvidia employees for having an extramarital affair. The company said it was initiating a search for a permanent CEO “and will consider internal and external candidates.” Huang has internally and externally pushed back on the need for a succession plan, according to employees and Huang’s public commentary. He has dozens of direct reports but no clear No. 2. Nvidia’s shares were trading down 12% in early trading on Thursday. In its statement, Nvidia said thanked Huang for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” It did not elaborate on the reasons for Huang’s departure. Nvidia said one of its directors, Harvey Jones, would become the company’s “first-ever chair of the board.” In a securities filing, Nvidia said the board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. His departure appeared to come quickly. As of Tuesday, Huang was operating normally within Nvidia, including preparing for next week’s quarterly earnings call, according to a person familiar with the situation. A Tuesday meeting with Nvidia’s executive staff—a group of 50 or so executives who mostly report directly to Huang—proceeded normally, other than Huang’s delivery of a short apology to his colleagues at the start of the meeting, that person said. But Huang faced other revelations that added to precariousness of his position at Nvidia. Several former employees told The Information that Huang was widely believed to have been in a separate relationship with Kimberly Powell, a vice president who ran healthcare technology-related initiatives at the company and reported directly to Huang. The alleged relationship was widely discussed by employees for years, these people said. Earlier Wednesday, The New York Times earlier reported that video evidence of the affair between the two executives had surfaced internally earlier this year. Huang and Powell, along with representatives for Nvidia and Huang, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Earlier in the week, Nvidia had hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the investigation into Huang’s conduct, and President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating Huang’s relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang. The Information reported Tuesday that Alice Huang worked at a Chinese firm that distributed hundreds of thousands of advanced Nvidia AI chips despite a U.S. ban on their sale to China. Huang’s firing is a major blow to a company that he has become synonymous with since he co-founded it in 1993. Nvidia has soared to Olympian heights during the current AI boom, in part through Huang’s relentless style of leadership and aggressive efforts to stay ahead of its competition. Nvidia’s graphics processing units are the dominant chips for training and running AI models, turning the company into a business juggernaut that reported $216 billion in revenue last year. In recent years, Huang told some senior colleagues that he planned to run Nvidia until he is 120 years old, according to a former Nvidia manager who heard the comments (Huang is currently 63). “This company was built around him for 30 years,” this person said. “This is unimaginable.” Huang’s ouster also creates uncertainty for the broader AI sector. He has been one of the most high-profile public advocates for AI, rebutting concerns about its safety even as others in the industry have raised them. And he has aggressively pumped Nvidia’s cash into a new crop of cloud companies that rent out its server chips to AI developers, as well as into AI developers such as OpenAI. Nvidia is planning to invest $10 billion in Anthropic’s initial public offering next week and has discussed providing credit guarantees related to a proposed data center in West Virginia that Anthropic plans to lease. As of earlier in the fall, Nvidia had $100 billion in equity investments in other companies. Huang’s ouster is likely to rattle stock market investors who have already been skittish about some of the smaller firms that depend on Nvidia server chips and capital to run their businesses. Huang’s successor will likely face questions about whether they plan to continue Nvidia’s practice of investing so freely in its customers. It also remains unclear whether any successor to Huang will have the clout to continue the tactics that helped make Nvidia so dominant—for example, its muscling of key partners like the chip manufacturer TSMC for capacity. The company is facing an array of competitors eager to chip away at its power. Google, AMD and Amazon offer competing server chips, and more potential competition is coming from Anthropic and OpenAI. “Jensen is so singular,” says an executive at a company that is a major customer of Nvidia’s chips. The fallout from Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang could spread beyond him. In recent days, The Information and other media organizations have reported on the reluctance of leaders in the Commerce Department in the past to impose export controls on AI chips and related technologies that would prevent China from getting access to them. Nvidia has lobbied aggressively against such rules in the past. (Late Wednesday, The Information reported that the Commerce Department is finalizing a new rule that would close a loophole that has allowed Chinese AI firms to remotely access advanced AI chips.) Lawmakers from both parties have begun calling for tougher export controls on Nvidia’s chips and related products, which Congress could pass in the coming weeks as part of a collection of legislation called the National Defense Authorization Act. A House subcommittee has also asked Huang to testify behind closed doors at a hearing in Washington next week about his relationship with Alice Huang. The outcome of that and other related probes could lead to further departures from Nvidia. Huang’s ouster could also be awkward for members of his family: His daughter and son, Madison and Spencer Huang , both work at Nvidia, along with Madison’s husband, Nico Caprez .
