title: SpaceX proposes 750 MW gas plant for Texas supercomputing hub
content: SpaceX is seeking approval to set up a 750-megawatt (MW) natural gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility at Starbase,Texas.The company separately confirmed on Thursday plans to invest more than $24 billion in the supercomputing project, which will generate its own electricity without drawing power from the public grid.The proposed facilities are part of a broader development plan for which SpaceX has sought a property tax abatement and a related economic development agreement, according to a public hearing notice issued by the City of Starbase. The city commission is scheduled to consider both requests at a public hearing on December 9.Multi-billion project​To develop the said facilities, the company has proposed an investment of $24 billion, which would be the largest private technology investment ever proposed in the Rio Grande Valley as the company seeks to expand its artificial intelligence computing capabilities.​The company said the proposed project would be built on roughly 444 acres near the Port of Brownsville and would combine a natural gas power plant with a large-scale data center designed to support AI workloads.The project has already generated more than 3,000 construction jobs and is expected to support more than 500 permanent positions once operational. The planned investment builds on more than $15 billion the company has already invested in Starship and related infrastructure at Starbase.​It would construct, own, and operate both the power plant and the supercomputing campus. The space company has been focusing on producing electricity from fossil fuels to power Musk’s larger ambitions in the AI space. Building its own power generation facility could allow SpaceX to avoid lengthy waits for grid connections, an increasingly common challenge for developers of large AI data centers.According to SpaceX, the supercomputing facility will train frontier intelligence systems for applications spanning medical research, emergency response, advanced manufacturing and national security. It will also help develop and test technologies for future space-based computing.​The proposal also aligns with Elon Musk’s broader AI ambitions. SpaceX has rapidly expanded beyond its traditional launch business by investing heavily in computing infrastructure that supports AI services. The company has reported strong growth in AI-related revenue while renting computing capacity to customers including Google and Anthropic.The company also announced a $220 million project to expand Brownsville’s water and wastewater infrastructure. The company described this as the largest private contribution to the city’s water future in its history and said it has already provided $40 million to the Brownsville Public Utilities Board to begin the work.The proposed water projects could add approximately 20 million gallons per day of additional capacity through potable water reuse and expanded brackish-groundwater treatment. The investment is intended to strengthen regional water security and reduce dependence on the Rio Grande.SpaceX’s other natural gas projects ​In October, SpaceX sought approval for a 32.4-mile natural gas pipeline in Florida to supply fuel for its Starship rockets as the company prepares to expand launch operations at Cape Canaveral.The proposed 16-inch transmission pipeline would run through Brevard County and connect SpaceX facilities with the existing Florida Gas Transmission interstate pipeline, and bring natural gas directly from the interstate network to customers including SpaceX.Florida is not SpaceX’s first attempt to build a dedicated natural gas connection for Starship. The company has also sought approval for an approximately 8-mile pipeline serving its Starbase launch complex near Boca Chica in South Texas.The two projects point to a broader effort to establish dedicated fuel infrastructure around SpaceX’s major Starship launch sites. The Florida pipeline would be about four times as long as the proposed Texas connection.Once approved, the Starbase project would rank among the largest private investments in South Texas and further transform the company’s launch site into a hub for both space exploration and AI infrastructure. The December 9 hearing will determine whether SpaceX receives the requested tax incentives needed to move the project forward.

title: SpaceX's 6-gigawatt campus will use dry cooling, skip groundwater use
content: SpaceX plans to invest around $50 billion in a supercomputing campus in Arizona, using a dry-cooling system designed to reduce the facility’s reliance on water. The project is part of a wider expansion worth more than $74 billion across Arizona and Texas as the company scales up its computing infrastructure.The proposed campus in Cochise County would use air-based cooling instead of conventional water-intensive systems. SpaceX also said it does not plan to use industrial groundwater for the facility, an important distinction for a project planned in an arid region where water availability is a major concern.Dry cooling limits water useThe Arizona facility is expected to create around 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent positions, according to SpaceX. The company is also working with local electric cooperatives to supply electricity to the campus.SpaceX said the development could reduce electricity bills for cooperative members by up to 20 percent. The project would require significant power infrastructure, with its plans outlining a campus of nine computing buildings and capacity of up to 6 gigawatts when fully developed. However, the development is not yet approved. SpaceX needs permission from Cochise County, where the proposal has drawn opposition from some residents. A petition with around 2,400 signatures has asked county officials to reject the project, with a public hearing scheduled for December. Texas brings water investmentThe Arizona campus is one part of SpaceX’s planned expansion. The company has also announced an investment of more than $24 billion in a supercomputing facility at its Starbase site in Texas.Unlike the Arizona project, the Texas facility is expected to generate its own electricity rather than draw power from the public grid. A separate public filing describes a proposed 750-megawatt natural gas-fired power plant alongside the computing campus. The gas plant remains a proposal and should not be confused with SpaceX’s announcement of the supercomputing facility. The Texas development has also brought a major water infrastructure commitment for nearby Brownsville. SpaceX has pledged up to $220 million for water and wastewater projects in the city and Cameron County, with $40 million provided initially under the agreement.The company said the investment would support projects capable of adding 20 million gallons of water capacity per day. However, Brownsville’s approved plans identify two projects expected to add approximately 18 million gallons daily: an 8-million-gallon-per-day potable water reuse system and a 10-million-gallon-per-day expansion of the Southmost Regional Water Authority facility. The agreement does not give SpaceX ownership of the water infrastructure or reserved capacity in the system. The projects are intended to strengthen the region’s water supply as Brownsville and surrounding communities continue to grow.Together, the two campuses represent a major expansion of SpaceX’s computing ambitions, with the Arizona project highlighting an approach to reducing industrial water demand and the Texas development combining dedicated power generation with a substantial regional water investment.

title: Spacecraft refueling port costs just $1 ahead of historic orbital test
content: Spacecraft could soon share a common refueling connection, potentially changing how operators manage satellites in orbit. Spaceium has released OpenPort, an open-source interface that any company can license and manufacture for just $1.The design lets spacecraft receive fuel after launch instead of relying entirely on their onboard reserves. It will also undergo an orbital demonstration aboard the International Space Station.Common refueling standardMost satellites carry a fixed supply of propellant for their planned missions. Once that supply runs low, operators often retire otherwise functional spacecraft. Their electronics and other systems might remain operational, but limited fuel can end their usefulness.A lack of standardized connections has also complicated orbital refueling efforts. Different manufacturers develop their own interfaces, forcing operators to consider compatibility before arranging fuel transfers. A tanker built by one company might not connect with another manufacturer’s spacecraft.OpenPort aims to address that problem through an identical connection on both spacecraft. Its androgynous design allows either vehicle to supply or receive propellant. That means a satellite could potentially refuel another spacecraft instead of relying exclusively on dedicated tankers.The interface also replaces a conventional fill-and-drain valve. Those connections typically serve ground fueling operations before launch. OpenPort keeps the connection functional after a spacecraft reaches orbit.Spaceium says its design handles higher pressures and greater docking misalignment than competing refueling interfaces. These capabilities could help spacecraft establish reliable connections during demanding orbital operations.Xenon transfer reaches orbitOpenPort’s upcoming demonstration will take place aboard the International Space Station. Spaceium plans to fly the hardware as a NASA-approved external payload through Voyager Technologies’ commercial payload service.During the demonstration, the interface will transfer xenon between two tanks in orbit. Spaceium describes this as the first-ever xenon transfer performed in orbit. The mission will test whether spacecraft can exchange propellant through a standardized connection.The demonstration follows another Spaceium mission in February 2026. Its precision robotic actuator successfully completed its first space mission after launching aboard a SpaceX rideshare.Building a refueling networkSpaceium wants OpenPort to become a widely adopted connection across the spacecraft industry. Its broader business model centers on automated orbital stations that sell propellant as a service.Co-founder and CEO Ashi Dissanayake says the company sees the stations as its primary business. Every spacecraft equipped with OpenPort could eventually become a potential customer.“The port isn’t the business. The stations are,” Dissanayake said. He believes widespread adoption will create demand for orbital refueling services, including those operated by competitors.Founded by aerospace and mechanical engineers Dissanayake and Reza Fetanat, Spaceium joined Y Combinator’s Summer 2024 batch. Its commercial customers include operators pursuing orbital transfer vehicles, lunar missions and geostationary satellites.The company plans to establish refueling stations across low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit. Its longer-term ambitions also include stations along routes to the Moon.A common connection could eventually help satellite operators extend spacecraft lifespans. It could also allow lunar missions and orbital transfer vehicles to travel farther without carrying all their propellant from Earth.Spaceium is expanding its engineering team as it prepares for the ISS demonstration and its first refueling station. OpenPort’s adoption will ultimately determine whether different spacecraft manufacturers embrace a shared standard.

title: US tears down 10 historic, highly contaminated Cold War-era buildings
content: Ten historic, heavily contaminated buildings at the heart of Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) have been reduced to rubble. The demolition marks the end of a six-year environmental cleanup campaign.Known collectively as Isotope Row, the tightly packed cluster spanned more than 12,000 square feet across the laboratory’s central campus. Removing the derelict structures eliminates long-standing radiological risks. It also frees up prime real estate for next-generation science.“After decades standing at the heart of ORNL, Isotope Row is gone and ORNL’s skyline is forever changed,” said Clint Wolfley, senior vice president of end state delivery for prime cleanup contractor United Cleanup Oak Ridge (UCOR).Coordinating a delicate teardownThe US Department of Energy’s (DOE) Oak Ridge Office of Environmental Management worked alongside UCOR to execute the project. Preparing the aging complex took six years of meticulous engineering. However, crews demolished the physical buildings in just two months.To keep neighboring laboratories running without disruption, demolition teams limited heavy teardown work to afternoon hours. This schedule required close coordination with laboratory operator UT-Battelle and the DOE’s Office of Science. Workers also disposed of most demolition debris directly on site. This approach spared taxpayers the high cost of hauling contaminated rubble to distant facilities.Isotope Row dates back to the late 1940s through the early 1960s. For decades, scientists inside these buildings produced radioisotopes used in medicine, industry, scientific research, and national defense.Operations shut down in the early 1990s. The facilities were left behind with radioactive isotopes, mercury, asbestos, and contaminated machinery still inside. Before demolition equipment could move in, crews had to sever all utility connections and strip out hazardous insulation. This preparatory phase is known as transitioning the buildings to “cold-and-dark” status.Clearing complex hazardsDeactivation teams entered the buildings in 2020 to tackle the interior hazards step by step. Multidisciplinary workers removed combustible materials, six contaminated hot cells, and several specialized gloveboxes. They also hauled out four 2,000-pound tanks that previously stored inert gas. In total, teams removed nearly three million pounds of waste from the site.The trickiest engineering challenge hung 10 to 15 feet above the laboratory floors. Central ventilation and process off-gas pipes were partly made of a concrete-and-asbestos blend that had soaked up radioactive contamination over decades. Crews used strict containment barriers and specialized packaging to dismantle the overhead ducts without releasing hazardous dust.Federal Project Director Michael Griswold said the project demanded high-level technical skill and an unwavering focus on worker safety.“This accomplishment reduces risks today while opening new opportunities for the laboratory’s tomorrow,” Griswold said.Wolfley credited the cleanup workforce for six years of creative problem-solving. He noted that their efforts have turned one of ORNL’s most hazardous footprints into an asset for future discovery.“After decades standing at the heart of ORNL, Isotope Row is gone and ORNL’s skyline is forever changed, clearing the way for its next generation of scientific discovery,” concluded UCOR.

title: Gas flow assisted flash evaporation deposits perovskite films at over 1 µm per minute without solvents
content:
Gas flow assisted flash evaporation deposits perovskite films at over 1 µm per minute without solvents
Researchers at the University of Valencia’s Institute of Molecular Science (ICMol) in Spain, together with
Oxford PV
, have developed a solvent-free vacuum technique for depositing perovskite films at rates above 1 µm per minute. The method, called gas flow assisted flash evaporation (Gas-FE), deposits films from a single pre-formulated powder, which the team says gets around the difficulty of controlling many separate sources in conventional co-evaporation.
In co-evaporation, each component needs its own source, and controlling the film composition gets harder as formulations become more complex, especially with trace additives. Deposition times can also run to hours. Earlier flash-evaporation approaches fed small amounts of powder into a heated crucible, which limited throughput. In Gas-FE, a ball-milled perovskite powder is fed by an auger screw into a nitrogen gas flow, forming an aerosol. The aerosol passes through a vaporizer held at 500 °C, and the vapor is carried through a heated showerhead onto a temperature-controlled substrate holder, at a roughing-pump vacuum of about 10 mbar. The team says this shortens turnaround between batches compared with high-vacuum deposition.
The researchers say the method transferred a mixture of components with widely different volatilities, including guanidinium iodide, amantadine hydrochloride, benzylphosphonic acid, lithium TFSI, formamidinium bromide, methylammonium iodide and lead iodide. They also report X-ray diffraction evidence of film formation from FA/Cs mixed-cation and mixed-halide powders.
For the main tests, the team used methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI₃) with 10 mol% methylammonium chloride and 8 mol% lithium TFSI. Films 100 to 1,100 nm thick were deposited by varying the powder injection time from 7 to 60 seconds, with a measured growth rate of about 18.6 nm/s (roughly 1.1 µm per minute). On a 10 × 10 cm² substrate area, the I:Pb ratio varied by less than 5% and the film thickness by 4%. Run-to-run variation was 6% to 8%.
The researchers integrated 250 nm films into a fully vacuum-deposited p-i-n solar cell (glass/FTO/MeO-2PACz/perovskite/C60/SnO₂/Cu). The best 0.05 cm² device reached a power conversion efficiency of 9.6%, with an open-circuit voltage of 0.91 V, a short-circuit current density of 16.8 mA/cm² and a fill factor of 63.3%. The team calls this a moderate, proof-of-concept result and says the spread in voltage and fill factor suggests that further improvement should focus on the interfaces and trap density.
The work was part of Spain’s PERTE Chip project, funded by NextGenerationEU.

title: China’s highways could generate 182 TWh of solar annually - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers at China’s Tongji University have developed a framework to assess highway PV potential based on solar irradiance, terrain and road networks. They estimate that China’s highways could generate enough solar power to cover 1.85% of national electricity consumption.
Lior Kahana
13 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
Illustration of roadside PV
A research team at China’s
Tongji University
has developed a new framework to assess the PV generation potential of highway networks. The approach combines solar irradiance, terrain and road-network characteristics and can be adapted to different countries by adjusting its parameters to local conditions.
“This research creates an irradiance-terrain-road network coupling model for highway PV assessment,” corresponding author Xiaojun Shen told
pv magazine
. “Unlike prior studies that only calculate available land, we integrate solar resources, terrain occlusion and road distribution, and categorize highway usable space. Furthermore, we propose three tailored operation schemes for off-grid, weak-grid and strong-grid scenarios, which helps planners match highway PV solutions to local grid conditions.”
The framework estimates annual highway PV generation potential based on solar irradiance, terrain effects and available installation area. It considers three categories of space: roadside areas, including medians and slopes; structural areas at tunnel entrances and exits; and service-area rooftops. The calculations account for installation geometry, module efficiency and system losses. The researchers also proposed three operating strategies: self-consumption with surplus energy storage in off-grid areas, grid support during electricity shortages in weak-grid areas and surplus electricity exports in strong-grid areas.
For the Chinese case study, the researchers used NASA Power irradiance data for 2025, with a spatial resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°, to define four solar-resource zones using ArcGIS. They divided terrain into three elevation categories – above 3,000 meters, between 500 meters and 3,000 meters, and below 500 meters – and assigned correction factors of 0.55, 0.75 and 0.95, respectively. They then used OpenCV to combine the resulting maps with China’s 185,000 km highway network. The calculations assumed a module tilt angle of 35 degrees, median widths of 1.5 meters, roadside slope widths of 5 meters and module efficiency of 17.5%, resulting in an overall conversion efficiency of 13.66% after accounting for losses.
“We were surprised to find that the dense highway network in central and eastern China creates substantial PV potential, even though the solar resource level there is lower than the west,” Shen said. “In addition, terrain shading imposes a dramatic reduction on power output for mountain highways, which is often overlooked in large-scale potential estimates.”
The results showed that China’s 185,000 km highway network has an estimated annual PV generation potential of 182 TWh, equivalent to approximately 1.85% of the country’s total electricity consumption in 2025. Roadside areas account for the largest share of the potential, followed by service-area buildings, while structural areas contribute less than 0.5%.
The researchers identified three major challenges to large-scale highway PV deployment: high installation costs and long payback periods that limit economic viability; potential conflicts with roadside ecology and traffic safety; and fragmented, site-specific demonstration projects that lack coordinated regional planning and systematic operation and maintenance.
“As for follow-up work, we plan to study the techno-economic performance of highway PV-storage configurations in service areas,” Shen said. “Traffic safety constraints for roadside PV installations will also be included to form practical deployment guidance.”
The findings are presented in “
Photovoltaic generation potential assessment of highway systems based on irradiance–terrain–road network coupling
,” published in
Next Energy

title: Chinese PV Industry Brief: Energy China shortlists 23 module suppliers for 15 GW tender - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, JinkoSolar has secured certification under new Chinese PV standards and Trina Solar is expanding into AI data center energy solutions, Drinda has canceled its Oman factory project, while GCL SI has secured a module supply contract, and polysilicon oversupply continues to weigh on prices.
Vincent Shaw
13 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy China
has shortlisted 23 manufacturers for its 2026 centralized procurement of 15 GW of solar modules, including LONGi, Tongwei, JinkoSolar, JA Solar and Trina Solar. The tender covers 10.7 GW of tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) modules, 1 GW of heterojunction (HJT) modules and 3.3 GW of back-contact (BC) modules. Shortlisted bids range from CNY 0.695 ($0.102)/W to CNY 0.779/W. The announcement identifies shortlisted bidders, with final contract awards yet to be confirmed.
JinkoSolar
said it is among the first manufacturers to secure certification under two mandatory Chinese national standards: GB 47739-2026, covering PV module safety requirements, and GB 47740-2026, covering PV module nameplate and marking requirements. The certifications were issued by the China Quality Certification Centre (CQC) and China General Certification Center (CGC). The standards introduce stricter requirements for module safety, labeling and manufacturing consistency.
Trina Solar
and Intel showcased an integrated energy and computing solution for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers at the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai. Trina Solar presented grid-forming battery energy storage systems, AI-driven energy dispatch technology and an 800 V high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) power supply solution. The companies launched a pilot project in September to coordinate energy supply and computing operations. The collaboration is part of Trina Solar’s expansion into energy infrastructure solutions for AI data centers.
has canceled plans to build a 5 GW solar cell manufacturing facility in Oman, citing escalating international trade tensions, geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and changes to China’s PV technology export policies. The Chinese solar cell manufacturer said the developments had undermined the project’s viability. Drinda signed a letter of intent with the Oman Investment Authority in June 2024 to develop a 10 GW TOPCon cell manufacturing facility with an estimated investment of $700 million. The project was originally planned in two 5 GW phases.
GCL System Integration (GCL SI)
has secured a module supply contract for a 1 GW solar project developed by Xinjiang Xingqihang New Energy in Wusu, Xinjiang region. The contract covers approximately 776,840 modules rated at 710 W each, representing about 551.6 MW of DC capacity. Final delivery volumes will depend on project implementation. The agreement also includes transportation, installation guidance, technical support and after-sales services.
TrendForce
said China’s polysilicon inventories remained above 570,000 metric tons, while domestic production was expected to fall to approximately 95,000 metric tons in November. Despite further production cuts, polysilicon supply continues to slightly exceed demand from downstream ingot producers. Wafer inventories stood at around 27 GW, while average prices for 183 mm wafers fell to CNY 0.95 ($0.14) per piece. Weak module orders and persistent oversupply continue to put downward pressure on prices across the PV supply chain.

title: Dark clouds gather over Germany’s solar sector - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar module prices are stagnating, while battery energy storage system prices are expected to rise for the first time. Germany’s solar market could face significant challenges if policymakers fail to push through reforms to Germany’s Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) in time, according to Martin Schachinger of pvXchange.
Martin Schachinger, pvXchange.com
13 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Just as nature often falls calm before a storm, Germany is currently experiencing a period of apparent inactivity, particularly within the governing coalition when it comes to legislative reforms in the energy sector. Instead of swiftly finalizing reforms that would at least avoid undermining the renewable energy sector and secure approval from the relevant authorities, the government appears more focused on making concessions to major players in the fossil fuel industry.
Whether deliberately or through sheer irresponsibility, the federal government is delaying necessary decisions and postponing the finalization of the EEG 2027, Germany’s Renewable Energy Sources Act, and a package of measures concerning the electricity grid. This is fueling uncertainty about the future and threatening the viability of numerous business models and the companies that depend on them. The question is whether this is merely a passing shower or a major storm brewing on the horizon.
Solar module price trends this month, by contrast, resemble a gentle breeze, offering some relief. Price reductions in the Full Black and Mainstream categories have been marginal, while prices in the other two categories have remained unchanged. A slight increase in demand in the second half of the year has been met with generally good module availability. As a result, the market is experiencing neither significant oversupply nor shortages, apart from certain ultra-high-efficiency products. Although the overall trend remains slightly downward, manufacturers are not expected to make any further significant price cuts before the end of the year.
The situation is quite different for energy storage products. For years, battery prices moved in only one direction: downward. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, in particular, benefited from steadily declining costs thanks to improvements in energy density and economies of scale. However, prices now appear to have reached a floor. Rising energy and transportation costs are prompting manufacturers to introduce significant price increases for the first time. These increases have been announced gradually over recent months, and by January at the latest, products from various brands are expected to cost more than they do today, at least in the residential storage segment. As wholesalers, we are preparing for a sharp increase in demand toward the end of the year.
This tendency to bring forward purchases, along with similar developments, is currently boosting order books across the sector. But how long can this surge last? Until Christmas, or perhaps even into the first quarter of 2027?
A more serious storm is brewing over the European Commission’s state aid approval for the planned reform of Germany’s Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG). If approval is not secured in time, there is a risk that subsidies for solar power could be suspended from Jan. 1, 2027. The current authorization expires at the end of this year. If the new legislation is not adopted and submitted to the European Commission in time, new solar projects could face considerable legal and investment uncertainty, particularly those that depend on public subsidies or the financial security provided by guaranteed support mechanisms. This would primarily affect medium- and large-scale, debt-financed PV installations, while conventional residential systems designed for self-consumption would be less exposed.
Nevertheless, I believe a market-wide downturn cannot be ruled out. Some competitors I have spoken with are less pessimistic. They point to a growing number of large-scale, subsidy-free solar projects that can operate profitably without EEG support. In the small and medium-sized segments, too, emerging business models and service providers, including those offering direct marketing services, suggest that new installations could remain economically viable.
However, every installation needs a grid connection, and the process of securing one should be as straightforward as possible. Unfortunately, despite the stated political goal of reducing bureaucracy, more and more obstacles are being introduced. These additional requirements impose costs on system operators, potentially making many projects economically unviable.
Prices in November, including changes from the previous month (as of Nov. 10).
Martin Schachinger has studied electrical engineering and has been active in the field of photovoltaics and renewable energy for almost 30 years. In 2004, he set up the pvXchange.com online trading platform. The company stocks standard components for new installations and solar modules and inverters that are no longer being produced.

title: Malaysia extends residential solar rebates for approved applicants - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Malaysia’s residential solar rebate scheme has MYS 90 million ($22.1 million) remaining. Approved applicants will now be given until March 2027 to complete their PV installations and claim rebates.
Patrick Jowett
13 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Highlights
Residential
Malaysia will continue providing residential solar rebates to approved applicants under its Sustainable Rebate and Incentive Assistance (SuRIA) Home programme into 2027, the country’s Energy Transition and Water Transformation Minister Fadillah Yusof has confirmed.
The SuRIA Home programme
launched in June
with a MYS 150 million ($36.7 million) budget. The scheme offers eligible households a rebate of MYS 600 ($147.11)/kW of installed solar capacity up to a maximum of MYS 3,000 per household for a 5 kW PV system.
Yusof’s update to parliament earlier this week confirmed that applicants whose installations have not been completed by the programme’s scheduled Dec. 31, 2026 end date will remain eligible for their approved rebates, provided their solar systems are installed by March 2027.
There is currently MYS 90 million worth of funding support remaining, the minister added.
Government statistics state that 12,374 households had received support through the scheme as of September 15, worth a combined MYS 36.2 million. The government set a target of supporting 50,000 homeowners under the scheme at the time of its launch.
Yusof also provided parliament with an update on Malaysia’s Solar Accelerated Transition Action Programme (Solar ATAP), which allows residential, commercial and industrial customers to install solar for self-consumption while exporting surplus power to the grid. It
came into effect at the start of the year
The programme had approved 24,291 applications representing 391.85 MW of solar capacity as of September 15, Yusof said, compared to with 135.92 MW approved as of April 30, representing an increase of almost 190% in approved capacity over four and a half months.
Yusof also highlighted solar leasing and rent-to-own arrangements as alternative financing options that could reduce upfront costs and make residential solar installations more accessible to lower- and middle-income households in Malaysia.

title: Norway enters carbon credit agreement with Indonesia - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Norwegian government says the deal, covering 12 million tonnes of emission reductions, will help to accelerate the development of renewable energy sources in Indonesia.
Patrick Jowett
13 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Norway has agreed to purchase up to 12 million tonnes of emission reductions from Indonesia via a new carbon credit agreement.
Under the terms of the agreement, set to last ten years according to a statement published by the Norwegian government, Norway will purchase verified emissions reductions generated through new renewable energy projects in Indonesia.
Revenue from the sales “makes it possible for Indonesia to build projects that would otherwise not be realised,” the government’s statement adds.
The agreement was signed by the Global Green Growth Institute, acting on behalf of Norway, and Indonesian state-owned utility PLN.
It operates under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to cooperate on emissions reductions through the transfer of carbon credits between nations.
The deal builds on a climate cooperation agreement signed by Norway and Indonesia in June last year, which established a framework for using carbon-market financing to support floating solar power plants on reservoirs.
Norway’s Minister of Climate and Environment Sigrun Aasland said the new cooperation will help to ensure that more of Indonesia’s electricity comes from solar rather than coal, which currently covers over 70% of the country’s electricity production.
“[The agreement] shows how international cooperation can contribute to both emission cuts and a faster transition to renewable energy,” Aasland added.
The deal arrives as Indonesia begins implementing a
large-scale solar programme
aiming to deploy
100 GW of solar by 2029
. The country surpassed 1 GW of solar capacity in 2025, with total capacity reaching
Earlier this year, the Norwegian government backed a
carbon finance procurement facility
in Zambia that sees Norway purchase carbon credits generated by renewable energy projects. The project launched with a
300 MW solar tender
for projects connected to on-site storage.

title: Shinsung E&G unveils 650 W bifacial TOPCon solar modules with 23.25% efficiency - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
South Korean solar manufacturer Shinsung E&G has introduced new n-type TOPCon solar modules for ground-mounted, floating PV and agrivoltaic applications. The bifacial panels feature power outputs ranging from 640 W to 650 W and maximum conversion efficiencies of 23.25%.
Emiliano Bellini
13 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
South Korea-based solar module manufacturer
Shinsung E&G
has unveiled two new series of bifacial solar modules based on n-type tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) cell technology.
The new products include the SS-JM-TK series for ground-mounted solar installations and the SS-JM-TN series for floating photovoltaic and agrivoltaic applications. Both product lines are available in three versions, with nominal power outputs of 640 W, 645 W and 650 W.
The modules feature 156 bifacial monocrystalline solar cells and offer conversion efficiencies ranging from 22.89% to 23.25% under standard test conditions (STC).
The ground-mounted modules measure 2,465 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weigh 33.5 kg. The largest model, the SS-JM650TK, delivers a maximum power output of 650 W and an efficiency of 23.25%. It features an open-circuit voltage of 55.71 V and a short-circuit current of 14.52 A.
Under the manufacturer’s bifacial nominal power irradiance (BNPI) conditions, the ground-mounted series delivers power outputs of 700 W to 710 W, with corresponding efficiencies of up to 25.40%. Actual rear-side power generation depends on ground reflectivity and installation conditions.
The floating PV and agrivoltaic modules have the same length and width but feature a thicker, 35 mm frame. They also weigh 33.5 kg and provide maximum front-side power outputs of 650 W, with efficiencies reaching 23.25%.
Under BNPI conditions, the floating and agrivoltaic series delivers outputs of 705 W to 717 W, with the highest-rated model achieving a bifacial-equivalent efficiency of 25.65%.
Both product lines feature a dual-glass construction comprising 2.0 mm heat-strengthened glass on the front and rear sides, an anodized aluminum alloy frame, and an IP68-rated junction box with three bypass diodes.
The modules are designed for operation at a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and temperatures ranging from -40 C to 85 C.
According to the manufacturer, the ground-mounted modules have a maximum power temperature coefficient of -0.34%/C, compared with -0.29%/C for the floating and agrivoltaic variants.
The ground-mounted series is rated for mechanical test loads of 5,400 Pa on the front and 2,400 Pa on the rear. The floating and agrivoltaic modules offer a 5,400 Pa test-load rating on both sides.
Shinsung E&G provides a 12-year product warranty and a 30-year performance warranty for both series. The company guarantees at least 99% of the initial power output after the first year and 87.4% after 30 years, with maximum annual degradation of 0.4%.
In August, Shinsung E&G
opened a new 350 MW solar module production line
at its Gimje factory in South Korea, bringing the facility’s total production capacity to 600 MW. The company said the line would manufacture n-type solar modules for projects in the Saemangeum development region, including an 80 MW ground-mounted installation, another 74 MW project and a 300 MW floating solar facility.

title: Sodium-ion batteries close gap with lithium-ion as utility-scale storage opportunities grow - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Sodium-ion batteries are approaching lithium-ion performance in key areas, with commercial cells reaching energy densities of 175 Wh/kg and offering strong low-temperature performance. Silvia Bodoardo, professor at the Polytechnic University of Turin, told
pv magazine
that utility-scale energy storage represents the technology’s most promising market, as manufacturers ramp up production.
Sergio Matalucci
13 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Singeng sodium-ion battery project in Hubei
Sodium-ion batteries are emerging as a viable alternative to lithium-ion technology for stationary energy storage, driven by improvements in energy density, cycle life, safety and manufacturability.
According to Silvia Bodoardo, full professor at the Polytechnic University of Turin and scientific representative for the Batteries European Partnership Association (BEPA), the most significant development over the past 12 months has been the growing technological maturity of sodium-ion batteries.
“Sodium-ion technology clearly represents the most important development,” Bodoardo told
pv magazine
. “The fundamental shift is no longer just about material performance, but the convergence of energy density, cycle life, safety, and manufacturability.”
Commercial sodium-ion cells have reached energy densities of around 175 Wh/kg, compared with approximately 205 Wh/kg for advanced lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. The narrowing gap is particularly relevant for stationary storage, where weight is less critical than in electric vehicles.
“The gap is therefore becoming relatively small for stationary applications, where gravimetric energy density is not the dominant key performance indicator,” said Bodoardo.
Low-temperature performance is another area of progress. CATL’s second-generation sodium-ion technology reportedly operates across a temperature range of -40 C to 70 C, retaining around 90% of its capacity at -40 C.
Cycle life is also improving, with commercial-grade cells demonstrating capacity retention above 95% after 5,000 full-depth cycles, according to Bodoardo.
Beyond sodium-ion, non-lithium battery technologies are increasingly targeting different storage durations rather than competing directly with lithium-ion across all applications.
“The market is starting to split into roughly two- to six-hour batteries and true long-duration energy storage systems,” Bodoardo said.
Vanadium redox flow batteries, for example, are progressing toward installations with capacities of tens or hundreds of megawatt-hours, while gigawatt-hour-scale projects have also been proposed. Zinc-based and iron-air technologies are similarly targeting long-duration applications.
“In short, non-lithium batteries are increasingly differentiating by application, with sodium-ion emerging as a direct competitor to LFP for multi-hour storage, while flow, zinc, and iron-air technologies are increasingly geared toward long-duration storage,” Bodoardo said.
Commercial activity is accelerating, particularly in China.
CATL launched its sodium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) in June 2026
and expects cumulative shipments of around 1 GWh by the end of the year, with international deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027.
The development marks a significant step for a technology that accounted for less than 1% of global lithium-ion battery production in 2025.
Europe is also making progress. In September 2026, Altris, Clarios and InoBat reported that their European sodium-ion battery platform had successfully completed customer validation.

title: Sodium-ion pouch cells target cold-climate industrial niche - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Grepow has launched five sodium-ion pouch cells from 2 Ah to 7 Ah, aimed at industrial equipment and cold-climate applications that need high pulse power.
Vincent Shaw
13 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Assembly line of Grepow
Shenzhen-based battery manufacturer Grepow launched the series on Nov. 12, adding sodium-ion as a third core chemistry alongside its established nickel-metal hydride and lithium polymer lines.
The range is aimed at industrial equipment, cold-weather power systems, and specialty applications that require short bursts of high current.
All five models have a nominal voltage of 3.0 V. The four smaller cells, from 2 Ah to 6.5 Ah, have a charge cutoff of 3.4 V, while the 7 Ah flagship is rated to 4.0 V. Under specified lab conditions, the series supports discharge at up to 45C for 30 seconds and pulse discharge at up to 100C for two seconds, the company said.
Winter performance
In Grepow’s internal testing, a cell completed repeated three-second 28C pulse discharges after a four-hour rest at -20 C, and the same protocol at 20C after resting at -30 C. The company said the cells can also sustain continuous 0.2C discharge at -20 C for lower-rate output in prolonged cold.
In a separate internal comparison under selected conditions, Grepow said its sodium-ion cell showed stronger high-rate pulse discharge than a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cell at -20 C. The figures have not been independently verified, and performance will vary with pack design and operating conditions.
On cycle life, Grepow said a development cell retained 94% of its original capacity after 2,000 cycles in internal testing at 25 C with 1C charging and 30C discharging, compared with 83% for an LFP cell in the same test. Based on the current degradation curve, the company projects the cell could exceed 4,000 cycles before falling to 80% capacity.
Its product page states that the 4,000-plus figure is a projection rather than a completed test result, and that actual service life will depend on operating conditions and system design.
Core markets
The pouch format sets the series apart in a sodium-ion market where prismatic cells dominate volume production. Grepow has supplied nickel-metal hydride batteries for nearly three decades and, since 2012, high-rate lithium polymer packs for drones under its Tattu and Gens Ace brands, giving it an existing channel into the specialized, lower-volume markets the new series targets.
The company offers customization in cell selection, pack structure, and battery management systems for non-standard voltage, current, and form-factor requirements.
Grepow cited target applications including cold-weather vehicle starting and jump starters, auxiliary power for construction machinery, backup power for telecom base stations in cold regions, mobile robotics, and small stationary storage. That sets it apart from the large-format prismatic sodium-ion cells in China’s energy storage and electric vehicle pipelines, where cost competition is intensifying.
Whether the industrial pouch-cell segment proves commercially durable will depend on how the cycle-life projection holds up in real-world use and how customers weigh sodium-ion against established LFP options.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: Uniper and VNG Produce first green hydrogen at 30 MW facility in Germany - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The hydrogen will be transported through a roughly 25 km former natural gas pipeline converted to carry hydrogen, with deliveries to a TotalEnergies’ refinery scheduled to begin in 2027.
Sergio Matalucci
13 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Hydrogen
Utility-scale
The 30 MW electrolysis plant in Germany
have produced their first green hydrogen at the 30 MW electrolyzer facility at the Bad Lauchstädt Energy Park in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. The facility uses renewable electricity from a connected wind farm and is now entering a testing phase to assess the components of the integrated energy system. The hydrogen will be transported through a roughly 25 km former natural gas pipeline converted to carry hydrogen, with deliveries to TotalEnergies’ refinery in Leuna scheduled to begin in 2027. The project aims to demonstrate an integrated hydrogen value chain combining renewable power generation, electrolysis, storage, pipeline transport, and industrial consumption. Full commissioning is expected in 2027, when the facility is scheduled to begin supplying industrial customers.
Researchers
have assessed potential hydrogen transport corridors connecting West Africa to Europe via existing and planned natural gas pipeline routes, estimating a combined transport capacity of up to 7.16 million metric tons of green hydrogen per year. The study, conducted by Yifei Lu, Abeeb Adekunle Garba, Thiemo Pesch, and Andrea Benigni, examined transport scenarios involving the West African Gas Pipeline (WAGP), Nigeria-Morocco Gas Pipeline (NMGP), Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), and Maghreb-Europe Gas Pipeline (MEGP). The researchers compared a coastal corridor through Morocco and Spain with an inland route through Niger and Algeria, as well as a combined configuration using both corridors. They found that the combined configuration could transport almost twice as much hydrogen as either individual route, requiring a pipeline network spanning approximately 15,082 km and an estimated investment of €25.3 billion. Using a two-stage framework combining mixed-integer linear programming optimization and physical gas network simulations, they also assessed pressure drops, flow velocities, and compression requirements. At operating pressures of 80 bar to 100 bar, the combined configuration would require 34 compressor stations with a total installed capacity of 661 MW. Reducing the minimum operating pressure to 50 bar could increase hydrogen flow velocities to 22.37 m/s, exceeding the assumed nominal design velocity of 15 m/s. In their study, published in the
International Journal of Hydrogen Energy
, the researchers said developing both export corridors could diversify Europe’s renewable hydrogen supply routes. However, they cautioned that the estimated capacity represents a long-term technical planning scenario rather than a deployment forecast, as actual hydrogen availability will depend on regional demand, infrastructure development, investment, and cross-border cooperation.
Hydroplane
will lead the development of a hydrogen fuel cell-powered watercraft designed to transport modular hydrogen tank containers across New York’s inland waterways. The project, supported by the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA), aims to reduce the costs, emissions, and logistical complexity of clean hydrogen distribution across the state. “Hydroplane will lead a consortium that includes Serco North America, Hornblower Group, Pacific Hydrogen, Messer North America, and Unitrove,” the company said.
India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
has agreed to extend the commissioning deadlines for approximately 1.5 GW of subsidized electrolyzer manufacturing capacity awarded under the first tranche of its Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT) program, according to
The Economic Times
. The decision affects several manufacturers, including Reliance, Ohmium, and John Cockerill Greenko, which received support under a funding program worth approximately $220 million. The delays reportedly reflect slower-than-expected growth in India’s green hydrogen market, with a lack of confirmed orders and delays in reaching financial close for several hydrogen and green ammonia projects weighing on demand for electrolyzer equipment.

title: US firm claims 96,000-wafer-per-hour deposition line for tandem cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
NAED Energy Holding has said its new vertical deposition platform is rated at 96,000 wafers per hour and designed to make perovskite-silicon tandem cells targeting 30% efficiency.
Brian Publicover
13 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
tandem cells
Miami-based NAED Energy Holding said its PV-1 PECVD-V, a vertical in-line deposition platform for solar cell manufacturing, is rated at 96,000 wafers per hour, double the 48,000 wafers per hour of its previous XL-class platform.
The platform combines
plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD)
and physical vapor deposition (PVD) on a single shared-carrier line. Wafers travel upright through each stage, and to reach the second side, the entire carrier is lifted and turned 180 degrees rather than the wafers being flipped individually, which NAED said reduces direct wafer handling between process steps.
NAED said the line is designed to produce its T2X two-terminal perovskite/heterojunction (HJT) tandem cell, which targets 30% cell efficiency, and that it plans to sell the cells for terrestrial and space applications alongside glass-glass modules starting at 600 W.
According to the company, six of the line’s 13 process tools are complete and the remaining seven are in production. NAED said it designs the tools in-house, machines them in its own facility in the United States, and is now taking reservations for production tool slots from manufacturers.
“Going vertical let us double throughput and build the line around tandem cells from day one, rather than retrofitting tandem onto a platform designed for something else,” said Malcom Longair, media and development lead at NAED.
Rated figures
NAED said the 96,000 wafers-per-hour figure is a rated throughput and that 30% is a target efficiency, with full specifications and measured station test data available to qualified manufacturers on request. The release does not specify wafer size, yield or uptime, and does not name customers, investors, executives or the location of the production facility.
The company said the line, the carrier-turning mechanism, the wafer-retention carrier and the T2X cell are the subject of pending US patent applications, and that its intellectual property has been appraised at $179 million under an ASC 820 Level 3 fair-value methodology, an accounting standard that values assets using unobservable inputs such as management assumptions. NAED did not name the appraiser.
NAED describes itself as an aerospace, engineering and utility-energy company with operations in South Florida, New York and Nevada and a presence in Indonesia.
Perovskite-silicon tandem cells have already exceeded NAED’s target in the lab. Longi set a
world record of 35.5% efficiency
for a perovskite-silicon tandem cell in July. In the United States, Tandem PV
launched commercial perovskite-silicon manufacturing

title: China’s TOPCon M10 cell prices slip as export rush fades, domestic demand weakens - pv magazine Global
content:
China’s TOPCon M10 cell prices slipped as the earlier buying rush linked to U.S. Section 232 measures slowed and domestic demand weakened, according to market participants. Export demand for 210R cells, by contrast, remained relatively stable.
According to the Nov. 10 OPIS Global Solar Markets Report, free-on-board (FOB) China TOPCon M10 cell prices fell 1.13% week on week to $0.0439/W. TOPCon 210R cell prices were unchanged at $0.0459/W.
The earlier buying rush may have contributed to September’s rebound in Chinese cell exports, market participants said, as buyers brought forward purchases ahead of U.S. Section 232 measures on polysilicon and its derivatives, due to take effect on Dec. 4.
Chinese customs data showed cell exports rose more than 50% month on month by number of cells in September, following weak shipments in July and August. Energy think tank Ember estimated September shipments at approximately 14.28 GW.
Export destinations have also shifted sharply. The U.S., Kenya, Nigeria and the Philippines together accounted for nearly half of China’s cell exports by number in the third quarter, up from about 2% a year earlier. A trader said much of the supply delivered to the three emerging destinations may have been intended for U.S.-bound production.
India’s share of China’s cell exports, meanwhile, fell to about 1% in the third quarter from roughly 50% a year earlier, with Indonesia emerging as a major destination in its place. Market participants said Chinese cells were most likely being transshipped through Southeast Asia, which supplied more than 90% of India’s cell imports in July and August.
Domestic demand has offered little support. Changes to electricity pricing have weighed on project economics, weakening China’s traditional fourth-quarter installation rush, according to market analysts.
On the supply side, cell makers are responding to weaker demand and are expected to cut production further as they prioritize drawing down inventories and hold back wafer purchases, according to the Silicon Industry Branch of the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNMIA).
Beyond near-term cuts, manufacturers continued to announce line upgrades ahead of China’s mandatory module-efficiency standard, which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. During a Bank of America Global Research call on Nov. 6, Longi estimated that strict enforcement could eliminate around 30% of non-compliant production capacity, with only a limited number of manufacturers expected to successfully upgrade their facilities.
Other manufacturers have halted production altogether. One listed Chinese solar manufacturer said its main solar subsidiaries had been idle for about two months, with no orders in production. It cited industry oversupply, loss-making orders, falling domestic installations and a tighter overseas trade environment.
Looking ahead, market participants expect export demand to lose momentum as the Section 232 buying rush ends and rerouting through Southeast Asia slows ahead of India’s Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) requirement for cells. CNMIA expects downward pressure on cell prices across formats, with weakening cost support and installation demand insufficient to sustain a recovery.
Upstream, FOB China n-type M10 wafer prices fell 0.68% week on week to $0.145/pc, while 210R wafer prices declined 1.31% to $0.151/pc. The decline marked the first change in the 210R wafer assessment since mid-September.
Market participants attributed the wafer declines to weaker end-user demand, falling downstream product prices and production cuts among downstream manufacturers. M10 cell prices fell more sharply in percentage terms than M10 wafer prices, while 210R cell prices held steady despite cheaper wafers.
Wafer manufacturers have also reduced operating rates to varying degrees, according to industry sources. Most producers are operating at around 50% capacity, with leading manufacturers below that level. One specialized manufacturer has maintained a comparatively high operating rate of above 80%.
China’s wafer output totaled 55.17 GW in October, down 0.18% from September, according to CNMIA. Production is expected to decline further to approximately 52–53 GW in November.

OPIS APAC Solar Weekly Report

title: Ecuador scraps two taxes on solar equipment and energy storage systems - pv magazine Global
content:
The Ecuadorian government has introduced a 0% rate for value-added tax (VAT) and the tax on foreign currency outflows (ISD) on certain equipment and components used in the electricity sector, including solar PV and energy storage systems. The measure is established under Executive Decree 530, signed by President Daniel Noboa and published on Nov. 11 in the Fifth Supplement to Official Gazette No. 407.
The decree amends Article 194 of the regulations implementing the Internal Tax Regime Law. It covers equipment, turbines, inverters, generators, machinery, materials, supplies, components and systems, as well as associated parts and accessories. Eligible goods must be intended for the installation, expansion, rehabilitation, modernization, operation or maintenance of electricity infrastructure.
The 0% tax rates apply to equipment used in solar PV, wind, hydropower, thermal and geothermal generation facilities, among other technologies. They also cover energy storage systems and their components, as well as electricity transmission, distribution and retail infrastructure.
The Ministry of Environment and Energy has issued Ministerial Agreement MAE-MAE-2026-0118-AM, identifying 55 categories of goods eligible for the 0% VAT rate on the domestic market. The list includes solar cells, modules, panels, generators, inverters, power optimizers, charge controllers, mounting structures, tracking systems and direct-current (DC) solar cables.
For energy storage, eligible products include stationary battery cells and modules, battery banks, integrated storage systems, bidirectional converters and battery management equipment.
The agreement also establishes 104 tariff subheadings covering imports eligible for the 0% ISD rate. The tax benefits apply exclusively to goods and transactions expressly listed in the official annexes.
Article 55 of the Internal Tax Regime Law already provided for a VAT exemption on solar PV generation equipment and accessories. The new decree clarifies the regulatory scope of that provision and establishes the ISD treatment for imports included in the official list.
Both the decree and the ministerial agreement were published on Nov. 11, with the new rates taking effect on Nov. 12, 2026.
The decree also includes a transitional provision covering domestic purchases and imports made between Jan. 1, 2026, and the date the reform entered into force. Taxpayers may deduct VAT paid on eligible goods as an expense for the 2026 income tax year, provided the amounts have not already been claimed as input tax credits or offset against VAT collected on sales.
The measure forms part of broader regulatory changes in Ecuador’s electricity sector. The country has been seeking to accelerate private investment in renewable energy following the electricity shortages and widespread blackouts of 2024.
In August 2025, the government had authorized
643 MW of private renewable energy projects, including solar and hydropower
. The total comprised 179.1 MW of distributed generation projects intended to supply the electricity market and 464.6 MW of self-generation capacity for corporate consumers, with the option to sell surplus electricity.
According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), Ecuador had 131.35 MW of cumulative installed solar PV capacity at the end of 2025, up from approximately 84 MW in 2024.

title: Heliene announces commercial production of perovskite tandem modules using Caelux glass - pv magazine Global
content:
Solar module maker
and perovskite company
have announced the start of commercial-scale production of perovskite/silicon tandem solar modules at the Heliene module assembly facility in Minnesota.
The modules feature Caelux’s “Energy Producing Glass” layered on top of a traditional silicon solar module, which the companies say achieves efficiencies of 27% or more. The glass, which Caelux produces at its facility in Baldwin Park, California, contains a thin film of perovskite material that adds a second energy generation layer to a solar module.
The two companies say they have entered into a long-term multi-gigawatt agreement to commercialize the perovskite/silicon hybrid modules, and are targeting module efficiency of 29% by 2028.
In a recent presentation during
pv magazine USA Week 2026
, Caelux CEO Scott Graybeal outlined his company’s technology roadmap, explaining that silicon solar modules made with the current generation of Caelux glass can achieve efficiencies of between 26.7% and 28.2%, depending on the cell architecture of the underlying silicon layer. The CEO said his company expects to reach a milestone of greater than 30% efficiency in tandem module configurations with TOPCon, HJT and back-contact cell designs by 2028 or 2029.
Caelux’s approach to perovskite integration with silicon relies on what is known as four-terminal (4T) perovskite technology. In a 4T perovskite module, the perovskite layer is deposited onto glass and the silicon cells strung and laminated separately. The technology gets its name because the top and bottom light-absorbing layers of the finished module operate as completely independent electrical circuits, each requiring its own positive and negative electrical contacts, or terminals. In addition to Caelux, companies like Tandem PV and CubicPV are pursuing 4T perovskite tandems for commercial use.
This differs from two-terminal (2T) perovskite tandems, in which a perovskite layer is deposited directly on top of the silicon during the cell manufacturing phase. Also known as “monolithic” perovskite tandem solar cells, this technology is being pursued by companies like
Swift Solar
Oxford PV
Heliene CEO Martin Pochtaruk says Heliene chose to work with Caelux partly because of the 4T architecture and partly because it manufactures perovskite glass domestically.
“One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely new production setup,” Pochtaruk said in a statement. “With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar, besides the fact that partnering with true friends also makes it fun.”
The two companies plan to display one of the perovskite-silicon tandem modules at the Heliene booth at RE+ 2026. Commercial shipment of the modules is expected in 2027.

title: India's ReNew plans polysilicon manufacturing - pv magazine Global
content:
ReNew Energy has announced plans to invest around INR 80,000 crore ($8.9 billion) in digital infrastructure and clean energy manufacturing projects in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh.
The proposed investments include an INR 67,000 crore, 1 GW green hyperscale data center in Anakapalli; INR 11,000 crore in polysilicon and metallurgical silicon manufacturing facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore; and an INR 1,500 crore permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli.
The company also plans to establish the ReNew Centre for Technical Excellence (R-CTE) in Visakhapatnam under the Indian government’s PM SETU scheme.
The polysilicon and metallurgical silicon facilities will strengthen India’s domestic solar manufacturing supply chain. They will complement ReNew’s existing investments in solar manufacturing, including a 6.5 GW ingot and wafer production facility in Anakapalli, which is expected to be commissioned by March 2028.
The proposed 1 GW hyperscale data center in Anakapalli will be powered by renewable energy, expanding ReNew’s presence in digital infrastructure.
ReNew also plans to invest INR 1,500 crore in a permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli, with commissioning scheduled for March 2029.
As part of its workforce development initiatives, ReNew will collaborate with the Andhra Pradesh government to develop a cluster of five industrial training institutes (ITIs) in Gajuwaka, Visakhapatnam, into the ReNew Centre for Technical Excellence.
The initiative falls under the PM SETU framework, which provides for indicative investments of up to INR 241 crore over five years for a typical hub-and-spoke ITI cluster. The center will focus on developing industry-relevant technical skills and improving employability in renewable energy, advanced manufacturing and related sectors.
ReNew currently operates 717 MW of wind and 60 MW of solar capacity across 10 sites in Andhra Pradesh.
As of Oct. 30, 2026, the company’s gross clean energy portfolio stood at 20.5 GW, including 1.7 GW/6.2 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS).
ReNew also has 6.4 GW of solar module and 2.5 GW of solar cell manufacturing capacity. It is adding another 4 GW of solar cell production capacity, which is expected to become operational in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

title: Mexico lifts planned investment to $10.6 billion for 8 GW renewables - pv magazine Global
content:
Mexico’s state-owned electricity company Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE) has increased its planned investment to $10.6 billion for 38 renewable energy projects being developed through mixed-investment arrangements with private companies.
The updated portfolio includes 8,026 MW of renewable generation capacity and more than 2,500 MW of storage power, according to CFE Director General Emilia Calleja Alor during an appearance before the Chamber of Deputies.
Calleja said CFE has a portfolio of 60 renewable generation projects for 2024–2030, representing 9,184 MW of new capacity. Of these, 22 will be developed directly by the state-owned company and account for 1,158 MW. The remaining 38 projects fall under mixed-investment arrangements and represent approximately 87.4% of the planned capacity.
Under the model, the state holds a 54% stake and the private partner 46%. Private companies provide the financing required to execute the projects, while CFE participates as the majority shareholder and electricity buyer. The contracts provide for CFE to purchase 70% of the electricity generated, with the remaining 30% available for sale on the market.
The latest figures update previous announcements about the mixed-investment project calls. As
pv magazine México reported in June
, the first selection comprised 37 projects totaling 7,411 MW. These included 33 solar projects with approximately 6,710 MW and four wind projects totaling about 700 MW. The estimated investment at that stage was $7.4 billion.
In October, CFE reported a portfolio of 8,025 MW and investment exceeding $10 billion. The latest announcement raises those figures to 8,026 MW and $10.6 billion, but CFE has not provided a breakdown showing the changes by technology or individual project.
Calleja said the mixed-investment projects include more than 2,500 MW of storage power. However, CFE did not specify the corresponding energy capacity in MWh, the planned duration of the systems or their allocation among individual projects. It also did not provide an updated breakdown of the solar capacity included in the 38-project portfolio.
Projects CFE will develop with its own resources include further phases of the Puerto Peñasco solar plant in Sonora, the Chicoasén II hydropower project in Chiapas and hydropower developments in Sinaloa. According to CFE’s
2026–2030 development program
, sections III and IV of Puerto Peñasco will add 580 MW, with commissioning scheduled for 2028.
Calleja also stressed the need to coordinate renewable energy expansion with new transmission and distribution infrastructure, as well as backup and storage systems. During her appearance before lawmakers, she announced a review of solar power plants that remain awaiting connection to the national electricity grid.

title: Osaka Gas buys Japanese residential solar and battery installer - pv magazine Global
content:
Japanese utility Osaka Gas said its wholly owned subsidiary Osaka Gas Marketing has signed an agreement to acquire all shares of Truach, a company that sells, installs, and maintains residential solar and battery systems. It did not disclose the financial terms of the deal.
Osaka Gas said Truach was founded in Nara in 2021 and has since expanded across the Kansai, Chubu, and Kanto regions. It will become Osaka Gas Marketing’s first wholly owned subsidiary and is set to be renamed Daigas Truach on April 1, 2027. Truach had revenue of JPY 1.6 billion ($10 million) in its third fiscal year, according to reports by Jiji Press.
Truach also runs a service called Truach Club, which draws on its sales and installation know-how to support homebuilders across Japan in selling solar and battery systems, Osaka Gas said.
Osaka Gas said demand for residential solar, batteries, and vehicle-to-home systems is rising in Japan, driven by environmental awareness, volatile electricity prices, and preparations for natural disasters. It said the spread of net-zero energy homes and growing interest in energy management should expand the residential smart energy market further.
The company said the Daigas Group will make active use of partnerships, investments, and acquisitions to bring in specialist expertise, describing the Truach deal as the first step.
The acquisition also builds on Osaka Gas’ push into home storage. In July, the company began selling
Kyocera’s Enerezza Plus II home battery
for new solar-equipped homes, and it is developing a service called Sumai Battery EX that would aggregate customers’ batteries to offer flexibility in Japan’s balancing and capacity markets. Osaka Gas said it aims to launch the service as early as this year.
Other Japanese utilities are also turning to home batteries. In February, a Japanese utility
launched a residential battery demand response pilot
a survey published in August
found that Japanese buyers of solar and storage rank cost savings above disaster preparedness.

title: Rinnai launches new residential heat pump water heaters - pv magazine Global
content:
Rinnai America Corporation, the U.S. unit of Japanese heating specialist
Rinnai Corporation
, has introduced the REHPW series of electric heat pump water heaters for residential applications in the United States.
“It’s a bar-raising debut,” the company said in a statement.
The product range comprises three models with nominal storage capacities of 50 gallons (189 liters), 65 gallons (246 liters) and 80 gallons (303 liters). The systems achieve a uniform energy factor (UEF) of 3.75 for the smallest model and 4.0 for the two larger units.
According to the manufacturer, the water heaters extract thermal energy from the surrounding air to heat domestic hot water. They use R134a refrigerant and feature a 500 W compressor, alongside 4.5 kW electric resistance heating elements for backup operation.
The heat pump can operate at ambient temperatures as low as 2.8 C. The units are designed for connection to a 208 V or 240 V single-phase electrical supply at 60 Hz and require a 30 A circuit breaker.
The smallest model, REHP50W, provides a first-hour hot water delivery rating of 71 gallons (269 liters), while the REHP65W and REHP80W offer 80 gallons (303 liters) and 91 gallons (344 liters), respectively.
The units measure 551 mm, 650 mm and 650 mm in diameter, with respective heights of 1,687 mm, 1,663 mm and 1,885 mm. Their weights range from approximately 99 kg to 132 kg.
The new range features top and side water connections, as well as a top-mounted air inlet and exhaust arrangement intended to increase installation flexibility. The manufacturer said the systems can be installed in garages, basements and laundry rooms. An optional ducting kit is available for applications with limited space.
The water heaters also incorporate a variable-speed fan, a third tank temperature sensor and five operating modes. Wi-Fi connectivity enables monitoring and control, while CTA-2045 Level 2 demand-response functionality allows the units to adjust electricity consumption in response to grid signals.
According to Rinnai, the REHPW series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 efficiency requirements and complies with California’s Title 24 energy standards.
The manufacturer offers a 10-year warranty on the storage tank and other parts, alongside one year of labor coverage.

title: Shared grid connections could improve bankability of residential solar-plus-storage systems - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team in the Netherlands has developed an optimization model for sizing and operating battery storage systems in solar-powered apartment buildings, finding that shared grid connections could significantly improve the economics of energy storage.
“Our study uses real operational data from a 58-apartment building in Utrecht to investigate how battery storage can improve solar self-consumption and reduce grid peaks,” corresponding author Simone Coccato told
pv magazine
. “A key contribution is showing how grid connection configurations and network tariffs can significantly influence the economic value of batteries.”
Coccato said the team is now extending its research to clusters of residential buildings operating as virtual power plants (VPPs). “We are investigating how coordinated batteries can reduce grid congestion, improve renewable energy integration, and provide flexibility to electricity markets,” he said.
The researchers tested the model on an apartment building equipped with 356.6 kW of rooftop and building-integrated facade PV capacity and 70 kWh of battery storage.
The case study focused on a 10-story, 58-apartment building constructed in Utrecht in the 1970s and renovated to a positive-energy standard between 2019 and 2020. In 2022, the building consumed 200 MWh of electricity and generated 255 MWh from its PV systems. Its two 35 kWh batteries currently serve shared facilities, including heat pumps, elevators and common utilities, while each apartment retains an individual grid connection.
The researchers examined two scenarios: a hypothetical configuration in which the apartments and shared facilities operate under a single grid connection with import and export limits of 110.4 kW, allowing the batteries to serve the entire building; and the existing configuration, in which storage serves only shared facilities.
Using a full year of measured data, the team developed a linear programming optimization model to evaluate battery capacities of up to 500 kWh under three operating strategies: minimizing peak grid imports, maximizing PV self-consumption and combining both objectives.
“We found that a relatively small 70 kWh battery could eliminate 122 hours of grid export-limit violations under a hypothetical shared-connection scenario, enabling potential savings of over €20,000 ($22,154) annually in grid connection costs,” Coccato said. “Interestingly, optimizing the existing battery operation could also increase solar self-consumption by more than 15 percentage points compared with its default control strategy.”
The results showed that, under the hypothetical shared-connection scenario, the economically optimal battery capacity was approximately 280 kWh, delivering a net annual benefit of €32,829 (36.318,89) and a payback period of 1.7 years. The existing 70 kWh system achieved a modeled net annual benefit of €25,297 and a payback period of approximately 0.55 years.
The researchers presented their findings in “
Unlocking flexibility in buildings through batteries: a case study of the Netherlands
,” published in
Applied Energy
. The research team included scientists from the Netherlands’
Utrecht University
and building energy systems developer Inside Out Technologies.

title: Türkiye, China sign $15 billion renewables investment plan - pv magazine Global
content:

Further details on the projects, including a timeline for project development, are yet to be released.

signing of eight financial agreements
