title: How Peak Energy Chose Sodium-Ion for Grid Storage
content:
Stationary Batteries
Materials
Battery Manufacturing
Interviews
Peak Energy develops sodium-ion battery storage for the grid, focused on safety, lower costs, and US manufacturing for large-scale energy deployment.
November 13, 2026
7 Min Read
Peak Energy has garnered more than $1 billion in commercial customer agreements.
Peak Energy.
Cameron Dales was certain that he was done with launching and managing startup organizations. It was 2023, and his career to that point was almost completely dedicated to introducing the high-tech hub that is California’s Silicon Valley to new companies. As a member of the founding teams for Symyx Technologies, a former materials science group that developed high-throughput robotic tools and software for the discovery and processing of advanced materials before being acquisitioned, and the advanced lithium-ion battery outfit
, where he led commercial strategy and operations, Dales had no doubts — the time was right for a new direction.
When an opportunity to join Eclipse Ventures in Palo Alto, a firm that he had brought to Enovix as its largest investor, was presented to serve as an operating partner, he accepted. “I really thought my days of company-building were over,” said Dales, president and chief commercial officer at Peak Energy, a startup that produces a battery energy storage system (BESS) based on sodium-ion technology. And he continued to feel that way up to and including the first day of his new job, when a chance meeting with former Tesla executive Landon Mossburg.
Related:
This Tech Issue Is Reshaping the 2026 Midterm Elections
“I remember distinctly telling Landon that nothing could ever beat lithium-ion,” Dales recalls. “That you couldn’t make money in grid storage and, by the way, that I would never be interested in starting another company. But I did wish him good luck.” Within a few months’ time, however, Dales came to the conclusion that lithium-ion was not going to be the best long-standing platform for an anticipated multi-decade infrastructure uprising in the grid storage sector.
ESS Gigafactory Sacramento. Courtesy of Peak Energy.
Why Peak Energy chose sodium-ion for grid-scale energy storage
Demand for longer storage durations at lower costs was only going to escalate, even before factoring in the expansion of renewable energy and data centers. “The most exciting opportunity in all of energy was going to be this massive build-out that is happening,” said Dales. “A trillion dollars would be going into the ground over the next 10 years, and it would be the linchpin to speed-to-electrons for data centers. It would be the key to low-cost electricity given the growing demand across the economy. It’s an incredibly exciting market. And we realized that we could develop at a scale that had never been seen before in stationary batteries that were being built on the wrong technology platform.”
Today, Peak Energy, has garnered more than $1 billion in commercial customer agreements and has recently announced $108 million through its most recent round of financing capital to begin installations of the company’s proprietary
passively cooled
sodium-ion BESS, which is said to be the first of its kind in the United States.
Related:
How Gotion Built Its 40-GWh Gigafactory in Illinois
How Peak Energy’s sodium-ion BESS improves safety and lowers OPEX
Dales built a career advancing battery and aerospace technologies. With engineering degrees from Cornell and Stanford, he developed spacecraft hardware at Lockheed Martin, co-founded Symyx Technologies’ Tools unit, and led automated research tool development. At Enovix, he helped establish infrastructure, technology, and partnerships for manufacturing ultra-high-performance 3D silicon-wafer batteries successfully.
He can lay claim to more than 100 patents as an inventor. He says that one of the key takeaways he learned along the pathway that led him to Mossburg and the staff that they’ve cultivated at Peak, which consists of founding members largely from Tesla, Enovix, and
Northvolt,
is that lithium-ion is essentially developed for mobile technology. “It is focused on high-energy density as opposed to the things that really matter in stationary storage, with cost being No. 1 as well as fire safety, and, more importantly, the security of the supply chain,” Dales said.
Related:
Should Batteries Be Beautiful? Torus Thinks So.
Alongside this reality, he saw what he calls the “sister technology” of lithium-ion emerging in China—the class of sodium-ion batteries. “After spending a significant amount of time visiting factories in China, we became convinced that this was really going to reach scale, which is a prerequisite for any chemistry or any technology to actually make any difference in the battery space,” said Dales. “And we believed that it was going to reach scale faster than anybody really was expecting in the Western world. With that, we launched Peak Energy with a vision to not just be a battery company but to attack the most impactful part of the challenge first, which is the storage piece. We’ve recruited an amazing team that could rethink how to design and architect a stationary storage system when you're starting with a different building block.”
Despite some inherent differences, sodium remains quite similar to
lithium iron phosphate (LFP)
in several ways and can be manufactured on the same platform. “With lithium-ion, you can literally switch over an LFP production line to sodium-ion,” explained Dales. “So we had a running start in terms of scale.”
Peak's grid storage product. Courtesy of Peak Energy.
Why passive architecture matters for grid-scale battery safety
“This can be mitigated at the system level, but that comes at the expense of complexity and cost,” said Dales. “You build very complex systems to keep them safe, especially when you've got hundreds of giant container-sized batteries together to form a project. As we started rethinking how energy storage should be done with this different building block, sodium, we found that the main disadvantage of sodium-ion is that it's somewhat lower energy density. That means it's definitely not the right choice for your cell phone.” In the context of stationary storage, however, the density impact was not determined to be significant. “What we found as we started working with it and designing specifically for that chemistry — was that its unique properties were really around stability,” said Dales. “Stability over its lifetime. Stability over cycle life. And stability for safety reasons. It's less volatile and highly stable at high temperatures.”
While lithium-ion batteries have become less expensive and the cost around facilities built with large stationary batteries has decreased, almost all of that reduction has come from the cell and doesn’t solve the real ongoing economic difficulty, which lies with the systems, said Dales. “It's in the installation. It’s in sending an army of electricians to the field to wire systems up over weeks, sometimes months. And the biggest piece of the pie is the operating expense (OPEX) line. The cost to operate what are essentially power plants for decades. And the OPEX line is driven by a host of factors, such as the degradation of batteries over time and the need to then replace them to live up to power purchase agreements, as well as preventive maintenance.”
Since launching the company in 2023, Dales says he and his team have substantially improved the capabilities of sodium-ion at high temperatures. “They now allow us to build a system that is ideal in simplicity,” he said. “Our units have no cooling system and no fire-suppression system required because of the safety properties of the chemistry. It's a fully passive architecture. There’s no moving parts and no coolants to leak, which typically is how fires start. It's not the cell spontaneously combusting, it's the ancillary electronics and coolants. There's no preventive maintenance required for our system.”
Peak Energy’s Sacramento factory, customer pipeline, and GM partnership
This summer, Dales and his colleagues announced that Sacramento, CA, will be home to Peak’s first US manufacturing facility dedicated to grid-scale sodium-ion BESS. The
183,000-square-foot facility
located in Sacramento's Metro Air Park is expected to enter production with shipments beginning in the first quarter of 2027 and will reportedly produce up to 4 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery systems annually, in addition to more than 6 GWh of customer commitments already in place.
Secured customer agreements include those with Jupiter Power, Energy Vault, and RWE Americas. The company also recently announced a
strategic partnership with General Motors
that will reportedly combine Peak's BESS technology with GM's battery cell development expertise to deliver more affordable and reliable stationary storage. “And then there is a robust pipeline of additional projects and longer, larger offtakes that we expect to sign over the course of the rest of this year,” said Dales.

title: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike
content:
Micah Toll
| Nov 14 2026 - 5:02 am PT
I’ve been
waiting years
for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.
Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.
When it debuted earlier this year
, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.
USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare.
Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it
barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model
that’s slowly starting to ship.
The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition.
, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.
Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.
And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.
Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.
If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.
Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.
Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.
The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.
I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.
It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.
And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.
Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.
But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.
I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.
But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.
For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.
Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

title: Tesla Cybercab's autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn't move
content:
Tesla Robotaxi
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Nov 14 2026 - 5:33 am PT
Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.
And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
What Cybercab owners agree to
The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company
started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use
at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.
The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.
Here’s what else is in there:
Tesla can change the subscription price with one month’s notice. You pay $29,990 up front, and the car’s usefulness then depends on a monthly fee Tesla sets.
The Cybercab only works inside Tesla-enabled Robotaxi geofences. Driving outside them is prohibited and can be technically blocked, and Tesla “may expand, reduce, relocate, or otherwise modify the operating area at any time.”
Tesla can suspend or cancel the subscription for “unauthorized or inappropriate use.” Three or more “strikeouts” for improper or unsafe use trigger a one-week suspension of autonomous driving, during which the car may not operate. Your payment isn’t prorated.
Tesla can remotely access, locate, restrict, or control the car, place it in a “safe state,” or end your access, and the agreement says those actions don’t give you remedies beyond what’s in the terms.
Tesla collects “Autonomy Data,” including image data from the cabin camera above the rear-view mirror, kept for 30 days by default.
It’s for personal use only. You can’t put your Cybercab on Tesla’s Robotaxi network, Uber, a delivery app, or a rental platform without Tesla’s written authorization.
No wraps, tint, or wheel changes except through Tesla or an authorized provider, or your subscription can be suspended.
That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.
Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was
between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps
, and parts of the Houston map have been
called “fake” by the person tracking it
. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.
Mark Valorian, who went through the terms
, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.
Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.
Tesla says the Model Y runs the same thing
This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.
Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network
around Q2 2027
. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.
So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.
Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.
Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.
Electrek’s Take
I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.
You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.
And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.
A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.
So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
content:
Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate
artificial intelligence
, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level
AI ethics
governance
, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.
“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.
Technology leads and systems engineers are
responsible
for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the
European Union
, the U.S.
National Institute of Standards and Technology
, and the
International Organization for Standardization
The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as
systemic bias
, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.
Most traditional computer science, software, and
electrical engineering
degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.
Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.
Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance,
AI ethics
, and governance.
The benefits of microcredentials
Skills-based microcredentials
represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.
Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.
For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects
software engineering
and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.
Translating standards into microcredentials
Bridging
technical capability and ethical responsibility
requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in
socio-technical standards
, most notably through the
IEEE 7000 series
for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.
IEEE Credentialing Program
translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

title: Diesel Prices Are Surging. This Electric Trucking Company Is Seeing More Interest
content:
The CEO of Einride, an electric freight company, says he's seeing more customer interest in electric trucking due to high fuel prices.
Photo by:
8:00am ET
High gas prices have helped drive more interest in electric cars this year. But it’s not just everyday drivers who are looking to ditch fossil fuels.
Eye-watering diesel costs are pushing more shippers to consider a switch to electric trucks, Roozbeh Charli, CEO of electric and autonomous freight company Einride, told me in an interview.
“You’re definitely seeing an upswing in both customer conversations and just general narrative” around electrification, he said.
Diesel prices have risen far more severely than prices for regular gasoline, putting extra pressure on commercial operators. The average cost of diesel in the U.S. has shot up by more than 60% since the war with Iran began,
to over $6 per gallon
. Shippers are facing far higher fuel costs in Europe too. It all means customers who told Einride they’d revisit the idea of electric freight sometime down the line are deciding to get the ball rolling.
“A lot of those customers are coming back now, saying ‘let’s get started, rather sooner than later,’” Charli said.
Einride says customers are taking a closer look at electric trucking due to high and volatile diesel prices.
Photo by: Einride
There’s some evidence that those conversations are generating actual business. Einride, which was founded in 2016 and sells electric freight services and software, says its sales pipeline tripled year over year during the first half of 2026. Its conversion rate doubled over the same period.
And it isn’t the only one noticing an uptick in demand. In September, a coalition of shippers like PepsiCo
placed an order for 2,500 electric trucks
in a deal that’s set to double the U.S. fleet of electric Class 8 trucks. Catalyst Mobility, one of the nonprofits running the program,
has said
it’s noticed more interest in EV trucks from companies that weren’t involved in the deal due to diesel prices.
Charli chalks the increased interest up to a couple of things. The pricing pain today is part of it. It means there’s a broader range of customer use cases where electric trucks are price-competitive with, or cheaper than, using traditional big-rigs. Those are typically what he calls “middle-mile” applications of, say, 100-200 miles back and forth, with high utilization. That last part is key, since battery-powered trucks still tend to cost more than diesel ones.
The situation is also making some companies realize just how exposed they are to drastic swings in the price of diesel, Charli said.

Our weekly newsletter breaks down the biggest mobility news every Friday
The trend is encouraging for reasons beyond economics. Heavy-duty trucks make up a relatively small portion of the U.S. fleet, but they account for a disproportionate share of fuel consumption and harmful air pollution.
“Any exposure to diesel exhaust is going to be harmful to your health,” says Ray Minjares, heavy-duty vehicles program director at the International Council on Clean Transportation. “And so since there's really no safe level, the obvious solution, particularly in a world where commercial zero-emission vehicles are already available, is to switch to that technology.”
The Tesla Semi represents a "step-change" for electric trucking hardware in the U.S., Einride CEO Roozbeh Charli said.
Photo by: Tesla
High diesel prices aren’t the only tailwind helping to drive trucking electrification this year, Charli said. The
long-awaited launch
Tesla Semi
not only helped bring more attention to electric trucking, but it also introduced a genuinely groundbreaking offering to the U.S. market, he said.
“The Tesla Semi, in a U.S. context, is definitely a step-change in the capabilities of the hardware” in terms of range, performance, and price, he said.
In August, Einride announced plans to deploy 500 Semis to service Amazon and other North American customers, tripling its fleet. Tesla’s truck is several years late to full-scale production. But given the diesel situation these days, maybe it’s right on time.
“They timed it well,” Charli said.

title: Tesla Opens Self-Driving Cybercab Orders To 'Select Customers' At $29,990
content:
Tesla Opens Self-Driving Cybercab Orders To 'Select Customers' At $29,990
The Cybercab will be Tesla's cheapest vehicle, but there's a catch: autonomous driving will cost you $299 per month.
- Tesla said it is starting to invite "select customers" to order Cybercabs.
- The steering wheel-free two-seater could be the first Level 4 autonomous vehicle people can actually own.
- Customers will also need to purchase an autonomous driving subscription for the Cybercab to work, Tesla said.
Tesla will soon start selling its steering wheel-free Cybercab for personal use, the company announced on Friday.
The Cybercab will cost $29,990, undercutting the Model 3 by $7,000 and making the golden two-seater Tesla's cheapest vehicle ever. According to a screenshot of the order page shared by Tesla, deliveries will begin as soon as next month.
There are a few catches. The Cybercab won't operate anywhere in the country, Tesla says, but rather in "supported service areas." It will also require a $299-per-month autonomous driving subscription to operate, with the first month included for no charge. That totals to some $3,600 per year just to use the vehicle, before insurance or maintenance costs.
And the model will be sold to hand-picked buyers, at least to start. "Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use," the company said in a tweet on its Robotaxi X account. Tesla said initial availability is limited.
It's not clear when or if sales will expand to the general public. But the sale of a car one can actually own that is capable of driving itself without supervision would be a massive milestone for both the automotive world and for Tesla in particular.
Putting autonomous cars in the hands of regular people has been one of Elon Musk's central promises for about a decade, and he's missed his self-imposed deadlines year after year. Meanwhile, today's driverless cars are owned and operated by companies running ride-hailing services, like Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla—not by individuals. The Cybercabs in operation today are part of Tesla's Robotaxi service, which opened for business last year and now shuttles riders around in a handful of U.S. cities, including Austin and Miami.
Tesla's biggest boosters online cheered the news. But it's also sure to tick off some of the many Tesla owners who have paid for Full Self-Driving over the years and have been waiting patiently for their Model 3s and Model Ys to become autonomous. Most recently, Musk said that will happen in the second quarter of next year in areas where the Robotaxi service operates.
The Tesla Cybercab has two seats and no steering wheel or pedals.
Tesla is far from the only company looking to sell autonomous cars to the public someday. Rivian plans to introduce lidar and a new in-house chip to the R2 in the hopes of giving it self-driving capability someday. General Motors plans to introduce an eyes-off version of Super Cruise to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. It'll operate on highways first before expanding to other road types, GM says.
Tesla advertises the personally-owned Cybercab as "fully autonomous" and says owners will be able to monitor their vehicles and manage rides via the Tesla app. But overall, the announcement raises almost as many questions as it answers.
For example, there was no mention of whether customers would be able to add their cabs to the Robotaxi fleet and earn passive income, another longtime Musk promise. It's also not clear where the Cybercab will be able to operate, nor whether Tesla will expand that territory quickly enough to make buying one worthwhile beyond a handful of cities.
Another cloud of uncertainty looming over the Cybercab's rollout is regulatory in nature. The Cybercab's unconventional design has caught the attention of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which questions how exactly Tesla determined that the vehicle complies with motor vehicle safety standards. The Tesla lacks a steering wheel, pedals, and side-view mirrors, all things that are typically required for a car to be street-legal.
The federal government lets companies apply to roll out noncompliant vehicles, but those deployments are capped at 2,500 vehicles per year. (Zoox, for its part, was recently granted an exemption to commercially deploy 5,000 of its autonomous pods over two years.) NHTSA has said it's working to streamline autonomous-vehicle rules, which could work in Tesla's favor here.
If Tesla can pull this off, it'll be one for the history books. Of course, the company has made numerous ambitious promises around self-driving cars—like 1 million robotaxis by 2020, and unsupervised self-driving pretty much every year since—and it has generally fallen short. Whether the Cybercab rollout breaks that streak is still to be determined.

title: The VW ID. Buzz Is Getting A New Job As A Robotaxi
content:
May Mobility plans to bring 10,000 driverless ID. Buzzes to a road near you.
Photo by:
Suvrat Kothari
12:37pm ET
May Mobility plans to build out a massive fleet of Volkswagen ID. Buzz EVs.
It plans to launch 10,000 driverless Buzzes over the next five years.
A partner-first approach means that Uber, Lyft, and other ride-hailing companies may be the first to get these EVs starting in 2028.
Volkswagen ID. Buzz
hasn't exactly been a smash hit in the U.S. But that hasn't stopped commercial customers from eyeing up the nostalgic electric van for something it's particularly good at: moving people.
May Mobility
announced on Thursday that it plans to integrate its autonomous driving systems into the Buzz to give it a job wherever driverless taxis are welcome.
Photo by: Volkswagen
May wants to use its existing tech stack to equip up to the ID. Buzzes with hardware and software that can see "up to 10 seconds into the future."
—May's tech uses onboard predictive modeling to anticipate how the world around it will move, similar how a human assess other drivers around them. It creates multiple scenarios in its digital brain and uses the model's reasoning to determine which one is most suited for its environment.
The tech would also make the cars capable of integrating with any of the "global robotaxi platforms," which is one of the ways that May is approaching its partnership-first business model. Presumably, that means its existing fleet partners like Lyft, Uber, and other ride hailing services around the world.
May's approach is also a silent win for folks who want to make sure that Buzz doesn't fizzle out.
One of the biggest blockers to Buzz adoption on the consumer side has been the
that could change in the coming months
, the van's initially high price tag and just so-so range made it a fairly lukewarm offering to EV buyers looking to park the Buzz in their own driveway. That's why Robotaxis might be the best use of the Buzz yet.
It's roomy enough to comfortably haul plenty of passengers (and whatever cargo they bring along), plus it has the easy ingress and egress of a minivan. Other companies seem to agree, even
VW's own MOIA arm
that recently began
testing an autonomous version of the Buzz in Los Angeles
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
So far, May has completed about 600,000 commercial driverless rides in the U.S. and Japan. And while it hasn't said how many cars it operates, May is pretty open about its long-term goal for the Buzz.
It plans to put 10,000 of these autonomous ID. Buzzes on the road by 2031. That all starts with road testing early next year, followed by delivering the first fleet vehicles to customers by 2028.

title: SpaceX 星舰第 15 次试飞升空：超重型助推器中途改道墨西哥湾溅落放弃回收，飞船继续飞行中
content:
IT之家 11 月 14 日消息，美国太空探索技术公司（SpaceX）重型运载火箭“星舰”于当地时间 11 月 13 日下午 4:47（北京时间次日 06:47）从得州星际基地发射升空，实施第 15 次试飞。
发射窗口于美国中部时间当天下午 4 时 45 分开启，星舰从轨道发射台 2 号升空。
此次任务使用超重型助推器 B22 号和飞船 S42 号，原计划首次实现助推器与飞船双双返回发射场并由发射塔机械臂实施空中捕获回收，同时部署 26 颗第三代星链卫星。
发射升空后不久，星舰及超重助推器完成热分离（hot-staging），飞船猛禽发动机成功点火，超重型助推器按计划执行返回机动。
不过 SpaceX 官方随即确认，超重型助推器已改道至墨西哥湾近海溅落着陆，发射塔空中捕获任务取消。飞船上升段燃烧结束后进入预定亚轨道轨迹，团队正检查各系统状态，以确认是否继续执行入轨操作。
分离后继续点火，S42 约 8 分钟后完成第一次燃烧，最终在约 275 公里高度进入低地球轨道（LEO）。这是星舰第二次成功入轨（上次是 Flight 14）。
根据任务设计，若飞船获准进入近地轨道，将在约 275 公里高度完成约 14 圈飞行，任务时长超过 22 小时后再尝试返回星舰基地实施捕获。此前超重型助推器曾三次成功被发射塔捕获，但飞船空中捕获尚无先例。此次试飞是星舰系统第二次执行轨道级别任务。
IT之家注意到，SpaceX 在发射前已获得相关监管批准，发射过程实时通过官方平台直播。目前飞船仍在按计划飞行，后续是否入轨及最终回收结果有待进一步确认。

title: “像一大群蜜蜂”：亚马逊 Prime Air 送货无人机噪音过大，遭当地居民投诉
content:
11 月 14 日消息，据休斯顿纪事报报道，亚马逊旗下的超快无人机配送服务 Prime Air 曾承诺，无论是午间零食、日用百货还是紧急医疗用品，只要重量在 5 磅
（IT之家注：约 2.3 千克）
以内，最快都能在 30 分钟内通过空中直送消费者家门口，然而当地居民对该服务并不买账。
在亚马逊开展该项服务的得克萨斯州各社区中，噪音污染已成为居民频繁投诉的焦点。
“刚推出时，这确实挺酷、挺新奇的，但现在简直快把我逼疯了。”当地居民表示，“
这听起来就像一大群蜜蜂在耳边盘旋，音量比普通的蜂群大得多，而且从早到晚响个不停
。”自 Prime Air 无人机进驻该地区以来，当地居民针对噪音污染的投诉便接连不断。
“理查森眼下经历的一切很快就会在全美各地上演，到那时人们终将相信我们的话 —— 让这么多无人机整天在头顶飞来飞去，确实是一个极其严重的问题。”一位理查森居民在接受纽约时报采访时说道。
亚马逊在一份声明中回应称，公司一直虚心听取理查森等城市居民的早期反馈，已派遣团队与当地居民及市政领导层会面，并据此调整了飞行运营方案。
“在包裹投递阶段，无人机的音量低于停靠在路边怠速运转的配送卡车，且仅持续约 30 秒，”亚马逊方面表示，“而在高空巡航阶段，其声响仅相当于低档位运行的窗式风扇，通常在室内根本听不到。”
亚马逊同时强调，外界对其 Prime Air 无人机以及“30 分钟内送达”服务的总体评价“压倒性地积极”。
除噪音外，部分居民还对无人机导航摄像头带来的隐私问题以及个别投递失误（如包裹落入泳池、无人机擦撞建筑等）表示担忧。
对此，亚马逊已采取将出港飞行最低平均高度提升至 225 英尺
（约 68.6 米）
、允许居民申请在系统地图中模糊自家住宅图像等改进措施。

title: “黑苹果”有望卷土重来，新项目探索将 macOS 搬上骁龙和 x86 架构电脑
content:
IT之家 11 月 14 日消息，过去几十年里，不想花钱买 Mac、却又希望使用 macOS 的用户，可以通过组装“黑苹果”电脑实现。不过，自从苹果改用自研 Arm 芯片后，黑苹果的安装难度大幅提高。
据外媒 TechSpot 今天（14 日）晚间报道，近期出现的至少两个新项目，则试图让 macOS 登陆骁龙和 x86 平台。
其中一个项目开发了 Arm 转 x86 指令翻译层，计划让大多数较新的英特尔和 AMD 处理器能够运行 macOS，早期版本现已开放试用。另一个项目则在搭载骁龙处理器的华硕 Zenbook 笔记本上成功启动 macOS，部分基本功能也能正常使用。
黑苹果的历史可以追溯到 20 世纪 80 年代，但在非苹果设备上运行 macOS 直到 21 世纪初才逐渐流行。
2006 年，苹果放弃 PowerPC 处理器，转而采用英特尔芯片。由于 Windows 电脑广泛使用英特尔处理器，安装黑苹果也变得容易许多。后来，苹果又转向采用自研 Arm 架构的 Apple Silicon 芯片，一度让外界认为黑苹果将彻底退出历史舞台。
工程师米格尔 · 克鲁兹上个月公布的 Snapintosh 项目，则有望首次尝试利用高通骁龙芯片，让 macOS 不再依赖 Apple Silicon。其演示了一台华硕 Zenbook A16 笔记本成功启动 macOS，不仅能够切换不同桌面模式，还能打开多个应用程序。不过，距离正常使用仍有很长一段路要走。
Snapintosh 暂时只支持搭载骁龙 X2 Elite 处理器的 Zenbook A16，运行时还需要连接另一台 Mac，无法单独使用笔记本电池供电。Wi-Fi、声音、摄像头、蓝牙、睡眠和外接显示器等功能也尚未实现，画面帧率无法稳定达到 60fps。至于何时会在 GitHub 发布测试版，项目尚未给出明确时间。
另一名工程师泰勒 · 史密斯开发的 Stela 项目则瞄准了更广泛的 PC 平台。Stela 利用 Arm 转 x86 指令翻译技术运行 macOS，开放测试版支持采用 Nehalem 及更新架构的英特尔处理器，以及 Bulldozer 及更新架构的 AMD 处理器。此外，电脑至少需要 8GB 内存，并配备英伟达 GTX 16 系列或更新型号的显卡。
IT之家获悉，用户可以从 Stela 的 GitHub 代码仓库下载测试版，在 Windows 电脑上运行安装程序，再选择 U 盘制作安装介质。在线安装版需要 8GB 空间，离线安装版需要 32GB，安装 macOS 的目标硬盘还需预留 60GB 空间。Stela 同样暂不支持 Wi-Fi 和声音，但蓝牙功能可以正常使用。

title: 中国科学院揭示大脑仅用少量神经元就能解码手部三维运动轨迹，打开脑机接口研发新路径
content:
IT之家 11 月 14 日消息，据新华社昨晚报道，中国科学院自动化研究所团队通过灵长类动物实验研究，揭示大脑仅用少量神经元就能解码手部三维运动轨迹，为研发更高效的新一代脑机接口提供神经科学依据。
在以往的运动皮层研究中，实验往往将猕猴的运动范围限于少量离散位置，研究人员难以分辨神经元的编码方式。
为了解开这个难题，研究团队设计了一个无约束的三维抓取任务，并在猕猴左侧的初级运动皮层和前运动皮层植入微电极阵列。通过对三维空间运动过程中细胞放电率的计算，研究人员发现负责规划运动的前运动皮层，以及发出运动执行指令的初级运动皮层中，都有部分神经元对手的实时位置进行编码，从而呈现手在空间中运动的位置。
实验数据显示，初级运动皮层和前运动皮层都仅需少量位置调谐细胞即可解码三维轨迹，印证了大脑编码的极高效率。
“我们对大脑理解越深，脑机接口的效能就可以发挥得越好。”中国科学院自动化研究所研究员余山说，未来，脑机接口若能直接提取大脑中的运动轨迹，不仅能更加高效地执行行动方案，也能让外部设备控制更顺滑。

content:

title: 填补 40 年观测空白：三氢正离子 H₃⁺ 禁戒纯转动光谱首次被捕获
content:
11 月 14 日消息，天文学家利用詹姆斯 · 韦布空间望远镜（JWST），在仙王座 A 西部（Cepheus A West）的 HH 168 天体中，
首次探测到约四十年前理论预言的三氢正离子（H₃⁺）禁戒转动光谱。
Pan 与 Oka 于 1986 年计算了 H₃⁺的禁戒转动光谱，并提出可以利用它探测星际 H₃⁺。在此后的约四十年里，这类光谱一直未在实验室或天文观测中被探测到。本次研究报告利用韦伯空间望远镜，在 HH 168 中首次探测到这类光谱。
赫尔比格-哈罗天体 HH 211 的壮观喷射，天文学家还发现了此前未见的光谱特征 H₃⁺。图源：欧空局、美国宇航局
IT之家注：禁戒是光谱学术语，指某种能级跃迁受到特定规则限制，不能通过常规最容易发生的方式吸收或发出光。原子、分子只能处于某些特定能量状态，从一个状态变到另一个状态，叫作“跃迁”。发光，就是它从较高能级跃迁到较低能级时，以光子的形式释放能量。
量子力学中存在“选择定则”，会根据角动量、对称性等条件，限定哪些跃迁能够发生。对于最常见的方式称为“电偶极跃迁”，不符合相应条件的跃迁就被称为“禁戒跃迁”。
三氢正离子（H₃⁺）的平衡结构是一个对称的等边三角形，没有永久电偶极矩，也就是没有通常有利于产生转动辐射的那种电荷分布不对称。因此，在理想的刚性结构近似下，它没有普通的电偶极纯转动光谱。
三氢正离子中原子核的排列形成一个等边三角形。
但真实分子并非完全刚硬，旋转造成的离心畸变，可以诱导出微小的电偶极矩，让原本受到抑制的转动跃迁产生微弱光谱。而这类微弱信号此前既未在实验室中测得，也未在天体中被观测到。相关研究于 11 月 6 日在预印本平台 arXiv 公开。
HH 168 中受震气体的地图，展示了新检测到的三氢发射如何沿着热分子氢的分布分布。
天文学家借助韦布空间望远镜的中红外仪器，在两个观测区域中，共捕获 26 条显著性超过 5σ 的相关谱线，最强的一条位于 16.325 微米。这些信号的空间分布和运动速度与受到激波冲击的高温氢分子一致，表明它们来自炽热的分子气体。分析显示，激发这些信号的气体温度至少约为 2,000 开尔文。
团队还在 HH 211 的韦伯存档数据中发现同类光谱。这意味着，新方法有望帮助研究人员追踪星际气体受冲击后的电离与化学变化。

title: 智能体帮你联络商家或保险公司，Meta 旗下 Muse 上线代打电话功能
content:
IT之家 11 月 14 日消息，Meta 旗下 AI 智能体 Muse 推出代打电话功能，开通高级付费订阅后，用户就能让 Muse 代自己联系美国商家。Meta 称，Muse 可以帮助用户处理各种烦琐事务，完成待办事项。
13 日凌晨，Meta 首席 AI 官汪滔在 X 上发文宣布：“Muse 能帮你打完所有不想亲自打的电话。”
据悉，用户可以借助 Muse 联系保险公司或有线电视服务商、预约美国车管部门的业务办理时间，或是打电话向餐厅订位。
Muse 会使用 AI 合成语音与商家工作人员交谈，但这类功能并非总能顺利完成任务。部分商家的工作人员听出对方是 AI 后便直接挂断电话，有人是为了防范诈骗，也有人认为这类来电可能是恶作剧，只会浪费时间。
Meta 此前已面向早期体验用户测试了几个月，现向 Meta AI 最高级别的付费订阅用户开放。订阅价格为每月 19.99 美元（IT之家注：现汇率约合 133.6 元人民币）起。
Muse 并非首款支持代打电话的 AI 工具。谷歌 Gemini 的 Call for Me 功能支持 Pixel 11 和 Pixel 10，能够通过用户本人的电话号码拨打电话，另一款热门 AI 智能体 Instinct 也从 9 月开始测试代打电话功能。

title: 曝小米与“AMG 之父”创办的 HWA 秘密合作，希望打造“载入史册”新车
content:
感谢IT之家网友
11 月 14 日消息，当地时间 11 月 5 日，意媒 Quattroruote 援引不具名知情人士消息称，小米与 HWA 或在秘密合作开发一款
，部分知名零部件供应商也有望参与其中。
IT之家注：HWA 由 AMG 创始人汉斯 · 维尔纳 · 奥夫雷希特创办，
脱胎于 AMG，长期负责奔驰的赛车项目
，这其中就包括德国房车大师赛（DTM）。
双方据称希望打造一款
性能前所未有、足以载入汽车史册
的车型。新车的具体形式仍未确定，既有可能是全新的旗舰车型，也有可能是小米现有两款车型（SU7/YU7）的极致性能版。
▲ 现款小米 SU7 Ultra
过去几周，多辆采用更激进设计的 SU7 Ultra 测试车现身纽博格林赛道。该媒体分析称，不排除小米已在开发
更侧重赛道性能的 SU7 Ultra 升级版
接近项目的技术人员此前透露，小米主要
针对 SU7 Ultra 现有的薄弱环节进行改进
新车的底盘经过重新调校，以更好地适应纽北赛道，车轮定位设定更加激进，尤其是外倾角；制动系统也进行了强化，不仅增大了规格，还改进了散热设计。
动力系统则将进一步
提高输出功率和散热效率
，空气动力学设计也有所优化，以增加下压力，并改善热气流的排出。
目前仍无法确定 HWA 是否参与了 SU7 Ultra 升级方案的研发，还是双方计划共同推出一款全新车型。
据该媒体分析，如果是全新车型，可能有两种方向。一种是采用先进技术和现代化设计、性能达到全新高度的
，造型和车身比例或借鉴中置发动机跑车；另一种则是
以 HWA 190 Evo（下图）为基础
进一步开发，因此有可能改变其原本的特色。
HWA 去年推出了 190 Evo 项目，以现代化复刻的形式改装了经典奔驰 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II 。其采用碳纤维车身，造型极为方正。

title: 白宫“超级智能工作组”呼吁放宽问责政策，鼓励 AI 企业报告网络安全事件
content:
IT之家 11 月 14 日消息，据彭博社报道，当地时间 13 日，美国政府新设的“超级智能工作组”在白宫开会，建议联邦机构放宽网络安全事件的问责政策，鼓励 AI 企业主动报告重大安全事件。
一名不愿具名的政府官员透露，工作组认为，过去处理网络安全事件时采用的监管处罚标准可能不再适用，甚至会让企业不敢分享重要的安全信息。
工作组因此敦促各机构，未来 12 个月内应限制企业因安全事件承担的监管责任，并考虑进一步延长期限。
此次政策建议意味着工作组的立场发生转变，从此前倾向于依法处罚开发不安全产品的企业，改为通过减轻责任鼓励 AI 开发商报告安全事件。就在上个月，工作组还警告开发商，必须报告并解决安全事件，否则可能面临尚未明确的处罚。
据IT之家了解，“超级智能工作组”于今年 9 月底成立。此前，一系列失控 AI 模型引发安全事件，公众对 AI 可能造成灾难性后果的担忧持续升温。

title: 黄仁勋辞任 CEO 后，英伟达诞生地丹尼餐厅移除纪念铭牌、又宣布将重新挂回
content:
感谢IT之家网友
11 月 14 日消息，据 NBC News 报道，在一家丹尼餐厅（Denny’s）路边店内，硅谷历史的一角仿佛凭空消失了。
30 多年前，黄仁勋与两位好友正是在这里构想出了英伟达，而如今纪念这一确切位置的牌匾已不翼而飞。牌匾上的铭文曾写道：“开启一家万亿美元公司的卡座”，如今只剩下一片空荡荡的砖墙和剥落的墙漆。两名店员证实，牌匾已被撤下。
▲ 2023 年，丹尼餐厅 CEO Kelli Valade 与英伟达创始人黄仁勋在加利福尼亚州圣何塞的丹尼餐厅同框
IT之家注意到，在该媒体发文后，丹尼餐厅的一位发言人表示，该连锁餐厅正在“重新安装这块牌匾，以纪念在丹尼餐厅促成英伟达诞生的那些对话”。
“黄仁勋最初是在丹尼餐厅当洗碗工起家的。多年后，他和联合创始人们聚在我们的一个卡座里，探讨了后来演变为英伟达的构想。这块牌匾正是这段共同历史的见证，”该发言人说道。
英伟达创立于 1993 年，黄仁勋担任公司首席执行官的时间远超科技界同行。他一向乐于谈及自己作为移民的草根出身，常提起 15 岁时在俄勒冈州波特兰一家丹尼餐厅打的第一份工。
“我洗过盘子、收拾过餐桌，也当过服务员，”黄仁勋在 2023 年公司官方博客刊登的一次访谈中回忆道，“没人能比我一次端更多的咖啡杯。”

Octave Expands Industrial AI Offering After Cerebre Takeover
Prioritise Us
on Google
Octave is strengthening industrial AI insights with its acquisition of Cerebre. Credit: Getty Images
Octave Intelligence has acquired Cerebre, adding a contextual model to strengthen industrial AI insights, explains Jeff Robbins, CEO at Cerebre
For customers in industrial environments, such as the oil and gas sector, there is a business need for AI insights to improve
resilience and performance
across the supply chain.
However, the insights also have to draw on expertise based on real-world conditions in order to be reliable.
Octave is responding to this need through its acquisition of Cerebre, which will broaden the scope and improve the accessibility of its industrial AI tools for its customers.
Supply chain transformation
Octave, a global leader in mission-critical software, has announced its acquisition of Cerebre. Cerebre is a US-based software company that uses its technological capabilities to transform fragmented engineering schematics, plant data and engineering knowledge into a connected model.
Octave is a technology company which helps organisations make informed decisions across the entire asset lifecycle. Through this, it ensures performance, safety and reliability are interwoven throughout the entire process.
Cerebre’s model means that any AI system, agent or engineer can make informed decisions from real plant knowledge, acting as the contact layer above raw data. This is particularly critical in the engineering sector, as it acts as one of the first steps in a
physical supply chain.
“Our customers run facilities where being wrong is not an option,” explains Mattias Stenberg, Chief Executive Officer of Octave.
Mattias Stenberg, Chief Executive Officer of Octave
“For years we have been building the record to design, build, operate and protect those facilities from one connected view. Cerebre provides insights into existing facilities, serving as a context engine for a unified plant model. Introducing Cerebre to Octave’s installed base, which covers 60% of Fortune 500 companies, supports our strategy of accelerated Annualised Recurring Revenue (ARR) growth and new licensing models.”
At a glance
Octave solutions are purpose-built for the domain
It makes use of context driven AI
Octave has a total revenue of US$415m - a 6% year-over-year increase
The company reports an 18% SaaS revenue growth since the year prior
Octave’s Data-as-a-Service has saved customers hundreds of work hours per year
Reducing fragmentation
Octave understands what its customers need, having the engineering system and record of each design. Major companies in the oil and gas sectors use Cerebre to place plant configuration, conditions and real-time knowledge in one process. This helps the plant maintain operations as it changes with external shifts.
Cerebre’s model begins with the plant, building off the context provided to the model in order to
develop a tailored solution
. Engineers can capture and govern plant-specific data which is often siloed, which then is used to explore how each team operates.
When combined with Octave’s AI applications and customer base, Cerebre helps shorten time to action and continues to operate alongside existing tools.
“We’ve spent years operating in stealth, pushing our technology to the limits with the world’s largest and most demanding operators,” says Jeff Robbins, Chief Executive Officer of Cerebre.
Jeff Robbins, Chief Executive Officer of Cerebre
“We built Cerebre so engineers and AI can reason over the same trusted, real-time model of the plant. By joining Octave, we are positioned to underpin industrial AI and expand across our combined customer base and beyond.”
Octave’s customer base will be able to have access to Cerebre’s capabilities, increasing the efficiency of the engineering and operations solutions. As the acquisition develops, further details will explore how global supply chains can benefit from this union.
Our customers run facilities where being wrong is not an option.
Mattias Stenberg, Chief Executive Officer of Octave
Key Partners
Octave delivers mission-critical software enabling organizations to make informed decisions throughout the asset lifecycle-Design, Build, Operate, and Protect. The platform transforms complex operational data into actionable intelligence, connecting expertise with real-world conditions and enterprise insights. Octave enhances performance, resilience, and incident response in environments where safety, reliability, and performance are essential and failure is unacceptable.
Cerebre builds context infrastructure for industrial AI operations. While engineers use plant knowledge to reason-equipment relationships, flow, control logic-AI systems need the same structured understanding. Cerebre creates and maintains this contextual model layer, enabling AI agents to reason over real plant knowledge rather than raw data.
Pfizer is a leading global biopharmaceutical company founded in 1849, headquartered in New York. Known for developing breakthrough medications and vaccines, Pfizer produces treatments across immunology, oncology, cardiology and rare diseases. The company gained worldwide prominence with its COVID-19 vaccine developed with BioNTech. With revenues exceeding US$100 bn, Pfizer invests heavily in research and development to advance healthcare innovation globally.
BHP is the world's largest mining company, headquartered in Melbourne, Australia. BHP extracts and processes iron ore, copper, coal, nickel and petroleum. Operating across Australia, Americas, and globally, the company is a major commodity supplier to industrial markets, particularly China. BHP emphasises sustainable mining practices while maintaining its position as a critical player in global resources and energy sectors.

Headquartered in Stuttgart, it's the world's largest automotive supplier, producing components, power tools, home appliances and industrial technology. Employing over 400,000 people globally, Bosch invests significantly in innovation, particularly electric mobility, IoT solutions, and smart home technology, maintaining leadership across multiple industrial and consumer sectors.
Siemens AG is a German conglomerate founded in 1847, specializing in industrial manufacturing, energy, healthcare and infrastructure. Major products include medical imaging equipment, industrial automation systems, power generation technology and transportation solutions. With operations in over 200 countries and approximately 300,000 employees, Siemens remains a global technology powerhouse.

The launch of this new route is strengthening maritime connections and offering access to new and expanding markets.

Exiger, a market-leading supply chain risk management company, has been awarded a US$12 million contract by the US Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center. Jabil has consolidated five acquired businesses into a single Procurement & Supply Chain Services portfolio. The move brings together ProcureAbility, Retronix, ID8 Global, Velocity Electronics and Rebound Electronics under one operational structure.
The company operates more than 120 sites across the globe and employs 3,500 procurement and supply chain professionals. Jabil maintains relationships with more than 40,000
suppliers through its network

data harvested from more than 100,000 industrial operating hours and tens of millions of handled cases, this second-generation platform introduces hardware, electrical, and structural upgrades designed to maximise unit availability, and improve dock-door throughput.

The new multi-year agreement expands the scope of Walmart's existing collaboration with Zipline. The two companies have been working together on drone deliveries since 2021.

title: 10 largest nuclear power plants in the US ranked by generating capacity
content: Electricity demand can swing sharply over the course of a day, but the grid needs power long after the evening rush has passed. Nuclear power helps meet that round-the-clock demand, supplying roughly one-fifth of US electricity with reactors that typically run for months between refueling outages and produce no carbon dioxide while generating power.Some nuclear stations can deliver more electricity than others simply because they have more reactors. Others can generate just as much power with fewer, larger reactors. Here are the ten largest operating nuclear power plants in the US, ranked by net summer generating capacity.1. Plant Vogtle, Georgia (4,530 MW)Wikimedia CommonsPlant Vogtle’s rise to the top was nearly four decades in the making. Its first two reactors entered commercial service in 1987 and 1989, and the site remained a two-reactor station until Unit 3 came online in 2023.Unit 4 followed in April 2024, making the eastern Georgia plant the only operating four-reactor nuclear station in the country. The two newer units account for nearly half of Vogtle’s capacity, giving it a lead of almost 600 megawatts over Palo Verde.2. Palo Verde Generating Station, Arizona (3,937 MW)Drive about 55 miles west of downtown Phoenix, and you’ll find three nuclear reactors in a place with no major body of water beside them. Palo Verde solved that siting problem by drawing on a resource the Phoenix area already produced in abundance. The resource was municipal wastewater.The station takes treated wastewater from nearby communities and processes it further for use in its cooling towers. Arizona Public Service says Palo Verde recycles more than 20 billion gallons a year, helping sustain a plant that supplies electricity across several Southwestern states.3. Browns Ferry Nuclear Plant, Alabama (3,662 MW)Browns Ferry takes its name from a ferry crossing on the Tennessee River in northern Alabama. The Tennessee Valley Authority began generating nuclear power there in 1974, and a third reactor entered commercial service in 1977.All three units are boiling-water reactors, which produce steam directly in the reactor vessel to drive their turbines. Together they put Browns Ferry more than a gigawatt ahead of fourth-place Oconee, the largest drop between any two neighbors on this list.4. Oconee Nuclear Station, South Carolina (2,600 MW)When Oconee’s first reactor entered service in July 1973, Duke Energy was building what would briefly become the world’s largest nuclear station. The three reactors still make Oconee the largest nuclear plant in Duke’s fleet and give it a narrow edge over the South Texas Project in this ranking.The plant sits on Lake Keowee, where two generations of power technology share the same waterfront. The lake supplies water for plant cooling, and the nearby Keowee hydroelectric station has historically supplied standby power as well as electricity for the grid.5. South Texas Project, Texas (2,580 MW)Wikimedia CommonsThe South Texas Project gets within 20 megawatts of Oconee with one fewer reactor. Its two pressurized-water units, which entered commercial service in 1988 and 1989, each have a net summer capacity of roughly 1,290 megawatts.The plant sits between Bay City and Palacios near the Texas Gulf Coast, but its cooling water comes from a reservoir of its own. At around 7,000 acres (about 2,830 hectares), that reservoir gives a sense of how much land the infrastructure around a two-reactor station can occupy.6. Peach Bottom Atomic Power Station, Pennsylvania (2,549 MW)Peach Bottom’s generating units are numbered 2 and 3, a reminder that the site near Delta started out with a very different reactor. Unit 1 was a high-temperature, gas-cooled demonstration reactor that shut down in 1974, the same year its two larger neighbors entered service.The operating units use boiling-water technology and together put Peach Bottom within about 31 megawatts of the South Texas Project. They also give Pennsylvania its largest nuclear station, with Susquehanna close behind.7. Susquehanna Steam Electric Station, Pennsylvania (2,494 MW)Susquehanna’s two reactors entered service in the 1980s, decades before the data center campus next door became part of the plant’s story. In June 2025, operator Talen Energy announced an expanded deal to supply electricity from the station to Amazon Web Services.The deal covers Amazon’s adjacent campus and allows deliveries to other sites in Pennsylvania. That gives the plant a role in meeting demand from cloud computing and AI at a station built more than 40 years ago.8. Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant, Texas (2,400 MW)Texas’ second entry sits inland near Glen Rose, southwest of Fort Worth. Comanche Peak’s first reactor entered commercial service in 1990, and its second followed three years later, bringing another large block of nuclear capacity onto the Texas grid.Both reactors draw cooling water from the neighboring reservoir, which absorbs heat released as steam condenses back into water. Between Comanche Peak and the South Texas Project, Texas has nearly 5,000 megawatts of nuclear generating capacity at just two sites.9. Braidwood Generating Station, Illinois (2,332 MW)Both Braidwood reactors began commercial operation in 1988, making the Will County station younger than several others on this list. Their combined capacity puts Braidwood at the top of Illinois’ nuclear fleet, ahead of Byron by roughly 32 megawatts.The plant’s cooling lake doubles as a fishing spot and waterfowl refuge. It was filled with water pumped from the Kankakee River in the early 1980s, flooding several former strip-mine pits in the process.10. McGuire Nuclear Station, North Carolina (2,316 MW)Wikimedia CommonsLake Norman was already producing electricity before McGuire’s first reactor came online. Duke created the lake in 1963 by damming the Catawba River at the Cowans Ford hydroelectric station, then built the nuclear plant on its shore near Charlotte.McGuire’s two reactors entered commercial service in 1981 and 1984, and the station uses the lake for cooling. It takes the final spot by just 5.5 megawatts over Duke’s Catawba Nuclear Station in neighboring South Carolina.ConclusionTogether, the ten largest nuclear power plants in the US have about 29 gigawatts of generating capacity. That’s nearly a third of the country’s nuclear capacity concentrated at just ten sites.Most of these plants have been generating electricity for decades. With newer reactors like those at Plant Vogtle now in service, the US relies on a mix of old and new units to keep power flowing around the clock.

title: 5,000-year-old Chinese brewing secret: red mold, cloth lined filters
content: Brewers in China used red mold and bast-fiber textiles to filter rice-based alcoholic beverages approximately 5,000 years ago, according to a new study.University of Arizona researchers examined 16 pottery vessels and five specialized filters from the Wayaoli archaeological site in China’s Zhejiang Province. Using microscopic residue analysis, they identified starch grains, phytoliths, fungi, and microfibers preserved on the pottery. These residues indicated that the vessels were used to produce rice-based alcoholic beverages, including red-colored alcohol made with Monascus mold.Ancient brewers used red mold to ferment riceArchaeologists first found five unusual pottery filters with connected upper and lower bowls. Based on their design, they suspected they might have been used to produce alcohol, although it appeared they could also have supported other processes, including grain processing and water purification.However, residue analysis revealed rice starch and traces of Monascus mold, which is associated with traditional red rice brewing, on all five filters. Its enzymes break down rice starch into sugars that can then be fermented, the study reported. Additionally, the mold produces red pigments, suggesting that the Ancient Chinese drank red alcohol.Some starch grains showed damage consistent with cooking and fermentation, providing further evidence that the vessels were used in alcohol production. Researchers also discovered several starchy plant fibers, including foxnut, Job’s tears, and underground storage organs.The residue evidence aligns with an earlier study conducted at the Shangshan archaeological site in Zhejiang Province, dating back 10,000–9,000 years, which indicated that Monascus was used to ferment rice-based beverages. Another processing techniqueResearchers found traces of microscopic fibers identified as bast-fibers, which stem from the inner bark of plant stems and can be used to manufacture textiles.That suggests ancient brewers placed woven fabric inside the upper bowls of the pottery filters to separate the liquid from solid material.“These bast fibers were likely woven into textiles and placed on the upper filter bowl to improve alcohol filtration,” said researchers.The study states that bast-fiber textiles were used for filtration, improving both the taste and clarity of alcoholic beverages. However, researchers found no intact cloth at the archaeological site.Alcohol held ritual significanceAccording to the study, most of these pottery filters came from burials excavated at the site.These vessels frequently appeared alongside other pottery associated with household activities, including jars, plates, and cooking pots.The researchers interpreted the presence of filters in burials as evidence of alcohol’s importance in the community’s social and ritual traditions.Late Neolithic societies in the Lower Yangzi River region were known for their intensive rice agriculture, technological innovation that increased social complexity, and elaborate ritual practices. Rice fermentation played a role in advancing culture and manufacturing techniques. By analyzing the microscopic residues on ancient pottery, researchers uncovered a major feature of these cultures. They identified evidence of both fermentation and filtration techniques used about five millennia ago.The study findings demonstrated the production of rice-based fermented beverages using Monascus molds and bast-fiber textiles. It suggested the significance of alcohol during the social and rituals during the Late Songze and Early Liangzhu periods.

title: China debuts 4,000-kilowatt rescue ship with 360-degree propulsion
content: China has completed its first batch of five domestically designed medium-sized maritime rescue vessels, strengthening its ability to respond to emergencies along its coastline. The final vessel, Donghai Jiu 152, officially joined the Ministry of Transport’s Donghai Rescue Bureau on November 13, 2026. The 4,000-kilowatt vessel brings several specialized capabilities to China’s eastern coastal waters. Its propulsion and positioning systems allow crews to operate in challenging maritime conditions. The ship can also support rescue missions involving large numbers of survivors.The delivery marks the end of a nearly seven-year procurement program. China delivered the first vessel, Donghai Jiu 151, in December 2019.Designed for coastal emergenciesMeasuring 69.5 meters (228 feet) long and 14.6 meters (48 feet) wide, Donghai Jiu 152 targets rescue operations across China’s eastern waters. Its hull and onboard systems accommodate demanding conditions along exposed coastlines.The vessel can withstand strong winds and carries an external firefighting system. It also has enough capacity to accommodate up to 100 rescued people. That capacity gives rescue crews additional flexibility during large-scale maritime emergencies.Its equipment also supports operations beyond conventional search and rescue missions. An advanced azimuthing electric propulsion system provides precise maneuverability. This setup helps the vessel navigate confined waters and maintain control during demanding operations.A Class 2 dynamic positioning system (DP-2) further expands its operational capabilities. The system helps the ship maintain a designated position without relying entirely on conventional anchoring. Such technology proves particularly useful when crews conduct operations near islands, reefs, or other difficult coastal terrain.Electric propulsion improves controlDynamic positioning plays an important role in modern offshore and maritime operations. DP-2 systems use computerized controls to coordinate propulsion and maintain a vessel’s position. They can compensate for external forces such as wind, waves, and currents.Donghai Jiu 152 also carries a three-point anchoring arrangement. Captain He Feng said the system helps the vessel remain stable in shallow water. It can maintain that position under Sea State 3 conditions, according to CCTV News.That capability supports diving operations, which require a relatively stable working platform. Maintaining position in shallow water can prove difficult when currents and changing weather affect a vessel. The additional anchoring arrangement gives the crew another way to manage those conditions.Seven-year construction programChina began receiving the first vessel in this series in December 2019. The Donghai Rescue Bureau took delivery of Donghai Jiu 151 on December 25 that year. The vessel established the foundation for four subsequent ships.In December 2022, China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC) signed contracts for four additional vessels. The shipbuilder developed the new designs using Donghai Jiu 151 as their foundation.The subsequent vessels also incorporated upgrades to digital systems and network connectivity. These improvements aim to support better coordination during maritime rescue operations.Completing the five-vessel program gives China’s rescue authorities additional coverage across nearshore waters. The broader emergency response network combines vessels of different sizes with maritime, land, and aerial resources. Together, these assets help authorities coordinate operations across varying distances and rescue scenarios.The new fleet also addresses a gap in China’s nearshore emergency response capabilities. Its medium-sized vessels can handle missions that may demand more capacity than smaller rescue boats provide. Their specialized equipment also allows crews to tackle operations in challenging coastal environments.

title: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years
content: A new study has found that China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents. That’s not to say China owns much of the technology used in these setups, but it does reveal how active it has been in patenting in this field.The study’s findings come from two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026. It appears to show that technological focus has shifted quite dramatically over this time.Before about 2014, patents were dominated by American, Norwegian, and Canadian researchers exploring underwater enclosures and pressure protection. Between about 2015 and 2020, attention turned to cooling, electrical supply, and long-term reliability. From 2021, Chinese researchers became the dominant source for patents, particularly focusing on modular construction and maintenance. They also found that China holds the lion’s share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.China appears to hold the most patentsChinese patents in particular focus on the actual construction, installation, connections, and maintenance of them at scale. This appears to show that China is shifting focus to the more practical elements rather than proving experimental technology. All very interesting, but why all the interest? Well, data centers generate an enormous amount of heat when in operation. This comes from the conversion of electricity into heat by the vast number of computer processors.Typically, this is handled by using a combination of fans, chillers, cooling towers, and liquid-cooling systems to manage temperatures. That is costly in terms of hardware and additional electricity costs.If the centers could be placed underwater, they could take advantage of the ocean’s near-limitless supply of very cold seawater. Obviously, you can’t just submerge the hardware directly into the ocean, so they need to be placed inside sealed, pressure-resistant containers first.These are then lowered and secured to the seabed, and connections are made to the shore for power and data cables. Once there, the heat from the servers can be transferred to the cold ocean water using special internal cooling systems. To this end, the seawater acts as a massive heat sink, potentially eliminating much of the mechanical cooling equipment needed on land. This doesn’t make the computers themselves consume less electricity, but it can reduce the energy spent keeping them cool.China is taking the lead in underwater data centersAnd it is not just a theoretical technology either. Famously, Microsoft deployed one, called Project Natick, off the coast of Scotland in 2018. The project ran for around two years, and results were very encouraging.According to Microsoft, the underwater data center had just one-eighth of the failure rate of similar land-based setups. Yet despite this, Microsoft chose not to commercialize the technology, and confirmed in 2024 that the project had been discontinued.So, is the 80 percent figure something other nations should sit up and take notice of? Yes, and no. It is clear China has established some kind of lead here in terms of patents, but the engineering challenges of actually deploying them are enormous. The shift in focus to modularity likely reflects China’s ambitions to scale the technology commercially. But it is important to note that patents tend to be territorial in nature. Holding a large share of patents in a particular field doesn’t automatically give a country control of the technology worldwide.

title: China spots likely supermassive neutron star over 1.8x bigger than sun
content: Chinese astronomers examining data from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) have found a likely supermassive neutron star accompanying a red giant, that is, neither big enough to be a black hole nor small enough to be a neutron star. This is a rarity even for astronomers and could help us understand the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes.Neutron stars are the remains of high-mass stars that have exploded. After the explosion, a star with a mass around 1.4 times that of our Sun fits into a sphere no larger than 12 miles ( 20 kilometers) across.Black holes, on the other hand, are remnants of even larger stars with mass at least five times that of the Sun to begin with. With no neutron star spotted with mass greater than 2.5 times that of the Sun, there remains a mass gap of 2.5 – 5 solar masses between them and the black holes. So, a rare spotting of an object in this mass gap opens up opportunities to understand where neutron stars give way to black holes.What did the astronomers spot? The astronomers spotted a new binary system, named J0008+0128. The binary system consists of the red giant and its companion, which was not visually confirmed. Instead, astronomers inferred its existence from its gravitational effects. This is not the first time astronomers have made such an association. However, its inferred mass, between 1.8 and 2.8 times that of the Sun, places it somewhere in the upper range of the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes, a rare and valuable find.The researchers found that the pair completes an orbit in 3.3 years, showing sufficient separation between the two. Yet the duo follows a near-circular path despite their separation. The absence of light other than that of the red giant signifies that the companion is not another regular star but a neutron star.In similar binaries, neutron stars draw material from other companions, adding to their own mass. But in this case, the neutron star is too far away to pull material from the red giant either.A neutron star or more? The astronomers conducted more than than 300,000 simulations involving binary systems to understand how such a system has been formed. Yet, none of these simulations could explain the mass and orbital properties of the system. The closest resemblance the team has for this system is Gaia NS1, a neutron star with a mass of about 1.9 suns and a two-year orbit. While J0008+0128 is a bit more extreme, it does fit all explanations. One possible explanation is that the binary system is actually a triple system with two very close small neutron stars or a neutron star and a white dwarf orbiting the red giant. Alternatively, it may have been a triple system in which the smaller bodies merged, the researchers suggest. The astronomers are confident that the formation of the system cannot be ruled out in principle and may have required a combination of extreme yet plausible parameters.The research findings were published in Science Advances.

title: China’s Arcfox launches two new EVs with 99-second battery swaps
content: Chinese automaker BAIC’s electric vehicle brand Arcfox has launched two new battery-swappable models in China, expanding the technology into a more affordable segment of the market. The Beta S3 535 Ultra+ LiDAR Swappable Edition and Beta T1 Swappable Edition both use CATL’s Chocolate battery-swapping network, with prices starting at 52,000 yuan ($7,800) under a battery-leasing arrangement.The launch builds on a partnership between BAIC and CATL to develop a shared battery-swapping ecosystem. Both cars can swap depleted battery packs in about 99 seconds, allowing drivers to resume their journeys without waiting for conventional charging.Beta S3 gets LiDAR and 535-km rangeAccording to Car News China, the Beta S3 535 Ultra+ is a front-wheel-drive electric sedan powered by a permanent-magnet synchronous motor producing 159 kW (213 hp) and 250 Nm of torque. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (62 mph) in 7.1 seconds and has a top speed of 165 km/h (103 mph).Its battery delivers a claimed range of 535 km (332 miles) under China’s CLTC testing cycle. The vehicle also supports conventional fast charging.The new edition’s main technology highlight is its driver-assistance system. It combines a 192-line LiDAR sensor with Horizon Robotics’ Journey J6M computing chip to support highway and urban navigation assistance, as well as automated parking.Inside, the sedan features a 15.6-inch central touchscreen, an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8155 cockpit processor. Its starting price is 78,800 yuan ($11,800) with battery leasing.Beta T1 brings swapping to a lower priceThe smaller Beta T1 targets buyers looking for a more affordable electric car. It measures 4,337 mm (170.7 in) long, 1,860 mm (73.2 in) wide, and 1,572 mm (61.9 in) tall, with a 2,770-mm (109.1 in) wheelbase.Its electric motor produces 95 kW (127 hp), while its CATL-manufactured lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supports the swapping system. The car has a top speed of 150 km/h (93 mph), although Arcfox has not disclosed the range of this new edition.The T1 starts at 52,000 yuan ($7,800), with a higher trim priced at 60,000 yuan ($9,000), both under battery-leasing plans.CATL expands its battery-swapping networkThe two launches are part of CATL’s wider effort to make battery swapping available across multiple vehicle brands. BAIC, CATL, and service partner CAES signed a cooperation agreement in April 2026 covering compatible vehicle development and battery-swapping infrastructure.CATL reported that its Chocolate network had more than 1,470 stations across 99 Chinese cities at the time, with a target of exceeding 3,000 stations by the end of 2026. In October, BAIC and CATL also announced a broader partnership targeting one million battery-swapping vehicles.Under battery leasing, customers purchase the car without owning its battery outright, paying a recurring fee to use a pack maintained within the swapping network. For the new Arcfox models, monthly plans start at 399 yuan ($60) for a 5,000-km (about 6,200 miles) allowance, while unlimited monthly mileage costs 599 yuan ($90).Arcfox is also offering buyers 10,000 km (about 3,100 miles) of free battery-swapping mileage through 20 vouchers. The promotion applies to Beta S3 swapping-edition purchases made by January 31, 2027, and to Beta T1 customers.The challenge for the technology will be expanding station availability. A battery exchange that takes just 99 seconds is useful only when compatible infrastructure is accessible. By bringing more affordable vehicles into the same network, BAIC and CATL are betting that shared infrastructure can make battery swapping a more practical alternative to conventional EV charging.

title: China’s BYD targets nine-minute charging with new plug-in hybrid SUV
content: Chinese EV giant BYD is preparing to launch the Fang Cheng Bao Ti 9, a full-size six-seat plug-in hybrid SUV built around a combination of high-output electric motors, a 66.48 kWh Blade Battery, and an unusually fast charging system. The company said its flash-charging technology can take the battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in nine minutes, potentially making charging speed one of the model’s main selling points.The Ti 9 will officially launch in China on November 19, ahead of its public appearance at the 2026 Guangzhou Auto Show. Fang Cheng Bao general manager Xiong Tianbo said earlier that display vehicles had reached 21 dealerships across 12 cities, with deliveries underway in another 20 cities.The launch follows the opening of reservations earlier in November. A Ti 9 also rolled off BYD’s Xi’an production line that day as the company’s 19 millionth new energy vehicle, marking a production milestone for the Chinese automaker.Dual electric motors deliver 536 hpThe Ti 9 uses BYD’s sixth-generation DM-i plug-in hybrid system, pairing a 1.5-liter turbocharged gasoline engine with two permanent magnet synchronous electric motors.The combustion engine produces 154 hp, while each electric motor is rated at 268 hp. Together, the motors provide a combined peak electric output of 536 hp. According to reports, the configuration gives the SUV substantial electric propulsion capacity while retaining a gasoline engine for longer journeys.Energy comes from a 66.48 kWh second-generation lithium iron phosphate Blade Battery. BYD claims an all-electric driving range of 193 miles under the Worldwide harmonized Light vehicles Test Cycle (WLTC). With a full battery and fuel tank, the Ti 9 has a claimed combined range of 1,013 miles under China’s CLTC testing standard. The estimated equivalent under the WLTP cycle is about 808 to 861 miles, though real-world range depends on driving conditions and vehicle configuration.When the battery is depleted, fuel consumption is rated at 36.8 mpg under WLTC testing. These figures position the Ti 9 as a large hybrid SUV designed to combine substantial electric driving capability with the flexibility of a conventional fuel-powered vehicle.Nine minutes flash chargingThe most notable technology claim for the Ti 9 model is the flash-charging system. BYD claims the system can charge the battery from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes and reach 97 percent in nine minutes.The company also claims that the system can charge the battery from 20 percent to 97 percent in 12 minutes at temperatures as low as minus 22 degrees Fahrenheit. That cold-weather figure is particularly relevant because low temperatures can reduce battery charging performance and increase charging times.The 66.48 kWh Blade Battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry, which BYD has developed across its electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle lineup. The second-generation battery is central to the Ti 9’s claimed electric range and rapid-charging capability.However, BYD has not disclosed the peak charging power, the precise charging infrastructure required to achieve the advertised times, or the conditions under which the figures were recorded. Those details will be important for assessing how readily the technology can be used outside controlled testing conditions.
